hello: the word that opens every door, even at the bakery
food: Seafood platter
Oysters, whelks and prawns, to share on a terrace facing the sea.
France.respect: Say bonjour when you walk into a shop and respect the priority rules in the water: the surfer closest to the peak goes first.

hello: “hi”, rounded off with an obrigado (thank you) or obrigada depending on who is speaking
food: Grilled sardines
Served on a slice of country bread, especially in summer.
Portugal.respect: Life moves at a gentle pace: take time for a coffee at the counter and give way to locals at busy peaks.

hello: “hi”, followed by a buenos días in the morning
food: Tapas
Small plates to share at the bar, from ham to fried squid.
Espagne.respect: People eat late, often after 9 pm. In the water, wait your turn and avoid paddling against the flow of the locals.

food: Fish and chips
Fried fish and chips, eaten down by the harbour.
Royaume-Uni.respect: Queuing is sacred, at the counter as in the line-up. Always thank the driver when you get off the bus.

hello: “hello” in Irish, which always raises a smile
food: Seafood chowder
A creamy fish and seafood soup, served with soda bread.
Irlande.respect: At the pub, everyone buys a round in turn. On reef breaks, listen to the locals’ advice: the sea is powerful here.

hello: “hi” and “bye”, best kept for people you know well
food: Spaghetti alle vongole
Pasta with clams, garlic and parsley, facing the sea.
Italie.respect: Cover your shoulders to enter a church and avoid wandering around town in your swimwear.

hello: “hello”, said with a smile to the taverna owner
food: Grilled octopus
Marinated in olive oil and oregano, dried in the sun outside the tavernas.
Grèce.respect: Cover your shoulders and knees to visit monasteries. Don’t pick up stones or ancient fragments.

food: Black risotto (crni rižot)
A cuttlefish-ink risotto, a speciality of the Dalmatian coast.
Croatie.respect: In the old towns, don’t walk around shirtless or in swimwear: some municipalities hand out fines.

hello: “good morning” in Maltese, a legacy of Italian
food: Pastizzi
Flaky pastries filled with ricotta or peas, to munch at the village café.
Malte.respect: Modest dress is required in the churches, which are numerous and busy. Don’t touch the Posidonia seagrass when snorkelling.

food: Salmon and dried cod (tørrfisk)
Two treasures of the coast, from the smokehouse to the wooden drying racks.
Norvège.respect: Allemannsretten lets you camp in nature, away from houses, as long as you leave no trace. Fires are often banned in summer.

food: Plokkfiskur
A fish and potato stew, served with rye bread.
Islande.respect: Stay on marked trails: moss takes decades to grow back. Check safetravel.is before every outing.

food: Smørrebrød
Open rye-bread sandwiches topped with herring, prawns or egg.
Danemark.respect: The dunes are protected: stay on the boardwalks and don’t camp outside designated sites.

hello: the northern “hi”, good at any time of day
food: Fischbrötchen
A bread roll filled with herring or smoked mackerel, down at the harbour.
Allemagne.respect: Recycling is taken seriously and beaches often charge a fee in summer (Kurtaxe).

food: Raw herring (haring)
Served with onions, eaten tail-first at the market stalls.
Pays-Bas.respect: Cycle lanes have priority: look carefully before crossing, the bikes come fast.

hello: “peace”, the everyday greeting, to which you reply wa alaykoum salam
food: Fish tagine
Slow-cooked with preserved lemon, olives and vegetables, often shared from one dish.
Maroc.respect: Cover your shoulders and knees away from the beach, ask before photographing anyone and eat with your right hand.

food: Fish couscous
A recipe from the Tunisian coast, spiced up with harissa.
Tunisie.respect: Away from the beaches, covering up is appreciated. During Ramadan, avoid eating in public during the day.

hello: “peace be upon you”, the everyday greeting
food: Cumin-grilled fish
Picked from the stall and grilled in front of you, with rice and salads.
Égypte.respect: Don’t touch or stand on the coral, use mineral sunscreen and keep your distance from the dolphins.

hello: “how are you?” in Wolof, to which you reply maa ngi fi
food: Thiéboudienne
Rice with fish and vegetables, the national dish, shared from a large bowl.
Sénégal.respect: Greetings are long and important: take time to ask how people are before getting down to business.

hello: “hi”, followed by a sorriso (smile): that’s morabeza, the local hospitality
food: Cachupa
A stew of corn, beans and fish or meat, an everyday dish.
Cap-Vert.respect: Life here is stress-free: morabeza is met with patience. Keep your distance from the turtles nesting at night.

hello: “welcome” in Twi, which you’ll hear often
food: Fufu and fish soup
A cassava and plantain dough to dip into a spicy soup.
Ghana.respect: Greet people before asking for anything and use your right hand to give or receive.

hello: “how are you?”, the best-known local greeting
food: Palm butter soup
A palm-nut stew, served with rice.
Liberia.respect: The Robertsport surf community is small and close-knit: introduce yourself, support the local schools and share the waves.

hello: “hi”, and bom dia in the morning
food: Muamba de galinha
Chicken slow-cooked in palm oil with okra.
Angola.respect: Ask before photographing people or official buildings. Travel with a local contact on long dirt roads.

hello: “hello” in Afrikaans, understood all along the coast
food: Walvis Bay oysters
Farmed in the cold waters of the Benguela, among the most renowned in Africa.
Namibie.respect: Stay on authorised tracks: 4x4 tyre marks scar the desert for decades.

hello: “hi, how’s it going?”, the South African beach greeting
food: Braai
The South African barbecue, with boerewors and grilled snoek.
Afrique du Sud.respect: Find out about shark activity and follow the Shark Spotters’ flags. Leave nothing visible in your car.

hello: “hi”, and bom dia in the morning
food: Piri-piri grilled prawns
Marinated in chilli and garlic, grilled over a wood fire.
Mozambique.respect: Watch whale sharks and manta rays without touching them, from a distance, with a responsible operator.

hello: “hello” in Swahili, with a hakuna matata thrown in
food: Zanzibar spiced pilau
Rice fragrant with cloves and cardamom.
Tanzanie.respect: In Zanzibar, which is mostly Muslim, cover your shoulders and knees away from the beaches, especially in Stone Town.

hello: “hello”, to which you reply jambo sana
food: Fish in coconut milk (samaki wa kupaka)
Grilled, then coated in a spiced coconut sauce, a Swahili speciality.
Kenya.respect: On the Swahili coast, dress modestly in town and ask before taking photos.

food: Romazava
A meat broth with brèdes, the local leafy greens.
Madagascar.respect: Respect the fady, local taboos specific to each region: ask for advice before swimming or visiting a sacred site.

food: Dholl puri
Split-pea flatbreads filled with curry, the island’s favourite street food.
Maurice.respect: Hindu temples are visited barefoot and with covered shoulders and knees. Don’t walk on the coral at low tide.

food: Coconut fish curry (cari coco)
A mild coconut-milk curry, served with rice and chatini.
Seychelles.respect: Turtles and coco de mer are strictly protected. Don’t collect any shells from the beaches.

food: Rougail saucisse
Sausages simmered with tomatoes, onions and chilli, served with rice and beans.
La Réunion.respect: Swimming is regulated because of the shark risk: stick to authorised zones and the rules in force.

hello: “hi”, often followed by a how’s it going?
food: Fish tacos
Grilled or fried fish, cabbage and a creamy sauce, the emblem of surf towns.
États-Unis.respect: A tip (15 to 20%) is part of the price at restaurants. Respect the line-up pecking order: never drop in on anyone.

hello: “hi”, or bonjour depending on the province
food: Wild salmon
Grilled on a cedar plank, a Pacific coast tradition.
Canada.respect: Store your food out of reach of bears and learn about the First Nations territories you pass through.

food: Tacos de pescado
Fried or grilled fish in a corn tortilla, with lime and salsa.
Mexique.respect: In cenotes and on reefs, use only biodegradable sunscreen, or none at all as you’re often asked to.

food: Rice and beans
Rice and red beans cooked in coconut milk, with chicken or fish.
Belize.respect: The barrier reef is fragile: touch nothing, don’t feed the fish and choose a licensed operator.

Honduras.lang: Spanish, Creole English on the islands
food: Baleada
A flour tortilla filled with beans, cream and cheese.
Honduras.respect: On the Bay Islands, pay the marine park fee and don’t collect coral or conch.

food: Pupusas
Corn cakes stuffed with cheese and beans, served with curtido.
Salvador.respect: The coast’s surf communities are welcoming: buy local, share the waves and stay humble at the point breaks.

food: Gallo pinto
Fried rice and beans, served morning, noon and night.
Nicaragua.respect: Many spots are on private land: use the authorised access points and respect the fishermen.

hello: “pure life”, used as hello, thank you and goodbye
food: Casado
A full plate: rice, beans, plantain, salad and fish or meat.
Costa Rica.respect: Don’t feed the monkeys and respect the turtle nesting beaches, which are closed at night.

food: Sancocho
A chicken soup with yuca and coriander, the national dish.
Panama.respect: In Indigenous territories such as Guna Yala, ask permission and pay the communities’ access fees.

hello: the joyful Puerto Rican exclamation, alongside the classic hola
food: Mofongo
Mashed fried plantain with garlic, often topped with seafood.
Porto Rico.respect: On shallow reefs, go in and out through the channels the locals use to spare the coral and your feet.

food: La bandera dominicana
Rice, red beans and stewed meat, the flag on your plate.
République dominicaine.respect: Haggle with a smile and favour small local businesses.

hello: “hello”, said with the islands’ sing-song accent
food: Conch salad
A salad of raw conch marinated in lime, with peppers and chilli.
Bahamas.respect: Don’t collect live conch and respect the protected fishing seasons.

food: Cayman-style fish
Snapper or wahoo stewed with peppers, onions and tomatoes.
Îles Caïmans.respect: The marine parks are protected: no fishing and no anchoring outside designated spots. With the stingrays, follow your guide’s instructions to the letter.

food: Flying fish and cou-cou
Spiced flying fish with okra cornmeal, the national dish.
Barbade.respect: Wearing camouflage clothing is banned on the island. Swimwear on the beach only.

food: Keshi yena
A ball of cheese stuffed with spiced chicken, baked in the oven.
Aruba.respect: Sunscreens containing oxybenzone are banned to protect the reefs.

food: Stoba
A goat or beef stew slow-cooked with spices.
Curaçao.respect: Shore diving is king: enter the water at the marked access points and don’t touch the coral.

food: Fried fish with funchi
Grilled or fried fish with a local cornmeal polenta.
Bonaire.respect: The Nature Fee is compulsory to dive or swim in the marine park. No gloves and no contact with the reef.

food: Accras de morue
Spicy salt-cod fritters, to nibble with a drink before dinner.
Guadeloupe.respect: Say hello to everyone, even in passing. Don’t walk on the seagrass beds and watch turtles from a distance.

food: Colombo
A Caribbean curry of chicken or goat, flavoured with colombo spice mix.
Martinique.respect: Greet people when you arrive and avoid beachwear in town. Turtles are for watching, not touching.

food: Arepa
A corn cake with any filling you like, from fish to cheese.
Venezuela.respect: Check the local situation before you go and choose posadas run by local people.

food: Pescado frito con patacones
Fried fish, smashed plantains and coconut rice on the coast.
Colombie.respect: Avoid joking about the country’s violent past: Colombians are proud of their country as it is today.

food: Ecuadorian ceviche
Prawns marinated in lime in a tomato sauce, served with toasted corn.
Équateur.respect: In the Galápagos, stay two metres from the animals and always follow your naturalist guide.

hello: “hi”, followed by a habla causa among friends
food: Ceviche
Raw fish marinated in lime and ají chilli, the national dish.
Pérou.respect: The caballitos de totora are a living heritage: admire them, and ask before photographing the fishermen.

food: Empanadas de mariscos
Pastries filled with seafood and cheese.
Chili.respect: The Pacific is cold and powerful: wear a thick wetsuit and respect the locals at the points.

hello: “hi, how are you?”, to which you reply tudo bom
food: Moqueca
A fish stew with coconut milk and palm oil.
Brésil.respect: Don’t bring out your valuables on the beach and share the waves: surfing is a religion here.

food: Chivito
The national sandwich, filled with beef, ham, egg and cheese.
Uruguay.respect: Sharing mate is a gesture of friendship: don’t stir the bombilla and hand it back to the person serving.

food: Asado
The Argentine barbecue, a Sunday ritual.
Argentine.respect: Mate is shared: only take it when it’s handed to you, and say gracias only when you don’t want any more.

hello: the Australian “hello”, often followed by mate
food: Seafood barbecue
Grilled prawns and fish, with a cold beer at sunset.
Australie.respect: Swim between the red and yellow flags, patrolled by the lifesavers. Never drop in on a local’s wave.

hello: “hello” and “thank you” in Māori, used by everyone
food: Hoki fish and chips
Wrapped in paper and eaten on the beach.
Nouvelle-Zélande.respect: Respect Māori sacred sites (wāhi tapu) and the principle of kaitiakitanga, guardianship of nature.

food: Kokoda
Raw fish marinated in lemon and coconut milk.
Fidji.respect: When visiting a village, cover your shoulders and knees, take off your hat and offer kava to the chief (sevusevu).

hello: “hello” in Tahitian, with a big smile
food: Poisson cru (raw fish in coconut milk)
Raw tuna marinated in lime, with crunchy vegetables and fresh coconut milk.
Polynésie française.respect: Marae are sacred sites: don’t climb on the stones. At Teahupoo, locals always have priority.

hello: “hello” in Drehu (Lifou), one of the 28 Kanak languages
food: Bougna
Yam, sweet potato, banana and chicken or fish cooked in coconut milk in banana leaves.
Nouvelle-Calédonie.respect: On customary land, perform the coutume: introduce yourself to the chief with a small offering before settling in.

food: Lap-lap
A yam or cassava paste cooked in leaves in a stone oven.
Vanuatu.respect: Many beaches are customary land: ask permission and pay the small access fee the village asks for.

food: Oka
Raw fish marinated in lemon and coconut cream.
Samoa.respect: Sunday is for church and rest: avoid noisy swimming near villages. At dusk, respect sa, the prayer time.

food: Ota ika
Raw fish marinated in lemon and coconut milk.
Tonga.respect: Sunday is sacred by law: no swimming and no sport. Cover your shoulders in town.

hello: “may you live long”, the local greeting
food: Ika mata
Raw fish marinated in lemon and coconut milk.
Îles Cook.respect: Rāui protects certain areas of the lagoon: no fishing or collecting where it applies.

food: Grilled fish with taro
Fresh lagoon fish, served with taro.
Palaos.respect: The Palau Pledge, stamped in your passport, commits you to protecting the island. Reef-harmful sunscreens are banned.

food: Mumu
Meat and vegetables steamed under hot stones.
Papouasie-Nouvelle-Guinée.respect: Reefs belong to the clans: surf camps pay a fee to the villages, which limit the number of surfers.

hello: “good morning”; terima kasih means thank you
food: Nasi goreng
Spiced fried rice, often topped with an egg, for breakfast as well as dinner.
Indonésie.respect: Wear a sarong to enter a temple, give and receive with your right hand and don’t step on offerings placed on the ground.

food: Kinilaw
Raw fish marinated in coconut vinegar, ginger and chilli.
Philippines.respect: In marine protected areas, pay the access fees and don’t touch turtles or coral.

food: Nasi lemak
Coconut rice with sambal, fried anchovies and a hard-boiled egg.
Malaisie.respect: Away from the beaches, cover your shoulders and knees, especially in villages and near mosques.

hello: “hello”, with ka for a woman and khrap for a man
food: Tom yam goong
A hot and sour soup with prawns, lemongrass and galangal.
Thaïlande.respect: Never touch someone’s head, don’t point your feet at a Buddha and cover up in temples.

food: Bánh xèo
A crispy pancake with prawns, to roll up in fresh herbs.
Vietnam.respect: Take off your shoes when entering someone’s home and avoid sticking your chopsticks upright in your rice.

hello: “long life”, said with palms pressed together
food: Rice and curry
Rice surrounded by several vegetable and fish curries and coconut sambol.
Sri Lanka.respect: Never pose with your back to a Buddha statue for a photo, and cover your shoulders and knees in temples.

hello: “I greet you”, with palms pressed together
food: Fish curry
A fish curry with coconut milk, a speciality of the west coast.
Inde.respect: Take off your shoes before entering a temple or a home, and eat with your right hand.

hello: the everyday greeting; kihineh? means “how are you?”
food: Garudhiya and mas huni
A tuna broth and a mix of tuna, coconut and chilli, for breakfast.
Maldives.respect: On inhabited islands, bikinis are for bikini beaches only, alcohol is banned and covering up is expected.

food: Kaisendon
A bowl of rice topped with the day’s raw fish, a harbour-town speciality.
Japon.respect: Leave no litter behind: public bins are rare, so carry a bag. No visible tattoos in some onsen.

food: Night markets
Squid skewers, oyster omelettes and bubble tea.
Taïwan.respect: In temples, enter through the right-hand door and leave through the left, without stepping on the thresholds.

food: Hainan seafood
Crab, prawns and Wenchang chicken, the stars of the island.
Chine.respect: Carry your passport with you and set up a mobile payment method: cash is used less and less.

food: Shuwa
Spice-marinated meat slow-cooked underground, for special occasions.
Oman.respect: Cover up away from hotel beaches, avoid public displays of affection and ask before taking photos.

food: Sayadieh
Fish and rice with caramelised onions, a speciality of Aqaba.
Jordanie.respect: Accept the tea you’re offered, it’s a sign of hospitality. Cover your shoulders and knees away from the beaches.

hello: “hi”, pronounced “hey”, good at any time of day
food: Seafood smörgåsbord
Pickled herring, gravlax salmon and prawns on crispbread.
Suède.respect: Allemansrätten lets you camp for a night in nature, away from houses, leaving no trace and lighting no fires in dry spells.

food: Salmon soup (lohikeitto)
Salmon, potatoes and dill in a creamy broth.
Finlande.respect: In the sauna, you go in naked or in a towel depending on local custom, and shower first. Quiet and personal space are highly valued.

food: Pierogi
Dumplings filled with curd cheese, potatoes or meat.
Pologne.respect: On the Baltic, the dunes and pine forests are protected: stay on the marked paths down to the beach.

hello: “hello” in Swiss German; bonjour or buongiorno depending on the region
food: Fondue and perch fillets
Two classics of the Swiss lakeshores, for sharing.
Suisse.respect: Punctuality matters, and so does recycling. On the lakes, respect the swimming zones and boat traffic.

hello: “hi”, Austrian style, for both hello and goodbye
food: Alpine lake trout
Caught in the lakes and grilled, often served with parsley potatoes.
Autriche.respect: Alpine lakes are often lined with private or paying beaches: look for signposted public access.

food: Bled kremšnita
A vanilla cream cake, the speciality of Lake Bled.
Slovénie.respect: Nature parks such as Triglav are strictly protected: no wild camping and no drones without a permit.

food: Lángos
Fried flatbread topped with sour cream and cheese, the king of Balaton’s beaches.
Hongrie.respect: On Lake Balaton, respect the storm warning lights: the wind can pick up very quickly on this shallow lake.

food: Ohrid trout
Caught in Lake Ohrid, an endemic species now protected and often replaced by farmed trout.
Macédoine du Nord.respect: Lake Ohrid is a UNESCO World Heritage Site: leave no litter and cover up to visit churches and monasteries.

food: Njeguši ham
A smoked, air-dried mountain ham, served with local cheese.
Monténégro.respect: In old towns such as Kotor, people don’t walk around in swimwear.

hello: “hello” in Greek, in the south of the island
food: Grilled halloumi
A sheep’s and goat’s milk cheese that grills without melting.
Chypre.respect: Turtle nesting beaches are closed at night in summer: no torches and no parasols planted near the nests.

food: Balık ekmek
A grilled fish sandwich, sold right on the quays.
Turquie.respect: Cover your shoulders and knees and take off your shoes to visit a mosque; women cover their hair.

food: Hummus and falafel
Chickpeas mashed with tahini and fried balls, served in pitta.
Israël.respect: During Shabbat, from Friday evening to Saturday evening, transport and shops slow right down: plan your journeys ahead.

food: Machboos
Spiced rice with fish or meat, flavoured with dried lime.
Émirats arabes unis.respect: Away from the beaches, covering up is expected, and public displays of affection are frowned upon.

food: Grilled fish and jollof rice
The day’s fresh fish and spicy red rice, on the peninsula’s beaches.
Sierra Leone.respect: Ask before photographing anyone and support the community’s small businesses and surf schools.

food: Chambo
A fish from Lake Malawi, grilled or fried, served with nsima.
Malawi.respect: The lake is a nature reserve for its cichlids: don’t take any fish and dress modestly in the villages.

hello: “hello” in Khmer, with palms pressed together
food: Amok
A coconut-milk fish curry cooked in a banana leaf.
Cambodge.respect: Cover your shoulders and knees in pagodas and never touch someone’s head.

hello: a polite “hello”, with a slight bow
food: Hoe and market seafood
Raw fish sliced to order, eaten on the spot at the harbour market.
Corée du Sud.respect: Don’t start eating before your elders and don’t stick your chopsticks upright in your rice.

food: Dim sum
Small steamed bites, shared over tea.
Hong Kong.respect: On lifeguarded beaches, swim inside the shark-net enclosure and respect the flags.

food: Fish in coconut milk
Fresh lagoon fish cooked in coconut milk, with taro.
Îles Salomon.respect: Almost all land and reefs are customary: ask the village for permission and pay the diving or surfing fees.

hello: “hello” in English, understood in every state of Micronesia, where each island has its own language
food: Grilled fish with breadfruit
Lagoon fish and breadfruit, the staple of island meals.
Micronésie.respect: Yap and Chuuk have strong customs: cover your thighs and ask before entering a village.

food: Ropa vieja
Shredded beef stewed in tomato, served with rice and black beans.
Cuba.respect: Stay in a casa particular to support families, and carry cash: internet and bank cards remain hit-and-miss.

food: Jerk chicken
Chicken marinated in chilli and allspice, smoked over pimento wood.
Jamaïque.respect: Always ask before photographing anyone, and haggle with a smile.

hello: “hello”, said with the islands’ sing-song accent
food: Fungi and fish
Okra cornmeal with fish in Creole sauce.
Îles Vierges britanniques.respect: Use the marine park’s mooring buoys rather than your anchor and don’t touch the coral.

food: Conch pâté
A fried pastry filled with spiced conch, sold at small stands.
Îles Vierges des États-Unis.respect: Sunscreens containing oxybenzone are banned to protect the reefs.

food: Roasted breadfruit and fried jackfish
The national dish, served at small local eateries.
Saint-Vincent-et-les-Grenadines.respect: In the Tobago Cays Marine Park, pay the entry fee and let the turtles swim without approaching them.

food: Oil down
A stew of breadfruit, salt fish and coconut milk.
Grenade.respect: Nutmeg is the island’s pride: buy directly from the cooperatives. Pay the underwater park fee.

food: Callaloo
A soup of dasheen leaves and coconut milk.
Dominique.respect: Buy the nature sites pass and leave the whales and dolphins in peace, with a licensed operator.

food: Green fig and saltfish
Green bananas and salt cod, the national dish.
Sainte-Lucie.respect: The Soufrière Marine Park charges an entry fee and bans fishing and contact with the coral.

food: Conch fritters
Conch fritters, the speciality of the archipelago.
Îles Turques-et-Caïques.respect: Don’t collect conch or coral, and don’t feed the rays or fish in the marine parks.

food: Pepián
A spiced stew with toasted seeds, a national dish with Mayan roots.
Guatemala.respect: Ask before photographing local people, especially in Mayan villages.

hello: “hello” in Creole, or hello on the Dutch side
food: Accras and johnny cakes
Salt-cod fritters and small fried breads, between French and Caribbean culture.
Saint-Martin.respect: The nature reserve covers many of the islets: no anchoring on seagrass beds and no fishing.

food: Mataba
Pounded cassava leaves cooked in coconut milk.
Mayotte.respect: Mayotte is mostly Muslim: cover up away from the beach. The lagoon is a marine park, so watch turtles and dolphins from a distance.

hossegor.vibe: Basque-Landes villas tucked among the pines, a saltwater lake where oysters are farmed and surf-brand shops on every street corner: Hossegor lives for the wave, and the whole town keeps a close eye on the swell.
food: Duck magret and confit
The classics of Landes fattened duck, served with homemade chips or in a Landes salad.
hossegor.respect: At La Gravière, the line-up is packed and very local: watch for a long time from the beach, never snake anyone’s priority and stay on the sand if the barrels are beyond your level.
hossegor.season: September to November: powerful autumn swells, offshore wind in the morning and sandbanks often at their best.

around.d: Tidal saltwater lake lined with villas and oyster beds, ideal for a stroll.
Protected wetland where you can watch migrating and wintering birds from purpose-built trails.
Old town of colourful half-timbered houses on the banks of the Nive, ramparts and a lively covered market.
Traditions, pelota, fishing and rural life of the Basque Country told in a handsome riverside mansion.
Boardwalk trail on stilts through a swampy forest and a freshwater pond in Seignosse.

lacanau.vibe: A seaside resort built for the people of Bordeaux, Lacanau Océan has lived to the rhythm of surfing for decades: a lively seafront, a high dune retreating before the ocean, pine forest and a big calm lake behind.
food: Entrecôte à la bordelaise
Grilled over vine cuttings and topped with a red wine sauce, with a glass of Médoc.
lacanau.respect: Cross the dune only via the marked paths: the chestnut fencing protects a fragile ridge that erosion nibbles away every winter. Respect the swimming zones too.
lacanau.season: September to October: consistent swells, wind often calmer in the morning, water still mild and peaks freed from the summer crowds.

around.d: Large freshwater lake fringed with pines, perfect for paddleboarding, sailing or a wave-free swim.
Trails and boardwalks through marshes, heathland and forest, with shy wildlife to spot.
The largest natural lake in mainland France, with sandy beaches and cycle paths.
Wooded dunes, damp dune slacks and unspoilt marshland between the lake and the ocean.

latorche.vibe: At the tip of the Pays Bigouden, land of tall lace headdresses and the fishing ports of Penmarch and Le Guilvinec, La Torche faces Audierne Bay, with its dolmen and windsurfers on the horizon.
hello: “hello” in Breton, always well received in the Pays Bigouden
food: Le Guilvinec langoustine
Landed live at the Le Guilvinec fish auction and best enjoyed simply, with homemade mayonnaise.
latorche.respect: Rip currents are treacherous near the point: stay in your zone, give the surf schools space and don’t trample the fragile vegetation around the dolmen.
latorche.season: September to November: well-lined-up westerly swells, water still bearable and a beach deserted after summer.

around.d: Tall granite lighthouse on the Penmarch headland: climb to the top for the view along the coast.
Major small-scale fishing port: watch the trawlers come in and the bustle of the fish auction.
Capital of the Pays Bigouden, with its castle housing a museum of costumes and headdresses.
Prehistoric burial mound set on the point, facing the ocean and the long sweep of Audierne Bay.
Charming little port at the mouth of the Odet, opposite Bénodet, with its café terraces and chapels.

biarritz.vibe: A former imperial resort of Belle Époque villas, Biarritz saw the birth of European surfing on these waves below the cliffs; longboarders, schools and regulars gather on the beach as soon as the tide drops.
hello: “hi” in Basque, said with a smile
food: Gâteau basque
Shortcrust pastry filled with custard or black cherry jam, perfect to take to the beach.
biarritz.respect: At high tide the beach vanishes beneath the cliffs: check the tide times, and share the waves with the schools and longboarders, who are out in force here.
biarritz.season: September to October: clean autumn swells, water still mild and fewer students in the water than in high summer.

around.d: Former Art Deco sea museum, with seals and Bay of Biscay wildlife, facing the Rocher de la Vierge.
Basque village of white houses with red shutters, at the foot of La Rhune and its caves.
Gothic cathedral with soaring spires and a cloister, in the heart of Grand Bayonne.
Former fishing village perched on the coast, with its little harbour and pelota court.
Small protected lake between Biarritz and Bidart, circled by a shady walking path.

anglet.vibe: Between the mouth of the Adour and the Biarritz lighthouse, Anglet lines up its sandy beaches facing the Pyrenees, linked by a promenade where joggers, surfers and families cross paths around the Chambre d’Amour.
hello: “hi” in Basque, said with a smile
food: Bayonne ham and Espelette pepper
Cured ham and the region’s mild chilli, to nibble as tapas with a glass of Irouléguy.
anglet.respect: At Les Cavaliers, the locals know every sandbank: wait your turn at the peak, don’t sit inside those paddling for a wave and take your rubbish with you when you leave the beach.
anglet.season: September to November: hollow autumn swells, frequent offshore wind in the morning and water still pleasant.

around.d: Old town of colourful half-timbered houses on the banks of the Nive, ramparts and a lively covered market.
Basque village whose façades are covered in strings of chilli peppers drying in the sun.
Traditions, pelota, fishing and rural life of the Basque Country told in a handsome riverside mansion.
Former Art Deco sea museum, with seals and Bay of Biscay wildlife.
Basque village of white houses with red shutters, at the foot of La Rhune and its caves.

quiberon.vibe: A granite peninsula battered by the Côte Sauvage on one side, a sheltered bay on the other: Quiberon has always lived from the sea, between sardine canneries, fishing ports, thalassotherapy and boats to Belle-Île.
hello: “hello” in Breton, always well received on the peninsula
food: Salted butter caramel
Born on the peninsula, you can try it as sweets, on a crêpe or in a jar to take home in your suitcase.
quiberon.respect: On the Côte Sauvage, swimming is dangerous because of the currents and rocks: only go in the water with an instructor, and stay on the path without trampling the heath.
quiberon.season: May to June and September: moderate swells, warming water and beaches far quieter than in August.

around.d: Cliffs, coves and granite arches along a spectacular coastal path facing the open sea.
Large rocky island reached by boat: the Port-Coton needles, colourful harbours and coastal paths.
Imposing fortress remodelled by Vauban, towering over the port of Le Palais as soon as the boat arrives.
Long rows of Neolithic standing stones lining the roadside at Erdeven.
Quiberon’s old fishing port turned marina, with its little lighthouse and quays.

seignosse.vibe: A resort born among the pines, Seignosse Océan hides its holiday homes behind a high dune, with freshwater lakes further inland; here, the day is set by the tide and the sandbanks.
food: Pastis landais
Light brioche flavoured with orange blossom and rum, nothing to do with the aperitif of the same name.
seignosse.respect: Les Bourdaines draws a crowd as soon as the swell picks up: share the peaks, and park in the designated car parks rather than in the forest or at the foot of the dune.
seignosse.season: September to November: solid autumn swells, offshore wind in the morning and a calmer line-up than in summer.

around.d: Wild river between forest and dunes, to float down in a traditional boat all the way to the ocean.
Boardwalk trail on stilts through a swampy forest and a freshwater pond.
Tidal saltwater lake lined with villas and oyster beds, ideal for a stroll.
Peaceful lake surrounded by pines and reeds, popular with anglers and walkers.
Protected wetland where you can watch migrating and wintering birds from purpose-built trails.

capbreton.vibe: Capbreton keeps the soul of a fishing port, with its wooden pier and fish stalls, while at La Piste old graffiti-covered bunkers stand guard over barrels fed by the nearby Gouf underwater canyon.
food: Chipirons à la plancha
Baby squid seared with garlic and parsley, served all along the Basque and Landes coast.
capbreton.respect: The bunkers at La Piste are sinking and tilting in the sand: don’t climb on them. At high tide, the shorebreak hits hard, even for swimmers.
capbreton.season: September to November: powerful autumn swells, early-morning offshore wind and water still mild.

around.d: Long wooden jetty topped by its lighthouse, for watching the surfers and the sunset.
Tidal saltwater lake lined with villas and oyster beds, ideal for a stroll.
Protected wetland where you can watch migrating and wintering birds from purpose-built trails.
Old town of colourful half-timbered houses on the banks of the Nive, ramparts and a lively covered market.
Traditions, pelota, fishing and rural life of the Basque Country told in a handsome riverside mansion.

lafitenia.vibe: Just north of Saint-Jean-de-Luz, a town of tuna boats and shipowners where Louis XIV married the Infanta, Lafitenia Bay opens between green cliffs and Basque farms; on swell days, you watch it peel from the path.
hello: “hi” in Basque, said with a smile
food: Ttoro
Fish and shellfish soup of the Saint-Jean-de-Luz fishermen, spiced with Espelette pepper.
lafitenia.respect: The Lafitenia right is highly sought after: one surfer per wave, priority to whoever is on the peak, and no sneaking inside. The small car park fills up fast, so come early.
lafitenia.season: September to December: westerly swells strong enough to make the right peel, with offshore wind in the morning.

around.d: Fishing port, shipowners’ houses, the church where Louis XIV was married and a large sheltered beach.
Neo-Gothic castle-observatory perched on the Hendaye clifftop road, with a lavishly decorated interior.
Fishermen’s quarter facing Saint-Jean-de-Luz, birthplace of Maurice Ravel and home to Socoa Fort.
Basque village of white houses with red shutters, at the foot of La Rhune and its caves.
Typical Basque village with a Roman bridge over the Nivelle, a starting point for La Rhune.

guethary.vibe: A former fishing village clinging to the cliff, Guéthary has kept its little slipway harbour and pelota court; when the big swell arrives, the whole village settles on café terraces to watch the guns tackle Parlementia out at sea.
hello: “hi” in Basque, said with a smile
food: Veal axoa
Minced veal simmered with onions and Espelette pepper, a festive dish of Basque villages.
guethary.respect: Parlementia breaks far out on a reef: when it’s holding big, stay on the shore unless you have the right experience and equipment, and give priority to the peak’s regulars.
guethary.season: October to February: big winter swells that wake up the reef, often with offshore wind in the morning.

around.d: Fishing port, shipowners’ houses, the church where Louis XIV was married and a large sheltered beach.
Neo-Gothic castle-observatory perched on the Hendaye clifftop road, with a lavishly decorated interior.
Basque village of white houses with red shutters, at the foot of La Rhune and its caves.
Small hilltop village gathered around its church, pelota court and cemetery facing the Pyrenees.
Former Art Deco sea museum, with seals and Bay of Biscay wildlife.

sauveterre.vibe: Between the vast Olonne state forest and the salt marshes, Sauveterre remains a wild beach a stone’s throw from Les Sables-d’Olonne, a fishing and offshore-racing port from which the Vendée Globe sailors set off.
food: Mogettes with Vendée ham
Melt-in-the-mouth white beans on toasted bread, with a slice of Vendée ham.
sauveterre.respect: Reach the beach by the marked paths through the forest and dune, and never light a fire: the pine forest is highly vulnerable to wildfires in summer.
sauveterre.season: September to November: consistent westerly swells, wind often calmer in the morning and quiet forest car parks.

around.d: The seafront promenade, the big beach, the fishing port and the channel from which the Vendée Globe yachts depart.
Former salt marshes where you can watch waders and migrating birds on foot or by bike.
Old fishermen’s quarter of narrow lanes facing the port, with its Arundel Tower.
Ruins of a medieval fortress overlooking the town of Talmont-Saint-Hilaire.
Modern and contemporary art in a former abbey, with a fine collection of works by Gaston Chaissac.

latranche.vibe: A family resort in southern Vendée, La Tranche-sur-Mer stretches its sandy beaches sheltered by pine woods, facing the Pertuis Breton strait and the Île de Ré, with a long tradition of growing flower bulbs.
food: Vendée brioche
Plaited brioche scented with orange blossom, traditionally served at weddings in the Vendée.
latranche.respect: Near the Belle-Henriette breach, the reserve protects a fragile dune and nesting birds: keep out of fenced-off areas and keep your dog on a lead.
latranche.season: June to September: small, easy swells, warmer water and surf schools open; aim for June or September to have some space.

around.d: Flat, luminous island with whitewashed villages, salt marshes and cycle paths.
Harbour town fortified by Vauban, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with lively quays and ramparts.
Protected coastal lagoon and dunes, rich in birdlife, between La Tranche and La Faute.
Former Benedictine abbey in the heart of the coastal Poitevin Marsh, with its chapter house.
Lighthouse on a wooded headland with views across the Pertuis Breton to the Île de Ré.

lapalue.vibe: At the tip of the Crozon Peninsula, in the Armorique Regional Nature Park, La Palue opens between sandstone cliffs and heather moorland, on a coast of former crayfish ports such as Camaret.
hello: “hello” in Breton, always well received on the peninsula
food: Kouign-amann
Born in Douarnenez, just across the bay: flaky pastry, salted butter and caramelised sugar.
lapalue.respect: Swimming is forbidden at La Palue because of violent currents: only go in the water if you have real experience, and stay on the paths to protect the dune and the heath.
lapalue.season: September to November: powerful westerly swells, beautiful light and a nearly empty beach after summer.

around.d: Dizzying cliffs facing the Tas de Pois rocks, one of the finest panoramas in Brittany.
Wild headland extended by a rock arch nicknamed Dinan Castle.
The peninsula’s southern cape, with heathland, a coastal path and views over Douarnenez Bay.
Harbour of colourful houses, a boat graveyard and a UNESCO-listed Vauban tower on the shingle spit.
Bare, heath-covered summit with a 360-degree view over the peninsula and the bays.

penhors.vibe: The little harbour of Pouldreuzic, home of the famous Breton pâté, Penhors lines the long Audierne Bay and its shingle bank; above the beach, the chapel hosts a major Breton pardon every year.
hello: “hello” in Breton, always well received in the Pays Bigouden
food: Crêpes and buckwheat galettes
A galette complète made with buckwheat, then a salted butter crêpe, with a bowl of farmhouse cider.
penhors.respect: The shingle bank protects the marshes behind it: don’t take any pebbles, don’t walk on the vegetation and park in the designated car parks.
penhors.season: September to November: consistent westerly swells, wind often lighter in the morning and water still reasonable.

around.d: Tall granite lighthouse on the Penmarch headland: climb to the top for the view along the coast.
Traditional boats afloat and on the quay, for a dive into Breton maritime history.
Small historic town with cobbled lanes running down to the Goyen, and its Notre-Dame church.
Rocky headland and legendary board-sports spot, with a dolmen and a view over the whole of Audierne Bay.
Capital of the Pays Bigouden, with its castle housing a museum of costumes and headdresses.

lapalmyre.vibe: Razed at the end of the war and then rebuilt in a bold modern style, Royan still has its Belle Époque villas at Pontaillac, around a sheltered cove facing the estuary and the Cordouan lighthouse.
food: Marennes-Oléron oysters
Matured in claires in the neighbouring basin, to enjoy with a glass of Pineau or white wine.
lapalmyre.respect: Pontaillac cove is small and packed in summer: surf outside the marked swimming zones and give the schools space on their peak.
lapalmyre.season: May to June and September: small, easy swells, warming water and a less crowded cove than in summer.

around.d: Monumental lighthouse standing at sea at the mouth of the estuary, UNESCO-listed and open to visitors by boat.
Village of flower-filled lanes, oyster farmers’ huts and craft workshops on the Seudre.
Cliffs riddled with troglodyte caves overlooking the Gironde estuary.
Romanesque church long buried in sand, a stop on the Way of St James, on the other side of the estuary.
Resort of old villas, with a coastal path, coves and the Pont du Diable.

mimizan.vibe: Set on either side of the stream linking Lake Aureilhan to the ocean, Mimizan Plage mixes old villas, pine woods and long lifeguarded beaches, with the Landes forest as its hinterland.
food: Landes salad
Confit gizzards, dried duck breast and foie gras on green salad, the great classic of Landes tables.
mimizan.respect: Don’t go in the water near the mouth of the Mimizan stream: the outflow from the lake creates violent currents, especially on a falling tide. Surf between the marked zones.
mimizan.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells, early-morning offshore wind and water still mild.

around.d: Romanesque remains of a priory with a carved doorway, UNESCO-listed (Way of St James).
Large lake lined with pines and a promenade, ideal for paddleboarding or family cycling.
Lighthouse with a black-and-white spiral in the forest, whose top offers a view of the coast.
Small museum devoted to local history, from the medieval priory to life in the Landes forest.
Seaplanes, models and archives in Biscarrosse, a former base from the golden age of seaplanes.

capferret.vibe: At the end of a tongue of sand and pines, Cap Ferret lives between ocean and bay: oyster villages of wooden huts, pinasse boats at anchor and, opposite, the Dune du Pilat closing off the horizon.
food: Arcachon Bay oysters
Enjoyed in an oyster farmer’s hut with crépinettes sausages and a glass of dry white wine.
capferret.respect: At the point, the tidal currents in the channel are extremely violent: never go in the water on a falling tide without knowing the spot, and respect the no-go zones.
capferret.season: September to November: clean autumn swells and well-formed sandbanks, always keeping an eye on the tidal coefficients.

around.d: Europe’s highest dune, to climb for a vast view over the ocean, the forest and the Banc d’Arguin.
Red and white lighthouse whose top offers a view over the bay, the point and the Dune du Pilat.
Island in the middle of the bay, famous for its cabanes tchanquées perched on stilts, best seen by boat.
Winter Town of whimsical villas, piers, seafront and a lively market.
Shifting sandbanks at the entrance to the bay, a seabird refuge reached by boat.

bidart.vibe: A Basque village perched on the cliff, Bidart gathers a church, a pelota court and a half-timbered town hall around its square, while down below the beaches follow one another at the foot of green cliffs.
hello: “hi” in Basque, said with a smile
food: Ossau-Iraty sheep’s cheese
Matured sheep’s cheese from the Pyrenees, served with Itxassou black cherry jam.
bidart.respect: The Pavillon Royal peak is narrow and hotly contested: respect priority and don’t paddle inside the locals. The cliffs crumble, so don’t settle at their foot.
bidart.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells, offshore wind in the morning and sandbanks often well placed.

around.d: Fishing port, shipowners’ houses, the church where Louis XIV was married and a large sheltered beach.
Neo-Gothic castle-observatory perched on the Hendaye clifftop road, with a lavishly decorated interior.
Former fishing village perched on the coast, with its little harbour and pelota court.
Basque village of white houses with red shutters, at the foot of La Rhune and its caves.
Small protected lake between Biarritz and Bidart, circled by a shady walking path.

nazare.vibe: Nazaré keeps its fishing traditions alive, between women in layered skirts and fish drying in the sun on the beach, while below the fort, Praia do Norte has become the world stage for giant waves.
food: Nazaré dried fish
Horse mackerel split open and sun-dried on racks by the beach, sold by the fishermen’s wives.
nazare.respect: On big swell days, stay well back from the cliff edge and the shoreline: the waves can wash over the whole beach. Let the jet-ski and rescue teams do their work.
nazare.season: October to March: big winter swells funnel into the underwater canyon and raise the giant waves.

around.d: Fort and lighthouse above Praia do Norte, a lookout for the giant waves with a surf exhibition.
UNESCO-listed Gothic and Manueline masterpiece, with its Unfinished Chapels.
Town built around a vast UNESCO-listed Cistercian monastery, with the tombs of Pedro and Inês.
Baroque church in Sítio, the clifftop quarter, with a plunging view over the town and the beach.
Almost enclosed shell-shaped bay with calm waters, ideal for swimming.

supertubos.vibe: Peniche is a major fishing port set on a clifftop peninsula, known for its bobbin lace, its fortress turned museum of resistance to the dictatorship, and its dozens of surf camps.
food: Caldeirada
Stew of fish and potatoes simmered in layers, a speciality of ports such as Peniche.
supertubos.respect: When Supertubos is barrelling, the line-up fills with locals and pros: wait your turn, and leave nothing visible in your car in the beach car parks.
supertubos.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells and early-morning offshore wind that hollow out the barrels.

around.d: Protected archipelago reached by boat, with a fort perched on an islet and crystal-clear waters.
Walled medieval village of white, flower-filled lanes, famous for its ginjinha.
Former political prison of the dictatorship, now the Museum of Resistance and Freedom.
Headland of ocean-sculpted cliffs, with its lighthouse and a view of the Berlengas.
Portugal’s largest coastal lagoon, perfect for kitesurfing, paddleboarding and birdwatching.

ericeira.vibe: A former fishing village of white houses trimmed in blue, Ericeira has become Europe’s first World Surfing Reserve; the boats are still hauled up onto the fishermen’s beach, at the foot of the cliffs.
food: Pão de Mafra
Country bread with a floury crust and an airy crumb, from the ovens of nearby Mafra.
ericeira.respect: Coxos breaks over sharp rocks and the line-up is very local: watch first, respect the pecking order at the peak, and don’t go in at low tide without knowing the bottom.
ericeira.season: October to March: powerful west-northwest swells and offshore wind that make the rights peel along the reefs.

around.d: Brightly coloured Romantic palace perched on the Sintra hills, surrounded by a wooded park.
Town dominated by a vast UNESCO-listed Baroque palace-convent, with its library.
White village clinging to a cliff above a natural pool carved into the rock.
The westernmost point of mainland Europe, wind-battered cliffs and a lighthouse.
Medieval ramparts winding along the ridges of Sintra, with views as far as the ocean.

mundaka.vibe: A small Basque port nestled at the mouth of the Urdaibai estuary, a biosphere reserve, Mundaka lives to the rhythm of the tides; from the church forecourt on the point, the whole village scans the sandbank.
hello: “hi” in Basque, the everyday language in Mundaka
food: Marmitako
Stew of tuna, potatoes and peppers, a dish of the fishermen of Bermeo, the big neighbouring port.
mundaka.respect: The Mundaka left is a matter of metres: priority to the locals at the peak, and beware of the estuary’s powerful current on a falling tide. If you lack the level, watch from the harbour.
mundaka.season: October to February: powerful northwest swells that draw long barrels over the estuary sandbank.

around.d: Symbolic town of the Basque Country, with its sacred oak, its Assembly House and its Peace Museum.
Estuary of marshes, forests and beaches, to explore on foot, by bike or by kayak.
Cave decorated with prehistoric paintings, discovered through a guided visit and a reconstruction.
Major Basque fishing port, with its old quarter, colourful quays and fishermen’s museum.
Centre for watching migrating birds in the heart of the reserve’s marshes.

thurso.vibe: At the far end of mainland Scotland, in Caithness with its flagstone fences and Norse-derived place names, Thurso looks out towards Orkney; the river pours peat-brown water right next to the wave.
food: Cullen skink
Creamy soup of smoked haddock, potatoes and onions, perfect after an icy session.
thurso.respect: Thurso East breaks over a flat, shallow rock slab: paddle in and out via the channel, respect the small local community at the peak, and bring something to warm up with.
thurso.season: September to November: well-lined-up North Atlantic swells and days still fairly long; bring a thick wetsuit.

around.d: 16th-century castle, former residence of the Queen Mother, with walled gardens facing the sea.
Legendary village at the northeastern tip of Scotland, departure point for boats to Orkney in summer.
The northernmost town on the British mainland, with its ruined old church and its beach.
Forest planted behind the dunes of Dunnet Bay, criss-crossed by easy trails.

bundoran.vibe: An old-fashioned seaside resort with amusement arcades and fish and chips, Bundoran has become Ireland’s surf capital, facing Donegal Bay and the flat-topped silhouette of Benbulben.
bundoran.respect: The Peak breaks over a flat reef right in front of the town: give priority to the locals, avoid the spot at very low tide, and don’t walk on the slippery rocks without boots.
bundoran.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells and the warmest water of the year, before the winter storms.

around.d: Fishing village overlooked by Classiebawn Castle, famous for its giant waves.
Lake framed by cliffs, with a waterfall that inspired the poet Yeats.
Uninhabited island holding the remains of an early Christian monastery within a stone enclosure.
Long beach of soft sand, perfect for walks and beginner surfing.
Large lake straddling the border, renowned for its wild trout and peaceful shores.

rodiles.vibe: At the head of the Villaviciosa estuary, the Asturian capital of cider, the beach backs onto a pine wood and a nature reserve where birds spend the winter; after your session, head to a sidrería to watch cider poured from a height.
food: Fabada and Asturian cider
White beans slow-cooked with chorizo and black pudding, with cider poured from a height.
rodiles.respect: The estuary is a nature reserve: don’t trample the mudflats where birds land, park in the pine-wood car park and let the locals run the peak at the river mouth.
rodiles.season: October to March: the big northwest swells of autumn and winter finally make the river-mouth right peel.

around.d: Small town of old lanes, the heartland of Asturian apple orchards and cider houses.
Small pre-Romanesque Asturian church, a stone gem amid the meadows.
Large port city, with its old fishermen’s quarter of Cimadevilla and its town beach.
Rural houses, hórreos and everyday objects to help you understand Asturian culture.
All about apples, presses and the ritual of pouring cider from a height.

somo.vibe: Opposite Santander, you reach Somo by small ferry across the bay; the village lives from its surf schools, its long spit of dunes and the Cantabrian families who spend their summers there.
food: Rabas
Fried strips of squid, nibbled as an aperitif in the bars around Santander Bay.
somo.respect: The dunes of El Puntal and Loredo are fragile: cross them on the boardwalks and leave room for the surf lessons set up on the inside sandbanks.
somo.season: June to October: more moderate swells and milder water for learning; September avoids the August crowds.

around.d: Royal summer palace set on a green peninsula, with a park and views over the bay.
Cove on the Costa Quebrada bristling with blades of rock, superb at low tide.
Vast coastal marshes where many migrating birds stop over.
Santander’s Belle Époque beach, lined with gardens, villas and a casino.
Gothic cathedral built over a medieval crypt, in the heart of the city.

zarautz.vibe: A Basque seaside resort where surf schools line the promenade, between pintxos bars and txakoli vineyards clinging to the hills; right next door, Getaria keeps its fishing port and smoking grills.
hello: “hi” in Basque, said with a smile
food: Txakoli and Getaria grilled fish
Lively white wine poured from a height, with turbot or anchovies cooked over embers.
zarautz.respect: In summer, lifeguards mark out swimming and surfing zones: stay in yours. At the peak, priority goes to the surfer closest to where the wave breaks.
zarautz.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells, water still mild and a beach freed from the summer crowds.

around.d: Old town of pintxos bars, La Concha Bay and seafront promenades.
Fishing village at the foot of the rocky “mouse”, a lively harbour and txakoli vineyards.
Layered flysch cliffs between Zumaia and Mutriku, to follow on foot or by boat.
Former convent turned museum of Basque society, from yesterday to today.
Wooded hills, trails and old ironworks above the coast.

pantin.vibe: On the Costa Ártabra, between green cliffs, hórreos and the Valdoviño lagoon, the villages of Ferrolterra have lived from the sea and from surfing ever since the Pantín contest started stopping here.
hello: “hi” in Galician, without the Spanish h
food: Cedeira percebes
Goose barnacles prised from swell-battered rocks, simply boiled in salted water.
pantin.respect: The Ferrolterra locals care about the rules of the peak: wait your turn, and park in the car park rather than on the tracks of the neighbouring farms.
pantin.season: September to November: powerful, well-lined-up autumn swells, before the winter storms.

around.d: Primeval Atlantic forest at the bottom of a valley, with ferns and a wild river.

around.n: Monastery of San Xoán de Caaveiro
around.d: Medieval monastery perched on a rocky spur, in the heart of the Fragas do Eume.
Lighthouse on a windswept cape, with views over the cliffs of the coast.
Old town on the estuary, with its long stone bridge and narrow lanes.
Medieval keep perched on a hill, with a fine view over the estuary and the valley.

lasanta.vibe: A fishing village of white houses set on a coast of black lava where the Atlantic crashes; the whole island bears the mark of César Manrique, who wedded architecture to volcanic landscapes.
food: Papas arrugadas with mojo
Small potatoes boiled in salted water, served with a red or green mojo sauce.
lasanta.respect: The La Santa line-up is run by demanding locals: watch for a long time, leave them the sets and don’t paddle to the peak without the level, as the lava reef is very shallow.
lasanta.season: October to March: the northwest winter swells light up the reefs, with fewer trade winds than in summer.

around.d: Lava tube landscaped by César Manrique, with its underground lake and tiny white crabs.
Visit a vast lava tunnel with astonishing colours, beneath La Corona volcano.
Volcanic wall towering over the long Famara beach and the island of La Graciosa.
The island’s former capital, white colonial houses and a big Sunday market.
Former quarry transformed by Manrique into a garden of cacti from around the world.

anchorpoint.vibe: A former Amazigh fishing village of white and blue houses, Taghazout lives to the rhythm of its surf houses, but the boats still come back to the harbour and argan trees cover the surrounding hills.
hello: “hi” in Amazigh, the Berber language of the Souss
food: Amlou
Spread of roasted almonds, argan oil and honey, for breakfast.
anchorpoint.respect: In the village, cover your swimsuit with a T-shirt or sarong. In the water, the Anchor line-up is busy: respect priority and jump off the rocks between sets.
anchorpoint.season: November to March: North Atlantic winter swells make the right peel, under gentle sunshine.

pipeline.vibe: On the North Shore, life stays rural: roadside fruit stands, wooden houses and Hawaiian surfers who are heirs to the watermen, for whom the wave is to be respected as much as it is surfed.
hello: “hello” in Hawaiian, a word that also carries the idea of love and kindness
food: Kahuku garlic shrimp
Prawns sautéed in garlic and butter, served with rice from the food trucks.
pipeline.respect: At Pipe, the pecking order is strict and the locals make the rules: watch from the beach if you don’t have the level. Keep your distance from resting turtles and monk seals.
pipeline.season: November to February: North Pacific winter swells make the wave barrel, at the height of contest season.

around.d: Sacred Hawaiian valley, botanical garden and a trail to a waterfall.
The largest Hawaiian temple on the island, perched above Waimea Bay.
Legendary big-wave bay in winter, a calm lagoon for swimming in summer.
Living museum of Pacific cultures: dances, canoes and recreated villages.
Sheltered bay where you often see green turtles, with coastal trails.

mavericks.vibe: Around Pillar Point Harbor, fishing boats sell their catch on the docks and Pacific fog wraps the cliffs; a corner of farms and pumpkin fields that comes alive in winter when the giants rise.
food: Dungeness crab
Big North Pacific crab, sold cooked on the harbour docks in season.
mavericks.respect: Watch the sessions from Pillar Point Bluff without going near the edge of the unstable cliffs; in the Fitzgerald reserve tide pools, take nothing and leave the seals in peace.
mavericks.season: November to March: big North Pacific winter swells wake up the wave, in cold water.

around.d: Rock pools to explore at low tide: anemones, starfish and seals.
Clifftop trails with a plunging view of the Mavericks wave.
Former coastal road turned trail above spectacular sheer drops.
A climb through the chaparral to a summit open to the ocean and the bay.
Long wild beaches lined with dunes and a coastal trail.

trestles.vibe: You reach the wave on foot by a trail that follows San Mateo Creek and passes under the railway bridge; surfers fought to save this little valley from a motorway, on ancestral Acjachemen land.
trestles.respect: The trail crosses the sacred Acjachemen site of Panhe: stay on the path. In the very crowded line-up, pros and locals take the sets, so don’t sit at the peak without the level.
trestles.season: May to October: south swells and swells from Mexican Pacific hurricanes make the rights and lefts of Lowers peel.

around.d: 18th-century Spanish mission, ruins of the stone church and gardens.
Legendary beach of old-school longboarders, cliffs and coastal trails.
Small adobe and wooden houses among the oldest in California.
Spanish Colonial-style villa, gardens and a view of San Clemente Pier.
Beach at the foot of the cliffs, with a trail and a campsite up on the bluffs.

malibu.vibe: Once the Chumash land of Humaliwo, the point saw the birth of Californian surf culture in the Gidget years; the first World Surfing Reserve, it mixes classic longboards, a protected lagoon and villas along the Pacific Coast Highway.
malibu.respect: At First Point, the line-up is packed and the local longboarders care about priority: don’t drop in. Malibu Lagoon is protected, so stay on the trails.
malibu.season: June to October: south swells make the First Point right peel, with warmer water.

around.d: Rocky headland with a trail, views over the bay and migrating grey whales.
Wild canyon, volcanic rocks and a natural pool in the heart of the Santa Monica Mountains.
1920s villa decorated with the famous Malibu tiles, facing the wave.
Shady trail to a waterfall and the ruins of a modernist house.
Vast beach of golden sand, one of the busiest in Los Angeles.

puerto.vibe: A fishing port on the Oaxaca coast turned hangout for surfers from all over the world; in the morning, the boats are pulled up onto the main beach and the stalls overflow with mezcal, chocolate and Oaxacan chillies.
food: Tlayudas
Large crispy tortilla topped with beans, quesillo and grilled meat.
puerto.respect: Zicatela is not a swimming beach: the shorebreak and currents there are violent. Leave the peak to locals and experts, and go for a swim in a sheltered cove.
puerto.season: May to September: Pacific southern-hemisphere swells make Zicatela barrel, in the heat of the rainy season.

santateresa.vibe: A former fishing and cattle hamlet at the tip of the Nicoya Peninsula, Santa Teresa stretches along a dusty track lined with surf shops, yoga studios and a jungle full of howling monkeys.
santateresa.respect: Drive your quad at walking pace on the main track, which is shared with pedestrians. Depending on the tide, rocks show in front of some peaks: spot them before going in.
santateresa.season: May to November: green season, consistent south swells and fewer people, with offshore winds in the morning.

around.d: The country’s first protected area: rainforest, monkeys and a trail to a wild beach.
Bohemian seaside village, known for its waterfalls in the forest.
Neighbouring hamlet that has stayed peaceful, with rocky coves and fishing boats.

chicama.vibe: At the end of a windswept coastal desert, Puerto Malabrigo lives from its long fishing pier and its endless left; the La Libertad region still bears traces of the Moche and Chimú cultures.
food: Shambar
Thick soup of wheat, pulses and pork, served on Mondays in the Trujillo region.
chicama.respect: The pier and the harbour are still workplaces: let the fishermen through. When walking back up the point, never cut across the path of whoever is riding the wave.
chicama.season: April to October: southern-hemisphere winter swells make the left peel for hundreds of metres.

puntadelobos.vibe: Pichilemu, Chile’s surf capital, keeps its wooden houses, its huasos and the hand-harvested Cáhuil salt pans; at the point, surfers and residents rally to protect the cliffs from development.
puntadelobos.respect: The cliffs at the point are protected: stay on the marked trails and park in the designated car parks. At the peak, the locals jump off the rocks and have priority.
puntadelobos.season: March to October: southern-hemisphere autumn and winter swells make the left peel, in cold water.

around.d: Lagoon village of traditional salt pans, where you can buy salt straight from the producer.
Seaside resort with old-fashioned charm, a meeting place for young Chilean surfers.
Early 20th-century former casino and its palm park facing the sea.
Hill topped by a cross, the best viewpoint over the town and the bay.
Coastal lagoon where you can watch black-necked swans and waterbirds.

jbay.vibe: A small Eastern Cape town known for its shells, its surf-brand factory shops and its aloes; when the swell comes in, the whole town crowds onto the wooden boardwalks overlooking Supertubes.
food: Port St Francis chokka
Squid caught on the line by the neighbouring fleet, served grilled or fried.
jbay.respect: Supertubes is packed with sharp locals: take your turn, never let go of your board and enter the water through the usual gaps between the rocks.
jbay.season: May to September: the southern-hemisphere winter sends long southwest swells and offshore winds that groom Supertubes.

around.d: Village of white houses with thatched roofs, lined with canals and beaches.
Historic lighthouse on the tip of Cape St Francis, with views over the rocks and the coast.
Calm river with dark waters, to explore by kayak or paddleboard down to the sea.

bells.vibe: At the start of the Great Ocean Road, Torquay saw the birth of surf brands that went global; at Easter, the contest winner rings the bell at the foot of the red clay cliffs and coastal bush.
bells.respect: The clay cliffs crumble: go down to the beach by the built stairways. At the Bells peak, the locals are many and experienced, so stay humble.
bells.season: March to October: the southern-hemisphere autumn and winter bring southwest swells in cold water.

around.d: Boards, photos and the history of Australian surfing, from Duke Kahanamoku to today’s champions.
Wild cliffs, a coastal trail and protected reefs to explore with a mask.
Surf capital of the Surf Coast, shops, cafés and lifeguarded beaches.
Peaceful coastal village, famous for the kangaroos grazing on its golf course.
Lifeguarded beach at the foot of the cliffs, popular with local surfers.

snapper.vibe: On the border of Queensland and New South Wales, Coolangatta has raised several world champions; sand pumped from the mouth of the Tweed feeds the Superbank and the surf lifesaving clubs set the rhythm of the beach.
snapper.respect: This is one of the most crowded line-ups in the world: to jump off the Snapper rocks, wait for a lull and never cut across the line of whoever is surfing.
snapper.season: February to May: late-summer cyclone and easterly swells make the Superbank peel for hundreds of metres.

around.d: Headland straddling two states, ideal for whale watching in winter.
Protected islet where you can snorkel among sea turtles and tropical fish.
Historic wildlife park: koalas, kangaroos and rainbow lorikeets.
Australian wildlife in the forest, with platypuses and nocturnal birds.
Quiet little seaside town, with a beach, an estuary and a seafront promenade.

margaret.vibe: On Wadandi land in southwest Australia, the wave breaks close to vineyards and karri forests; at Prevelly, surfers cross paths with hikers on the Cape to Cape Track and lovers of fine wine.
food: Marron
Large freshwater crayfish from southwest Australia, often served grilled.
margaret.respect: Main Break is run by seasoned locals: watch before you paddle out. Stay on the Surfers Point paths to protect the dune vegetation.
margaret.season: March to May: the southern-hemisphere autumn combines big Southern Ocean swells with offshore winds in the morning.

around.d: Large limestone cave with spectacular formations, rich in fossils.
Jarrah and marri forests along the river, with walking trails.
Lively little town in the heart of the wine region, with cafés and farmers’ markets.
Protected coastline between the two capes, reefs, dolphins and migrating whales.
Tiny surfers’ village tucked into a sheltered bay, on the Cape to Cape Track.

uluwatu.vibe: At the end of the limestone Bukit Peninsula, bamboo warungs cling to the cliff above the cave that leads to the water, and every evening the kecak dance is performed at the temple facing the sunset.
hello: the Balinese Hindu greeting, palms together, wishing peace and well-being
food: Babi guling
Spit-roasted suckling pig stuffed with Balinese spices, served with rice and sambal.
uluwatu.respect: At Uluwatu Temple, wear a sarong and keep an eye on your glasses and phone: the macaques snatch them. In the crowded line-up, give priority to Balinese surfers.
uluwatu.season: April to October: dry season, southern Indian Ocean swells and southeast trade winds blowing offshore on the west coast.

around.d: Hindu temple perched on the cliff edge, with a kecak dance at sunset.
Temple set on a wave-battered rock, a Balinese pilgrimage site.
Fishing village with its fish market, and grilled seafood dinners on the beach.
Small cove of golden sand nestled between the rocks, reached by a staircase.
Art from Asia and the Pacific, with European painters inspired by Bali.

padang.vibe: You reach the little cove by a staircase that squeezes through a crack in the cliff; here surfing blends into Balinese daily life, between offerings laid on the sand, family warungs and the lanes of Pecatu.
hello: the Balinese Hindu greeting, palms together, wishing peace and well-being
food: Sate lilit
Skewers of spiced minced fish, wrapped around lemongrass stalks.
padang.respect: The reef sits just below the surface: only go out if you have the level, and wear mineral sunscreen. Leave the sets to the Balinese locals, who run this short and hotly contested peak.
padang.season: June to September: dry season and big southern swells, the only ones able to make this left barrel.

around.d: Hindu temple perched on the cliff edge, with a kecak dance at sunset.
Temple set on a wave-battered rock, a Balinese pilgrimage site.
Fishing village with its fish market, and grilled seafood dinners on the beach.
Ancient temple on Serangan Island, bustling during the major religious festivals.
Giant statue of Vishnu riding Garuda, and Balinese dance performances.

cloudbreak.vibe: South of the Mamanucas, boats leave from the islands and the Viti Levu coast to reach this offshore reef; long reserved for Tavarua guests, the wave has been open to all since 2010, but ashore the culture of bula and kava still reigns.
cloudbreak.respect: Cloudbreak is surfed from a boat: go with Fijian boatmen who know the reef and respect the rotation at the peak. The coral is razor-sharp, so reef boots are recommended.
cloudbreak.season: May to September: the dry season brings big southern swells and trade winds that are often favourable in the morning.

around.d: Large, colourful Hindu temple in Nadi, a reflection of the Indo-Fijian community.
Mamanuca island of white beaches and clear waters, with a Fijian village.
Hilly volcanic island in the Mamanucas, with villages, beaches and reefs.
Small island next to Malolo, with a sheltered lagoon, a marina and sandy beaches.

teahupoo.vibe: At the end of the road on Tahiti Iti, where the asphalt stops facing the mountain, the village lives from fishing, va’a and the lagoon; you reach the wave by boat, and it has hosted the Olympic surfing events.
teahupoo.respect: The village has only one narrow road: drive slowly and park in the designated spots. To reach the pass, go out with a local boat rather than paddling out alone.
teahupoo.season: May to September: the southern-hemisphere winter sends the big southwest swells that make the wave roar.

around.d: Roadless wild coast of Te Pari, with cliffs, waterfalls and valleys to explore.
South-coast village where Paul Gauguin lived and painted, with gardens and a lagoon.
The peninsula’s crossroads, from where a road climbs to the plateau and its lookouts.

floripa.vibe: On Santa Catarina Island, fishing villages of Azorean origin, with their lacemakers and oyster farms, sit alongside the surf shops; behind Joaquina, the big dunes welcome sandboarders.
food: The island’s oysters
Farmed in the bays of Santa Catarina, served raw, gratinated or with garlic.
floripa.respect: The Joaquina dunes are protected: sandboard only in the designated areas. In the water, respect the swimming zones marked out by the guarda-vidas.
floripa.season: April to September: the southern-hemisphere autumn and winter bring consistent south swells and less crowded beaches.

around.d: Large lagoon lined with dunes and hills, with restaurants, kitesurfing and nightlife.
Protected islet with turquoise waters, rock carvings and marked trails.
Azorean colonial village, colourful houses, oysters and sunsets over the bay.
Historic suspension bridge linking the island to the mainland, the city’s emblem.
Sandy beach framed by rocks, with powerful surf and paragliding over the hills.

puntaroca.vibe: At Puerto de La Libertad, the fishermen’s boats are hoisted onto the old pier and the fish market comes alive at dawn; the country is betting on its “Surf City”, but the port keeps its working-class soul.
food: Cóctel de conchas
Raw black clams with lime and onion, sold near the harbour pier.
puntaroca.respect: Punta Roca breaks over cobbles and rocks: go in and out through the passage the locals use, and give them priority at the peak.
puntaroca.season: March to October: southern Pacific swells make the right peel, with offshore winds in the morning.

around.d: Small surf village at the foot of the hills, with a pebble beach and a renowned right.
Historic pier, fishing boats and a very lively fish market.
Cool town at the foot of the volcano, with its lively pedestrian street and El Carmen church.

raglan.vibe: A small black-sand town on Whāingaroa Harbour, Raglan lives to the rhythm of surfers, artists and farms on the volcanic hills; Māori culture and surf spirit meet in the cafés on the main street.
raglan.respect: On the Manu Bay left, give priority to the surfer closest to the peak and never paddle into the path of those riding down the wave; rocks show at low tide.
raglan.season: March to October: southwest swells of the southern-hemisphere autumn and winter make the point peel; bring a thick wetsuit.

around.d: Bohemian main street, art galleries, cafés and a wharf on the calm-water harbour.
Forested former volcano overlooking the coast, with a hiking trail and views over the Tasman Sea.
Large wild inlet lined with hills and small communities, far from the crowds.

saquarema.vibe: Between lagoon and ocean, the old fishing town of Saquarema lives for the waves of Itaúna, watched over from their rock by the white church of Nossa Senhora de Nazaré; here, surfing is passed down through families.
saquarema.respect: At Itaúna, the wave is powerful and the line-up very local: wait your turn, don’t sit at the peak as soon as you arrive and avoid contest days if you’re a beginner.
saquarema.season: May to September: south swells of the southern-hemisphere winter wake up the Itaúna beach break, often with offshore wind in the morning.

montanita.vibe: Bamboo huts, cocktail stalls and hammocks: Montañita is the bohemian stopover on the Santa Elena coast, where the commune’s fishermen and travellers from all over the world meet on the beach every evening.
montanita.respect: The point breaks over rocks: wear reef boots at low tide, give priority to the peak’s regulars and, at night, stay in a group in the party streets.
montanita.season: December to April: consistent north swells, warm water and sunshine; the atmosphere peaks at carnival time.

around.d: Neighbouring village with a long, quiet beach, overlooked by a sanctuary perched on the cliff.
Peaceful hamlet at a river mouth, between coastal forest, a wild beach and small waves.

lobitos.vibe: Wooden houses from the oil era, pumpjacks in the desert and pelicans on the pier: Lobitos has traded oil for surfing without losing its fishing-village soul.
lobitos.respect: The lefts break over a rock bottom: let the locals go at the peak, take your rubbish with you and don’t get in the way of the fishermen working on the pier.
lobitos.season: April to October: south swells of the southern-hemisphere winter line up the lefts, with a south wind that is often offshore.

around.d: Fishing village famous for big-game fishing and Hemingway’s stay, with a barrelling wave.
The westernmost point of mainland South America, with cliffs and deserted beaches.

mardelplata.vibe: Argentina’s great seaside resort, Mar del Plata mixes a monumental rambla, a casino and a fishing port of yellow boats where sea lions lounge; this is where Argentine surfing took off.
food: Mar del Plata alfajores
Biscuits filled with dulce de leche and coated in chocolate, made famous by Havanna, founded here.
mardelplata.respect: In January, the town beaches are packed: surf in the authorised zones, away from swimmers, and respect the flags and instructions of the guardavidas.
mardelplata.season: March to May: more consistent south swells, water still mild and beaches freed from the summer crowds.

around.d: Argentine fine art in Villa Ortiz Basualdo, an elegant Anglo-Norman-style mansion.
An icon of modern Argentine architecture: a house set like a bridge over a stream.
Water tower that looks like a medieval manor, with a lookout over the city and the ocean.
Neo-Gothic brick basilica facing Plaza San Martín, in the heart of downtown.
Lake surrounded by a nature reserve and hills, for picnics, pedalos or birdwatching.

arica.vibe: At the foot of El Morro, Arica blends the Atacama Desert, Aymara heritage and the Chinchorro culture, whose mummies are among the oldest in the world; surfers hunt the barrels off Alacrán Island.
food: Azapa olives
Plump and purplish, they grow in the neighbouring oasis and turn up on every table.
arica.respect: El Gringo breaks over a very shallow slab: only venture out with real experience, and give priority to the locals and the bodyboarders who are regulars at the peak.
arica.season: April to September: southwest swells of the southern-hemisphere winter hollow out the barrel, under skies that are almost always dry.

around.d: Headland overlooking the city and the port, with a history museum and a view along the whole coastline.
Prefabricated iron church attributed to the Eiffel workshops, in the heart of the old town.
Oasis of olive groves in the middle of the desert, with an archaeological museum devoted to the Chinchorro mummies.
Former 19th-century customs house turned cultural centre and national monument, near the port.

itacare.vibe: A former cocoa port at the mouth of the Rio de Contas, Itacaré keeps its colourful lanes, its capoeira rodas and its coves hidden in the Atlantic Forest, reached by trails.
food: Acarajé
Bean fritter fried in dendê oil, filled with prawns and vatapá, typical of Bahia.
itacare.respect: The beaches are linked by forest trails: don’t walk them alone after dark, and at Tiririca, leave the waves to the regulars if you’re a beginner.
itacare.season: April to September: more consistent southeast swells; in summer, the sea calms down and suits very first attempts.

shonan.vibe: The former capital of the shoguns, Kamakura sits next to Shonan surf culture: between Zen temples, the little Enoden train running along the coast and weekend surfers from Tokyo, Sagami Bay lives at two speeds.
food: Shirasu-don
A bowl of rice topped with tiny sardine fry, caught in Sagami Bay.
shonan.respect: Keep your swimsuit for the beach and don’t wander the streets of Kamakura in it; at the peak, one surfer per wave, as the line-ups overflow at weekends.
shonan.season: Late August to October: typhoon swells liven up Sagami Bay, with water still warm.

around.d: Huge bronze Buddha seated in the open air since the Middle Ages, a symbol of the city.
Small island linked by a bridge: shrines, sea caves, a lighthouse lookout and views of Mount Fuji.
