Kamakura’s great Shinto shrine, at the end of a long cherry-lined avenue.
Hillside temple with a wooden Kannon statue, hydrangea gardens and a view over the bay.
Large Zen monastery nestled in a cedar forest, with old buildings and a listed bell.

arugam.vibe: Fishermen’s outrigger canoes pulled up on the sand, crocodile lagoons and Tamil and Muslim villages: for decades Arugam Bay has blended surfing backpackers with the coastal life of eastern Sri Lanka.
hello: “hello” in Tamil, the language of the east coast, said with palms together
arugam.respect: The neighbouring villages are mostly Muslim and Tamil: keep your swimsuit for the beach and cover your shoulders and knees whenever you go into town.
arugam.season: May to September: the southwest monsoon blows offshore on the east coast and the point peels consistently.

around.d: Small park around a reservoir where wild elephants come to graze in the late afternoon.
Ancient Buddhist temple set in the dunes by the ocean, in Pottuvil.
Ruins of an ancient monastery in the jungle, with a stupa, moonstones and statues.
Hindu temple at the foot of rocks, starting point of the walking pilgrimage to Kataragama.

cloud9.vibe: Coconut groves as far as the eye can see, fishermen’s bancas and habal-habal motorbike taxis: Siargao has built its surf culture around Cloud 9 and its boardwalk, while keeping the quiet life of its fishing villages.
cloud9.respect: The Cloud 9 line-up is very busy and the reef is shallow: stay on the shoulder if you don’t have the level and give priority to local surfers at the peak.
cloud9.season: September to November: Pacific swells and a wind that is often offshore hollow out the barrel; it’s contest season.

around.d: Teardrop-shaped islet covered in coconut palms, a classic stop on island-hopping boat trips.
Fishing village known for the Magpupungko natural pools, best seen at low tide.

waikiki.vibe: The beach of Hawaiian kings and then of the beach boys, Waikiki is where Duke Kahanamoku introduced surfing to the world; his statue facing the waves and the outrigger canoes gliding on the swell keep that bond alive.
hello: “hello”, “goodbye” and “affection” in Hawaiian, far more than a greeting
food: Poke
Cubes of raw fish seasoned with soy sauce, sesame oil and onion.
waikiki.respect: Hawaii bans sunscreens containing oxybenzone: bring a mineral sunscreen, and in the packed line-up, never let go of your board among the beginners and canoes.
waikiki.season: May to September: South Pacific swells make the gentle waves of Oahu’s south shore peel.

around.d: Iconic volcanic crater, climbed by a trail up to a lookout over Waikiki.
Marine reserve in an old crater, for snorkelling among reef fish.
Dizzying Koʻolau cliffs, a view over the windward coast and a key site in Hawaiian history.
Replica of a Japanese temple at the foot of lush green cliffs, with a pond and gardens.
Century-old waterfront aquarium devoted to the marine life of Hawaii and the Pacific.

unstad.vibe: In this remote cove on Vestvågøy, between farms and peaks, Arctic surfing was born from the daring of a few local pioneers; here you surf under the midnight sun in summer and the northern lights in winter.
unstad.respect: The hamlet is tiny: park in the designated car park, don’t camp in the farm meadows and check with the local surfers before going in the water.
unstad.season: September to March: North Atlantic storms send the swell, with the northern lights as a bonus, but the water is icy.

around.d: Very well-preserved fishing village, with its red rorbuer at the end of a narrow fjord.
18th-century red wooden church facing the sea and the mountains of Flakstadøya.
Working fishing port on a small island, with cod-drying racks and houses on stilts.
South-coast fishing village, a Hurtigruten port of call, surrounded by steep peaks.

skeletonbay.vibe: On the edge of the Pelican Point peninsula, the Namib dunes plunge into the icy Benguela Atlantic: fur seals, flamingos from the Walvis Bay lagoon and sand-laden wind surround this remote wave.
skeletonbay.respect: Fur seals and jackals prowl around the spot: leave no food behind, drive on the hard-sand track and never come alone, as help is far away.
skeletonbay.season: May to September: the big south-west swells of the southern winter line up the barrel, often under morning fog.

around.d: A huge sand dune to climb on foot for the view over the desert, or to race down on a sandboard.
A lighthouse at the end of a long sand spit where fur seals and pelicans laze about.
A Namibian port and its lagoon, where flamingos feed in their hundreds along the seafront.

mentawai.vibe: On Sipora, the village of Katiet lives off coconut palms and fishing in front of the reef; the archipelago is home to the Mentawai people, known for their traditional tattoos and sikerei shamans, especially on Siberut.
mentawai.respect: In these remote villages, cover up out of the water and ask before taking photos; at the peak, take turns with the other boats and camps, because the very shallow reef is unforgiving.
mentawai.season: April to October: Indian Ocean swells are at their most consistent, with winds often light in the morning.

dungeons.vibe: At the foot of the Sentinel, Hout Bay lives between its snoek fishing harbour, boats to Seal Island and the Imizamo Yethu township; Dungeons itself only comes alive with the big winter storms.
food: Bobotie
Spiced curried minced meat baked under an egg custard, a Cape Malay heritage dish.
dungeons.respect: Dungeons is for big-wave specialists only: if you’re not one, watch from the boat or the harbour, and respect the rules of the marine protected area.
dungeons.season: May to August: southern winter storms send the big south-west swells that wake the wave up, in cold water.

around.d: A road carved into the cliff between Hout Bay and Noordhoek, with spectacular ocean views.
Mountains, fynbos and wild beaches all the way to the Cape of Good Hope and Cape Point.
A neighbourhood of colourful houses on the slopes of Signal Hill, the historic heart of Cape Malay culture.
A lively fishing harbour with a market, fish and chips and boat trips to the fur seal colony.
A surfers’ village facing the Atlantic, with a long beach and the Slangkop lighthouse.

bluehole_belize.vibe: Made famous by Cousteau’s team, the Great Blue Hole is reached at dawn from Caye Caulker or San Pedro after a long crossing, for a dive among the stalactites of ancient drowned caves.
food: Grilled lobster
Caught around the cayes and grilled over a wood fire, only during the fishing season.
bluehole_belize.respect: Stick close to your guide and respect the announced depth, often around 40 m: the descent is fast and the atoll is protected, so nothing may be taken.
bluehole_belize.season: April to June: dry season, calmer seas for the long crossing and good visibility, before hurricane season.

around.d: An islet listed as a natural monument, with a red-footed booby colony and a wall famous among divers.
A remote atoll of coral walls and turquoise lagoons, the setting for Blue Hole trips.

sipadan.vibe: Off Semporna, Sipadan has to be earned: limited daily permits and a dawn departure from Mabul; all around, the Bajau Laut, sea nomads, still live on their boats and in stilt houses.
sipadan.respect: Permits for Sipadan are limited each day: book early through an approved centre and, on the island, stay within the permitted area. Ask before photographing Bajau families.
sipadan.season: April to September: calm seas and often excellent visibility, ideal for the walls and barracuda tornadoes.

around.d: A low-lying island home to Bajau families, a paradise for “muck” diving and small critters.
A sandbank topped with stilt bungalows, with dives over sandy bottom and reef.

rasmohammed.vibe: At the southern tip of Sinai, where the Gulfs of Suez and Aqaba meet, dive boats leave Sharm el-Sheikh for Shark and Yolanda Reef, while the Bedouin keep up their tradition of tea and hospitality in the nearby desert.
rasmohammed.respect: In the national park, pay the entrance fee, take no shells or coral, and make sure your boat moors only to the designated buoys.
rasmohammed.season: June to October: the water is at its warmest and big schools of jacks and barracuda gather around Shark Reef.

around.d: A 19th-century British cargo ship lying upside down on a reef, colonised by coral and fish.
A Sinai seaside resort with its old market, shisha cafés and dive harbour.
Sharm el-Sheikh’s lively bay, with a beach, a promenade and a reef you can snorkel.

thistlegorm.vibe: Discovered by Cousteau’s team in the 1950s, the wreck lies in the Gulf of Suez, off Sinai; you reach it at dawn by boat from Sharm el-Sheikh or Hurghada, or on a liveaboard dive cruise.
thistlegorm.respect: This is a war grave: bring nothing up, enter the holds only with a guide and avoid grabbing the structure, which is deteriorating.
thistlegorm.season: April to November: warmer water and often manageable seas, but the current on the wreck can be strong all year round.

around.d: A triangular reef nicknamed the ships’ graveyard, where several wrecks lie waiting to be explored.
A 19th-century British steamship run aground on Abu Nuhas, its ribs carpeted in coral.

tulamben.vibe: Beneath Mount Agung volcano, Tulamben is a fishing village of black-pebble beaches, where Balinese porter women carry dive tanks on their heads down to the water’s edge.
hello: a Balinese Hindu greeting, hands pressed together, wishing peace and goodwill
food: Babi guling
Suckling pig stuffed with Balinese spices and spit-roasted, served with rice and sambal.
tulamben.respect: The volcanic pebbles roll underfoot: wear booties to get into the water, never hold on to the wreck and pay the tank porters fairly.
tulamben.season: April to October: dry season, calm seas and good visibility on the wreck; come early in the morning to avoid the crowds.

around.d: A temple whose split gates frame Mount Agung, on the slopes of Mount Lempuyang.
A former royal water palace: pools, fountains and stepping stones amid gardens.
A Bali Aga village with preserved traditions, famous for its double-ikat geringsing weaving.
A string of fishing villages with colourful jukungs, for snorkelling off black-sand beaches.
An active volcano climbed at night to watch the sunrise over its crater lake.

greatbarrier.vibe: From Cairns and Port Douglas, boats head out every morning to the outer reef; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, traditional custodians of this Sea Country, pass on their stories here.
food: Barramundi
A fish from Queensland’s tropical waters, served grilled or as fish and chips.
greatbarrier.respect: Never touch the coral, wear a stinger suit during stinger season (November to May) and respect the marine park zoning.
greatbarrier.season: June to October: dry season, clear water, moderate trade winds and few jellyfish, with slightly cooler water.

silfra.vibe: At Þingvellir, where the Vikings held the open-air Althing from the 10th century, meltwater from the Langjökull glacier filters through the lava for decades before filling the fissure, icy and crystal clear.
food: Hverabrauð
Sweet rye bread baked for a whole day in the geothermal ground, as in Laugarvatn.
silfra.respect: Silfra can only be dived with an approved guide and drysuit experience; don’t touch the walls and stay within the national park boundary.
silfra.season: September to April: fewer groups in the fissure and superb low-angled light; the water stays at 2-4 °C all year round.

around.d: UNESCO-listed site of the ancient Icelandic parliament, among fissures, meadows and a lake.
A waterfall dropping into the Almannagjá fissure, a few minutes’ walk from the site.
Iceland’s largest natural lake, ringed by lava and mountains, for walking or fishing.
A lake and village with hot springs, and geothermal baths by the water.
A volcano with waymarked trails, fumaroles and hot rivers you can bathe in.

cenote_dosojos.vibe: Deep in the Yucatán jungle, on land managed by a Maya community, Dos Ojos opens onto a vast network of flooded caves; for the Maya, cenotes were gateways to the underworld.
food: Cochinita pibil
Pork marinated in achiote and bitter orange, slow-cooked in a banana leaf.
cenote_dosojos.respect: Shower before entering the cenote, with no sunscreen or repellent, and never venture into the passages without a certified cave-diving guide.
cenote_dosojos.season: December to April: dry season and clear skies, when shafts of light plunge into the water around midday.

around.d: A fortified Maya city perched on a cliff above the Caribbean Sea.
A small archaeological site in the forest, with remains of murals and a cenote.

medes.vibe: Facing L’Estartit, the Medes Islands, once a refuge for privateers, have become a marine sanctuary: the village lives off diving, while Montgrí Castle watches over the rice fields of Pals.
hello: “good morning” in Catalan, the proper greeting in the morning
food: L’Escala anchovies
Salted and cured following an age-old tradition in the neighbouring port of L’Escala.
medes.respect: In the reserve, fishing and collecting are forbidden and dives are supervised: go through an approved club and never feed the groupers.
medes.season: June to October: warmer water and good visibility; September still offers mild seas and fewer people.

around.d: An unfinished fortress atop the massif, reached on foot for a view over the whole bay.
A medieval castle given by Dalí to Gala and decorated by the painter, now a house museum.
Coastal marshes crossed by trails and hides for spotting flamingos, storks and waders.
A fishing village of white houses and arcades, nestled around small coves.
A museum in Torroella de Montgrí devoted to Mediterranean landscapes, sounds and crafts.

portcros.vibe: No cars here: you land at the little harbour lined with colourful houses, then head off on foot beneath pines and holm oaks. Fishermen and park rangers together watch over Posidonia seagrass meadows that have been protected for decades.
food: Provençal aïoli
Salt cod, steamed vegetables and whelks topped with a mayonnaise of crushed garlic and olive oil.
portcros.respect: Don’t smoke outside the village, pick nothing and, whether by kayak or boat, never drop anchor in the Posidonia meadows: they are protected.
portcros.season: June to September: water above 20 °C and often calm seas; June and September avoid the August crowds.

around.d: The largest of the Hyères Islands: sandy beaches, vineyards and car-free cycle tracks.
A fort overlooking Port-Cros bay that hosts exhibitions about the national park.
A garden of the world’s Mediterranean regions facing the islands, with a guided underwater trail in summer.
A hilltop village of flower-filled lanes and cobbled steps, with a view over the roadstead.
A peninsula linked by two tombolos, with a coastal path and salt pans with flamingos.

calanques.vibe: Sugiton has to be earned: you walk down from the Luminy campus, cool box on your back, like the Marseillais at the weekend. Further on, Morgiou and Sormiou keep their cabanons and fishermen’s pointus moored at the foot of the cliffs.
food: Bouillabaisse
Marseille’s rockfish soup, served with rouille, croutons and the fish on the side.
calanques.respect: In summer, book your free access to Sugiton on the park website and check whether the massifs are open: they close on days of high fire risk.
calanques.season: June to October: milder water and often calm seas between bouts of mistral, with far fewer people from September.

around.d: A fishing port with pastel façades, terraced vineyards and boats leaving for the calanques.
Dizzying ochre cliffs above the sea, to explore along the Route des Crêtes.
A long pine-fringed harbour calanque, the gateway to the trail towards Port-Pin and En-Vau.
A wild limestone island off the calanques, renowned for its dive sites and seabirds.
Town of shipyards and the Eden cinema, with its Figuerolles calanque and old harbour.

richelieu.vibe: This horseshoe-shaped rock barely breaks the surface, in the waters of the Surin Islands park, where Moken sea nomads still live. Divers set out from Khao Lak or Khuraburi, often on a liveaboard of a few days.
food: Kaeng som
A sour and very spicy Southern Thai curry with fish, turmeric and tamarind.
richelieu.respect: Don’t hold on to the rock covered in soft corals and anemones, and keep your distance from whale sharks, never touching or chasing them.
richelieu.season: February to April: glassy seas, crystal-clear water and the best chances of whale sharks; the park closes from mid-May to mid-October.

rajaampat.vibe: The Papuan stilt villages live from fishing and still practise sasi, which temporarily closes certain areas of reef to let the fish come back. You stay with local families, lulled by the lapping of water beneath the floor.
food: Papeda with yellow-broth fish
A sticky sago porridge served with fish cooked in turmeric and lime.
rajaampat.respect: Cover up when walking through the villages, which are often very devout, and buy the marine park entry card, which funds patrols and local communities.
rajaampat.season: October to April: generally calm seas and good visibility; from June to September, southerly winds whip up the sea.

galapagos.vibe: At the far end of the archipelago, these two uninhabited islets can only be reached on a dive liveaboard: you never set foot on them, it all happens underwater, in currents where cold and warm waters meet.
galapagos.respect: Stay grouped behind your guide in the current, never chase the sharks and touch neither the animals nor the living rock: the park rules are strict.
galapagos.season: June to November: cooler, richer water that draws big schools of hammerhead sharks and whale sharks.

maldives.vibe: On the local islands, life revolves around the mosque, the harbour and the dhonis, the traditional boats; in the late afternoon, people share tea and hedhikaa, little tuna and coconut snacks.
maldives.respect: At manta ray cleaning stations, settle on the bottom without moving, and give the whale sharks in the south of the atoll space, without touching them.
maldives.season: January to April: dry north-east monsoon, calm seas and top visibility on the walls and channels of the atoll.

hanauma.vibe: This collapsed crater open to the ocean was once a fishing ground prized by Hawaiian chiefs. Today you enter after a short lesson about the reef, and parrotfish cross paths with the humuhumunukunukuāpuaʻa.
hello: “hello”, “goodbye” and much more in Hawaiian: the welcoming spirit of the islands
food: Poke
Cubes of raw fish marinated in shoyu, sesame oil and seaweed, served on rice.
hanauma.respect: Book your entry slot online, use mineral sunscreen and never stand on the coral, even where the water is shallow.
hanauma.season: All year round, with the warmest water from April to October; arrive at opening time for clear water before the crowds.

around.d: An easy trail to the lighthouse, with views of the windward coast and, in winter, whales.
A sea geyser that spouts between volcanic rocks, near a small cove.
Fine sand and turquoise water facing the Mokulua islets, ideal at sunrise.
A garden of dryland plants nestled inside an old crater.
Honolulu’s beach district, cradle of modern surfing and its beach boys.

bonaire.vibe: At Sorobon, local kids learn to windsurf from childhood and several have become world freestyle stars. At the back of the bay, the mangroves and conch-shell piles of Lac Cai recall the fishing of old.
bonaire.respect: Keep out of the mangroves and seagrass at the back of the bay, where young fish and conch grow, and leave room for beginners from the Sorobon schools.
bonaire.season: January to August, peaking in June and July: strong, steady trade winds over a flat, warm lagoon.

around.d: Fringing reefs all around the island, reachable by shore diving at dozens of sites.
A cargo ship lying on the sand near Kralendijk, the island’s signature wreck dive.
Pink ponds, mountains of salt and flamingos, with the slave huts along the coast.
A small capital of colourful houses, with its seafront promenade and fort.
The island’s oldest village, tucked in a valley and proud of its traditions and harvest festival.

tarifa.vibe: Behind its ramparts, the white old town keeps its Moorish-looking lanes facing the Rif mountains. In the strait, dolphins and orcas cross paths with the bluefin tuna still caught by the almadrabas along the coast.
food: Almadraba bluefin tuna
Caught in spring in the strait and served as tataki, a la plancha or as tartare.
tarifa.respect: In summer, launch and land your kite only in the marked zones and corridors, away from swimmers, and beware of strong Levante winds that push you out to sea.
tarifa.season: April to October: the wind blows most often, powerful Levante or gentler Poniente, in water that is warming up.

around.d: Ruins of a Roman garum-making town by Bolonia beach and its great dune.
A Caliphate of Córdoba fortress overlooking the harbour, with views over the strait and Africa.
Cliffs, dunes and coastal trails facing Morocco, on a major bird migration route.
The southernmost point of mainland Europe, between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean.

dakhla.vibe: Between desert and ocean, the town lives off fishing and oyster farming in the lagoon. Under the khaima, you’ll be served tea in three glasses, a Sahrawi ritual that takes all the time it needs.
food: Dakhla oysters
Farmed in the lagoon, they are eaten freshly opened, with a squeeze of lemon.
dakhla.respect: Avoid sailing over the oyster beds and near fishing boats, and take time for tea when it is offered: it is a gesture of welcome.
dakhla.season: April to September: the thermal wind is at its strongest and blows almost daily; winter stays mild but a little less windy.

cabarete.vibe: A former fishing village turned Caribbean HQ for kiters, Cabarete lives with its feet in the sand: tables on the beach, merengue and bachata in the evening, motoconchos zipping along the coast road.
cabarete.respect: On busy Kite Beach, always launch and land with an assistant and keep clear of swimmers in front of the bay’s restaurants.
cabarete.season: June to August, then December to March: steady thermal trade winds in the afternoon, summer being the windiest period.

around.d: A wild palm-fringed beach, the most consistent surf spot on the north coast.
A seaside town with a sheltered bay, ideal for snorkelling, and a museum on its Jewish history.

lemorne.vibe: At the foot of the mountain, once a refuge for runaway slaves and now a place of remembrance, the Creole fishing villages live to the rhythm of séga, born on these shores. On Sundays, families picnic under the casuarina trees.
lemorne.respect: At One Eye, the wave belongs first to locals and regulars: watch for a long time before paddling out. In the lagoon, stay in the kite zones, away from swimmers.
lemorne.season: May to October: southern winter and strong south-east trade winds, perfect for the lagoon as well as the wave.

around.d: A UNESCO-listed mountain, symbol of resistance to slavery, with a view over the lagoon from the summit.
Dunes of volcanic soil in ochre, red and purple hues, in the heart of Chamarel.
Native forest, viewpoints and trails where you can spot endemic birds and monkeys.
A crater lake sacred to Hindus, lined with temples and monumental statues.
An upland village with its waterfall, rum distillery and Creole table d’hôte restaurants.

cumbuco.vibe: This fishing village has kept its jangadas, triangular-sailed rafts that still head out to sea. After your session, you race by buggy across the dunes to the lagoons, for fried fish with your feet in the water.
food: Caranguejada
Mangrove crabs cooked in a spicy broth, cracked open with a little mallet.
cumbuco.respect: In the lagoons, leave room for swimmers and jangadas, and before a downwinder, always tell someone your route and arrival time.
cumbuco.season: July to January: powerful, steady trade winds almost every day, peaking from September to November.

essaouira.vibe: At the harbour, blue boats land sardines and sea bream that are grilled on the spot. In the medina, thuya woodworkers and Gnawa musicians set the tempo, beneath ramparts battered by the trade wind.
food: Grilled sardines at the harbour
Pick your fish from the harbour stalls: it’s grilled before your eyes and served with bread and salad.
essaouira.respect: At the harbour, ask before photographing the fishermen; on the beach, launch well away from swimmers and camel drivers, and cover up to go back into the medina.
essaouira.season: April to September: the trade wind blows hard almost every day; the water stays cool, so bring a good wetsuit.

around.d: A UNESCO-listed fortified old town, with white and blue lanes, souks and workshops.
A cannon bastion overlooking the fishing harbour, with views of the ramparts and Mogador Island.
A house of memory devoted to the town’s Jewish heritage, in the mellah.
A small surfers’ village by a long wild beach, around its white marabout shrine.
A protected island facing the bay, a refuge for Eleonora’s falcon, to admire from the coast.

lafranqui.vibe: Between lagoon and sea, Leucate lives to the rhythm of the tramontane: oyster farmers on the lagoon, fishermen’s huts and the old villas of La Franqui at the foot of the plateau cliffs.
food: Leucate oysters
Farmed in the Salses-Leucate lagoon, to enjoy at the producers’ with a local wine.
lafranqui.respect: When the tramontane blows, the wind pushes offshore: never sail alone, stay within the authorised zones in summer and don’t trample the dunes of the sand bar.
lafranqui.season: September to June: frequent, powerful tramontane, especially in spring and autumn; in summer, the sea breeze is gentler.

around.d: A circular village around its tower, with salt pans, lagoons and beach chalets on stilts.
A large museum of Roman Narbonne, with a spectacular wall of stone inscriptions.
A ruined fortress amid the vineyards of the Corbières, with views all the way to the sea.
An old village at the foot of the plateau, with a cliff path above the sea.
A Roman and medieval town, with a cathedral, archbishops’ palace and lively covered market.

jericoacoara.vibe: Here the streets are sand and you walk barefoot. At sunset, the whole village climbs the big dune, then capoeira breaks out on the beach before nights of forró.
food: Tapioca
A cassava-starch crêpe filled with coalho cheese, coconut or dried meat.
jericoacoara.respect: Pay the environmental tax on arrival, stay on the tracks in the fragile dunes and, when kiting, keep well away from swimmers at the village beach.
jericoacoara.season: July to January: strong trade winds almost every day, peaking from September to November, with the lagoons nice and full.

around.d: Dunes, mangroves and cliffs, with the Pedra Furada rock arch to reach on foot.
A small town beside a turquoise freshwater lagoon, with hammocks strung above the water.

hookipa.vibe: A stone’s throw from Paia, a former sugar town turned windsurfers’ village, the beach follows an unwritten code: surfers in the morning, sails in the afternoon when the trade wind picks up, and green turtles coming to sleep on the sand.
hello: “hello”, “goodbye” and much more in Hawaiian: the welcoming spirit of the islands
food: Plate lunch
Rice, macaroni salad and teriyaki meat or kalua pig, the Hawaiian workers’ lunch.
hookipa.respect: Follow the local rule: surfing in the morning, windsurfing only from 11 am. On the beach, keep your distance from resting turtles.
hookipa.season: March to May and October to November: frequent trade winds and still-solid north swells, the best mix for the wave.

around.d: A lush valley in the West Maui mountains, dominated by the spire of the Iao Needle.
A legendary giant wave, visible from the cliffs on days of very big winter swell.
A tropical garden on the Road to Hana, with native plants and taro patches.
A former missionary house in Wailuku that tells the history and culture of Maui.
A wetland for watching Hawaiian stilts and coots, both endangered species.

pozo.vibe: A small fishing hamlet on an arid pebble coast, Pozo has seen generations of Canarian windsurfers grow up, including women world champions. Between sessions, everyone gathers facing the waves.
food: Papas arrugadas with mojo
Small potatoes boiled in salted water, served with red and green mojo sauces.
pozo.respect: Leave the wave zone to experts and locals, take care launching over the pebbles and never get in the way of a rider heading back out.
pozo.season: June to August: trade winds of rare strength, often over 30 knots, and perfect waves for jumping.

around.d: A nature reserve of golden dunes between palm grove, lagoon and ocean.
A green gorge with cave houses and restaurants carved into the rock.
An old town of colourful lanes around its church and shady squares.
A sacred cave of the ancient Canarians, pierced by four openings facing the plain.
A volcanic crater with a trail and viewpoint, looking over the east of the island.

gardalake.vibe: A former fishing village that long remained Austrian, where Goethe stopped on his way to Italy, Torbole lives to the rhythm of sails, among olive trees, mountain forts and Arco’s climbing cliffs.
food: Carne salada
Beef cured with salt and herbs, served in thin slices or grilled with beans.
gardalake.respect: Always give way to ferries and scheduled boats, stay out of marked swimming areas and rig your gear in the centres’ dedicated areas.
gardalake.season: May to September: the Pelèr and Ora blow almost every day, driven by the temperature difference between lake and mountains.

around.d: A range overlooking the east shore, rich in alpine flowers, reached by cable car from Malcesine.
A town of cobbled lanes at the foot of its Scaliger castle, perched on a rock above the lake.
Ruins perched above the olive groves, with views over the Sarca valley and the lake.
A waterfall roaring at the bottom of a narrow, damp gorge above Riva.
A small turquoise lake amid the forests, ideal for a cool swim.

hoodriver.vibe: Among pear and apple orchards and craft breweries, the small town has reinvented itself around windsurfers. On the riverbanks, Native American fishermen still catch salmon from their wooden platforms.
hoodriver.respect: Respect the platforms and nets of Native American fishermen, whose fishing rights are guaranteed by treaty, and stay well away from the river’s barges and tugs.
hoodriver.season: June to August: the west wind funnels into the gorge almost every afternoon, drawn in by the heat of the interior.

around.d: A canyon of basalt cliffs and waterfalls, to explore along the historic highway and its trails.
A steep hike to meadows full of flowers in spring, with a plunging view of the river.
A former railway turned trail along a wild river, on foot or by bike.
A large collection of vintage planes and cars, many of them still in working order.

annecy.vibe: Above the lake, paragliders take off from the Col de la Forclaz. On the water, professional fishermen still haul in féra and Arctic char, in a lake that local residents cleaned up decades ago.
food: Lake féra
A white fish from the lake, served as fillets meunière in the waterside restaurants.
annecy.respect: Give way to the lake company’s boats, avoid the protected reed beds along the shore and don’t go near private jetties.
annecy.season: June to September: pleasant water in high summer and a glassy lake in the morning, before the breeze picks up in the afternoon.

around.d: A former prison shaped like a ship’s prow in the middle of the Thiou canal, emblem of the old town.
The castle of the Counts of Geneva overlooking the old town, with a museum on Alpine lakes.
A wooded mountain above the lake, whose summit offers a panorama as far as Mont Blanc.
A village on the east shore beside a sheltered bay, around its former abbey.
A limestone massif of mountain pastures and forests, criss-crossed by trails and tome cheese farms.

verdon.vibe: The lake swallowed the old village of Les Salles-sur-Verdon, rebuilt higher up the shore. Around it, the lavender fields of the plateau and the faience workshops of Moustiers tell the story of Haute-Provence.
food: Banon
A goat’s cheese matured in chestnut leaves tied with raffia.
verdon.respect: Wild camping, bivouacking and fires are forbidden around the lake; in the gorges, don’t land on the fragile banks and let boats heading back down pass.
verdon.season: May to June and September: the water is already mild and the gorges far less crowded than in July and August, when pedalos jam the entrance.

around.d: A village clinging to the cliff, with its suspended star and faience workshops.
A vast plateau of lavender and wheat, in flower from late June to mid-July.

around.n: Museum of Prehistory of the Verdon Gorges
around.d: A museum on the human presence in the gorges since prehistory, with a reconstructed village.
A hilltop village above the lake, the starting point of the Corniche Sublime.
A hilltop village of stone lanes, with open views over Provence.

glenan.vibe: You come here under sail or by launch from the Cornouaille coast. The Glénan sailing school has trained sailors here since the post-war years, and Saint-Nicolas protects a narcissus that grows nowhere else.
hello: “hello” in Breton, to call out on the quay
food: Buckwheat galettes and cider
A galette complète browned in butter, washed down with a farmhouse cider from the Fouesnant area.
glenan.respect: On Saint-Nicolas, stay on the marked paths of the reserve that protects the Glénan narcissus, don’t trample the dunes and take your rubbish back to the mainland.
glenan.season: June to September: the clearest, mildest water of the year; aim for a day without strong wind and with a small tidal coefficient.

around.d: A walled town on an islet in the heart of the harbour, with ramparts to walk and lively lanes.
Dune grasslands where the endemic Glénan narcissus blooms in spring.
A museum of Breton fishing in the walled town, with a trawler to visit at the quay.
A former military fort covering almost all of Cigogne island, base of the sailing school.
A protected wetland behind the dune barrier, rich in birds, with a trail.

capri.vibe: Far from the chic Piazzetta, Capri keeps its mule tracks, lemon trees and the fishermen of Marina Grande. Made-to-measure sandals and limoncello are still produced here, facing the Faraglioni.
food: Ravioli capresi
Ravioli filled with caciotta and marjoram, topped with a basil tomato sauce.
capri.respect: Don’t swim in the Blue Grotto, where swimming is forbidden, and in a kayak keep your distance from the boats and shuttles crowding in.
capri.season: May to June and September: calm, warm seas, with fewer boats around the island than in high summer.

around.d: A sea cave lit up in intense blue, entered lying down in a rowing boat.
Ruins of Emperor Tiberius’s palace, perched atop a cliff.
Terraced gardens with views of the Faraglioni and the hairpin bends of Via Krupp.
The island’s highest point, reached by chairlift from Anacapri, with views over the whole gulf.
A natural rock arch above the sea, at the end of a path through the pine woods.

palombaggia.vibe: Between twisted umbrella pines and reddish granite rocks, facing the Cerbicale islets, the beach lives to the rhythm of its beach shacks in summer, while the hinterland keeps its stone villages and Torrean sites.
hello: “hello” in Corsican, always appreciated at the village bar
food: Corsican charcuterie and brocciu
Figatellu, lonzu and fresh ewe’s milk cheese, to taste at an inn in the hinterland.
palombaggia.respect: Stay on the marked paths to spare the dune and, on a paddleboard or boat, never drop anchor in the Posidonia meadows.
palombaggia.season: June and September: water already warm or still mild, often calm seas and a beach far less crowded than in August.

around.d: A protected granite archipelago, coves of crystal-clear water and snorkelling among groupers.
A hilltop Genoese old town, ramparts and lively lanes above the former salt pans.
Wild islets facing the beach, a refuge for seabirds, to paddle along by kayak.
A Bronze Age fortress clinging to the mountain, with a view over the whole gulf.
A prehistoric Torrean site amid the maquis, among granite boulders.

praia_marinha.vibe: The Algarve’s golden limestone has been sculpted here into arches, caves and stacks; small colourful boats run along these cliffs to the sea caves, overlooked by a dizzying coastal path.
food: Seafood cataplana
Clams, prawns and fish simmered in a copper pot, an Algarve speciality.
praia_marinha.respect: Go down by the built staircase and never settle at the foot of the cliffs: the limestone crumbles. On the path, stay well back from the edges.
praia_marinha.season: June to September: often glassy seas in the morning and the mildest water; aim for June or September to avoid the crowds.

around.d: A red sandstone Moorish fortress overlooking the former capital of the Algarve.
A fishing village of white houses, a lively harbour and grilled sardines.

around.n: Fort of Nossa Senhora da Rocha
around.d: A white chapel perched on a headland, with a plunging view over the coves.
A white village nestled in a cove, with a walk over the sculpted rocks of Algar Seco.
A fortified old town and the spectacular cliffs of Ponta da Piedade.

navagio.vibe: On Zakynthos’s west coast, limestone cliffs drop sheer into water of an almost unreal blue; in the neighbouring villages, monasteries, olive groves and honey stalls tell of an island more rural than its beaches.
navagio.respect: The limestone cliffs are becoming fragile: stay behind the viewpoint barriers and follow the boatmen’s instructions about access to the cove.
navagio.season: May to June and September: often calm, clear seas on the west coast, with fewer boats than in high summer.

around.d: A small northern harbour from which boats leave for the Blue Caves of Cape Skinari.
A mountain village and its fortified monastery, surrounded by olive trees.
A mountain village in the north-west, with stalls of honey, olive oil and embroidery.
The island’s highest point, with views over the Ionian Sea and the mountain villages.

anse_source.vibe: On La Digue, people get around mostly by bike, among Creole houses, former copra and vanilla plantations and granite boulders polished by the rain; the pace remains that of an island village.
anse_source.respect: Access is through L’Union Estate, with an entry ticket. In the lagoon, use mineral sunscreen and never put your feet on the coral.
anse_source.season: April–May and October to November: between the two monsoons, light winds, calm seas and good visibility; swim preferably at high tide.

around.d: A UNESCO-listed primeval palm forest, realm of the coco de mer and the black parrot.
A former coconut and vanilla plantation, with a plantation house and giant tortoises.
Granite islets in a marine park, among the best snorkelling in the archipelago.
A wild white-sand cove on Praslin, fringed with tropical vegetation.
A special reserve for seabirds, where hawksbill turtles also nest.

whitehaven.vibe: In the heart of the Great Barrier Reef, the Whitsundays are best experienced by boat: yachts, kayaks and catamarans link forest-covered islands, the traditional territory of the Ngaro, a seafaring people who paddled bark canoes.
food: Grilled barramundi
Tropical Queensland’s signature fish, served grilled or as fish and chips.
whitehaven.respect: From November to May, wear a stinger suit against box jellyfish. National park: no fires, and you take all your rubbish home.
whitehaven.season: June to October: dry season, clear skies, moderate trade winds and a much lower jellyfish risk than in the southern summer.

around.d: The Hill Inlet lookout over swirling sandbanks, plus forests and trails.
A white-sand beach facing Whitehaven, with snorkelling on the nearby coral.
A national park island criss-crossed by trails leading to lookouts over the archipelago.
Wild islands of bush-covered hills and secluded bays, with waymarked walks.

wissant.vibe: Between the two capes, Wissant keeps its flobarts, fishing boats hauled up on the sand, and its Belle Époque villas; on a clear day, the English cliffs come into view opposite, and people sail here in all weathers.
food: Boulogne herring
Smoked or marinated, served warm with potatoes in oil, king of the Opal Coast ports.
wissant.respect: Leave space for swimmers and beached flobarts, respect the marked kite zones in summer and don’t walk on the protected dunes.
wissant.season: September to April: low-pressure systems bring strong, steady westerly winds; in summer, the breezes often stay lighter.

around.d: Chalk cliffs overlooking the strait, with views of the English coast on a clear day.
The closest point to England, with coastal paths and migrating birds.
A walled old town with a belfry and France’s leading fishing port.
A Second World War underground base turned museum, with tunnels to explore.
A fishing village of low houses, flobarts and crabs from the local catch.

letouquet.vibe: A resort born in pine woods planted on the dunes, Le Touquet mixes Anglo-Norman villas, forest and a vast foreshore where sand yachts and kites glide; in winter, the Enduropale sets the beach roaring.
food: Welsh
Cheddar melted with beer over bread and ham, an English legacy on northern French tables.
letouquet.respect: Kiting is allowed in the marked zones, away from lifeguard posts in summer; give way to sand yachts and spare the Canche bay.
letouquet.season: April to October: steady thermal breezes over a huge foreshore at low tide, perfect for progressing in shallow water.

around.d: A hilltop walled town with a citadel and cobbled lanes dear to Victor Hugo.
A wild estuary of dunes and salt meadows, rich in birds and sometimes seals.
A fishing port on the Canche, with a fish auction and quays that inspired a colony of painters.
A brick lighthouse open to visitors, with views over the Canche bay and the forest.
A museum of archaeology and local history, centred on the ancient port of Quentovic.

hardelot.vibe: A resort founded in the early 20th century by an English entrepreneur near Hardelot Castle, it mixes villas among the pines, the dunes of Mont Saint-Frieux and a long beach where kites, sand yachts and shrimp fishers cross paths.
food: Moules-frites
Moules marinières and home-made chips, the great classic of the Opal Coast beach shacks.
hardelot.respect: The dunes of Mont Saint-Frieux are protected: stay on the marked paths, and kite in the designated zones, away from swimmers.
hardelot.season: September to May: strong westerly winds carried by low-pressure systems; at low tide, the beach offers a huge stretch of water.

around.d: A large aquarium devoted to the oceans, with sharks, rays and sea lions.
A fortified old town, belfry and quays of France’s leading fishing port.
A fortified castle turned Entente Cordiale cultural centre, with an Elizabethan theatre.
A wooded dune among the highest on the coast, with trails and views over the Channel.
A dome dominating the upper town and a vast crypt with murals.

wimereux.vibe: Colourful Belle Époque villas lined up along the sea wall: it was from here that Marconi made the first radio link across the Channel in 1899, and people still gather shrimps and mussels on the rocks at low tide.
food: Welsh
Cheddar melted with beer over bread and ham, an English legacy on Opal Coast tables.
wimereux.respect: In summer, the lifeguarded beach is reserved for swimmers: launch your kite outside it. When foraging on the shore, respect minimum sizes and put rocks back in place.
wimereux.season: Autumn to spring: low-pressure systems bring strong, steady westerly winds; in summer, sessions mostly happen in the afternoon.

around.d: A large aquarium devoted to the oceans, with sharks, rays and sea lions.
A walled old town, belfry and quays of France’s leading fishing port.
A headland facing England, with coastal paths and migrating birds passing through.
A medieval fortified castle housing collections of archaeology and world art.
A coastal village with its Vauban fort set on the beach and the Slack estuary.

berck.vibe: A town of seaside hospitals since the 19th century, where children were treated in the fresh air, Berck lives facing the wind: in spring, its kite festivals fill the sky above the immense beach.
food: Caudière berckoise
A soup of fish, mussels and potatoes, handed down from fishing families.
berck.respect: Watch the seals of the Authie bay from afar, never approaching the sandbanks where they rest, and sail well away from swimmers.
berck.season: September to April: strong westerly winds and a huge stretch of water at low tide; in spring, the wind stays reliable and milder.

around.d: A vast bay of sand and salt meadows, with seals, birds and the harbours of Saint-Valery and Le Crotoy.
A wild estuary lined with dunes, where harbour seals rest.
A hilltop walled town with a citadel and cobbled lanes dear to Victor Hugo.
A Cistercian abbey with remarkable woodwork and wrought-iron gates.
A botanical garden of old roses and rare plants, at the foot of the abbey.

malolesbains.vibe: A sea wall lined with Belle Époque villas, sand from which the soldiers of 1940 embarked: Malo lives above all to the rhythm of the Dunkirk carnival, when costumed bands sing and herrings fly from the town hall balcony.
food: Potjevleesch
A Flemish terrine of white meats in jelly, served cold with chips.
malolesbains.respect: At carnival, dress up and follow the band without shoving; on the beach, launch your kite outside the lifeguarded swimming zones.
malolesbains.season: September to April: frequent west to north-west gales and an immense beach at low tide; in summer, the wind is scarcer.

around.d: A small fortified Flemish town with ramparts, canals and a belfry.
The history of the port, with models and boats afloat along the quays.
A large sail training ship moored in the harbour, to visit from deck to hold.
A contemporary art museum in a sculpture garden, facing the sea.
A 19th-century fort tucked in the dunes, with a trail on the 1940 battle.

lehavre.vibe: A city rebuilt in concrete by Auguste Perret and listed by UNESCO, Le Havre watches container ships go by from its pebble beach lined with white huts, where Monet painted dawn over the harbour.
food: Moules à la normande
Cooked in cider and topped with crème fraîche, the classic of seafront bistros.
lehavre.respect: Launch your kite outside the lifeguarded swimming zones and keep well away from the breakwaters and the harbour channel, reserved for ships.
lehavre.season: September to April: strong south-west to west winds with the low-pressure systems, sometimes with a small surfable swell.

around.d: A glass museum facing the sea, with a rich Impressionist collection around Boudin and Monet.
Perret’s concrete lantern tower, its interior bathed in coloured stained glass.
A former fort turned into gardens and greenhouses, with views over the city and the estuary.
A fishing port and seaside resort, with a fish market and grand villas.
Reed beds and mudflats of the estuary, a major stopover for migrating birds.

etretat.vibe: Courbet and Monet painted these chalk arches, Maurice Leblanc hid Arsène Lupin’s treasure here in the Hollow Needle, and on the shingle, old boats turned upside down as caloges recall the fishing past.
food: Teurgoule
Cinnamon rice pudding baked slowly in the oven, Normandy’s signature dessert.
etretat.respect: Don’t pick up pebbles, it’s forbidden, and check the tide times before passing the arches: it’s easy to get trapped at the foot of the cliffs.
etretat.season: June to September: calmer seas more often, less cold water and beautiful evening light on the cliffs; head out when the wind is light.

around.d: A huge Gothic abbey church, a major pilgrimage site of the Precious Blood.
Maurice Leblanc’s house, with a playful trail in the footsteps of the gentleman burglar.
A fishing village nestled between two cliffs, with a pebble beach and villas.
A museum on cod fishing and the history of the port, with a lookout over the town.
A contemporary garden of topiaries and sculptures, perched on the Amont cliff.

dieppe.vibe: A pioneer of sea bathing in France, Dieppe is still a real fishing port, a major name in scallops; its pebble beach also holds the memory of the 1942 Canadian raid.
food: Marmite dieppoise
Fish, mussels and scallops simmered in a cream sauce, the pride of the harbour’s tables.
dieppe.respect: Give way to swimmers in the lifeguarded zone and, in a kayak, keep away from the harbour entrance and the foot of the crumbling cliffs.
dieppe.season: July and August: the least cold water of the year and lifeguarded swimming; choose a calm-sea day with no offshore wind.

around.d: A fortified castle overlooking the beach, famous for its collection of carved ivories.
A clifftop village with a sailors’ church and the cemetery where Georges Braque lies.
An English-style park and gardens, with rhododendrons and sea views.
The imposing ruins of a medieval fortified castle on a spur above the valley.
A lighthouse on the Pointe d’Ailly, with a panorama of the Alabaster Coast cliffs.

siouville.vibe: At the tip of the Cotentin, La Hague lines up moorland, dry-stone walls and granite hamlets; at Siouville, Norman surfers take on cool water and a swell rolling straight in from the Atlantic.
food: Cotentin spider crab
Caught in pots along the Channel coast, served simply with mayonnaise.
siouville.respect: The line-up is small and loyal: wait your turn at the peak and say hello to the regulars. Park in the designated car parks, never on the dunes.
siouville.season: September to November: consistent Atlantic swells, water that still holds some of the summer warmth and deserted beaches.

around.d: A freshwater pond behind the dunes, a refuge for waterbirds with observation trails.
A rocky headland and customs officers’ path, with views of the Channel Islands.
A family resort with its harbour, its havre and its big dunes.
A Renaissance castle in the heart of a landscaped park with greenhouses and a pond.
Cherbourg’s fine arts museum, rich in works by Jean-François Millet.

vauville.vibe: A great wild bay lined with dunes and a bird pond, beneath the moors of La Hague: you mostly meet walkers, shore foragers and board riders who come for wind and swell facing the Nez de Jobourg.
vauville.respect: The bay’s dunes and the Mare de Vauville are protected: stay on the marked paths and don’t park your van on the dune verges.
vauville.season: October to March: big westerly swells and strong winds, for experienced surfers and kiters only; autumn often offers the best compromise.

around.d: A freshwater pond behind the dunes, a refuge for waterbirds with observation trails.
An ocean museum in the former transatlantic terminal, with a nuclear submarine to visit.
One of the most powerful tidal currents in Europe, to watch from Cap de la Hague.
A Renaissance castle in the heart of a landscaped park with greenhouses and a pond.

hauteville.vibe: On the Côte des Havres, the sea goes out a very long way, revealing oyster beds and mussel posts; the wind sends sand yachts and kites gliding between dunes and small havres where the rivers flow out.
food: Oysters and bouchot mussels
Farmed on the foreshore of the Cotentin’s west coast, to enjoy facing the sea.
hauteville.respect: At low tide, never cross the oyster beds and mussel posts on a sand yacht or kite, and watch out for the incoming tide, which is very fast here.
hauteville.season: March to June and September to November: steady westerly winds and spring tides that uncover a huge foreshore.

around.d: A granite archipelago whose landscapes change with the tide, with seals and seabirds.
A privateers’ town perched on its rock, with a fortified upper town and fishing port.
The romantic ruins of a Benedictine abbey in a wooded valley.
The ruins of a fortified castle on the edge of the Sienne havre.
Former lime kilns and a maritime museum on the history of the havre.

granville.vibe: A privateers’ town perched on its rock, Granville fitted out Newfoundland cod boats, saw Christian Dior grow up and holds its carnival every winter; at the foot of the upper town, the sea goes out as far as the eye can see.
food: Granville Bay whelks
Served warm with mayonnaise, the pride of Normandy’s great shellfish port.
granville.respect: The tide comes in very fast here: check the tide times before setting off by kayak or on foot, and beware of the currents around the Pointe du Roc.
granville.season: June to September: kinder seas and long days for reaching Chausey, timing your outing with the tides.

around.d: A rock crowned by its abbey, in the middle of a bay with immense tides.
A granite archipelago whose landscapes change with the tide, with seals and seabirds.
The couturier’s childhood villa and its clifftop garden, with fashion exhibitions.
Ramparts and granite lanes of the old town, with views over the bay.
A restored Premonstratensian abbey, nestled in a peaceful valley of the bocage.

saintmalo.vibe: Granite ramparts, memories of the privateers and of Jacques Cartier: facing the Sillon and its oak breakwaters, Saint-Malo lives by the sea, from where the Route du Rhum yachts set off every four years.
food: Cancale oysters
Rock or flat, enjoyed at the port of La Houle facing the oyster beds.
saintmalo.respect: Watch the tide if you walk to the Grand Bé: the causeway is quickly submerged. At high spring tides, waves break over the Sillon sea wall.
saintmalo.season: July and August: the mildest water of the year and long evenings; at low tide the sea goes out a long way, so aim for high tide.

around.d: An islet reachable at low tide, with Chateaubriand’s tomb facing the open sea.
The oyster port of La Houle, with oyster beds and tastings on the quays.
A wild headland on the Emerald Coast, with views over the bay of Mont-Saint-Michel.
A walled medieval town with half-timbered houses and a port on the Rance.
A fortified castle standing on a rocky spur, facing Cap Fréhel.

saintlunaire.vibe: A resort born in the Belle Époque around villas perched on rocky points, Saint-Lunaire gazes over the bay of Saint-Malo from the Pointe du Décollé; at Longchamp, the schools introduce you to surfing on the Emerald Coast.
food: Buckwheat crêpes and galettes
A complète with egg, ham and cheese, washed down with a bowl of cider at the village crêperie.
saintlunaire.respect: At Longchamp, priority goes to the surfer closest to the peak: keep clear of surf lessons and never let go of your board among beginners.
saintlunaire.season: September to November: more consistent but reasonably sized westerly swells, still-mild water and a beach free of holidaymakers.

around.d: Belle Époque villas, the Clair de Lune promenade and views of the Saint-Malo ramparts.
A fortified castle standing on a rocky spur, facing Cap Fréhel.
Pink sandstone cliffs, heather moorland and seabird colonies.
A medieval wall walk around the old town, with views over the Rance valley.
A village of sailors and painters, with small coves and a sheltered harbour.

erquy.vibe: Pink sandstone once cut into paving stones, heather and gorse moorland on the cape: Erquy also lives off its scallop fishing fleet, which makes its harbour one of the major ones in the bay of Saint-Brieuc.
food: Erquy scallops
Fished in winter in the bay of Saint-Brieuc, simply pan-fried in salted butter.
erquy.respect: On the cape, stay on the marked paths: the heather moorland is fragile and protected. In a kayak, keep your distance from the cliff birds.
erquy.season: June to September: calmer seas more often, clear water and long days for exploring the cape’s coves.

around.d: Pink sandstone cliffs, heather moorland and seabird colonies.
A fortified castle standing on a rocky spur, facing the sea.
An islet topped by a chapel, reached on foot along a shingle bar at low tide.
A small fishing and pleasure harbour tucked at the end of a ria.
A fortified castle remodelled in the Renaissance, surrounded by moats and gardens.

perros.vibe: Pink granite rocks shaped into strange silhouettes, chapels and pardons of the Trégor: at Perros, you read the sea from the customs officers’ path, facing the Sept-Îles where gannets and puffins nest.
hello: “hello” in Breton, always well received at the Trégor market
food: Buckwheat crêpes and galettes
A galette complète and a salted-butter crêpe, with a bowl of Breton cider.
perros.respect: In the Sept-Îles, landing is only allowed on Île aux Moines: watch the birds from a distance. On the path, don’t climb on the protected rocks.
perros.season: July to early September: the least cold water of the year, long days and warm light on the pink granite.

around.d: A protected archipelago with colonies of gannets, puffins and grey seals.
A peninsula of jumbled pink granite, for a walk among sculpted rocks.
A Gothic cathedral and its cloister, in the heart of a small town full of character.
The imposing ruins of a medieval fortified castle above the Léguer valley.
A huge telecommunications dome turned museum, on the history of satellite links.

imsouane.vibe: A fishing village where the blue boats come back into harbour among the surfers, Imsouane lives to the rhythm of the fish auction and the tide; you eat the catch of the day grilled facing the bay.
food: Grilled fish from the harbour
Picked as the boats come in and grilled on the spot, with tomato salad and bread.
imsouane.respect: The fishing boats pass close to the peak: always give them priority, and cover up as soon as you leave the beach to walk through the village.
imsouane.season: October to March: north-west winter swells wrap into the bay and peel off long, consistent rights.

safi.vibe: A town of potters and a major sardine port, Safi keeps its sea fortress from the Portuguese occupation; its right-hander, surfed by a handful of experts on big-swell days, remains a wave apart.
food: Safi sardines
Grilled or as meatballs in tomato sauce, in one of the sardine capitals.
safi.respect: An expert wave over a shallow rock slab: if you’re not at that level, watch from the shore. When it’s working, give priority to the locals.
safi.season: November to February: only big north-west winter swells, with a favourable wind, make the wave work.

around.d: A fortress overlooking the medina and housing the national ceramics museum.
A 16th-century Portuguese sea castle, standing face to the ocean.
Medina, fishing port and the potters’ hill with its kilns and glazed ceramics.

sidikaouki.vibe: A hamlet of low houses set in Haha country, where the little white marabout that gave the place its name watches over the beach; between sessions, dromedaries and horses amble along the sand and argan trees cover the hills.
food: Amlou and argan oil
Almond paste, argan oil and honey, spread on warm bread at breakfast.
sidikaouki.respect: The marabout of Sidi Kaouki is still a place of pilgrimage: admire it from outside. In the water, leave plenty of room between kites, windsurfers and surfers.
sidikaouki.season: October to March: steady Atlantic winter swells and lighter trade winds, which often leave clean mornings.

around.d: UNESCO-listed walled town, ramparts facing the ocean, souks and thuya-wood workshops.
Cannon-lined bastion above the fishing harbour and its blue boats.
Bird reserve off Essaouira, a refuge for Eleonora’s falcon, best watched from the shore.
House of memory devoted to Essaouira’s Jewish past, in the heart of the mellah.
Ruined watchtower half buried in sand, near the mouth of the Oued Ksob.

ngor.vibe: The Lebou village of Ngor lives from fishing: painted pirogues pulled up on the sand, nets hauled in at the end of the day, and a pirogue shuttle to the island where Senegalese surfing found one of its founding waves.
ngor.respect: The crossing is run by the village boatmen: pay for your seat before you board. At the peak, the wave is short and prized by locals: wait your turn.
ngor.season: November to April: well-angled North Atlantic winter swells and a northerly trade wind often favourable on the point.

around.d: Car-free lanes, colourful houses and little coves a stone’s throw from the coast.

around.n: Îles de la Madeleine National Park
around.d: Wild volcanic islets teeming with seabirds, reached by pirogue.
Giant bronze statue on one of the Mamelles hills, with views over the whole peninsula.
Lighthouse perched on a volcanic mound, with a panorama over Dakar and the ocean.
Westernmost tip of the African continent, swell-battered rocks and sunsets.

ouakam.vibe: Tucked into the corniche, the old Lebou village of Ouakam keeps its pirogues and sandy lanes, overlooked by the white minarets of the Mosque of the Divinity, which seem to rise out of the waves.
ouakam.respect: The area around the mosque is a place of prayer: cover your shoulders and legs as you walk through. In the water, the left is held by experienced locals: keep a low profile.
ouakam.season: November to April: steady North Atlantic winter swells, dry skies and cooler water.

around.d: UNESCO-listed island, colonial houses, flower-filled lanes and the House of Slaves.
Monumental bronze statue towering over Ouakam, with views over the whole Cap-Vert peninsula.
Lighthouse on top of a volcanic mound, with a panorama over the ocean and the city.

around.n: Îles de la Madeleine National Park
around.d: Protected volcanic islets, seabird colonies and clear water.
Small car-free island, sheltered beaches and colourful houses facing the village.

elandsbay.vibe: A West Coast hamlet between the icy ocean and the Verlorenvlei lagoon, rich in birdlife; crayfishing sets the rhythm of local life, and rock paintings adorn the nearby caves.
food: West Coast crayfish
The local “kreef”, grilled on the braai with garlic butter, star of West Coast tables.
elandsbay.respect: The paintings in Elands Bay Cave are fragile: do not touch them. At the point, the line-up is small and close-knit: greet the locals and wait your turn.
elandsbay.season: May to September: big South Atlantic winter swells that make the point peel; bring a thick wetsuit.

around.d: Prehistoric shelter decorated with rock paintings, with a view over the bay.
Protected wetland where flamingos, pelicans and herons feed among the reeds.
Cape gannet colony watched up close from a hide, at the end of the harbour.
West Coast fishing harbour, crayfish and open-air seafood restaurants.

muizenberg.vibe: A Victorian seaside resort on False Bay, with its brightly painted beach huts and its promenade; this is where South African surfing was born and where the Shark Spotters programme was launched.
food: Kalk Bay fish and chips
Fried snoek or hake at the neighbouring fishing harbour of Kalk Bay, eaten facing the boats.
muizenberg.respect: At Surfer’s Corner, the surf schools take over the whitewater: steer clear of beginner groups and always keep hold of your board near swimmers.
muizenberg.season: March to May: the south-easter eases, moderate swell and False Bay water still mild for learning.

around.d: Cove among granite boulders, with an African penguin colony to watch from the boardwalks.
Mountains, fynbos and cliffs all the way to the Cape of Good Hope and Cape Point.
Road carved into the cliff and a summit trail, with a plunging view over Hout Bay.
Lagoon and reed beds behind the beach, waterbirds and kayak outings.
Surf village on the Atlantic coast, Slangkop Lighthouse and Long Beach.

dahab.vibe: A former Bedouin fishing village turned freediving capital, Dahab faces the Sinai mountains; at the Blue Hole, plaques fixed to the rock remember the divers the sea has kept.
food: Bedouin herbal tea
Brewed over embers with desert herbs and served very sweet under Sinai tents.
dahab.respect: Never attempt the Arch without technical training. Enter the water through the marked entry points to spare the reef flat, and leave the memorial plaques untouched.
dahab.season: October to November: water still very warm, excellent visibility and the summer heat has eased.

around.d: Granite rocks painted blue by a Belgian artist in the middle of the Sinai desert.
Seafront promenade, Bedouin cafés, kitesurfing lagoon and starting point for Sinai treks.

nosybe.vibe: Off Nosy Be, the perfume island lined with ylang-ylang fields, Sakalava fishermen in outrigger canoes cross paths with dive boats heading for the little lighthouse on Tanikely.
food: Fish in coconut
Fresh fish simmered in coconut milk, a classic of Nosy Be’s street eateries.
nosybe.respect: Tanikely is a marine protected area: do not touch the turtles or the coral, do not feed the fish and do not take any shells home.
nosybe.season: September to December: calm sea, clear warm water, and whale sharks often spotted off Nosy Be.

around.d: Volcanic island of lemurs, a village of embroiderers and forest trails.
Large island with ylang-ylang distilleries, crater lakes and the Hell-Ville market.

watamu.vibe: A small town on the Swahili coast where dhows sail past coral coves; volunteers watch over the turtle nests here, and the remains of the city of Gedi recall the ancient trade of the Indian Ocean.
watamu.respect: On the beach, do not disturb the marked turtle nests and avoid torches and fires at night; in the marine park, do not pick up shells or coral.
watamu.season: December to March: gentler north-east monsoon, calm sea and clear water in the lagoon.

around.d: Protected lagoon with coral heads, reef fish and turtles, by glass-bottom boat.
Medieval Swahili city swallowed by the forest, coral mosques and palaces.

keramas.vibe: On Gianyar’s black-sand coast, the rice fields run almost down to the wave; Hindu processions come to purify their effigies in the sea, and the nearby villages keep painting, dance and carving alive.
hello: Balinese Hindu greeting, hands joined in front of the chest
food: Babi guling
Spit-roasted suckling pig stuffed with spices, the pride of Gianyar’s warungs.
keramas.respect: Make way for ceremonies coming down to the sea and do not step over offerings placed on the sand. At the narrow peak, wait your turn.
keramas.season: October to March: the west monsoon blows offshore on the east coast and southern swells keep the right hollow.

around.d: Royal hall of justice with ceilings painted in the Kamasan style, surrounded by a moat.
Holy water temple where Balinese purify themselves under the spouts of spring-fed pools.
Traditional village with gateways lined up along a paved street, and a bamboo grove.
Temple built in front of a cave home to thousands of bats, facing the sea.
Village renowned for its meticulous school of painting and its ancient temple.

nias.vibe: In southern Nias, hilltop stone villages keep their great houses on stilts and the tradition of stone jumping; below, Lagundri Bay, reshaped by the 2005 earthquake, lives to the rhythm of the surfers’ losmen.
hello: greeting and blessing in the Nias language, offered to everyone
nias.respect: In the traditional villages, introduce yourself to the elders and leave a contribution. At low tide the reef flat is exposed: do not walk on the reef.
nias.season: April to October: drier season and long southern Indian Ocean swells that keep the right holding.

gland.vibe: At the end of the Blambangan peninsula, the Alas Purwo forest, sacred to Javanese Hindus and home to monkeys and peacocks, stops dead at the reef: here, you live in a surf camp cut off from the world.
food: Banyuwangi rujak soto
Vegetable salad in peanut sauce drowned in a broth, a speciality of East Java.
gland.respect: Alas Purwo is a national park: do not feed the macaques, take all your rubbish away with you and stay inside the camp grounds at night.
gland.season: May to September: dry season, offshore south-east trade winds and long southern swells that keep the left holding.

komodo.vibe: Bare hills where monitor lizards prowl plunge into waters churned by currents; in the stilt villages, Bajo fishermen have lived from the sea for generations.
komodo.respect: On the islands, never walk without a ranger because of the dragons. Underwater, the currents are fierce: follow your guide and only hold on to bare rock.
komodo.season: April to June and September to November: calmer sea, good visibility and fewer boats than in high summer.

around.d: Ranger-led hike to meet Komodo dragons in the savannah and forest.
Padar and Rinca islands, viewpoints over the bays and pink-sand beaches.
Fishing village on stilts, colourful boats and everyday life by the water.

bunaken.vibe: Facing the cone of the Manado Tua volcano, Bunaken’s fishing villages live among coconut palms, mangroves and little churches; here, the Minahasa and Christian culture of North Sulawesi blends with that of the Bajo seafarers.
food: Tinutuan (bubur Manado)
Rice porridge with vegetables, corn and pumpkin, Manado’s signature breakfast.
bunaken.respect: Bunaken is a fee-paying marine park: keep your entry tag, do not touch the wall and never walk on the reef flat at low tide.
bunaken.season: April to November: calmer sea outside the north-west monsoon and often excellent visibility along the walls.

around.d: Capital of North Sulawesi, lively waterfront and fiery Minahasa cuisine.
Chinese temple with red and gold roofs, among the oldest in eastern Indonesia.

similan.vibe: Nine uninhabited granite islands off the Phang Nga coast, visited only by rangers, divers and boats from Khao Lak; giant boulders form arches and swim-throughs underwater.
food: Kaeng som
Sour, very spicy fish and tamarind curry, typical of southern Thailand.
similan.respect: The park limits visitor numbers: do not touch the coral or the sea fans, do not feed the fish and keep well away from moored boats.
similan.season: December to April: north-east monsoon, glassy sea and peak visibility while the park is open.

weligama.vibe: In the bay, fishermen’s outrigger canoes sit alongside rental boards; the little islet of Taprobane and its villa watch over the beach, and stilt fishermen still perch along the nearby coast.
food: Ambul thiyal
Sour tuna curry with goraka, cooked almost dry, a speciality of the south coast.
weligama.respect: Surf schools and fishermen share the bay: keep clear of the canoes and fishing lines, and cover up when you leave the beach.
weligama.season: November to April: north-east monsoon, offshore wind on the south coast and small, regular swells for learning.

around.d: UNESCO-listed fortified town, ramparts, colonial lanes and a lighthouse facing the ocean.
Crescent beach under coconut palms and boat trips to watch whales.
Mangrove-fringed lagoon, boat rides to islets and a temple.
Tall white lighthouse at the southern tip of the island, facing the Indian Ocean.
Rocky islet crowned by a villa, to admire from Weligama beach.

ichinomiya.vibe: A small town on the Kujūkuri coast, both surf town and shrine town: boards strapped to bikes, surf shops along the coast road and worshippers coming to pray at Tamasaki Shrine.
food: Namerō
Raw fish finely chopped by knife with miso, ginger and spring onion, a recipe of the Bōsō fishermen.
ichinomiya.respect: Park only in the paid beach car parks, do not get changed in the street and respect the lifeguarded swimming zones in summer.
ichinomiya.season: September to November: swells from typhoons and Pacific lows, water still mild and fewer people than in summer.

around.d: Ancient Shinto shrine in the heart of Ichinomiya, black lacquer and great sacred trees.
Kannon hall built on stilts atop a rock, deep in the forest.
Huge sandy beach running north, fishermen and surfers as far as the eye can see.
Cliffs facing the Pacific and a lookout over the long curve of Kujūkuri.
Museum devoted to contemporary Japanese realist painting, with bold architecture.

kerama.vibe: Islands of villages with coral-stone walls and red-tiled roofs, where Ryukyu culture is still alive; locals make their living from fishing, diving and, in winter, the passing humpback whales.
hello: “hello” in Okinawan, which the elders love to hear
food: Okinawa soba
Wheat noodles in a light broth, topped with braised pork, to try in the island’s little restaurants.
kerama.respect: Green turtles graze the seagrass close to shore: keep your distance, do not touch them and never chase them.
kerama.season: May to October: warm, clear water and a sea often calm between typhoons.

around.d: White-sand beaches, lookouts over the archipelago and whale watching in winter.
The largest of the Kerama Islands, Aharen and Tokashiku beaches at the foot of the hills.
Quiet little island home to Kerama deer, with reefs right by the shore.
Village of traditional houses surrounded by stone walls, linked by a bridge.

rincon.vibe: In the north-west corner of Puerto Rico, Rincón has lived to the rhythm of the swell ever since a world surfing championship was held there in the late 1960s; in winter, surfers and humpback whales share the open water.
rincon.respect: Tres Palmas is a marine reserve: do not walk on the elkhorn coral, do not fish, and give locals priority when the wave wakes up.
rincon.season: December to March: only the big North Atlantic winter swells wake up the Tres Palmas right.

around.d: Historic lighthouse above the waves, a whale-watching spot in winter.
Protected uninhabited island offshore, walls and exceptionally clear water for diving.
Surf beach below the former nuclear reactor dome, with a view of the lighthouse.
Sheltered public beach, calm water and sunsets over the Mona Passage.

pavones.vibe: A fishing and surfing village at the end of a long dirt road, south of the Golfo Dulce, where the rainforest runs down to the pebbles and all of life revolves around the swell and the tides.
pavones.respect: The line-up is like the village: small and close-knit. Say hello, wait your turn and do not sit at the peak on big days if you are a beginner.
pavones.season: April to October: green season and South Pacific swells that make the left peel along its full length.

around.d: Long wild beach between mangroves and the Golfo Dulce, calm water and offshore fishing.
Hamlet at the end of the coast road, between forest and reef, popular with surfers.

tamarindo.vibe: A former Guanacaste fishing village turned cosmopolitan surf town, Tamarindo keeps its sabanero culture of cowboys and rodeos inland; right opposite, leatherback turtles come to nest on Playa Grande.
food: Rosquillas and chorreadas
Cheesy corn rings and sweet corn pancakes, traditional treats of Guanacaste.
tamarindo.respect: Crocodiles live in the estuary: do not surf the river mouth at dusk. At night, Playa Grande belongs to the turtles.
tamarindo.season: December to April: dry season, offshore wind in the morning and moderate swell, ideal for learning.

around.d: Leatherback turtle nesting site, guided night visits with the park rangers.
Wild beach across the estuary, with a more powerful beach break.
Mangroves to explore by kayak or boat, birds, iguanas and crocodiles.
Rocky cove to the south, famous reef right and a village feel.
Beach made of crushed shells and turquoise water great for snorkelling.

sayulita.vibe: Dirt streets bright with papel picado, shops selling Huichol art in beads and wool yarn, fishermen’s pangas on the sand: Sayulita blends a Nayarit coastal village with a surfing community.
food: Pescado zarandeado
Whole butterflied fish, marinated in chillies and grilled over a wood fire, the pride of Nayarit.
sayulita.respect: At the right-hand peak, give priority to the local longboarders and stay with the other beginners in the whitewater, on the beach side.
sayulita.season: November to March: gentle, regular north-west swells, mild water and humpback whales in the bay.

todossantos.vibe: Off Ensenada, a fishing port and port of call in Baja California, Todos Santos Island keeps its lighthouse and its cold waters; big-wave hunters head out by boat from the marina.
food: Ensenada fish tacos
Battered, fried fish in a tortilla with cabbage and cream: Ensenada claims to have invented them.
todossantos.respect: Go with a captain who knows the peak, an impact vest and a jet-ski partner; do not land on the island without permission.
todossantos.season: November to March: big North Pacific winter swells that stand up the walls of Killers.

around.d: Lively port, fish market and gateway to the Valle de Guadalupe vineyards.
The oldest cantina in Baja California, sawdust on the floor and an old-time atmosphere.
Twin-towered cathedral in the heart of Ensenada, a venue for religious festivals.

islamujeres.vibe: A fishing island of colourful houses where people get around by golf cart; at its southern tip, the remains of a Maya shrine dedicated to Ixchel overlook the sea, and fish grilled with achiote is still the local pride.
food: Tikin xic
Fish marinated in achiote and bitter orange, grilled in a banana leaf.
islamujeres.respect: With whale sharks, the rules are strict: two swimmers at a time with a guide, no contact and no flash.
islamujeres.season: June to September: whale sharks gather offshore and the Caribbean stays warm and calm.

around.d: Modern archaeology museum on the Maya civilisations, with an open-air site.
Maya ruins in the middle of the hotel zone, roamed by iguanas.
Popular market in downtown Cancún, crafts and small eateries.

tofino.vibe: At the end of the road on Vancouver Island, Tofino lives on Nuu-chah-nulth territory, between forests of giant cedars and sea inlets; surfers share the coast with fishermen, kayakers and grey whale watchers.
tofino.respect: Wolves and bears roam the beaches: leave no food or rubbish on the sand and keep your dog on a lead.
tofino.season: September to November: well-lined-up North Pacific autumn swells, before the winter storms.

around.d: Maze of fjords, islands and old-growth forests, by kayak or water taxi.
Boardwalk trail among giant cedars several centuries old.
Huge beach in Pacific Rim park, between rocks, driftwood and rainforest.
Wild island reached by kayak, deserted beaches and rustic camping.

newsmyrna.vibe: Founded by Minorcan, Greek and Italian settlers who came to clear land in Spanish Florida, New Smyrna keeps its oak-shaded streets; at the inlet, local kids surf the jetty before school.
newsmyrna.respect: On the stretch of beach open to cars, drive at walking pace in the marked lanes. In summer, turn off your lights near loggerhead turtle nests marked with stakes.
newsmyrna.season: September to November: swells from tropical storms offshore, water still warm and a quieter beach after summer.

around.d: Tall red-brick lighthouse turned museum, with a view over the inlet from the top.
Coquina remains of a 19th-century sugar mill, among the palm trees.
Rehabilitation centre for sea turtles and birds, with aquariums on local wildlife.
One of the largest pre-Columbian shell middens in Florida, left by Native Americans.

montauk.vibe: At the tip of Long Island, Montauk remains a sport-fishing port far from the chic of the Hamptons; at Ditch Plains, locals and weekend New Yorkers share the peak, and autumn brings back storms and striped bass.
food: The lobster roll
Lobster in a brioche bun, cold with mayonnaise or hot with butter, served at the clam shacks.
montauk.respect: The Ditch Plains car park is reserved for town permit holders: come by bike or early. At the peak, there are plenty of regulars, so wait your turn.
montauk.season: September to November: swells from hurricanes and autumn storms, water still mild and the summer crowds gone.

around.d: Oldest lighthouse in New York State, perched on the point facing the Atlantic.
Cliffs, wooded trails and a former military base with its huge radar.
Clay cliffs above the ocean and Second World War bunkers.
Pine forest, wild beach and “walking dunes” on Napeague Bay.
