mancora.vibe: A former fishing village turned meeting place for South American surfers, Máncora lives between colourful boats on the sand, lively evenings and small-scale fishing off Los Órganos.
food: Seco de chabelo
Green plantain and dried meat stewed together, a typical dish of the Piura region.
mancora.respect: At El Ñuro, where you swim with green turtles near the fishermen’s pier, do not touch or feed them. At the peak, give locals priority.
mancora.season: November to March: north-west swells that make the left peel, bright sunshine and the warmest water of the year.

huanchaco.vibe: Below its hilltop sanctuary, the bay where the Chimú already fished watches fishermen come home skimming past the old pier; neighbouring Trujillo, cradle of the marinera, dances on the edge of the desert.
food: Shambar
Thick soup of wheat, pulses and smoked meat, served on Mondays in Trujillo and the surrounding area.
huanchaco.respect: Do not climb on the caballitos drying upright on the beach. At Chan Chan, stay on the walkways: the mud-brick friezes are fragile.
huanchaco.season: April to October: the most consistent southern swells on the left; bring a wetsuit, as the water stays cool.

around.d: Vast Chimú adobe city, walls carved with fish and seabirds.
Moche temple with polychrome murals still vivid, excavations ongoing.
Colonial centre with colourful façades and wrought-iron grilles around the Plaza de Armas.
Wetlands where the totora reed used to build the caballitos is grown.
Small, well-restored Chimú temple with friezes of rainbows and creatures.

iquique.vibe: A former saltpetre port, Iquique keeps its wooden houses with verandas along Calle Baquedano; paragliders take off from the dunes above the city, and Chilean bodyboarders have made El Colegio a proving ground.
food: Chumbeque
Layered biscuit filled with honey or fruit, an Iquique treat with Chinese roots.
iquique.respect: El Colegio breaks over a barely submerged reef shelf: only go if you have mastered barrels, wear reef booties and give priority to local bodyboarders.
iquique.season: April to September: the most powerful south-west swells, cool but bearable water under almost always dry skies.

around.d: Wooden houses from the saltpetre era, a theatre and the Calle Baquedano promenade.
White wooden tower, a national monument in the heart of Plaza Arturo Prat.
Ship sunk off the port during the Battle of Iquique, a replica of which has become a museum.

praiadorosa.vibe: A fishing hamlet of Azorean origin discovered by surfers and backpackers, Rosa has kept its pousadas in the hills and its trails to the Ibiraquera lagoon; in winter, the mullet-fishing nets return to the sand.
food: Sequência de camarão
Prawns served in a succession of dishes, fried, with garlic or in pastel, a ritual of the Santa Catarina coast.
praiadorosa.respect: Southern right whales are protected: no drones and no approaching on a paddleboard. During the traditional mullet fishing, respect the zones closed to surfing.
praiadorosa.season: March to June: consistent southern swells, offshore wind in the morning and quiet beaches after the Brazilian summer.

around.d: Former fishing village with a white church, surf beaches and the Siriú dunes.
Former whaling port turned surfers’ haunt, with lookouts for spotting whales.

noronha.vibe: A former prison island bristling with Portuguese forts, Noronha now lives to the rhythm of turtles and dolphins; every visitor pays a preservation fee, and the whole village gathers at sunset at the Boldró fort.
noronha.respect: At the Atalaia natural pool, sunscreen and fins are banned and access is limited; the Bay of Dolphins can only be viewed from the lookout.
noronha.season: September to February: dry season and peak visibility; when the swell hits the Mar de Dentro, dive on the Mar de Fora side.

ilhabela.vibe: Brazil’s sailing capital, the island also hides dozens of shipwrecks along its shores and caiçara communities, such as Bonete or Castelhanos, which still live from fishing, far from any road.
food: Azul-marinho
Fish stewed with green bananas that turn the sauce blue, a caiçara dish of the coast.
ilhabela.respect: In the caiçara coves, take your rubbish away with you and ask before taking photos. Bring repellent against the borrachudos that bite near the rivers.
ilhabela.season: April to September: drier season, the channel often glassy in the morning and coves deserted after summer.

around.d: Atlantic Forest, waterfalls and trails to the wild beaches of the east coast.
Small colonial centre of low houses, facing the island across the channel.
Long white-sand beach renowned for surfing, with the forest as a backdrop.

puntadeleste.vibe: A former fishing hamlet on the Arroyo Maldonado, La Barra comes alive in summer with galleries and bars; you arrive over the wavy bridge, while at the Punta harbour, sea lions wait for the fishermen’s scraps.
puntadeleste.respect: At the harbour, keep your distance from the sea lions waiting for fish: they can bite. At the peak, local surfers have priority, especially in winter.
puntadeleste.season: March to May: more frequent southern swells, water still mild and the resort emptied after the big January rush.

around.d: Carlos Páez Vilaró’s white sculpture-house, clinging to the cliff facing the sunset.

around.n: Isla de Lobos and its lighthouse
around.d: Rocky islet home to a huge sea lion colony, approached by boat.
Wooded island facing the harbour, small sheltered beaches and remains of Spanish batteries.
Giant fingers rising from the sand of Playa Brava, the resort’s emblem.
Whale skeletons, shells and seaside history, in the woods of La Barra.

ayampe.vibe: On the Manabí coast, Ayampe lines up its bamboo and palm-thatch houses between dry forest and a river mouth; the village lives from small surf schools, far from the bustle of Montañita.
food: Fish viche
Thick fish soup with ground peanuts, plantain and corn, the pride of Manabí cooking.
ayampe.respect: To see the whales or Isla de la Plata, choose a licensed Machalilla park operator who respects approach distances.
ayampe.season: December to April: consistent northern swells, warm water and sunshine, despite a few tropical showers.

around.d: Dry forest, Los Frailes beach and Isla de la Plata, nicknamed the “poor man’s Galápagos”.
Community that guides visitors around a Manteño site and a sulphurous lagoon you can bathe in.
Crescent-shaped fishing port, boats returning in the morning and departure point for whale trips.
Party surf village, a renowned point and lanes of bars and restaurants.

burleigh.vibe: Under the pandanus palms of the headland, Burleigh hill fills up at sunset; on the point, Gold Coast surfers watch for cyclone swells, on Aboriginal land whose story is told by the Jellurgal cultural centre.
burleigh.respect: The line-up is one of the most contested in the country: do not jump off behind the point without the skills and respect priority. On the headland, stay on the path.
burleigh.season: February to May: cyclone swells and south-east trade winds blowing offshore on the point.

around.d: Trail around the headland, rainforest, basalt boulders and a view of the point.
Upland rainforest, waterfalls, lookouts and the glow-worms of Natural Bridge.
Kangaroos, koalas and rainbow lorikeet feeding.
Wildlife park that pioneered platypus breeding, deep in the forest.
Ancient Aboriginal ceremonial ring preserved in the middle of the city.

byronbay.vibe: A former whaling and abattoir town, Byron was adopted by the surfers of the shortboard revolution and then by the hippies; on Arakwal land, organic markets and longboards sit alongside sunrise at the lighthouse.
byronbay.respect: The Pass is crowded and shared with the schools: one person per wave, and paddle out around the side rather than through the take-off zone. In the marine park’s sanctuary zones, fishing is banned.
byronbay.season: March to June: cyclone swells, then southern swells that wrap around the cape, water still warm and the summer crowds gone.

around.d: White lighthouse at the end of a coastal path, the most easterly point of the mainland and whales in winter.
Islets off the bay, a dive site renowned for its leopard sharks and turtles.
Waterfall plunging off a rhyolite cliff, rainforest hike.
Coastal rainforest running down to small wild beaches.
Hinterland village with a heritage main street, cafés and a monthly market.

manly.vibe: Lined with Norfolk Island pines, Manly lives to the rhythm of the ferries and the volunteer surf lifesaving clubs; it was at Freshwater, just to the north, that Duke Kahanamoku gave his surfing demonstration, still legendary in Australia.
manly.respect: In the Cabbage Tree Bay Aquatic Reserve, do not touch or feed the blue gropers; little penguins nest near the wharf, so keep your distance.
manly.season: March to June: more consistent south and east swells, water still temperate and a less crowded beach than in summer.

around.d: Former quarantine station on the headland, carved inscriptions and night tours.
Bushland and a freshwater lake for swimming, walking or mountain biking.
19th-century batteries and tunnels on a wooded headland facing the harbour entrance.
Dizzying sandstone cliffs above the ocean, coastal walk to Watsons Bay.
Small red-and-white striped lighthouse at the tip of South Head.

ningaloo.vibe: Here the red bush of the cattle stations meets the turquoise lagoon; between Coral Bay and Exmouth, you camp at the end of sandy tracks and live to the rhythm of whale sharks, manta rays and turtles nesting on the beaches.
ningaloo.respect: Never block a whale shark’s path and keep your distance, do not fish in the sanctuary zones and never put your fins down on the coral.
ningaloo.season: April to July: whale shark season, often calm seas and heat more bearable than the scorching summer.

piha.vibe: Below Lion Rock, a former Māori pā, Piha lines up its wooden baches at the foot of forested hills; a culture of surfing and volunteer lifeguards was born here, made famous by the series Piha Rescue.
piha.respect: Clean your shoes at the kauri dieback stations and respect closed tracks. In the water, swim between the flags: the currents are treacherous.
piha.season: March to May: consistent westerly swells, calmer winds and water still mild after summer.

around.d: Hills of native forest, waterfalls and trails between Auckland and the Tasman Sea.
Wild black-sand beach, waterfall and cliffs, the setting for the film The Piano.
Three-tiered waterfall at the end of a short forest walk, with a pool for swimming.
Long black beach and a gannet colony nesting on the rocks.
Wild beach, black-sand dunes and Lake Wainamu, reached on foot.

shipwreck.vibe: At the foot of the plateau where kauri gum was once dug, Ahipara is a village of the Te Rarawa iwi; the beach of Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē still serves as a road and as a place to gather tuatua.
shipwreck.respect: If you drive on the beach, stay on the hard sand and off the dunes. For shellfish, respect the quotas and the rāhui set by the iwi.
shipwreck.season: April to September: south-west swells wrapping around the points and offshore south-east winds.

around.d: Dune lake with brown waters and a sandy beach, ideal for a freshwater swim.
Remote estuary lined with hills and mangroves, a small Māori hamlet on the shore.
Far North town, with its regional museum on kauri gum and Māori history.

restaurants.vibe: In the heart of the Mamanucas, the Restaurants left is surfed from Namotu or Tavarua; the reefs fall within the villages’ customary fishing grounds, and since the end of the resorts’ exclusive rights, boats from Viti Levu share the peak.
restaurants.respect: The reef is exposed at low tide: wait for mid-tide, wear booties or a helmet and respect the rotation at the peak. Choose a mineral sunscreen.
restaurants.season: May to October: consistent southern swells of the austral winter and offshore trade winds on the left in the morning.

around.d: Large Dravidian-style Hindu temple with painted ceilings, heart of the Indo-Fijian community.
Volcanic island with Fijian villages, grassy hills and reef-fringed beaches.
Mamanuca island with clear waters, reef snorkelling and a Fijian village.

borabora.vibe: Around Mount Otemanu, Bora lives between Vaitape, the va’a outrigger canoes training on the lagoon and the cannons left by the American base of the Second World War; in July, the Heiva rings with song and dance.
borabora.respect: Never walk on the coral heads and avoid feeding the rays and sharks. On a paddleboard or kayak, stay out of the channels used by boats.
borabora.season: May to October: dry season, refreshing trade winds and an exceptionally clear lagoon, with fewer showers.

around.d: The island’s main village, local crafts, little food trucks and the start of the round-island bike ride.
Iconic volcanic peak towering over the lagoon, best admired from the motus.

jardimdomar.vibe: A village of car-free cobbled lanes clinging above terraced banana plantations, Jardim do Mar saw surfers rally against the seawall promenade that ate into its legendary wave.
food: Espada with banana
Fillet of black scabbardfish caught offshore, pan-fried and served with Madeiran banana.
jardimdomar.respect: You get in and out over boulders pounded by the swell: watch for a long time before going and give locals priority. Park at the top of the village.
jardimdomar.season: November to February: big north-west swells that finally wake up the right, in air that is always mild.

around.d: Trail along an irrigation channel through laurel forest, to a pool fed by waterfalls.
Natural pools carved into black lava, pounded by Atlantic waves.
Dizzying cliff with a glass platform suspended above the cultivated terraces.
Neighbouring fishing village at the foot of the cliffs, another powerful right and fresh fish.
Summit above the clouds, start of the ridge trail to Pico Ruivo.

santabarbara.vibe: On the north coast of São Miguel, between tea plantations and fishing villages such as Rabo de Peixe, Ribeira Grande lives in summer to the rhythm of the Holy Spirit festivals and surf contests on the black sand.
food: Cozido das Furnas
Stew of meats and vegetables slow-cooked for hours in the hot volcanic ground.
santabarbara.respect: The beach break is shared with surf schools: keep clear of their zone and give locals priority. Outside lifeguarded hours, the currents are powerful.
santabarbara.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells, water still mild and gentler winds than in midwinter.

around.d: Twin lakes, one green and one blue, at the bottom of a vast caldera.
Village of fumaroles and hot springs, iron-rich pools in the Terra Nostra garden.
Wild crater lake at the top of the Água de Pau massif, a fine hike.
Sea crater forming an almost round natural pool, reached by boat in summer.
Old centre of basalt and whitewash, Baroque churches and a bridge over the river.

capomannu.vibe: On the Sinis peninsula, between flamingo lagoons and beaches of quartz grains, the fishermen of Cabras make mullet bottarga; when the mistral blows, surfers from all over the island converge on the cape.
food: Cabras bottarga
Mullet roe from the nearby lagoons, grated over pasta or sliced as an aperitivo.
capomannu.respect: Do not take quartz sand from the Sinis beaches: it is forbidden and fined. Around Mal di Ventre, the marine protected area regulates anchoring and fishing.
capomannu.season: October to April, when the mistral blows for several days: well-lined-up swell on the reef and a line-up far from the summer crowds.

around.d: Punic and later Roman city on a peninsula, columns standing against the sea.
Stone statues of Nuragic warriors, displayed in the Cabras museum.
Flat, wild island in the marine protected area, crystal-clear waters for snorkelling.
White limestone arch plunging into a turquoise cove.
Lighthouse at the tip of the Sinis, cliffs and a view over the Gulf of Oristano.

isolabella.vibe: Below Taormina, perched on its hill since Greek antiquity, the bay of Mazzarò keeps its fishing boats; the islet, once the garden of an eccentric English aristocrat, is now a reserve where you swim facing Etna.
food: Granita with brioche
Almond, lemon or mulberry granita, served with a brioche for a Sicilian breakfast.
isolabella.respect: The islet is a nature reserve: enter only by the official access, pick nothing and leave the pebbles and shells of the sandbar where they are.
isolabella.season: June to September: calm, warm sea and crystal-clear water; aim for June or September to avoid the crowds on the sandbar.

around.d: Greco-Roman tiers open to the sea and Etna, a concert venue in summer.
Lively Corso, medieval palaces and gardens hanging above the sea.
Hilltop village above Taormina, castle ruins and a plunging view over the coast.
Canyon of basalt columns carved by an icy river, to explore on foot.
Archaeological park of the first Greek colony in Sicily, with its small museum.

zlatnirat.vibe: Bol stretches between houses of white Brač stone and a Dominican monastery facing Hvar; for decades, boards and sails have watched for the afternoon maestral here, while the vines climb the mountainside.
food: Vitalac
Brač lamb offal wrapped in caul fat and spit-roasted, a speciality of the island.
zlatnirat.respect: On the point, respect the buoys separating swimmers from boards: never sail among swimmers, and come in through the designated lanes.
zlatnirat.season: June to September: an almost daily thermal maestral in the afternoon, ideal for windsurfing as well as kiting.

around.d: Monastery clinging to a wild ravine, reached by a stone path.
Ancient Greek fields still farmed, dry-stone walls and vines, on the island of Hvar.
Small old town at the head of a bay, with the fishpond castle of Tvrdalj.
Cave decorated with reliefs carved by monks, above Bol, visited with a guide.
Oldest village on Brač, ancient walls and the island museum in a tower.

naxos.vibe: An island more agricultural than glamorous, Naxos grows potatoes, graviera cheese and citrons for kitron; at Mikri Vigla, sailing schools and family tavernas are scattered between dunes and junipers.
food: Naxos graviera
Hard cheese with a nutty flavour, to try with the island’s potatoes and a glass of kitron.
naxos.respect: In the protected juniper dunes of Alyko, stay on the paths. When kiting, keep to the corridor in the windy bay and leave the southern bay to swimmers.
naxos.season: June to September: the meltemi blows strong and steady from the north; June and September bring gentler wind and fewer people.

around.d: Huge marble doorway of an unfinished temple, facing the harbour, at sunset.
Venetian kastro, vaulted whitewashed lanes and a lively seafront.
Mountain village with marble lanes, Venetian towers and small museums.
Highest peak in the Cyclades, a trail to the Cave of Zeus and views over the Aegean.
Restored archaic marble temple among fields and olive trees.

biscarrosse.vibe: Between two large lakes and the ocean, Biscarrosse watched the giants of the skies take off: its lake was once home to a seaplane base. At the beach, life follows the pines, the dunes and the baïnes.
food: Arcachon Bay oysters
Close by, the oyster farmers serve them in their huts with a glass of dry white.
biscarrosse.respect: Baïnes create currents that drag you out to sea: surf away from the swimming zones and reach the beach only by the marked paths through the dune.
biscarrosse.season: September to October: consistent autumn swells, offshore wind in the morning and water still mild.

around.d: Highest dune in Europe, with a vast view over the ocean, the forest and the Banc d’Arguin.
Large clear-water lake lined with pines, perfect for swimming, sailing or paddleboarding.
Seaplanes, models and archives telling the story of the Biscarrosse base’s heyday.
Shifting sandbanks at the mouth of the bay, a seabird refuge reached by boat.
Ville d’Hiver with its whimsical villas, piers, seafront and lively market.

carcans.vibe: At the end of a straight road through the pine forest, Carcans-Plage keeps the feel of a small Médoc resort: a few streets behind the dune, cycle paths through the pines and the largest lake in France close by.
food: Bordeaux canelé
Small cake with a caramelised crust and a soft centre, flavoured with rum and vanilla.
carcans.respect: Baïnes are common on this coast: spot the currents from the dune before going in, and keep your distance from the lifeguarded swimming zones.
carcans.season: September to October: consistent autumn swells, wind often calm in the morning and a line-up far less crowded than in summer.

around.d: The largest natural lake in mainland France, with sandy beaches and cycle paths.
Trails and boardwalks through marshes, heathland and forest, with shy wildlife to spot.
Wooded dunes, wet dune slacks and unspoilt marshes between the lake and the ocean.
Large freshwater lake lined with pines, ideal for paddleboarding, sailing or a wave-free swim.
Two square brick towers hidden in the pine forest, behind the line of dunes.

hourtin.vibe: Separated from the village by miles of forest, Hourtin-Plage lives in summer to the rhythm of surfers and families, while Hourtin’s harbour, on the lake, brings together sailing boats, windsurfers and fishing boats.
food: Pauillac lamb
Milk-fed lamb raised with its mother in the Médoc, simply roasted and served with a local wine.
hourtin.respect: The dunes of the neighbouring nature reserve are protected: stay on the marked paths and never cut through the vegetation to reach the beach.
hourtin.season: September to October: well-lined-up autumn swells, early-morning offshore wind and a beach almost empty after summer.

around.d: The largest natural lake in mainland France, with its harbour, beaches and cycle paths.
Wooded dunes, wet dune slacks and unspoilt marshes between the lake and the ocean.
Two square brick towers hidden in the pine forest, behind the line of dunes.
Former Romanesque abbey among the Médoc vineyards, with its church and carved portal.
Medieval keep of Lesparre, the last remnant of its castle, overlooking the little town.

montalivet.vibe: Montalivet is the birthplace of family naturism in France: the pioneers settled in the forest here just after the war. The village also revolves around its covered market and the long beach facing the dunes.
food: Grenier médocain
Médoc charcuterie made from rolled, spiced pork belly lining, served cold in thin slices.
montalivet.respect: On either side of the central beach, long stretches are naturist: respect this custom, and never take photos of bathers.
montalivet.season: September to October: solid autumn swells, early-morning offshore wind and water still mild.

around.d: UNESCO-listed Renaissance lighthouse standing at sea at the mouth of the estuary, visited by boat.
Seaside resort with colourful brick and stone villas and pedestrian streets.
Romanesque church long buried under sand, a UNESCO-listed stop on the Way of St James.
Tip of the Médoc between the ocean and the Gironde estuary, with its lighthouse and a view of Cordouan.

soulac.vibe: At the tip of the Médoc, Soulac lines up its brick and stone villas, a legacy of the first sea-bathing days, around a basilica long swallowed by the sand. Here, the ocean is eating away at the coast and everyone talks about it.
food: Lamprey à la bordelaise
Caught in the estuary, it simmers for hours in a red wine and leek sauce.
soulac.respect: The coast is retreating fast here: do not go near collapsed dune foots and cross the dune line only at the designated access points. Watch out for currents near the estuary.
soulac.season: September to October: consistent autumn swells, water still mild and beaches quiet again.

around.d: UNESCO-listed Renaissance lighthouse standing at sea at the mouth of the estuary, visited by boat.
Romanesque church long buried under sand, a UNESCO-listed stop on the Way of St James.
Tip of the Médoc between the ocean and the Gironde estuary, with its lighthouse and a view of Cordouan.
Village bright with hollyhocks on a promontory, with its Romanesque church facing the estuary.
Remains of an ancient port, baths and a great temple above the estuary.

penermalo.vibe: On the doorstep of Lorient, a major fishing port and capital of Celtic music, Guidel-Plages stretches to the wooded mouth of the Laïta; surfers, kitesurfers and walkers share the sand depending on the wind.
hello: “hello” in Breton, always well received on the coast
food: Crêpes and buckwheat galettes
A galette complète and a bowl of cider in a crêperie, the Breton ritual after a session.
penermalo.respect: Near the mouth of the Laïta, the tidal currents are strong: stay out of the water on the ebb, and leave room between kites, boards and swimmers.
penermalo.season: September to November: consistent westerly swells, water still bearable and beaches deserted after summer.

around.d: Island of cliffs and coves, with the convex beach of Les Grands Sables and its coastal paths.
Small town where two rivers meet, with its old lower town and half-timbered houses.
Romanesque church with a circular plan inspired by the Holy Sepulchre, in the heart of the lower town.
Large state forest along the Laïta, criss-crossed by shady hiking trails.
Reconstruction of the inn where Gauguin and his painter friends stayed at Le Pouldu.

porscarn.vibe: Between La Torche and the rocks of Saint-Guénolé, Pors Carn opens onto the Bay of Audierne in the heart of Bigouden country, land of tall lace headdresses, fishing ports and old granite chapels.
hello: “hello” in Breton, always well received in Bigouden country
food: Buckwheat galettes
Filled with egg, ham and cheese, with a bowl of cider in a Bigouden crêperie.
porscarn.respect: Do not venture onto the rocks of Saint-Guénolé in a big swell: rogue waves sweep across them. On the beach, give the surf schools space.
porscarn.season: September to November: well-lined-up westerly swells, water still bearable and the bay deserted after summer.

around.d: Tall granite lighthouse at the Penmarch point: climb to the top for the view over the coast.
Major small-scale fishing port: watch the trawlers come home and the bustle of the fish auction.
Capital of Bigouden country, with its castle housing a museum of costumes and headdresses.
Menhirs, stelae and objects found in Finistère, displayed in the museum and its garden.
Prehistoric burial mound on the point, facing the ocean and the long Bay of Audierne.

tanchet.vibe: A fishing port and the start of great offshore sailing races, Les Sables-d’Olonne lives facing the sea: the La Chaume district with its low houses, the lively Remblai and, to the south, the rocky peaks of Tanchet.
food: Les Sables sardines
Landed at the Les Sables fishing port and served simply grilled on the quayside terraces.
tanchet.respect: At Tanchet, the wave breaks over a rocky bottom: wear booties at low tide, wait your turn at the peak and respect the regulars.
tanchet.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells, water still mild and a quieter town than in summer.

around.d: Old fishermen’s quarter of narrow lanes, with its Arundel Tower facing the channel.
Modern and contemporary art in a former abbey, with a large Gaston Chaissac collection.
Ruins of a medieval fortress, with a view from the keep and events in summer.
Former salt marshes and pools where you can watch many birds, on foot or by bike.
Remains of a medieval abbey near the coast, peaceful and south of the town.

baleal.vibe: A former island linked to the coast by a sandy isthmus, Baleal looks across to Peniche, a fishing port renowned for its bobbin lace; on either side of the peninsula, two beaches let you surf in almost any wind.
food: Óbidos ginjinha
Sour cherry liqueur served in a little chocolate cup, in the lanes of Óbidos.
baleal.respect: There are lots of surf schools in Baleal: if you surf independently, move away from beginner groups and leave the waves at the rocky peaks to the regulars.
baleal.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells, water still mild and beaches free of the summer crowds.

around.d: Protected granite archipelago, with clear waters, seabirds and a fort on an islet, reached by boat.
White medieval village encircled by ramparts, with flower-filled lanes to explore on foot.
Fortress turned political prison under the dictatorship, now a museum of the resistance.
Cliffs sculpted by erosion and a lighthouse at the end of the peninsula, facing the Berlengas.
Large lagoon with calm waters, ideal for paddleboarding, sailing or birdwatching.

arrifana.vibe: Below the Arrifana cliffs, a small fishing harbour still shelters its boats at the foot of a winding road, while on the nearby plateau lie the remains of a ribat, a fortified monastery from the Islamic period.
food: Aljezur sweet potato
Grown in the sandy soils of the coast, it is enjoyed roasted or in cakes.
arrifana.respect: You are in the Costa Vicentina natural park: sleeping in a van or camping outside authorised areas is banned and enforced. Reach the beach by the road, not down the cliff.
arrifana.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells that the bay shelters from the wind, water still mild.

around.d: Remains of a 12th-century Islamic fortified monastery, on a promontory facing the ocean.
Wild cliffs, coves and Rota Vicentina trails along the Atlantic.
Ruins of a castle of Islamic origin overlooking the white village and the valley.
Ruins of a fort on the cliff, a viewpoint over the bay and the surfers below.
Wooded mountains of the Algarve, with the summit of Fóia and its stone villages.

amado.vibe: Nestled in a valley between cliffs of colourful strata, Amado brings together surf schools and travellers’ vans; close by, Carrapateira remains a small farming village and goose-barnacle fishermen still climb down the rocks.
food: Medronho
Strawberry-tree brandy distilled in the Algarve hills, served in a small glass after the meal.
amado.respect: The beach is inside the natural park: keep to the existing tracks by car, do not sleep in the car park and leave the cliff vegetation intact.
amado.season: September to November: well-lined-up autumn swells and an open beach that picks up almost every direction.

around.d: South-western tip of Portugal, dizzying cliffs and a lighthouse, famous for its sunsets.
Fortress on a windswept promontory, associated with Henry the Navigator.
Remains of a medieval fishing hamlet on the Pontal, above the ocean.
Old walled town with cobbled streets, a marina and the golden cliffs of Ponta da Piedade.
Group of prehistoric standing stones in the countryside near Vila do Bispo.

bordeira.vibe: A river winds between the dunes before meeting the ocean at the foot of the cliffs: Bordeira is a vast, wild beach, revealed from the wooden boardwalks and the Carrapateira scenic road.
food: Seafood cataplana
Clams, prawns and chouriço simmered in a copper pot, the great Algarve classic.
bordeira.respect: Reach the beach by the boardwalks over the protected dunes, and beware of the current at the river mouth when the tide is going out.
bordeira.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells, calmer wind in the morning and an almost deserted beach.

around.d: South-western tip of Portugal, dizzying cliffs and a lighthouse, famous for its sunsets.
Fortress on a windswept promontory, associated with Henry the Navigator.
Remains of a medieval fishing hamlet on the Pontal, above the ocean.
Remains of a 12th-century Islamic fortified monastery, on a promontory facing the ocean.
Ruins of a castle of Islamic origin overlooking the white village and the valley.

carcavelos.vibe: Lisbon’s surf beach, reachable by train from the capital, Carcavelos stretches out below the fort of São Julião da Barra; students and office workers come here to ride a few waves after class or work.
food: Pastel de nata
A small custard tart in flaky pastry dusted with cinnamon, born near the Jerónimos Monastery in Belém.
carcavelos.respect: At weekends the line-up is packed: always keep hold of your board, never let go of it under a wave, and stay clear of the surf lessons set up near the shore.
carcavelos.season: October to March: fairly powerful winter swells wrap around the coast and finally get this south-facing beach working.

around.d: A brightly coloured Romantic palace perched on the Sintra hills, surrounded by wooded parkland.
Medieval ramparts snaking along the Sintra ridges, with views all the way to the ocean.
A royal palace in the heart of the town, recognisable by its two large conical chimneys.
A former fishing village turned elegant resort, with its bay, citadel and narrow lanes.
Lisbon’s great museum, rich in Portuguese and European painting, with a garden above the Tagus.

matosinhos.vibe: A fishing and canning port right next to Porto, Matosinhos smells of charcoal: outside the restaurants, fish grills on braziers in the middle of the street. To the north, in Leça, Álvaro Siza slipped tidal pools into the rocks.
food: Matosinhos grilled fish
Sardines, sea bass or red mullet grilled over charcoal outside the restaurants near the port.
matosinhos.respect: This is Porto’s beginner beach: if you surf independently, keep away from the groups of beginners and respect the lifeguarded swimming zones in summer.
matosinhos.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells, and the harbour wall shelters the beach when the sea gets bigger.

around.d: A contemporary art museum designed by Álvaro Siza, in a large park with an Art Deco villa.
A neo-Gothic bookshop with a famous carved red staircase, in the heart of Porto.
An angular concert hall designed by Rem Koolhaas, open for tours and full of life.
A palace housing the country’s oldest art museum, with Portuguese sculpture and painting.
A shipbuilding town with a large monastery, an aqueduct and a replica caravel.

espinho.vibe: A seaside town with numbered streets laid out on a grid, Espinho still has its arte xávega fishermen, who haul their big nets up the beach by hand, next to surfers watching the right-hander by the jetty.
food: Francesinha
A Porto sandwich filled with meats, smothered in melted cheese and a spicy beer sauce.
espinho.respect: When the xávega fishermen are working, keep clear of the nets and ropes on the beach and in the water, and let the tractors through.
espinho.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells, wind often calmer in the morning and water slightly less cold.

around.d: A contemporary art museum designed by Álvaro Siza, in a large park with an Art Deco villa.
The country’s oldest art museum, with Portuguese sculpture and painting in a Porto palace.
An angular concert hall designed by Rem Koolhaas, open for tours and full of life.
Romantic gardens, glasshouses and camellia hedges around a former merchant’s mansion.
A small fishing village right on the beach, with its boats and a peaceful atmosphere.

buarcos.vibe: A former fishing village backed by the Serra da Boa Viagem, Buarcos runs on from the resort of Figueira da Foz and its huge beach; along the sea wall, a right-hander peels towards the bay when the winter swell comes in.
food: Leitão da Bairrada
Roast suckling pig with crackling skin, a speciality of the neighbouring Bairrada, served with a sparkling wine.
buarcos.respect: The right breaks along a sea wall and over rocks: wear booties, don’t paddle into the path of surfers coming off the peak, and respect the regulars.
buarcos.season: October to March: big winter swells wrap around Cape Mondego and produce long peeling rights.

around.d: A large medieval castle on a hill, overlooking the rice fields of the Mondego valley.
A small wooded mountain above the sea, with trails and viewpoints over the coast.
A headland with cliffs rich in Jurassic fossils, topped by a lighthouse above the ocean.
A lively seaside resort with an exceptionally wide beach, a casino and a fort.

saotorpes.vibe: Below the big port of Sines, birthplace of Vasco da Gama, São Torpes long enjoyed water warmed by the neighbouring power station, now closed; further south begins the wild coast of the Alentejo.
food: Carne de porco à alentejana
Marinated pork pieces sautéed with clams, the Alentejo’s marriage of land and sea.
saotorpes.respect: Just to the south begins the Vicentine Coast natural park: don’t camp outside the authorised areas, don’t sleep in a van on the clifftops, and stay on the paths.
saotorpes.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells, water still mild and a quiet beach after summer.

around.d: A white village trimmed in blue around a square, above small coves among the rocks.
A rocky islet topped by a ruined fort, facing a beach watched over by another fort.
A medieval castle above the bay, with a small museum and the statue of Vasco da Gama.
A white town at the mouth of the Mira, between river and ocean beaches.

cordoama.vibe: You reach it by a track across the Vila do Bispo plateau before it drops down to a wild beach below high cliffs; here, goose barnacle gatherers still brave the swell-battered rocks.
food: Percebes
Goose barnacles prised from the swell-battered rocks, the pride of Vila do Bispo, boiled in salted water.
cordoama.respect: Don’t settle at the foot of the cliffs: rockfalls happen regularly. The beach is inside the natural park, so don’t sleep in the car park.
cordoama.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells, calmer wind in the morning and an almost deserted beach.

around.d: The south-western tip of Portugal, with dizzying cliffs and a lighthouse, famous for its sunsets.
A fortress on a windswept promontory, associated with Henry the Navigator.

around.n: Chapel of Our Lady of Guadalupe
around.d: A small, isolated Gothic chapel in the countryside, linked to the time of Henry the Navigator.
A group of prehistoric standing stones in the countryside near Vila do Bispo.
An old walled town with cobbled streets, a marina and the golden cliffs of Ponta da Piedade.

elpalmar.vibe: A long beach with no tower blocks, lined with chiringuitos, vegetable plots and low houses, El Palmar lies below Vejer, a white hilltop village; further south, the Trafalgar lighthouse watches over the waters of the famous naval battle.
food: Tortillitas de camarones
Thin, crispy fritters with tiny shrimps, a treat from the Bay of Cádiz.
elpalmar.respect: In summer, surf only in the zones marked out by the lifeguards, and reach the beach by the existing paths without trampling the dunes.
elpalmar.season: October to March: Atlantic winter swells, often groomed by the Levante, which blows offshore here.

around.d: A white village perched on a hill, with Moorish lanes, ramparts and views over the coast.
A low headland topped by a lighthouse, between dunes and beaches, facing the site of the 1805 battle.
A small bohemian village below wooded cliffs, with its coves and freshwater springs.
A fishing port of white houses, with its old tower, narrow lanes and long beaches.

hierbabuena.vibe: For centuries Barbate has lived from almadraba tuna fishing and salting; beyond the port, Hierbabuena beach hides below the pine-covered cliffs of La Breña natural park.
food: Almadraba bluefin tuna
Caught in spring off Barbate, it’s eaten as tataki, a la plancha or cured as mojama.
hierbabuena.respect: The beach is inside La Breña natural park: walk there along the path from the port, take your rubbish home and stay on the clifftop trails.
hierbabuena.season: October to March: only well-angled winter swells reach this sheltered beach, far from the summer crowds.

around.d: Pine forest on high cliffs, coastal trails and marshes where many birds nest.
A watchtower perched on the cliff edge, a lookout over the coast and as far as Morocco on clear days.
A white village perched on a hill, with Moorish lanes, ramparts and views over the coast.
A tuna-fishing village turned quiet resort, with the ruins of its castle.
A low headland topped by a lighthouse, between dunes and beaches, facing the site of the 1805 battle.

salinas.vibe: Avilés’s seaside resort, Salinas unrolls its long beach as far as the El Espartal dunes; on the point, an open-air museum displays old anchors, and in the evening people share cider poured from a height in the sidrerías.
food: Fabada and Asturian cider
A stew of beans and cured meats, with cider poured from high up to aerate it.
salinas.respect: To the east, the beach continues into the El Espartal dunes: don’t trample them and use the boardwalks. At the peak, give priority to the local club regulars.
salinas.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells from the Bay of Biscay, water still mild and a less crowded beach.

around.d: A fishing village of colourful houses clinging in an amphitheatre around its little harbour.
A UNESCO-listed pre-Romanesque palace on the slopes of Mount Naranco above Oviedo.
An old town of arcaded streets, palaces and lively squares, carefully restored.
A white dome and curving forms designed by Oscar Niemeyer, facing the Avilés estuary.
An open-air museum on the Salinas point, where old anchors face the sea.

loslocos.vibe: A former fishing port at the mouth of the San Martín de la Arena estuary, Suances has turned to surfing; its beaches, lined up below the cliffs, draw Cantabrian surfers as soon as the swell arrives.
food: Cocido montañés
A Cantabrian stew of white beans, cabbage and cured meats, perfect after a winter session.
loslocos.respect: The peak is very local and the beach is narrow below the cliffs: go down by the built access, watch before paddling out and leave the best waves to the regulars.
loslocos.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells, water still mild and a calmer line-up than in summer.

around.d: A faithful replica of the cave with its painted bison, plus a museum on life in the Palaeolithic.

around.n: Collegiate Church of Santillana del Mar
around.d: A Romanesque collegiate church with a carved cloister, in the heart of a medieval stone village.
A cave decorated with hand stencils and signs among the oldest in Europe, visited in small groups.
A village of Modernista palaces, including Gaudí’s El Capricho, between sea and hills.
A Costa Quebrada cove bristling with rock blades, superb at low tide.

canallave.vibe: On the edge of the Liencres Dunes natural park, where the Pas meets the sea, Canallave opens the Costa Quebrada, a coast of layered cliffs and islets well known to geologists and Cantabrian surfers alike.
food: Sobaos pasiegos
Soft butter cakes from the Pas valleys, perfect with a coffee after your session.
canallave.respect: The Liencres dunes are a natural park: stay on the marked paths. Watch out for currents near the Pas estuary and for rocks at low tide.
canallave.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells, water still mild and car parks free of the summer crowds.

around.d: A Costa Quebrada cove bristling with rock blades, superb at low tide.
A faithful replica of the cave with its painted bison, plus a museum on life in the Palaeolithic.

around.n: Collegiate Church of Santillana del Mar
around.d: A Romanesque collegiate church with a carved cloister, in the heart of a medieval stone village.
A royal summer palace set on a green peninsula, with a park and views over the bay.
A cave decorated with hand stencils and signs among the oldest in Europe, visited in small groups.

loredo.vibe: Facing Mouro Island and the entrance to the Bay of Santander, Loredo continues the Somo sand spit below the meadows of Trasmiera; in summer, surf schools set up among the Cantabrian families.
food: Santoña anchovies
Bay of Biscay anchovies salted then filleted by hand in the Santoña canneries, on good bread.
loredo.respect: Surf schools take over the shoreline in summer: if you surf independently, look for peaks further along and let beginners learn safely. Cross the dunes on the boardwalks.
loredo.season: September to October: consistent autumn swells, water still mild and a beach freed from the August crowds.

around.d: A royal summer palace set on a green peninsula, with a park and views over the bay.
Vast coastal marshes where many migratory birds stop over.
Santander’s Belle Époque beach, lined with gardens, villas and a casino.
A sloping medieval old town above a huge golden sand beach.
A Gothic cathedral built over a medieval crypt, in the heart of the city.

fistral.vibe: Newquay has lived to the rhythm of surfing for decades: shops, schools and vans line up above Fistral. On the neighbouring headland, the whitewashed Huer’s Hut recalls the days when lookouts watched for shoals of pilchards.
hello: “hello” in Cornish, the revived Celtic language of Cornwall
food: Cornish pasty
A golden pastry filled with beef, potato, swede and onion, to eat by the sea.
fistral.respect: Fistral is very busy: surf between the black-and-white chequered lifeguard flags, never in the red-and-yellow swimming zone, and respect priority at the peak.
fistral.season: September to November: consistent Atlantic swells, water still mild and a beach free of the summer crowds.

around.d: Spectacular cliffs and huge rock stacks planted in the sand, seen from the coast path.
A neo-Gothic cathedral with three spires, in the heart of Cornwall’s only city.
An Elizabethan manor house with carved gables, surrounded by peaceful gardens.
A vast stretch of wild dunes overlooking Perran Bay, ideal for walking.
A village of slate roofs and a wide beach at the mouth of the Gannel.

polzeath.vibe: Facing the Camel estuary, Polzeath is a bay for families and surfers where you walk down to the water in your wetsuit straight from the village. The coast path heads off towards Pentire and its Atlantic-battered headlands.
hello: “hello” in Cornish, the revived Celtic language of Cornwall
food: Cornish crab and lobster
Caught off the north coast and enjoyed in sandwiches or grilled in the nearby harbours.
polzeath.respect: At high tide the beach shrinks and the line-up tightens: share the waves with beginners and leave your car in the car parks rather than on the sand.
polzeath.season: September to October: clean autumn swells in the bay, water still mild and a quieter village.

around.d: A fishing harbour of narrow lanes and whitewashed cottages huddled around the quay.
A twin headland topped by an Iron Age fort, with vast views over the ocean.
A tiny unspoilt cove tucked into the cliffs, a peaceful stop on the coast path.
A village on the Camel estuary, linked to Padstow by a small ferry.
A centre that raises young lobsters before releasing them into the sea, open to visitors.

perranporth.vibe: Legend has it that St Piran, patron saint of tin miners, landed here from Ireland. His black flag with a white cross flies everywhere, and the cliffs, riddled with old tunnels, tell of the coast’s mining past.
hello: “hello” in Cornish, the revived Celtic language of Cornwall
food: Cornish cream tea
Warm scones, strawberry jam and then clotted cream on top, the Cornish way.
perranporth.respect: Rip currents are common on this long beach: surf in the chequered lifeguarded zone, and stay well away from the foot of the cliffs undermined by old mine tunnels.
perranporth.season: September to November: frequent Atlantic swells, water still mild and vast stretches almost empty.

around.d: Huge dunes hiding the remains of St Piran’s Oratory.
A mining village with engine houses perched on the cliffs, overlooked by St Agnes Beacon.
A beach between dunes and cliffs, facing the twin rocks of the Gull Rocks.
A village of slate roofs and a wide beach at the mouth of the Gannel.
A small surf village tucked into a valley that runs down to a sandy beach.

gwithian.vibe: At the far end of St Ives Bay, the Towans dunes face Godrevy Lighthouse, the one that inspired Virginia Woolf. Here you surf with views of seals, cliffs and the light that drew generations of painters.
hello: “hello” in Cornish, the revived Celtic language of Cornwall
food: Cornish pasty
A golden pastry filled with beef, potato, swede and onion, to take down to the beach.
gwithian.respect: Grey seals rest in the coves below Godrevy: watch them quietly from the clifftops, without climbing down or flying a drone, especially during the pupping season.
gwithian.season: September to November: autumn swells that fill the bay, water still mild and fewer people in the water.

around.d: An islet topped by a castle, reached on foot by a causeway at low tide.
A fishing harbour with cobbled lanes, art galleries and beaches bathed in famous light.
Clifftop paths facing the lighthouse, with grey seals in the coves below.
A historic ceramics workshop turned museum, where potters still work.
A granite hamlet between moorland and cliffs, known for the legend of its mermaid.

sidiifni.vibe: A former Spanish enclave, Sidi Ifni keeps its white-and-blue Art Deco façades, its central square and its lighthouse above the ocean. The town lives slowly, between the fishing port, paragliders above the cliffs and the Atlantic mists.
hello: “hello” in Amazigh, the Berber language spoken in the Souss and the Anti-Atlas
food: Amlou
A spread of roasted almonds, argan oil and honey, for breakfast on warm bread.
sidiifni.respect: In the evening, the beach is Ifni families’ living room: cover up when you leave the sand and, towards Legzira, never climb on the remaining arch, which is fragile.
sidiifni.season: October to March: consistent Atlantic winter swells, water still pleasant and skies often clear in the afternoon.

mirleft.vibe: A village perched above a string of coves, Mirleft has long drawn travellers, anglers and surfers in search of peace and quiet. Below the ochre cliffs, each beach has its own character and its own wave.
hello: “hello” in Amazigh, the Berber language spoken in the Souss and the Anti-Atlas
food: Amlou
A spread of almonds, argan oil and honey, served with bread and mint tea.
mirleft.respect: The tracks to the coves cross farmland: stay on the existing tracks, don’t wild camp near houses and take all your rubbish with you.
mirleft.season: October to March: well-angled winter swells in the coves, water still mild and a quiet village.

tamraght.vibe: Between Aourir and Taghazout, Tamraght is a former Amazigh village that has become a base for surfers from all over the world. Sloping lanes, rooftop terraces and the neighbouring banana groves of Aourir mingle with the surf schools.
hello: “hello” in Amazigh, the Berber language spoken in the Souss and the Anti-Atlas
food: Amlou
A spread of almonds, argan oil and honey made in the hinterland, for breakfast.
tamraght.respect: The local point breaks are very busy with schools: give priority to whoever is on the peak, and stay discreet and covered up when walking through the village.
tamraght.season: October to March: Atlantic winter swells peeling along the points, offshore wind in the morning and water still mild.

around.d: Atlas gorges with palm trees, clear rock pools and boulders to jump from.
Restored ramparts on the hilltop, with a view over the whole Bay of Agadir.
A small town nicknamed “Banana Village”, with its fruit stalls and lively souk.

durban.vibe: Durban is one of the birthplaces of South African surfing: on the Golden Mile, waves peel between the piers in front of the seafront towers. The city blends Zulu and Indian cultures, spice markets and joggers at dawn.
hello: “I see you”, the Zulu greeting of KwaZulu-Natal
food: Bunny chow
Half a loaf of white bread hollowed out and filled with curry, born in Durban’s Indian community.
durban.respect: The beaches are protected by shark nets: surf in the lifeguarded sections between the piers, and never leave your things unattended on the sand.
durban.season: April to August: more consistent south swells, frequent offshore winds in the morning and water that stays warm.

around.d: A large mosque with golden minarets, in the heart of the Indian quarter and its markets.
Africa’s oldest botanical garden still in operation, with rare cycads and orchids.
A large seafront aquarium set in a reconstructed shipwreck, with sharks and rays.
Wooded gorges, waterfalls and hiking trails in the hills above the city.

ballito.vibe: On the Dolphin Coast, Ballito stretches out between sugar cane fields and natural pools carved into the rocks. The resort hosts a stop on the pro tour every year, and local surfers meet here from dawn.
hello: “I see you”, the Zulu greeting of KwaZulu-Natal
food: Bunny chow
Half a hollowed-out loaf filled with spicy curry, the Indian speciality of the Durban area.
ballito.respect: Only surf in front of beaches with shark nets and lifeguards, and leave the natural pools to swimmers and children.
ballito.season: April to August: consistent south swells, offshore winds in the morning and the warm water of the Indian Ocean.

around.d: A rock shelter where archaeologists have found traces of very ancient human occupation.
A monument to the Zulu king Shaka, raised on the site of his grave in KwaDukuza.
A small coastal village with a natural pool and rocky coves.
A rocky promontory and quiet beaches just north of Ballito.

umhlanga.vibe: Umhlanga revolves around its red-and-white lighthouse and its seafront promenade. It’s also home to the organisation that manages the coast’s shark nets, an essential part of sea culture in KwaZulu-Natal.
hello: “I see you”, the Zulu greeting of KwaZulu-Natal
food: Bunny chow
Half a hollowed-out loaf filled with curry, a legacy of Durban’s Indian community.
umhlanga.respect: Reef and rocks break the surface in front of the promenade: get in and out over the sand, surf in the lifeguarded zone and follow the lifeguards’ instructions.
umhlanga.season: April to August: more frequent south swells, offshore winds at sunrise and water that’s always warm.

around.d: Boardwalks through the dune forest to the lagoon and a wild beach.
A remnant of native coastal forest, rich in birds and indigenous trees.
A big port city with Indian markets, a seafront and Zulu cultural life.
A large mosque with golden minarets, in the heart of Durban’s Indian quarter.

umdloti.vibe: A small holiday village on a rocky point, Umdloti has kept a laid-back feel away from the coast’s tower blocks. Its big natural pool draws families and swimmers, while surfers keep an eye on the nearby sandbanks.
hello: “I see you”, the Zulu greeting of KwaZulu-Natal
food: Bunny chow
Half a hollowed-out loaf filled with curry, the speciality born among Durban’s Indians.
umdloti.respect: Rocks and currents are treacherous around the point: spot the channels from the beach, stay close to the lifeguards and leave the natural pool to swimmers.
umdloti.season: April to August: more consistent south swells, offshore winds in the morning and warm water all season.

around.d: Boardwalks through the dune forest to the lagoon and a wild beach.
A mangrove at the mouth of the Umgeni, with crabs, fish and birds.
A remnant of native coastal forest, rich in birds and indigenous trees.
A seaside resort with a lighthouse, a long promenade and cafés facing the ocean.

capestfrancis.vibe: Cape St Francis became legendary with the film The Endless Summer and its perfect wave. Around it, the white houses with black thatched roofs of St Francis Bay and the squid-fishing fleet set the tone.
food: Port St Francis squid
Caught on lines by the local fleet, it’s eaten grilled or fried, freshly landed.
capestfrancis.respect: Seal Point is a powerful reef break surfed by locals: wait your turn, don’t sit on the inside, and respect the penguin rehabilitation centre near the lighthouse.
capestfrancis.season: May to August: big southern winter swells and a westerly wind that often blows offshore on the point.

around.d: A tall white-and-red lighthouse on the cape’s rocks, facing the surf spot.
South Africa’s surf capital, famous for the Supertubes wave and its surf shops.
A village of white houses topped with black thatch, criss-crossed by canals.
A peaceful estuary for paddleboarding, kayaking and birdwatching.
An isolated hamlet on a long beach backed by big dunes.

jaco.vibe: The closest surf town to San José, Jacó fills up at weekends with Ticos from the Central Valley. Surf schools, sodas (local eateries) and nightlife line a long dark-sand beach, with the forest as a backdrop.
jaco.respect: Rip currents are powerful at Jacó: check the signposted zones before going in, and leave nothing valuable on the sand or in the car.
jaco.season: April to October: consistent south swells, mornings often windless before the afternoon showers.

around.d: A transitional forest where you can spot scarlet macaws, monkeys and tropical birds.
A river famous for its huge crocodiles, visible from the bridge on the coast road.
A sheltered horseshoe bay, calmer for swimming and paddleboarding.

dominical.vibe: On the Costa Ballena, Dominical is still a surfers’ village with dirt roads, where the jungle comes right down to the sand. Offshore, humpback whales pass by every year, and travellers often stay longer than planned.
dominical.respect: Dominical’s beach break is powerful and its currents are strong: don’t go out if you’re a beginner, and follow the local surfers’ advice on the channels.
dominical.season: April to October: powerful, consistent south swells, warm water and mornings often without wind.

around.d: Gateway to Ballena Marine National Park, with its sand spit shaped like a whale’s tail.
Rainforest trails, mangrove and a wild beach, rich in birds and monkeys.

playagrande.vibe: Playa Grande is above all the beach of the leatherback turtles, protected by a national park that has held back building. Houses stay hidden behind the vegetation, and the Guanacaste of the sabaneros is never far away.
food: Guanacaste rosquillas
Small crunchy rings of corn and cheese, to nibble with a black coffee.
playagrande.respect: During nesting season, the national park beach closes at night: don’t go there after sunset, and never with a torch or flash, unless you’re with an accredited guide.
playagrande.season: April to August: consistent south swells on this exposed beach break, mornings often calm and a less crowded line-up.

around.d: Leatherback turtle nesting beaches, to be visited at night only with a guide.
A mangrove to explore by kayak or boat, with crocodiles and water birds.
A beach made of tiny crushed shells, with clear turquoise water.
A rocky beach known for its reef right-hander, made famous by surf films.

langosta.vibe: Just south of Tamarindo, Langosta keeps a quieter feel, between a rocky point and the mouth of a small river. Its beach is part of the turtles’ protected area, and evenings are spent watching the sun sink into the Pacific.
food: Guanacaste rosquillas
Small baked rings of corn and cheese, a classic of the province’s bakeries.
langosta.respect: The beach is a protected nesting site: no fires or torches at night, and never touch the nests or the baby turtles heading for the sea.
langosta.season: April to August: well-angled south swells on the point and the river mouth, mornings often without wind.

around.d: Leatherback turtle nesting beaches, to be visited at night only with a guide.
A mangrove to explore by kayak or boat, with crocodiles and water birds.
A beach made of tiny crushed shells, with clear turquoise water.
A rocky beach known for its reef right-hander, made famous by surf films.

avellanas.vibe: At the end of dusty tracks, Avellanas lines up several sand and reef peaks along a tree-lined beach. There’s no town here: a few houses, beach restaurants and the rural spirit of Guanacaste, between cows and dry forest.
food: Guanacaste rosquillas
Small crunchy rings of corn and cheese, sold in the village bakeries.
avellanas.respect: The reef peaks are surfed by a close-knit local community: wait your turn, respect priority and drive slowly on the tracks so you don’t cover the houses in dust.
avellanas.season: April to August: consistent south swells on the reefs and sandbanks, with mornings that are often glassy.

around.d: A rocky beach known for its reef right-hander, made famous by surf films.
Leatherback turtle nesting beaches, to be visited at night only with a guide.
A mangrove to explore by kayak or boat, with crocodiles and water birds.

junquillal.vibe: A long, wild and barely built-up beach, Junquillal attracts those fleeing the bustle of Tamarindo. Turtles come here to nest, and life follows the rhythm of the farms and tracks of rural Guanacaste.
food: Guanacaste rosquillas
Small rings of corn and cheese, best with a Costa Rican coffee.
junquillal.respect: Turtles nest on this beach: avoid any light at night, keep your distance from the marked nests and take your rubbish with you, as there are hardly any bins.
junquillal.season: April to August: consistent south swells on an open beach break, warm water and an almost empty beach.

around.d: A rocky beach known for its reef right-hander, made famous by surf films.
Leatherback turtle nesting beaches, to be visited at night only with a guide.

nosara.vibe: Nosara grew up away from the main roads: forest separates the houses, the tracks are still dirt and yoga studios sit alongside surf schools. The Nicoya Peninsula is also known for the longevity of its inhabitants.
nosara.respect: The village tracks are dusty and shared with pedestrians and cyclists: drive at walking pace, and don’t disturb the howler monkeys that live in the trees above the beach.
nosara.season: April to October: consistent south swells on the Guiones beach break, warm water and mornings often without wind.

around.d: The beach of the arribadas, mass nestings of olive ridley turtles on certain nights.
A mangrove-lined estuary to paddle up by kayak for birdwatching.
A protected islet in Sámara Bay, reachable by kayak from the beach.

esterillos.vibe: Between Jacó and Quepos, Esterillos unrolls long, almost empty beaches lined with oil palms and small farms. People come here to surf without crowds and live to the slow rhythm of the Central Pacific.
esterillos.respect: The beaches are rarely lifeguarded and the currents are strong: never surf alone, and keep a low profile near the homes of the families who live here all year round.
esterillos.season: April to October: consistent south swells on the sandbanks, warm water and deserted beaches on weekdays.

bejuco.vibe: A grey-sand beach between Jacó and Quepos, Bejuco draws surfers looking for consistent waves away from the bustle. Here the coast road runs through palm plantations and peaceful hamlets.
bejuco.respect: A quiet beach with powerful currents: don’t surf alone, and respect the turtles that come to nest on the neighbouring coast.
bejuco.season: April to October: powerful, consistent south swells on the beach break, warm water and few people.

around.d: A protected beach where sea turtles come to nest, near a renowned surf spot.
Little-visited hill forest, with trails and rivers in the hinterland.

huntington.vibe: Huntington Beach claims the nickname “Surf City USA”: around the pier, the Duke Kahanamoku statue, legends’ handprints on the pavement and major contests set the town’s rhythm. Over at the State Beach, campfires light up the evenings on the sand.
huntington.respect: At the mouth of the Santa Ana, a fenced area protects the nests of terns and plovers: never cross it, and only light fires in the designated fire rings.
huntington.season: September to October: the last south swells, more frequent offshore winds, water still warm and less crowded beaches.

around.d: A long historic pier from which you can watch surfers riding on either side.
Coastal wetlands crossed by trails, rich in migratory birds.
A marina, the Balboa Peninsula and surf beaches south of Huntington.
A Victorian wooden pavilion on the harbour, departure point for ferries and boat trips.

oceanbeachsf.vibe: Ocean Beach is San Francisco’s cold, uncompromising surf: fog, a thick wetsuit all year round and long paddles against the sandbars. Surfers from the Sunset and the Richmond form a tough, low-key community here.
food: Clam chowder in a sourdough bowl
A creamy clam soup served in a sourdough loaf, the city’s signature dish.
oceanbeachsf.respect: Rip currents here are formidable and the beach isn’t lifeguarded the way others are: don’t go without solid experience, and keep dogs away from the plovers in the dunes.
oceanbeachsf.season: September to November: more frequent offshore winds, less fog and the first clean north-west swells.

around.d: A clifftop trail through cypresses and the ruins of the Sutro Baths, with views of the Golden Gate.
A huge urban park of lakes, gardens, museums and windmills that runs all the way to the beach.
A landscaped garden with a pagoda, an arched bridge and a teahouse, in the heart of Golden Gate Park.
A former estate perched on the cliff, with a clear view over Ocean Beach.
A Pacifica headland with ridge trails, facing the ocean.

steamerlane.vibe: Santa Cruz is one of the birthplaces of surfing on the American mainland: Hawaiian princes are said to have ridden waves here as early as the late 19th century, and Jack O’Neill developed his wetsuits here. Below the lighthouse, Steamer Lane peels at the foot of the cliffs.
steamerlane.respect: Steamer Lane is a very localised, rocky peak: only go out if you can handle the entry from the cliffs, respect priority scrupulously and keep your distance from the sea otters.
steamerlane.season: September to November: the first north-west swells, more frequent offshore winds and less fog than in summer.

around.d: A small museum set in the lighthouse, telling the story of local surfing.
A natural arch in the sea, rock pools at low tide and a grove where monarch butterflies overwinter.
Trails beneath giant coast redwoods, along the San Lorenzo River.
A historic beachfront amusement park, with the Giant Dipper wooden roller coaster.
A former ranch with trails along wild cliffs and unspoilt coves.

lapuntilla.vibe: A chic seaside resort from the early 20th century, with its old casino and palm park, Pichilemu has become Chile’s surf capital: schools, boards and fishing boats share the point.
lapuntilla.respect: La Puntilla hosts the surf schools: give priority to locals at the peak and note the town’s tsunami evacuation signs.
lapuntilla.season: March to May: consistent southern swells, wind often calm in the morning and beaches emptied after the Chilean summer.

around.d: A lagoon-side village known for its traditional salt pans and sea salt.
The old Ross casino, a Belle Époque building converted into a cultural centre.
A garden of palms and clipped hedges facing the ocean, the historic heart of the resort.
The town’s highest point, topped by a cross, with views over the bay and the points.
A coastal lagoon behind the beach, frequented by water birds.

infiernillo.vibe: At the foot of Cerro La Cruz, Infiernillo shows Pichilemu’s other face: a more exposed, less urban beach, where you come to surf away from the schools and watch the sun sink into the Pacific.
infiernillo.respect: The current is strong and the beach rarely lifeguarded: don’t surf alone and follow the tsunami evacuation signs to higher ground.
infiernillo.season: March to May: consistent southern swells, wind often calm in the morning and beaches emptied after the Chilean summer.

around.d: A lagoon-side village known for its traditional salt pans and sea salt.
The town’s highest point, topped by a cross, with views over the bay and the points.
The old Ross casino, a Belle Époque building converted into a cultural centre.
A garden of palms and clipped hedges facing the ocean, the historic heart of the resort.

matanzas.vibe: A small fishing village in the commune of Navidad, Matanzas has seen windsurfers and kitesurfers arrive, drawn by the south-westerly afternoon wind. Here the dry hills plunge straight into the ocean.
matanzas.respect: On the shore, the fishermen’s boats have priority: rig well away from their caleta and avoid sailing among swimmers in summer.
matanzas.season: March to May: consistent southern swells, windless mornings for surfing and a calm beach after summer.

around.d: A river whose mouth forms a dune-lined lagoon, good for birdwatching.
Sea cliffs rich in fossils, a true geological archive of the coast.

puertecillo.vibe: At the end of a long track through the hills, Puertecillo is still an isolated hamlet of huts and surf camps, with no town around it: people come for its left-hander and the silence of the coast.
puertecillo.respect: Services are almost non-existent: bring water and food, take all your rubbish with you and respect the private land the track crosses.
puertecillo.season: March to May: consistent southern swells, wind often calm in the morning and a track more passable than in winter.

renaca.vibe: Viña del Mar’s iconic beach, Reñaca lines up its stepped apartment blocks clinging to the hillside. In summer, Santiago’s youth gather here; the rest of the year, surfers and bodyboarders take the beach back.
renaca.respect: In summer, swimming is supervised by lifeguards: surf outside the marked zones and give priority to local bodyboarders at the peaks.
renaca.season: April to September: more consistent south-west swells and a beach handed back to locals outside summer.

around.d: A wooded park home to the Vergara Palace and the amphitheatre of the Viña festival.
A vertical lift in Valparaíso cut into the hillside, with views over the city.
A small 1906 castle set on the rocks, facing the waves of Viña del Mar.
Forests and trails around a reservoir lake, a bird refuge near the coast.
A neighbouring resort known for its dunes and seafood restaurants.

elabanico.vibe: Maitencillo stretches out below cliffs from which paragliders take off. A resort of second homes and cabañas, it keeps a family-friendly, sporty feel, far from the concrete of Viña del Mar.
elabanico.respect: El Abanico breaks close to the rocks: watch the line-up before going in and park in the designated spaces, not in front of residents’ entrances.
elabanico.season: April to September: consistent south-west swells and quiet beaches outside the summer season.

around.d: An elegant resort with villas nestled in greenery, and a coastal path over the rocks.

around.n: Church of Our Lady of Mercy, Papudo
around.d: A church listed as a historic monument in the seaside town of Papudo.
A small seaside port at the head of a bay, with its beaches and seafront.

canggu.vibe: Between rice fields nibbled away by cafés and black-sand beaches, Canggu blends an international surf scene with Balinese village life: on Batu Bolong beach, a small temple still receives offerings and ceremonies.
hello: a Balinese Hindu greeting that wishes peace and blessings
food: Babi guling
Suckling pig roasted with Balinese spices, served with rice and spicy vegetables.
canggu.respect: Ceremonies take place on the beach near Batu Bolong temple: stay back, and at the peak let Balinese surfers go first.
canggu.season: April to October: dry season, south-east trade winds blowing offshore on the west coast and consistent southern swells.

around.d: Mengwi’s royal temple surrounded by moats, with tiered meru pagodas.
A sea temple perched on a cliff, famous for its kecak dance at sunset.
Palace-style pavilions showcasing Balinese art, costumes and ritual objects.
A village renowned for its meticulous painting style and its carved temple.
The Sanur home of Belgian painter Le Mayeur, with his canvases and Balinese objects.

kuta.vibe: A former fishing village turned Bali’s tourist heart, Kuta is the beach where generations of travellers caught their first wave. At sunset, schools, vendors and Balinese families take over the sand.
hello: a Balinese Hindu greeting that wishes peace and blessings
food: Babi guling
Suckling pig roasted with Balinese spices, served with rice and spicy vegetables.
kuta.respect: Surf in the zones marked out by lifeguards, away from the schools. On Nyepi, the Balinese New Year, the whole island observes silence: nobody on the beach.
kuta.season: April to October: dry season and a south-easterly wind blowing offshore on the west coast beach breaks.

around.d: A fishing village known for its fish market and its beach barbecues.
Palace-style pavilions showcasing Balinese art, costumes and ritual objects.
A Hindu temple on Serangan Island, a major pilgrimage site during the great festivals.
The Sanur home of Belgian painter Le Mayeur, with his canvases and Balinese objects.
A park on the Bukit dominated by a giant statue of Vishnu riding Garuda.

medewi.vibe: Far from the bustle of the south, Medewi is a village in west Bali where the rice fields almost touch the pebble beach. Fishermen haul their outrigger canoes up the sand here, next to the surfers.
hello: a Balinese Hindu greeting that wishes peace and blessings
medewi.respect: The bottom is made of pebbles and rocks: bring booties, and make room for the fishermen launching their canoes.
medewi.season: April to October: dry season, offshore wind in the morning and southern swells that make the left peel.

around.d: A sea temple perched above the ocean, linked to the priest Nirartha.
A sea temple marking the spot where Nirartha is said to have landed in Bali.
The capital of Jembrana, known for its buffalo cart races, the makepung.

selongbelanak.vibe: A big white-sand bay ringed by hills, Selong Belanak lives to the rhythm of the Sasak villages: at the end of the day, buffalo cross the beach while the last students come out of the water.
food: Ayam taliwang and plecing kangkung
Fiery grilled chicken and water spinach with sambal, two Lombok classics.
selongbelanak.respect: Lombok is mostly Muslim: cover your shoulders and knees away from the beach, especially in the villages and during Ramadan.
selongbelanak.season: April to October: dry season, offshore trade winds and southern swells that roll gently into the bay.

kohtao.vibe: “Turtle Island” has become one of the world’s great dive training centres. Between coconut groves, granite coves and dive boats, island life revolves around the morning trips.
kohtao.respect: Several of the island’s clubs are restoring the coral: keep your fins away from the reef, don’t feed the fish and don’t pick up shells or coral.
kohtao.season: March to September: calm sea and good visibility; from October to December, the monsoon churns up the gulf.

kohlipe.vibe: In the heart of Tarutao Marine Park, Ko Lipe is home to a village of the Urak Lawoi, sea nomads who have long lived by fishing. Longtail boats link the reefs of the neighbouring islets.
kohlipe.respect: You’re in a national marine park: pay the entrance fees, never walk on the coral at low tide and respect the Urak Lawoi village.
kohlipe.season: November to April: calm Andaman Sea and crystal-clear water; during the monsoon, boats become scarce.

moalboal.vibe: Panagsama is just one street of dive clubs and simple eateries along the reef, but a few metres from shore, huge schools of sardines swirl. Fishermen’s bangkas still set off from the shore every morning.
hello: “good morning” in Cebuano, the language of the Visayas
food: Cebu lechon
Roast suckling pig with crispy skin, stuffed with lemongrass, the island’s pride.
moalboal.respect: Don’t chase the sardine school and let the turtles surface to breathe: no touching, and pay the small municipal reef protection fee.
moalboal.season: December to May: dry season, calm sea and good visibility; the sardines are there all year round.

around.d: A protected limestone islet ringed by coral walls teeming with fish.
Tiered waterfalls with turquoise pools, deep in the jungle above Badian.
A castle-like monastery, Cebu’s great Marian pilgrimage site.

malapascua.vibe: With no cars or tarmac roads, Malapascua lives between fishing villages and dive clubs. Before dawn, bangkas head out to a shoal where thresher sharks come to be cleaned.
hello: “good morning” in Cebuano, the language of the Visayas
food: Cebu lechon
Roast suckling pig with crispy skin, stuffed with lemongrass, the island’s pride.
malapascua.respect: With thresher sharks, no flash and no torch pointed at them: stay behind the line set by the guides and don’t approach the cleaning station.
malapascua.season: March to May: calm sea and visibility at its best; thresher sharks appear at dawn all year round.

apoisland.vibe: A small volcanic fishing island, Apo was one of the first marine reserves managed by the community itself, with support from Silliman University. The result: intact corals and turtles with every fin kick.
hello: “good morning” in Cebuano, the language of the Visayas
apoisland.respect: The sanctuary is managed by the islanders: pay the fee on arrival, stay out of the no-go zone and keep your distance from the turtles.
apoisland.season: March to May: calm sea, warm water and excellent visibility, before the monsoon winds arrive.

around.d: A coastal village with marine sanctuaries renowned for black-sand macro diving.
A lively university town with its seafront promenade, Rizal Boulevard.
St Catherine’s Cathedral, flanked by an old stone bell tower.
An American-style wooden building, now Silliman University’s museum.

coron.vibe: Coron Bay holds the wrecks of a Japanese fleet sunk in 1944. Above the water, the limestone cliffs of Coron Island belong to the ancestral domain of the Tagbanwa, who guard its lakes.
coron.respect: Take nothing from the wrecks and only go inside them with the right training. On Coron Island, follow the rules set by the Tagbanwa.
coron.season: November to May: dry season, calm sea in the bay and the best visibility on the wrecks.

around.d: A brackish lake with crystal-clear water nestled between cliffs, managed by the Tagbanwa.
A jagged karst island with turquoise lagoons and hidden lakes.

bondi.vibe: Bondi saw the birth of one of Australia’s first lifesaving clubs, and its lifesavers in red and yellow are part of the scenery. Between the old pavilion and the seawater pool cut into the rocks, Sydney comes to swim, surf and run.
bondi.respect: Surfers have their own zone, marked separately from the swimming flags: respect it, and beware of the powerful rip current at the south end of the beach.
bondi.season: March to June: more consistent south and east swells, offshore westerlies in the morning and water still warm.

around.d: Headlands and coastal trails around Cook’s 1770 landing site.
A fortified islet at La Perouse linked by a footbridge, popular with divers.
A former military site turned natural area, with a clifftop trail.
A vast dune field south of Botany Bay, the last of its kind in Sydney.

freshwater.vibe: This is where Hawaiian Duke Kahanamoku gave a legendary surfing demonstration in the summer of 1914–1915: his board is kept at the surf lifesaving club and his statue watches over the headland.
freshwater.respect: The bay is small and the line-up close-knit: wait your turn at the peak and leave the area between the flags to swimmers and families.
freshwater.season: March to June: consistent south and east swells, offshore westerlies in the morning and water still warm.

around.d: Historic buildings and passenger graffiti, on a headland facing the harbour.
A headland joined by a tombolo, with protected rock platforms and seabirds.
A sandstone lighthouse at the tip of Palm Beach, reached by a trail with panoramic views.
Bushland and a reservoir surrounded by walking and mountain-bike trails.
19th-century batteries and tunnels at the entrance to Sydney Harbour.

noosa.vibe: Recognised as a “World Surfing Reserve”, Noosa is a temple of longboarding: its right-handers wrap along the national park, in front of the pandanus trees. Longboard surf culture still reigns here.
noosa.respect: On the crowded points, paddle around the line-up rather than through the wave’s path, and don’t cut in front of those waiting. Leave the park’s koalas in peace.
