noosa.season: February to May: cyclone and south-east swells that light up the points, with water still warm.

around.d: A coastal trail between coves and forest, where you may meet koalas and dolphins.
The lakes and meanders of the Noosa Everglades, to explore by canoe.
A long wild beach below cliffs of coloured sands, reached by 4WD.
A steep climb to a summit with views over the whole Sunshine Coast.

cottesloe.vibe: Perth’s iconic beach, Mudurup in Noongar, Cottesloe brings together swimmers, surfers and sunset crowds on the Indian Ocean. Every year, the Sculpture by the Sea exhibition sets up its works on the sand.
cottesloe.respect: A very busy swimming beach: surf away from swimmers and get out of the water straight away when the shark alarm sounds.
cottesloe.season: May to September: stronger southern winter swells and mornings without the sea breeze, the “Fremantle Doctor”.

around.d: A car-free island of turquoise coves, to explore by bike among the quokkas.
A large sandbar reaching out into the Swan River, good for swimming.
A Second World War coastal battery and its tunnels, on Buckland Hill.
An underwater tunnel and tanks showcasing the wildlife of the state’s coasts.

whangamata.vibe: A resort of baches, the Kiwi holiday homes, Whangamatā lives to the rhythm of its bar, a renowned left at the mouth of the estuary. In summer the little town fills up; the rest of the year, surfers and anglers share it.
whangamata.respect: On the bar, wait your turn behind the locals. On the beaches, walk around the marked nesting areas of the New Zealand dotterels.
whangamata.season: February to May: cyclone and east swells, water still warm and beaches free of holidaymakers.

around.d: A former gold town whose huge Martha Mine pit can be seen from a lookout.
A wild pine-fringed beach and protected sand spit, a refuge for shorebirds.
An island off the coast, popular with boaters and anglers.
An estuary village overlooked by Mount Paku, which you can climb for views of the coast.

mountmaunganui.vibe: At the foot of Mauao, an extinct volcano sacred to the iwi of Tauranga, “the Mount” blends Kiwi beach culture, a surf lifesaving club and joggers circling the mountain at dawn.
mountmaunganui.respect: Mauao is an ancestral Māori site: stay on the marked trails. At the beach, surf outside the lifeguarded swimming flags.
mountmaunganui.season: March to June: more consistent east and north-east swells, frequent offshore winds and a quiet beach after summer.

around.d: A volcanic dome to climb or walk around, with views over the Bay of Plenty.
A rocky islet linked to the beach, with a blowhole that roars in big swells.
A harbour city on the lagoon, with a lively waterfront and markets.
A museum of vintage aircraft at Tauranga airport.

kealakekua.vibe: A sacred bay on the Kona coast, Kealakekua is home to Hikiau temple and the white obelisk marking the spot where Captain Cook was killed in 1779. Spinner dolphins come to rest here above the protected reef.
food: Kona coffee
Grown on the volcanic slopes above the bay, to taste at the growers’ farms.
kealakekua.respect: Stay more than 45 metres from the dolphins, as federal rules require. Paddling to the Cook monument requires a permit: check before you go.
kealakekua.season: April to October: generally calm sea on the Kona side and crystal-clear water in the morning, before the afternoon wind.

around.n: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau National Historical Park
around.d: An ancient Hawaiian place of refuge, with a reconstructed temple and carved wooden tiki statues.
A small wooden church whose interior walls are entirely painted with biblical scenes.
A restored coffee farm telling the story of Japanese farming families.
A shallow bay protected by a breakwater, ideal for swimming among turtles.
A former summer residence of Hawaiian royalty, now a museum in Kailua-Kona.

poipu.vibe: On the sunny south coast of Kauaʻi, land of Kōloa’s old sugar plantations, Poʻipū sees green turtles and Hawaiian monk seals come to rest on the sand, next to the remains of an ancient Hawaiian village.
food: Poke
Cubes of raw fish marinated in soy sauce and sesame oil, a Hawaiian speciality.
poipu.respect: If a monk seal is sleeping on the beach, stay well back behind the marked-off area. Hawaii bans sunscreens containing oxybenzone: choose a mineral sunscreen.
poipu.season: November to March: the south coast stays calm while the north takes the winter swells, ideal for snorkelling.

around.d: A lava blowhole that shoots up plumes of water with every wave.
A tropical garden in a valley running down to the sea, by guided tour.
A wild coast of fossilised dunes and coves, followed by a coastal trail.
Hawaii’s largest limestone cave, a true archive of vanished wildlife.
A small town of colourful wooden façades, known for its art galleries and swinging bridge.

labaule.vibe: A seaside resort born with the railway, La Baule lines up Belle Époque villas and pines behind its long beach, a stone’s throw from the salt workers who harvest Guérande salt.
food: Guérande fleur de sel
Harvested by hand by the salt workers, it lifts fish, galettes and caramels.
labaule.respect: In summer, launch and come back in through the marked channels: the strip along the shore is reserved for swimmers.
labaule.season: June to September: a sheltered bay, often calm sea in the morning and the water at its mildest.

around.d: A mosaic of salt pans where the salt workers harvest salt the traditional way.
Complete ramparts, fortified gates and cobbled lanes around the collegiate church.

around.n: Wild coast of the Guérande peninsula
around.d: A coastal path between rocks, coves and sea caves.
A fishing port with shipowners’ houses and quays buzzing at the fish auction.
A Second World War bunker turned into a place for visits and exhibitions.

hendaye.vibe: A border town set on the Bidassoa bay, Hendaye lives on Basque time: a shuttle boat to Hondarribia, pelota at the fronton and a gentle wave where many learned to surf.
hello: “hi” in Basque, said with a smile
food: Gâteau basque
Shortcrust pastry filled with pastry cream or black cherry jam.
hendaye.respect: The beach hosts lots of schools: give beginners space and surf away from the lifeguarded swimming areas.
hendaye.season: September to November: more consistent autumn swells, still-mild water and a quieter line-up.

around.d: The neo-Gothic castle of a scholar and explorer, perched on the cliff road.
A walled old town with colourful balconies, reached by the bay shuttle boat.
La Concha bay, the old town and renowned pintxos bars.
A coastal ridge with sculpted sandstone cliffs, a fine hike facing the ocean.
A Basque village of white houses with red shutters, at the foot of La Rhune.

morgat.vibe: A former sardine port turned seaside resort, Morgat nestles at the head of its bay; the cliffs of coloured rock and the sea caves reveal themselves from water level.
food: Kouign-amann
Born in Douarnenez, just across the bay, this flaky cake oozes butter and sugar.
morgat.respect: Only enter the caves when the sea is calm and take no rocks: the coastline is protected for its geology.
morgat.season: May to September: a bay sheltered from westerly winds, often calm sea and long days for following the cliffs.

around.d: Dizzying cliffs facing the Tas de Pois rocks, at the tip of the peninsula.
Wild heathland and a coastal path above the Atlantic.
A crayfish port with a shingle spit, a chapel and a listed Vauban tower.
A heathland summit with a 360° view over the Bay of Douarnenez.
Remains of a medieval abbey and a museum on the banks of the Aulne.

saintjeandeluz.vibe: A tuna port of red and green half-timbered houses, Saint-Jean-de-Luz saw the wedding of Louis XIV; its bay, closed off by sea walls, offers calm water right in the heart of town.
hello: “hi” in Basque, said with a smile
food: Ttoro
A fish and shellfish soup handed down from the town’s fishermen.
saintjeandeluz.respect: On a paddleboard, keep clear of the harbour channel used by fishing boats, and of the lifeguarded swimming areas.
saintjeandeluz.season: June to September: the bay, protected by its sea walls, stays calm and the water reaches its mildest.

around.d: Colourful quays, Ravel’s birthplace and the Socoa fort facing the bay.
Façades hung with drying chillies and shops selling Basque produce.
The neo-Gothic castle of a scholar and explorer, on the Hendaye cliff road.
A Basque village at the foot of La Rhune, with a fronton and an old bridge.
A former whaling port with understated charm, known for its big wave.

bourget.vibe: France’s largest natural lake, sung by Lamartine, Le Bourget brings together lavaret fishermen, a spa town and a lakeside abbey, beneath the cliff of Mont du Chat.
food: Lavaret fillet
A white fish caught in the lake, served meunière by the water.
bourget.respect: Steer round the reed beds along the shore, which are protected nesting areas, and keep an eye on the wind, which can quickly whip up a chop.
bourget.season: June to September: pleasant water for swimming, calm mornings before the afternoon breeze.

around.d: A lakeside abbey, burial place of the princes of the House of Savoy.
A balcony over the Bauges with a plunging view of the lake and Mont Blanc.
A spa town with Belle Époque grand hotels and Roman remains.
An old town, the Elephant Fountain and the castle of the Dukes of Savoy.
Alpine pastures, forests and hiking trails in an unspoilt massif.

serreponcon.vibe: Created by a dam on the Durance, the lake swallowed the old villages of Ubaye and Savines; the Saint-Michel chapel rises from its islet, facing the peaks.
food: Tourtons
Small filled fritters, with potato or prunes, typical of the Hautes-Alpes.
serreponcon.respect: The lake level varies with the running of the dam: avoid exposed muddy banks and pick out your exit point in advance.
serreponcon.season: June to early September: a full lake, pleasant water and a lighter thermal breeze in the morning.

around.d: A restored Romanesque abbey in a wooded valley above the lake.
A great forest of larch and fir, with trails up to the Morgon cirque.
A small town perched on its rock, with old lanes and the Tour Brune.
A Romanesque cathedral of two-tone stone with a lion porch.
A village rebuilt on the shore, the starting point for boat trips.

saintecroix.vibe: A reservoir lake created on the Verdon, which drowned the old village of Les Salles, rebuilt higher up; its turquoise waters border a land of lavender and faience.
food: Lavender honey
Harvested beside the fields of the Valensole plateau, to buy at the markets.
saintecroix.respect: On the park’s shores, no fires and no wild camping; in the lower gorges, paddle in single file on your right and don’t stop in the narrow passages.
saintecroix.season: June to September: pleasant turquoise water; set off early to avoid the crowds and the afternoon wind.

around.d: A spectacular canyon of limestone cliffs, viewpoints and trails.
A village of faience makers clinging to the cliff, beneath its hanging star.
Lavender fields in bloom in early summer, among almond trees and wheat.
A hilltop village with a glazed-tile castle and a view over the whole lake.
Columns of a Roman temple and an early Christian baptistery.

donnant.vibe: On the wild coast where Monet painted the needles of Port-Coton, Donnant tucks its beach between dunes and cliffs; the island’s surf community gathers here as soon as a westerly swell rolls in.
food: Crêpes and buckwheat galettes
A galette complète or a salted-butter crêpe, with a bowl of cider.
donnant.respect: The Donnant dunes are protected: use the marked access paths, and beware of strong currents near the rocks.
donnant.season: September to November: consistent westerly swells, still-mild water and a calmer island after summer.

around.d: A wild headland pounded by the swell, with a lighthouse and flowering heath.
A star-shaped fortress overlooking the harbour, with ramparts and a museum.
A small harbour of colourful houses, tucked at the end of its ria.
The great lighthouse of the wild coast, near the needles of Port-Coton.
A small fort where the great tragic actress used to stay, facing the ocean.

laconcha.vibe: A Basque city of Belle Époque elegance, Donostia lives facing its bay: year-round swimming, rowing clubs and trainera regattas that bring the whole city together in September.
hello: “hi” in Basque, said with a smile
food: Pintxos
Small bites on bread, to graze on from bar to bar in the old town.
laconcha.respect: Launch outside the marked swimming areas; at the pintxos bar, say what you had when you pay.
laconcha.season: June to September: a bay sheltered by Santa Clara Island, warmer water and a sea often glassy in the morning.

around.n: Mount Urgull and La Mota Castle
around.d: A wooded hill and fortress with views over the bay and the city.
A museum of Basque society in a former convent in the old town.
A small island in the middle of the bay, reachable by boat in summer.
A fishing port of fish grills, home town of Elcano and Balenciaga.
A wooded coastal path between Donostia and Pasaia, above the cliffs.

macarella.vibe: On an island designated a biosphere reserve, Macarella reveals its white sand at the end of a pine-filled ravine; all around, navetas and talayots recall a unique prehistory.
hello: “good morning” in Catalan, the island’s language
food: Mahón cheese
A cow’s milk cheese with an orange rind, mild or aged, the emblem of the island.
macarella.respect: In summer, road access is restricted: come by bus or on foot along the Camí de Cavalls, and don’t trample the posidonia seagrass meadows.
macarella.season: June to September: warm, clear water; arrive early to enjoy the cove before the crowds.

around.d: A historic path that circles the island from cove to cove.
A cove of pale sand between cliffs and pines, with turquoise water.
A prehistoric tomb shaped like an upturned boat hull.
A large Talayotic village with towers, an enclosure and hypostyle halls.
The island’s highest point, with a sanctuary and a view over all of Menorca.

arrabida.vibe: Limestone cliffs covered in scrub plunging into turquoise water: the Romans were already salting fish here, and the dolphins of the Sado estuary cruise offshore.
food: Choco frito
Cuttlefish fried in strips, the speciality of Setúbal’s taverns.
arrabida.respect: The coastline is a marine reserve: take nothing from underwater and, in summer, use the shuttle bus, as car access is limited.
arrabida.season: June to September: a south-facing coast sheltered from the north wind, with clear, calm water for following the cliffs.

around.d: A serra covered in scrub, panoramic roads and a convent on the slopes.
Dizzying cliffs, a remote sanctuary and dinosaur footprints.
A lively fishing port, a town beach and grilled fish on the seafront.
A church with twisted columns, a milestone of Manueline art.
Remains of a Roman fish-salting factory.

maspalomas.vibe: At the tip of the island, a desert of golden dunes spills into the Atlantic at the foot of a century-old lighthouse; behind the touristy seafront, ravines and Canarian villages keep their calm.
food: Papas arrugadas with mojo
Small potatoes boiled in salted water, served with red and green mojo.
maspalomas.respect: In the dune reserve, stay on the marked trails and don’t build stone shelters: it is forbidden.
maspalomas.season: May to October: southerly swells wake up the south coast and the water reaches its mildest.

around.d: A nature reserve of shifting dunes and the Charca lagoon.
A volcanic monolith at the heart of the island, with a hike and a view of Mount Teide.
A white village at the bottom of a ravine of palms and ochre rock.
A harbour of flower-decked houses and canals, nicknamed Little Venice.
A green gorge with cave houses and Canarian caves.

balos.vibe: A lagoon of clear water and pink-tinged sand, facing the islet of Gramvousa and its Venetian fort, a former pirate hideout; you get there by dirt track or by caique from Kissamos.
food: Dakos
A Cretan barley rusk topped with tomato, mizithra and olive oil.
balos.respect: A Natura 2000 site: take neither sand nor shells, and stay off the dunes and the marked-off areas of the lagoon.
balos.season: June to September: warm, clear water; in June and September, fewer excursion boats.

around.d: A big sandy beach facing the sunset and the remains of an ancient harbour.
Ruins of a hilltop ancient city, with a view over the Gulf of Kissamos.
A seaside Orthodox monastery with icons and a small museum.
A small coastal town with seafront tavernas and boat departures.

brela.vibe: Below the cliffs of Biokovo, Brela lines up pebble coves and pines leaning over a crystal-clear Adriatic; higher up, the old stone village recalls a life of shepherds and fishermen.
food: Peka
Meat or octopus slow-cooked under a cast-iron bell covered in embers.
brela.respect: The pines come right down to the water: no fires or barbecues on the coast, the fire risk is very high in summer.
brela.season: June to September: warm, clear sea, glassy in the morning before the afternoon maestral.

around.d: A limestone massif towering over the coast, with mountain roads and trails.
Biokovo’s summit, with a view of the Dalmatian islands on a clear day.
A former pirate hideout at the mouth of the Cetina gorge.
A village of Brač white-stone masons, at the head of a bay.
A seaside resort with a small harbour and a promenade along the beaches.

diani.vibe: On the Swahili coast, Diani lines up white sand and a lagoon protected by the reef; the outrigger canoes of Digo fishermen cross paths with kites, and colobus monkeys live in the coastal forest.
food: Viazi karai
Potatoes fried in a turmeric batter, a street snack of the Swahili coast.
diani.respect: Don’t feed the colobus and vervet monkeys, and don’t walk on the reef at low tide.
diani.season: June to September (kusi) and December to March (kaskazi): steady monsoon winds over the lagoon.

around.d: Hills of forest and savannah, home to elephants and sable antelope.
A community corridor for elephants, among baobabs and a river.

tofo.vibe: A fishing village turned divers’ stopover, Tofo lives between the fish market, beach bars and trips offshore to meet manta rays and whale sharks.
tofo.respect: With whale sharks and manta rays, no contact: keep your distance, don’t chase them and avoid using a flash.
tofo.season: All year round for mantas and whale sharks; from June to October, humpback whales pass offshore.

around.d: A peaceful old colonial town, with a market and dhows on the bay.
A sandy point between ocean and mangroves, topped by a lighthouse.

paje.vibe: A Swahili village of coral-stone houses, Paje lives by the tides: at low tide, women farm seaweed on the lagoon that kites cross at high tide.
paje.respect: Paje is a Muslim village: cover your shoulders and knees away from the beach, and kite around the seaweed farms.
paje.season: June to September (kusi) and December to February (kaskazi): steady trade winds over the lagoon.

around.d: Forest and mangroves, home to the red colobus monkey, endemic to Zanzibar.
A fishing village in the south, known for the dolphins offshore.
One of the oldest mosques in East Africa, with Kufic inscriptions.
A neighbouring coastal village with a turquoise lagoon and seaweed farms.

anselazio.vibe: Sculpted granite boulders, leaning takamaka trees and translucent water: Anse Lazio sums up the granite coast of the Seychelles, on an island where the legendary coco de mer grows.
anselazio.respect: Don’t collect shells or coral, which are protected in the Seychelles, and don’t feed the fish when snorkelling.
anselazio.season: April to May and October to November: between the two monsoons, a calm sea and the clearest water.

around.d: A primeval forest of coco de mer palms, where you may hear the black parrot.
A national park with giant tortoises, mangroves and a coastal trail.
A beach on La Digue with pinkish granite boulders and shallow water.
A seabird reserve where hawksbill turtles also nest.
A wild neighbouring beach of white sand and granite rocks.

balandra.vibe: On the Sea of Cortez, a shallow bay of turquoise water, fringed by mangroves and desert hills, watched over by the mushroom-shaped rock that is the emblem of La Paz.
food: Almejas chocolatas
Big clams from the Sea of Cortez, baked au gratin or cooked in their shells.
balandra.respect: Don’t climb the fragile mushroom rock; access to the protected area is limited, so come early and take your rubbish away with you.
balandra.season: April to June and October to November: the sea is often calm, outside the winter north winds.

around.d: A protected desert island: coves, red cliffs and a sea lion colony.
A long beach facing Espíritu Santo Island, with fish palapas.
A malecón buzzing at sunset, a cathedral and marisquerías.

lajolla.vibe: Between the Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the cliffs of La Jolla, a neighbourhood turned towards the sea: surf schools, divers exploring the underwater canyon and sea lions on the rocks.
food: California burrito
Carne asada and fries rolled up in a tortilla, a San Diego invention.
lajolla.respect: In the underwater reserve, nothing may be taken; keep your distance from the sea lions and seals at the Cove.
lajolla.season: July to September: the warmest water, an often calm sea and harmless leopard sharks in the shallows.

around.d: A marine reserve of kelp forests, garibaldis and a deep canyon.
The Scripps Institution’s aquarium, with kelp tanks and ocean views.
A small beach sheltered by a sea wall, taken over by seals.
A historic surf spot with sandstone reefs and a palm-frond shack.
A clifftop path above the sea caves of La Jolla.

cabopulmo.vibe: A fishing village that switched to protecting its reef, Cabo Pulmo has seen schools of jacks, rays and sharks return since its marine park was created on the Sea of Cortez.
cabopulmo.respect: In the national park, no fishing and no contact with the reef; dive only with an authorised operator.
cabopulmo.season: August to November: warm water and visibility often at its best; in spring, the sea can be windy.

akumal.vibe: Akumal means “place of the turtles” in Maya: its reef-sheltered bays hold seagrass meadows where green turtles graze, and cenotes hide in the jungle.
food: Cochinita pibil
Pork marinated in annatto and bitter orange, slow-cooked in its own steam.
akumal.respect: In the bay, follow the marked routes wearing a life jacket, without touching or chasing the turtles, and with a sunscreen free of chemical filters.
akumal.season: November to April: the dry season, an often clear sea and less sargassum than in summer.

around.d: A natural inlet where fresh water and sea mingle, set up as a water park.
A long white-sand beach lined with palms, and quieter.

cozumel.vibe: An island where Maya women came on pilgrimage to the goddess Ixchel, Cozumel has become a legendary name in diving, with its drifts along coral walls.
food: Tikin-xic
Fish marinated in annatto and cooked in a banana leaf, a Maya recipe.
cozumel.respect: The marine park requires a licensed guide: don’t touch the reef, no gloves, and let yourself drift without holding on to the coral.
cozumel.season: April to July: calm sea, warm water and excellent visibility, before the hurricane season.

around.d: Coral walls and arches among the island’s flagship dive sites.
A marine protected area covering the great reefs of the southwest.
A wild point with a lighthouse, a lagoon and turtle nesting beaches.
The island’s small town, with a malecón, a main square and evening tacos.

holbox.vibe: A car-free island of sandy streets and mural-painted façades, Holbox lives between fishing, a lagoon with pink flamingos and, in summer, whale sharks passing offshore.
food: Lobster pizza
A thin crust topped with local lobster, the island’s culinary curiosity.
holbox.respect: In the Yum Balam reserve, don’t go near the flamingos; on the island, get around on foot, by bike or by golf cart.
holbox.season: March to June: lighter wind for paddling in the lagoon and the mangroves, before the summer rains.

buzios.vibe: A former fishing village put on the map by Brigitte Bardot in the 1960s, Búzios mixes colourful boats, lanes that come alive at night and some twenty beaches on its peninsula.
buzios.respect: Geribá gets very busy in summer: surf away from swimmers, respect the regulars at the peak and leave nothing unattended on the sand.
buzios.season: May to September: more consistent southern swells on Geribá and a far less crowded beach than in summer.

arraialdocabo.vibe: Nicknamed Brazil’s diving capital, Arraial do Cabo still lives from small-scale fishing, with its boats hauled up on the sand and its cool waters rising from the depths.
arraialdocabo.respect: In the marine reserve, fishing is reserved for small-scale fishermen: take nothing, don’t feed the fish and keep your fins well away from the bottom.
arraialdocabo.season: April to June: the summer crowds are gone and the sea is often calm; bring a wetsuit, as the upwelling of cold water cools the sea.

around.d: A protected island with turquoise water and Farol beach, reachable by boat.
A protected coastline where the dive sites and small-scale fishing are concentrated.
A seaside town with its colonial fort, dunes and long white-sand beaches.
Unspoilt lagoons, dunes and restinga along the Lakes Region.

ilhagrande.vibe: A former prison island long kept apart, Ilha Grande has no roads for cars: you get around on foot or by boat, between Atlantic forest and fishing villages.
ilhagrande.respect: Stay on the park’s marked trails, carry your rubbish back down to Abraão and don’t feed the monkeys.
ilhagrande.season: April to June and September: less rain than in summer, an often calm sea and quieter trails.

around.d: Atlantic forest crossed by trails to the beaches and Papagaio Peak.
A remote fishing village and wild beach on the coast facing the open sea.
The island’s main village, with its church, harbour and boat departures.

sanandres.vibe: On the island, the Raizal culture, English-speaking Creole and Protestant, sits alongside the duty-free bustle of the centre; all around, the sea of seven colours changes shade above the reef.
food: Rondón
Fish, conch and root vegetables stewed in coconut milk, the quintessential Raizal dish.
sanandres.respect: The archipelago forms the Seaflower Biosphere Reserve: collect neither coral nor shells and don’t touch the rays on boat trips.
sanandres.season: February to April: the dry season, very clear water and blue skies; October and November are the rainiest months.

amed.vibe: A string of fishing villages below Mount Agung, Amed lives to the rhythm of the jukung returning at dawn and the salt makers who still harvest sea salt the traditional way.
hello: Balinese Hindu greeting, palms pressed together in front of the chest
food: Sate lilit
Skewers of spiced minced fish, wrapped around lemongrass stalks.
amed.respect: Don’t walk on the coral as you get into the water, and make way for the fishermen’s jukung landing on the pebbles.
amed.season: April to October: the dry season, a sea often glassy in the morning and good visibility in the bays.

around.d: A temple whose split gates frame Mount Agung, at the foot of Mount Lempuyang.
A dive village famous for the wreck of the USAT Liberty, accessible from the shore.
Bali’s sacred volcano, climbed at night to see the sunrise from the summit.
A Bali Aga village of ancient traditions, known for its double ikat weaving.
A former royal palace of Karangasem, with pavilions and pools facing the sea.

nusapenida.vibe: A dry limestone island that has stayed agricultural, Nusa Penida lives between seaweed plots farmed at the water’s edge, temples renowned for their spiritual power and cliffs plunging into the strait.
hello: Balinese Hindu greeting, palms pressed together in front of the chest
nusapenida.respect: Currents are powerful around the island: dive with a local centre, never touch the manta rays and keep your distance.
nusapenida.season: July to October: sunfish season and regular mantas, but cooler water and strong currents.

around.d: A neighbouring island of mangroves, beaches and surf reefs, a few minutes away by boat.
A temple built in front of a cave home to thousands of bats.
A small ferry port with white-sand coves, a good snorkelling spot.
A quiet seaside resort with a lagoon-side promenade and boats to the islands.

pemuteran.vibe: A dry, peaceful fishing village on the north coast, Pemuteran has reinvented itself around its reef, which locals protect and regrow together with the dive centres.
hello: Balinese Hindu greeting, palms pressed together in front of the chest
food: Sate lilit
Skewers of spiced minced fish, wrapped around lemongrass stalks.
pemuteran.respect: Don’t touch the metal structures in the bay: these artificial reefs, carrying a weak current, help the coral grow back.
pemuteran.season: April to November: the dry season, a very calm sea on the north coast and excellent visibility towards Menjangan.

around.d: An islet in the national park with coral walls, Bali’s benchmark for snorkelling.
Forests, savannah and mangroves, refuge of the rare Bali starling.
A temple backed against the cliff facing the sea, frequented by macaques.

nusalembongan.vibe: A small island of fishermen and seaweed farmers, Lembongan keeps its mangroves in the north and its colourful jukung, while the reefs of its west coast draw surfers.
hello: Balinese Hindu greeting, palms pressed together in front of the chest
nusalembongan.respect: On the shallow reefs, give locals priority; at low tide, don’t trample the farmers’ seaweed plots.
nusalembongan.season: April to October: consistent southern swells and easterly trade winds, often offshore on the west-coast reefs.

around.d: A former royal court of justice with a ceiling painted in the Kamasan style.
A temple built in front of a cave home to thousands of bats.
The Belgian painter’s beachside house and studio, with canvases and Balinese objects.
A quiet seaside resort with a lagoon-side promenade and boats to the islands.

elnido.vibe: El Nido’s name recalls the swiftlet nests gathered from its limestone cliffs; the fishing town now lives to the rhythm of the bangkas that set off each morning for the lagoons.
food: Tamilok
A mangrove worm served raw in vinegar, a Palawan curiosity for the curious.
elnido.respect: Keep the eco-tourism fee receipt on you during trips and don’t put your feet or paddle on the coral in the lagoons.
elnido.season: March to May: the dry season, a sea often glassy in the Bacuit archipelago and crystal-clear water in the lagoons.

phuquoc.vibe: A fishing island facing the Gulf of Thailand, Phú Quốc smells of pepper and of fish sauce fermenting in its wooden barrels, between the port of An Thới and the islets of the south.
food: Phú Quốc nước mắm
Anchovy sauce fermented in wooden barrels, the pride of the island.
phuquoc.respect: Don’t take starfish out of the water for photos and don’t stand on the coral around the An Thới islets.
phuquoc.season: November to April: the dry season, a calm sea in the south of the island and the best visibility around the islets.

abeltasman.vibe: Golden granite sand, clear water and fern forest: this coast bears the name of the Dutch navigator who sailed past in the 17th century, and you explore it by kayak, on foot or by water taxi.
abeltasman.respect: Book the park’s campsites and huts with DOC, take all your rubbish away and keep your distance from the seals on the rocks.
abeltasman.season: February to April: still-mild water, a sea often calm in the morning and fewer people than in the summer holidays.

around.d: A great coastal walk from bay to bay, to combine with kayaking.
A marine protected area where seals rest on the islet’s rocks.
A beach of golden sand and turquoise water, the southern gateway to the park.
A dizzying shaft in the karst of Takaka Hill, at the end of a short forest walk.
A long beach backed by a large campsite, in the north of the park.

cathedralcove.vibe: In the heart of Mercury Bay, named by James Cook, who came to observe the transit of Mercury, the coast of the Ngāti Hei lines up white cliffs, arches and islets sculpted by the sea.
cathedralcove.respect: In the marine reserve, fishing and collecting are forbidden; land without blocking the beach and respect any closures of the access track.
cathedralcove.season: December to March: the warmest water and an often calm sea; set off early, before the boats and the afternoon wind.

around.d: A beach where you dig your own pool in sand warmed by springs, at low tide.
A long white-sand beach facing Mercury Bay, ideal for swimming.
A small seaside town with a marina, a passenger ferry and boat departures.
A volcanic peak with a rocky summit, a short climb for a view over the peninsula.

rottnest.vibe: A car-free island you criss-cross by bike, Wadjemup keeps the painful memory of its former Aboriginal prison and is home to quokkas, the small marsupials that have become its emblem.
rottnest.respect: Don’t feed or touch the quokkas, it is forbidden, and when snorkelling don’t walk on the shallow reefs in the protected zones.
rottnest.season: December to April: the warmest water and an often calm sea in the morning, before the afternoon sea breeze.

around.d: A natural pool of turquoise water protected by the reef, perfect for swimming.
A historic lighthouse in the centre of the island, with guided tours and views of the salt lakes.
The main settlement with colonial buildings, ferry arrivals and bike hire.

around.n: Arthur Head and the Round House
around.d: A Fremantle headland and its round prison, one of the oldest buildings in the state.
Perth’s iconic beach, with Norfolk pines and sunsets over the ocean.

cablebeach.vibe: A former mother-of-pearl capital where pearl divers from Asia once worked, Broome lives on Yawuru land, between red cliffs, huge tides and camel rides at sunset.
cablebeach.respect: Swim between the flags, especially from November to May when box jellyfish and crocodiles may come close, and only drive a 4x4 in the permitted zone.
cablebeach.season: May to October: the dry season, a clear sea and outside jellyfish season; waves stay small and infrequent.

around.d: Red ochre cliffs above a turquoise sea, with dinosaur footprints at very low tide.
A historic open-air cinema where you watch films under the stars.
Vast mudflats for migratory birds and the “Staircase to the Moon” on full-moon evenings.
The pearl town, with its historic quarter and mother-of-pearl shops.
A centre on the bay for watching shorebirds that fly in from Asia.

herveybay.vibe: A peaceful Butchulla town facing K’gari, Hervey Bay owes its reputation to the humpback whales that rest here with their calves on the way to Antarctica.
herveybay.respect: If a whale approaches, stop paddling and let it pass: approaching whales and dolphins is strictly regulated in the marine park.
herveybay.season: July to October: a sheltered bay, a sea often flat in the morning and humpback whales stopping over.

around.d: A long historic pier reaching out into the bay, ideal at sunrise.
Mangroves, dugong seagrass beds and sand islands, including K’gari.
Two historic lighthouses on a wooded island in the strait.

noumea.vibe: Facing a UNESCO-listed lagoon, Anse Vata is where Nouméa’s residents play after work: boards, kites and paddleboards wait here for the trade wind that picks up in the afternoon.
food: Bougna
Chicken or fish, yams and bananas cooked in coconut milk in banana leaves.
noumea.respect: Keep out of the shuttle-boat channel to Îlot Canard and the marked swimming areas; the lagoon’s turtles and dugongs are protected.
noumea.season: September to December: steady, well-established southeasterly trade winds and lagoon water that is warming up.

around.d: Renzo Piano’s huts dedicated to Kanak culture, with exhibitions and a botanical trail.
A metal lighthouse on a lagoon islet, with a climb to the top and snorkelling around it.
Living corals, nautiluses and fish of the New Caledonian lagoon.
Kanak and Oceanian collections: sculptures, traditional money and a great hut.
A small islet off the beach with a marked underwater trail.

vieuxboucau.vibe: Its name recalls the old mouth of the Adour, diverted towards Bayonne in the 16th century; the Landes village now lives between pine forest, a tidal lake and long family sessions.
food: Magret de canard
Duck breast grilled over embers and served with sautéed potatoes, Landes style.
vieuxboucau.respect: Stay between the flags, as the baïnes create strong currents, and use only the official access paths: the dune is protected.
vieuxboucau.season: June and September: moderate swells suited to beginners, mild water and a less crowded beach than in August.

around.d: A trip by boat or canoe down a wild river lined with bald cypresses.
A tidal saltwater lake lined with Basque-Landes villas and oyster beds.
A boardwalk trail through a swamp forest rich in birds.
A protected wetland and major stopover for migratory birds, with hides.
A fishing and leisure harbour with its fish auction and wooden jetty.

moliets.vibe: A resort nestled in the pine forest, Moliets recalls the days of the resin tappers who harvested the pines’ resin; many arrive by bike along the forest cycle paths.
food: Pastis landais
A brioche flavoured with rum and orange blossom, queen of Landes afternoon snacks.
moliets.respect: Beware of the currents near the mouth of the Courant d’Huchet and stay on the boardwalks: the dunes and riverbanks are a nature reserve.
moliets.season: September to November: more consistent autumn swells, offshore wind in the morning and a quieter line-up.

around.d: A trip by boat or canoe down a wild river lined with bald cypresses.
A large pine-fringed lake where the Courant d’Huchet begins, for swimming and sailing.
A tidal saltwater lake lined with Basque-Landes villas and oyster beds.
A fishing and leisure harbour with its fish auction and wooden jetty.

espiguette.vibe: Between lagoons, salt pans and bull ranches, the Gard Camargue lives here to the rhythm of the Grau-du-Roi trawlers and the white horses grazing behind the dunes.
food: Gardiane de taureau
Camargue bull slow-cooked in red wine, served with Camargue rice.
espiguette.respect: Rig and ride only in the zones set aside for board sports, away from swimmers; cross the protected dune only by the marked paths.
espiguette.season: Spring and autumn: frequent mistral and tramontane, an uncrowded beach; in offshore wind, stay close to the shore.

around.d: A medieval walled town, with the Tour de Constance and pink salt pans all around.
A lively fishing port where the trawlers come in through the channel in the late afternoon.
A Romanesque cathedral standing alone on a former island between lagoons and sea.
A resort born in the 1960s, famous for its pyramid-shaped buildings.
A medieval watchtower guarding the approach to Aigues-Mortes, with views over the marshes.

almanarre.vibe: On the western tombolo of Giens, the windsurfers’ beach runs alongside the Pesquiers salt pans and their pink flamingos, facing the remains of the Greek city of Olbia.
food: Tapenade
Crushed black olives, capers and anchovies, to spread at a Provençal apéritif.
almanarre.respect: Check the rules for the riding zone, which is regulated in summer, and don’t trample the fragile dune ridge that protects the road.
almanarre.season: Spring and autumn: frequent mistral and easterly winds, and a beach far less busy than in summer.

around.d: Former protected salt marshes where you can watch pink flamingos and water birds.
An island in the national park, with wooded trails and a marked underwater trail.
Remains of a fortified Greek trading post by the sea, with streets and baths.
Medieval lanes climbing to the castle ruins, with palm trees and villas.
A coastal path between rocky coves and pines, with views of the Îles d’Or.

porquerolles.vibe: A car-free island you explore by bike, Porquerolles keeps its village of military origin around the Place d’Armes, its vineyards and its botanical conservatory among the pines.
porquerolles.respect: Fires and cigarettes are banned in the island’s natural areas; by kayak or paddleboard, don’t land on the seagrass beds and leave the banks of posidonia in place.
porquerolles.season: June and September: warm, clear water above the seagrass beds, and far fewer people than in high summer.

around.d: An island in the national park, with wooded trails and a marked underwater trail.
An isolated fort at the western tip of the island, facing cliffs and coves.
A small fort perched above the sea, on the path leading to the beach.
Former protected salt marshes where you can watch pink flamingos and water birds.

rondinara.vibe: Amid the scrub and granite of southern Corsica, the round bay of Rondinara opens onto the Strait of Bonifacio, where free-roaming cows sometimes wander onto the sand.
food: Fiadone
A light cake made with brocciu and lemon zest, the quintessential Corsican dessert.
rondinara.respect: Wild camping is forbidden: don’t sleep on the beach, take your rubbish away and keep your distance from the free-roaming cows.
rondinara.season: June and September: already-warm water, a calm bay and a car park far less packed than in high summer.

around.d: An archipelago of sculpted granite and turquoise water, by boat from Bonifacio.
A Genoese old town perched on its ramparts, with lanes and lively terraces.
The southern tip of Corsica, a path along limestone cliffs facing Bonifacio.
A Bronze Age fortress perched above the Gulf of Porto-Vecchio.
Laricio pines, a lake and the Piscia di Gallo waterfall above Porto-Vecchio.

scandola.vibe: A roadless coast watched over only by Genoese towers, Scandola is followed along the shore as the fishermen of Galéria and Girolata once did, beneath the flight of ospreys.
food: Brocciu
A fresh ewe’s or goat’s milk cheese, in omelettes, in fritters or in fiadone.
scandola.respect: In the strict reserve, landing, fishing and diving are forbidden: follow the coast without going ashore and stay well away from osprey nests.
scandola.season: May, June and September: a sea often calm in the morning, crystal-clear water and fewer boats than in summer.

around.d: A jumble of red granite sculpted above the sea, with trails and a panoramic road.
A roadless fishing hamlet with its Genoese tower, reached on foot or by boat.
A wild headland topped by a Genoese tower, a fine hike facing the open sea.
A UNESCO-listed gulf, with Porto’s marina and a Genoese tower on its rock.
A fishing village at the foot of the mountains, near the wild delta of the Fango.

saintebarbe.vibe: At the start of the great dune ridge running towards Quiberon, Sainte-Barbe lives between dolmens, sardine canneries and surf shops, facing an ocean that is often cold and powerful.
hello: “hello” in Breton, a word that always goes down well
food: Quiberon sardines
Prepared by hand in the peninsula’s canneries, sometimes sold as vintages.
saintebarbe.respect: The dunes of the Gâvres-Quiberon site are fragile: stay on the marked access paths and park your van only in authorised car parks.
saintebarbe.season: September to November: consistent westerly swells, still-temperate water and a quieter line-up.

around.d: Some of the world’s most famous menhir alignments, and sheltered beaches.
A coastal path between cliffs, rock arches and coves battered by the ocean.
An islet linked by a causeway, with a Romanesque chapel and fishermen’s houses on the ria.
The largest known menhir, lying near the tumulus and the Table des Marchand.
Rows of menhirs by the roadside, less visited than those at Carnac.

oleron.vibe: In the north of Oléron, colourful oyster huts, fish weirs and shore fishing set the pace of life; you surf facing the Pertuis d’Antioche, between marshes and vineyards.
food: Marennes-Oléron oysters
Matured in the nearby claires, to enjoy on the spot at the oyster hut.
oleron.respect: When shore fishing, respect the minimum sizes and put stones back where you found them; stay on the marked access paths to protect the dunes.
oleron.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells, still-mild water and a far calmer line-up than in summer.

around.d: A black-and-white striped lighthouse at the tip of the island, with views over the straits and the fish weirs.
A stone fort set in the sea, to admire from the coast or on a boat trip.
A harbour fortified by Vauban, with flower-filled lanes and lively quays on the Île de Ré.
A small car-free island to explore by bike, between fortifications and coves.
The island’s main fishing port: trawlers coming home and a lively fish auction.

beauduc.vibe: At the end of the track, the fishermen’s cabins of Beauduc form a timeless hamlet, among salt flats, pink flamingos and Camargue bulls; here, life follows the wind.
food: Gardiane de taureau
Camargue bull slow-cooked in red wine, served with Camargue rice.
beauduc.respect: The track crosses protected areas: never drive off the tracks, keep your distance from the flamingos and take all your rubbish away.
beauduc.season: April to October: frequent mistral and sea winds over flat water; in spring and autumn, fewer people and fewer mosquitoes.

around.d: A vast lagoon in the delta, haunt of pink flamingos and water birds.
A salt workers’ village of brick houses, facing the salt pans and their salt mounds.
A small, isolated lighthouse on the sea wall, reached on foot or by bike.
Protected lagoons, salt flats and dunes, rich in migratory birds.

ribeiradilhas.vibe: Ericeira, Europe’s first World Surfing Reserve, keeps the soul of a fishing village: white houses trimmed with blue, boats pulled up on the slipway and sea urchins in pride of place.
food: Sea urchins and grilled fish
Specialities of Ericeira’s tascas, where the catch of the day comes straight from the harbour.
ribeiradilhas.respect: The peak is busy with skilled local surfers: wait your turn, don’t let go of your board and beware of the rock shelf at low tide.
ribeiradilhas.season: September to March: consistent North Atlantic swells that make the right-hander peel, with fewer people than in summer.

around.d: A vast Baroque palace-convent with a monumental library.
A brightly coloured Romantic palace perched on the Serra de Sintra.
Medieval ramparts on the ridge, with views over Sintra and the ocean.
A white village clinging to the cliff, with a natural pool below.
A cobbled old centre, small squares and a fishing harbour at the foot of the cliffs.

guincho.vibe: Between shifting dunes and the cliffs of the Serra de Sintra, Guincho lives to the rhythm of the nortada; the fish restaurants on the coast road welcome kiters and weekending Lisboetas.
food: Travesseiros de Sintra
Puff pastries filled with almond cream, a speciality of Sintra’s pastry shops.
guincho.respect: The currents are violent: don’t swim unsupervised, give surfers room and stay on the boardwalks across the protected dunes.
guincho.season: June to September: the nortada blows hard almost every afternoon, ideal for kiting and windsurfing in strong wind.

around.d: The westernmost point of mainland Europe, with windswept cliffs and a lighthouse.
A brightly coloured Romantic palace perched on the Serra de Sintra.
An Oriental-inspired villa surrounded by a lush botanical garden.
A tiny cork-lined convent hidden in the Sintra forest.
A former fishing port turned chic resort, with its citadel and bay.

tonel.vibe: On the Romans’ Promontorium Sacrum, anglers cast their lines from the clifftops and percebes gatherers brave the backwash; Sagres lives on surf, wind and raw sea.
food: Percebes
Goose barnacles prised from the rocks of the Costa Vicentina, served simply boiled in salted water.
tonel.respect: You are in the Costa Vicentina Natural Park: no bivouacking or sleeping in your van outside designated areas, and stay well back from the edge of the unstable cliffs.
tonel.season: September to November: consistent westerly swells, often lighter wind and still-temperate water after summer.

around.d: The southwestern tip of Europe, with a lighthouse and dizzying cliffs facing the sunset.
A walled enclosure on the headland, with its stone wind rose and cliffs.
A west-coast village, gateway to the wild beaches of Amado and Bordeira.
A small fishing village where boats still rest on the beach.

caparica.vibe: Lisbon’s favourite popular beach, Caparica still has its arte xávega fishermen who haul the nets in from the sand, while a little train runs along the dunes to the southern beaches.
caparica.respect: Surf between the groynes, away from the rocks and the zones reserved for schools; in summer, swim only between the lifeguarded flags.
caparica.season: April to June and September to October: moderate, consistent swells for beginners, without the summer weekend crowds.

around.d: A Manueline masterpiece in Belém, with a finely carved cloister and Vasco da Gama’s tomb.
A fortified Manueline tower on the banks of the Tagus, symbol of the Age of Discovery.
A monumental prow on the Tagus, with a view over Belém from the top.
A collection of gilded royal coaches, among the richest in the world.

razo.vibe: On the Costa da Morte, a land of shipwrecks, lighthouses and percebeiros, the villages of Bergantiños line up granite hórreos and fishing harbours battered by the Atlantic.
hello: “hi” in Galician, the everyday language on the Costa da Morte
food: Pulpo á feira
Octopus sliced on a wooden board, drizzled with olive oil and paprika.
razo.respect: The Razo dunes are fragile: use the wooden walkways and leave the rocks to the percebeiros who work there.
razo.season: June to October: gentler swells for progressing and often calmer wind; bring a thick wetsuit, the water stays cool.

around.d: A potters’ village renowned for its traditional ceramics and old kilns.
A Romanesque country church, near the medieval towers of Mens.
An Iron Age hillfort, with the foundations of round houses.
A tiny fishing harbour on a rocky cove of the Costa da Morte.

bolonia.vibe: At Bolonia, the Romans salted tuna and made garum facing Africa; today, cows, a giant dune and chiringuitos keep company with the levante and poniente winds.
food: Almadraba bluefin tuna
Caught in spring by the almadraba traps of Zahara and Barbate, served as tataki or a la plancha.
bolonia.respect: The dune is a protected natural site: use the marked paths, don’t camp on the beach and keep your lines well away from swimmers in summer.
bolonia.season: May to September: the levante and poniente of the strait blow hard and often, with milder water than in spring.

around.d: A beachside Roman town: forum, theatre and fish-salting tanks.
A walled white old town, Europe’s kitesurfing capital, facing Morocco.
A tuna-fishing village with long beaches and a laid-back feel.
Cliffs, pine woods and bird migrations over the Strait of Gibraltar.
A viewpoint over the strait and Morocco’s Rif mountains.

sotavento.vibe: On the Jandía peninsula, between pale dunes and bare mountains where majorera goats graze, the tide shapes a lagoon each day that windsurfers have known for decades.
food: Majorero cheese
The island’s goat’s cheese, often rubbed with paprika or gofio.
sotavento.respect: You are in Jandía Natural Park: don’t drive off the tracks, keep off the dunes and respect the separation between kite and windsurf zones.
sotavento.season: June to September: strong, almost daily trade winds, accelerated along the coast, with pleasant water.

around.d: A remote hamlet at the end of a dirt track, facing a vast wild beach pounded by the ocean.
A protected volcanic massif and dunes, with the Pico de la Zarza to climb.

cotillo.vibe: El Cotillo keeps its old fishing harbour, its defence tower and its low houses; surfers cross paths with fishermen here at sunset, far from the bustle of Corralejo.
food: Majorero cheese
The island’s goat’s cheese, often rubbed with paprika or gofio.
cotillo.respect: To the south, the shorebreak and currents are powerful: swim in the northern lagoons instead and let the fishermen work in peace at the old harbour.
cotillo.season: October to March: consistent, powerful northwesterly swells, with more moderate trade winds than in summer.

around.d: A protected islet with turquoise coves and a trail to the volcano and the lighthouse.
The sacred mountain of the ancient Majoreros, adorned with foot-shaped rock carvings.
Lighthouses facing the waves and a small museum of traditional fishing.
A round defence tower overlooking the old harbour and the coast.
A lively northern harbour, gateway to the great protected dunes.

medano.vibe: A village of sand rather than concrete, El Médano lives to the rhythm of the wind beneath Montaña Roja; windsurfers, kiters and locals meet on the square facing the beach.
food: Papas arrugadas with mojo
Small salt-wrinkled potatoes, served with red and green sauces.
medano.respect: Montaña Roja is a nature reserve: stay on the marked trails and keep the launch zones clear for other riders.
medano.season: June to August: trade winds accelerated by the terrain blow hard almost every day, with mild water as a bonus.

around.d: An iconic volcanic rock at the foot of Mount Teide, in the Roques de García.
A summit on the rim of the Cañadas caldera, with an immense view of Mount Teide.
A deep gorge to hike up to a waterfall, above Adeje.
A cave sanctuary dedicated to the first Canarian saint, a place of pilgrimage.

famara.vibe: Caleta de Famara, with its sandy streets and white houses, lives to the rhythm of surfers beneath the Risco cliff; the whole island bears the stamp of the artist César Manrique.
food: Papas arrugadas with mojo
Small salt-wrinkled potatoes, served with red and green sauces.
famara.respect: Currents are strong at Famara: swim only near the schools, don’t camp on the beach and give the paragliders space.
famara.season: September to November and spring: consistent northerly swells, but gentler than in the depths of winter.

around.d: A lava tube transformed by César Manrique, with an underground lake and blind crabs.
An island without paved roads, with deserted beaches and sandy tracks to explore by bike.
The former capital, with white lanes and a big Sunday market.
Underground lava galleries explored on a guided tour.
A former quarry transformed by Manrique into a garden of cacti from around the world.

calodesmoro.vibe: In south-east Majorca, villages of golden marès stone, fishing harbours where llaüts bob on the water and dry-stone walls line coves carved into the limestone.
hello: “good morning” in Majorcan Catalan, called out at any time of the morning
food: Pa amb oli
Bread rubbed with tomato and olive oil, topped with cheese or sobrassada.
calodesmoro.respect: The cove is tiny and very popular: come early, park only in authorised car parks and take your rubbish home.
calodesmoro.season: June and September: warm, clear water for swimming and fish-watching, with smaller crowds than in August.

around.d: A long white-sand beach lined with dunes and protected salt flats.
Majorca’s southern tip, with a lighthouse and wild coast facing Cabrera.
Remains of the Majorcan Iron Age, bearing witness to the talayot culture.
A quiet little harbour of white houses, tucked at the end of an inlet.

goloritze.vibe: On the Baunei coast, shepherds and goatherds traced the paths running down from the Supramonte to the sea; Ogliastra keeps a strong pastoral culture where Sardinian is still spoken.
food: Culurgiones
Ogliastra ravioli filled with potato, pecorino and mint, sealed in the shape of an ear of wheat.
goloritze.respect: The cove is a natural monument: boats stay beyond the buoys, don’t take any pebbles and carry all your rubbish back up, as there are no facilities.
goloritze.season: June to September: calm seas and warm water; in June and September the climb back up the path is less punishingly hot.

around.d: The harbour where boats and kayaks set off for the coves of the Gulf of Orosei.
A karst cave home to one of the tallest limestone columns in Europe.
A Nuragic site perched above the sea, looking out over the Gulf of Orosei.
A small harbour, an ancient church and thousand-year-old olive trees facing the islet of Ogliastra.

sarakiniko.vibe: Since ancient times Milos has lived off its volcanic rock, from obsidian to modern mines; in its inlets, the syrmata, boathouses with colourful doors, watch over the fishermen’s boats.
food: Pitarakia
Small Milos cheese pasties, fried or baked, to nibble at the taverna.
sarakiniko.respect: The white rock is soft and slippery: don’t carve into it, avoid risky jumps and take everything away with you, as there is no shade and no bins.
sarakiniko.season: June to September: warm, clear water in the channels; pick a day without a strong meltemi for a relaxed swim.

around.d: A white village perched at the top of the island, famous for its sunsets.
Objects from the island, including prehistoric obsidian and a copy of the Venus de Milo.
A peaceful neighbouring island, reached by boat from Pollonia.
A quiet fishing village with tavernas on the harbour and a sheltered bay.
A seaside Bronze Age site, among the most important in the Cyclades.

pounta.vibe: Facing Antiparos, Pounta is first and foremost a small ferry landing; Paros, the island of ancient marble, lines up whitewashed chapels and fishing harbours swept by the meltemi all summer.
pounta.respect: The ferry to Antiparos crosses the channel constantly: stay well clear of its lane and don’t rig up in the middle of swimmers.
pounta.season: June to September, especially July–August: the meltemi blows strong and steady through the channel almost every day.

around.d: A large Byzantine church in Parikia, known as the church “of a hundred doors”.
A laid-back neighbouring island, with its village and its cave full of rock formations.
The main port, with whitewashed lanes and a Venetian kastro.
Parian marble sculptures and remains from the island’s ancient history.
An uninhabited islet with an ancient sanctuary of Apollo still being excavated.

stiniva.vibe: Long a military base closed to foreigners, Vis has kept its vineyards and stone villages, and in Komiža the memory of the falkuša, the sardine fishermen’s boats.
food: Viška pogača
A flatbread filled with salted fish, onions and tomato, a speciality of Komiža and Vis.
stiniva.respect: The path is steep and stony: go down in closed shoes with water, and by kayak only pass through the opening when the sea is calm.
stiniva.season: June to September: often calm seas and warm water; arrive early in the morning, before the excursion boats.

around.d: A sea cave lit up in blue by the midday sun.
A fishing port at the foot of Mount Hum, with its Venetian fort and narrow lanes.
A port town of stone houses and remains of the Greek colony of Issa.
The island’s highest point, with views over the whole Vis archipelago.

comino.vibe: Almost uninhabited, Comino takes its name from cumin and was once a smugglers’ hideout; the Knights of Malta’s St Mary’s Tower still keeps watch over the channel between Malta and Gozo.
food: Ġbejniet
Small sheep’s cheeses from Gozo, fresh, dried or peppered.
comino.respect: The lagoon is packed in summer: come early or late in the day, avoid single-use plastic and stay out of the marked boat lanes.
comino.season: May to June and September–October: warm, very clear water, with far fewer boats than in August.

around.d: Megalithic temples on Gozo, among the oldest stone monuments in the world.
A fortified citadel in the heart of Gozo, with views over the whole island.
The old fortified capital with silent lanes, nicknamed the Silent City.
Protected garrigue, cliffs and coastal paths in north-west Malta.

gozo.vibe: At Dwejra, fishing boats rest in the shelters of the Inland Sea, facing Fungus Rock once guarded by the Knights; the Azure Window collapsed in 2017, but diving still reigns supreme.
food: Gozitan ftira
A flatbread topped with potatoes, tomatoes and anchovies, baked in the village oven.
gozo.respect: Dwejra is a protected site: don’t collect fossils or rocks, enter the water at the usual access points and give it a miss if the north-westerly swell is pounding the rocks.
gozo.season: June to October: warm water, excellent visibility and often calm seas for descending into the chimney.

around.d: A fortified citadel in the heart of Gozo, with views over the whole island.
Megalithic temples among the oldest stone monuments in the world.
A lagoon linked to the open sea by a tunnel through the cliff, to pass by boat or on a dive.
A narrow sea gorge cut into the cliff, with steps down to the water.
A small bay lined with salt pans cut into the rock, still in use.

croyde.vibe: Between whitewashed cottages, village pubs and the Saunton dunes, Croyde has lived for surfing for decades; here, a post-session cream tea is part of the ritual.
food: Devon cream tea
Warm scones, clotted cream and strawberry jam, with the cream spread first.
croyde.respect: At low tide the wave is hollow and crowded: respect priority, and park in the pay car parks rather than in the village lanes.
croyde.season: September to November: consistent Atlantic swells, water still mild for Devon and far fewer people.

around.d: A National Trust headland, with a coastal path and views over the bay.
A vast dune system, the heart of the North Devon Biosphere Reserve.
Vintage boards and the history of surfing in Britain.
A seafaring village with colourful lanes, at the mouth of the Torridge.
A seaside resort on a large golden-sand beach.

rhossili.vibe: At the end of the Gower Peninsula, sheep and horses graze on the clifftops, the wreck of the Helvetia pokes out of the sand and Worm’s Head can only be reached at low tide.
hello: “hi” in Welsh, always a welcome touch
food: Penclawdd cockles and laverbread
Cockles from the estuary and seaweed purée, served as part of a Welsh breakfast.
rhossili.respect: For Worm’s Head, check the tide times: the causeway is only passable around low water and the tide comes back in fast.
rhossili.season: September to November: consistent westerly swells, water at its warmest and car parks less busy.

around.d: A sheltered bay lined with dunes and woods, ideal for swimming and paddling.
A fortified medieval manor house overlooking the salt marshes of north Gower.
A remarkably well-preserved Norman castle above the Gwendraeth.
A Welsh surf village, the gateway to the northern end of the bay’s beach.
A former smugglers’ village beside a sheltered beach.

lahinch.vibe: A promenade facing the Atlantic, links golf and surf schools: Lahinch lives off the sea all year round, and in the evening traditional music rings out in the pubs of Clare.
lahinch.respect: The nearby reefs are powerful and reserved for experienced locals; start out on the beach break, near the lifeguards, and watch out for currents.
lahinch.season: September to November: consistent autumn swells and water at its mildest; a thick wetsuit is still essential.

around.d: Dizzying cliffs above the Atlantic, with bird colonies and a coastal path.
A village renowned for its traditional music sessions in the pubs.
Lunar limestone plateaus, rare flora and prehistoric sites.
A cave home to a huge hanging stalactite.
A small medieval cathedral surrounded by carved Celtic crosses.

mullaghmore.vibe: A small fishing port in Yeats Country, Mullaghmore looks out on Ben Bulben and the Atlantic; in winter, the village gathers on the headland to watch the best big-wave surfers.
mullaghmore.respect: The wave is reserved for big-wave surfers with jet-skis and safety cover: if that’s not you, watch from the headland, well away from the rocks.
mullaghmore.season: October to March: big North Atlantic winter swells, surfable only with an offshore wind.

around.d: A village at the foot of Ben Bulben, with Yeats’s grave and a Celtic cross.
A valley lake framed by cliffs, with a waterfall celebrated by Yeats.
An uninhabited island with the ruins of an early Christian monastery.
The ruins of a medieval Dominican friary in the heart of Sligo.

klitmoller.vibe: A former fishing village on the Thy coast, Klitmøller has kept its low houses among the dunes and heather; surfers and windsurfers have built a real community here.
klitmoller.respect: The stone reefs are shallow and the water cold: wear boots and a thick wetsuit, and respect the pecking order of a small, local line-up.
klitmoller.season: September to November: autumn North Sea storms bring consistent swell and wind; bring a 5 mm wetsuit.

around.d: Dunes, heaths and lakes along the North Sea, to explore on foot or by bike.
A fishing village with tarred huts on the landing beach.

sylt.vibe: Thatched Frisian houses, wicker beach chairs lined up on the sand and Biike bonfires in February: Sylt cherishes its Frisian traditions facing an often rough North Sea.
food: Sylt oysters
Farmed in the north of the island, around List, best enjoyed simply with a squeeze of lemon.
sylt.respect: The dunes are protected and fragile: stay on the wooden boardwalks and respect the marked zones separating swimmers, surfers and kiters.
sylt.season: September to October: autumn storms and more consistent swells, water still bearable and empty beaches.

around.d: An upmarket village of thatched houses above the red cliff of the Rotes Kliff.
A Neolithic passage grave where you descend into a chamber of great stones.
An old Frisian church watching over Keitum and its former sea captains’ houses.
A shallow bay at the very north of the island, among mudflats, dunes and birds.

scheveningen.vibe: A former fishing village of The Hague, Scheveningen still celebrates the arrival of the new herring in its harbour, while surfers meet between the groynes beneath the facade of the Kurhaus.
scheveningen.respect: Between the groynes the peaks are tight: wait your turn, give priority to the regulars and in summer respect the areas reserved for swimmers.
scheveningen.season: September to November: autumn storms on the North Sea, more consistent swells and a beach handed back to the locals.

around.d: An art museum in an Art Deco building, famous for its large Mondrian collection.
A neo-Renaissance palace housing the International Court of Justice, set in a park.
A sculpture museum tucked into the dunes, with terraces facing the sea.
A miniature park that sums up the Netherlands: canals, windmills, ports and towns on a small scale.

hoddevik.vibe: At the end of the Stad Peninsula, a cape feared by Norwegian sailors for centuries, this hamlet of farms and sheep at the head of a deep bay has become home to a small Nordic surf culture.
hoddevik.respect: The access road is narrow and steep: park only in the designated spaces and don’t cross the farm meadows where the sheep graze.
hoddevik.season: September to October: consistent autumn swells, water still around 12 °C and days long enough to fit in session after session.

taghazout.vibe: White and blue houses, fishing boats hauled up on the sand and argan trees on the hills: Taghazout keeps the soul of an Amazigh fishing village, where surfers have flocked since the hippie years.
hello: “hello” in Tashelhit, the Amazigh language of the Souss
food: Amlou and argan oil
A paste of almonds, argan oil and honey, spread on warm bread at breakfast.
taghazout.respect: At point breaks such as Anchor Point, wait your turn and give priority to the locals; in the village, cover up again when you leave the beach.
taghazout.season: October to March: North Atlantic winter swells get the points peeling, with offshore winds in the morning.

around.d: Palm-lined Atlas gorges with pools of clear water to swim in.
The ramparts of the old kasbah on the hill, with a panorama over the whole Bay of Agadir.

oualidia.vibe: Around its lagoon, Oualidia lives from oyster farming and fishing: colourful boats, oyster beds and tables where you eat shellfish facing the water, in a resort popular with Moroccan families.
food: Oualidia oysters
Farmed in the lagoon and served freshly opened, with a squeeze of lemon, facing the water.
oualidia.respect: The lagoon is home to oyster beds and many waterbirds: don’t trample the beds and keep your distance from the flamingos.
oualidia.season: June to September: a calm lagoon, warmer than the ocean, ideal for swimming; August is the busiest month.

salkite.vibe: Santa Maria was born from the salt trade: on its old pier, fishermen still land tuna and wahoo when the boats come in, and in the evening morna drifts out of the seafront bars.
salkite.respect: Pump up and launch away from swimmers, steer around the marked turtle nests in summer and never ride alone: the beach is isolated.
salkite.season: December to April: north-easterly trade winds at their strongest, steady almost every day, with a warm sea all year round.

around.d: Salt pans set in an old crater, where you float in very salty water.
Old salt basins where the town began, frequented by waterbirds.
A black lava point and legendary wave, to watch when the windsurfers take it on.
A colourful little town with a fishermen’s pier, fish market and live-music bars.

pontapreta.vibe: At the foot of a desert of rock and sand, this black lava point has hosted wave windsurfing world cup events, while Santa Maria lives to the rhythm of the returning fishing boats and morabeza.
pontapreta.respect: Shallow reef and strong current: only paddle out if you can handle big waves, and give priority to those already in position.
pontapreta.season: November to March: North Atlantic winter swells meet the trade winds, and the right-hander lives up to its reputation.

around.d: Salt pans set in an old crater, where you float in very salty water.
A natural pool in the black lava and a cave where the light makes a “blue eye” shine.
Old salt basins where the town began, frequented by waterbirds.
A colourful little town with a fishermen’s pier, fish market and live-music bars.

busua.vibe: Brightly painted pirogues and nets spread out on the sand: Busua is still an Ahanta fishing village, surrounded by old European forts, where local young people learned to surf before going on to teach.
food: Kenkey with fried fish
A ball of fermented maize cooked in leaves, served with fried fish, chilli and onion.
busua.respect: Fishermen haul their pirogues and nets up the beach: don’t get in the way of their work and always ask before photographing them.
busua.season: November to March: the dry season, with gentler, more consistent swells, ideal for learning in the bay.

around.d: A whitewashed British fort perched on a headland above Dixcove harbour.
A village between river and sea, overlooked by the ruins of Fort Batenstein on the hill.
Ghana’s southernmost point, with a lighthouse, forest and fishing coves.
Remains of the Brandenburg fort at Princes Town, facing the ocean.
A lively fishing port where you can watch the pirogues come in and the fish being sold.

robertsport.vibe: At the foot of Mount Cape Mount, among houses from the days of the first settlers and the pirogues of Vai fishermen, Robertsport saw a young community of Liberian surfers take shape after the civil war.
robertsport.respect: The points break over rocks: work out the ways in and out with a local before your session and let the local kids have their share.
robertsport.season: April to October: consistent southern swells that get the lefts peeling, even though it is also the rainy season.

around.d: A large lagoon lined with mangroves, crossed by fishermen’s pirogues and full of birds.
Tropical forest on the slopes of the mountain overlooking the town and the coast.

cabroledo.vibe: South of Luanda, beyond Quiçama Park, this fishing village on an arid coast has become the weekend getaway for surfers from the capital, far from any mass tourism.
cabroledo.respect: The bay belongs to the fishermen too: don’t surf in among the nets and the boats coming in, and drive carefully on the coast road.
cabroledo.season: May to September: the cool dry season, with the most consistent southern swells to get the long left peeling.

aliwal.vibe: At Umkomaas, dive boats launch from the beach through the shorebreak, and every winter KwaZulu-Natal’s South Coast watches out for the sardine run, with dolphins and Cape gannets in its wake.
hello: “I see you”, the Zulu greeting, to which you reply yebo
food: Bunny chow
Half a loaf of white bread hollowed out and filled with curry, a speciality of Durban’s Indian community.
aliwal.respect: In the marine protected area, don’t touch or chase the ragged-tooth sharks: stay calm near the bottom and let them pass.
aliwal.season: June to November: ragged-tooth sharks gather on the reef, and the sardine run sometimes livens up the coast in winter.

around.d: A South Coast seaside resort with a large lifeguarded beach and a seawater pool.
A provincial heritage lighthouse standing above the coastal rocks.

sodwana.vibe: In the heart of Maputaland, dive boats launch from the beach through the waves, and it was in the offshore canyons that divers came across coelacanths, fish once thought extinct.
hello: “I see you”, the Zulu greeting, to which you reply yebo
sodwana.respect: In iSimangaliso Park, never drive on the beach outside the launch ramp and only approach nesting turtles with an accredited guide.
sodwana.season: November to April: the warmest water of the year and turtles coming to nest on the nearby beaches.

around.d: The country’s largest freshwater lake, among wooded dunes, hippos and birds.
Coastal dune forest and small lakes to explore on foot, among monkeys and birds.

langebaan.vibe: On the Afrikaans West Coast, Langebaan combines white houses, beach restaurants where crayfish grills over a wood fire and a springtime burst of flowers in the nearby park, beside a waveless lagoon.
food: West Coast crayfish
Rock lobster from the cold Atlantic waters, grilled over a wood fire in the beach restaurants.
langebaan.respect: The lagoon is a zoned marine protected area: only ride in the sector open to kites and avoid the sandbanks where birds feed.
langebaan.season: November to March: the south-easterly blows hard almost every afternoon over a flat, shallow lagoon.

around.d: Lagoon, fynbos and turquoise coves, carpeted with wildflowers in the southern spring.
A fossil bed of extinct animals, with guided tours of the excavations.
A vast natural harbour with cold waters, fishing ports and seabird islands.

bigbay.vibe: Facing Table Mountain across the bay, Bloubergstrand keeps its fishermen’s cottages and the memory of the battle that handed the Cape to the British; in summer, kiters from all over the world meet here.
food: Bobotie
Minced meat spiced with mild curry, topped with egg and baked, a legacy of Cape Malay cooking.
bigbay.respect: Launch and land only in the kite zones, away from swimmers, and give priority to surfers on the peaks when the wind drops.
bigbay.season: November to March: the south-easterly blows hard almost every day over cold Atlantic waves.

around.d: The prison island where Nelson Mandela was held, a World Heritage Site.
A summit next to Table Mountain, a hike with views over the city and the bay.
Dunes, fynbos and a hill with one of the finest views of Table Mountain.
A protected wetland for watching flamingos, pelicans and waterbirds.

pontadoouro.vibe: A village of sandy tracks right on the South African border, Ponta do Ouro lives to the rhythm of RIBs launched from the beach and lively weekends around the marisqueiras.
pontadoouro.respect: In the marine reserve, swimming with dolphins is only allowed with an accredited operator, without touching them, chasing them or cutting across their path.
pontadoouro.season: June to November: often better visibility and humpback whales migrating along the coast.

bazaruto.vibe: Off Vilankulo, lateen-sailed dhows glide between giant dunes and sandbanks, and island fishermen still live by the tides and nets hauled in by hand.
bazaruto.respect: In the national park, don’t walk on the coral at low tide, don’t collect any shells and keep your distance from dugongs and turtles.
bazaruto.season: May to November: the dry season, with often calm seas and clear water, and humpback whales migrating in the southern winter.

around.d: The archipelago’s second island, with dunes, freshwater lakes and reefs to explore by snorkel.
A large island of dunes to climb, with views over the sandbanks and turquoise lagoons.
A small rocky island with crystal-clear coves, nicknamed Paradise Island.

ifaty.vibe: The Vezo, a people of nomadic sea fishermen, criss-cross the lagoon in their outrigger pirogues, while on land the spiny forest and its baobabs grow almost down to the sand.
ifaty.respect: Don’t walk on the reef at low tide, don’t bring back coral or shells, and agree the price of the pirogue trip before you board.
ifaty.season: April to November: the dry season, with a clearer lagoon, and humpback whales offshore from July to September.

lavanono.vibe: At the far end of Antandroy country, a dry land of cacti, zebu and decorated tombs, a few fishermen’s huts face reefs where you can surf almost alone.
lavanono.respect: Don’t go near the tombs unless invited and don’t photograph them; fresh water is scarce here, so use it sparingly.
lavanono.season: March to October: the southern winter swells arrive powerful and consistent on the reefs.

mnemba.vibe: Facing Matemwe, fishermen’s outrigger canoes cross paths with the dhows taking divers out, and at low tide women farm seaweed on the reef flat.
mnemba.respect: The islet is private: you can’t land there. In the conservation area, turn down boats that chase dolphins and never touch the turtles.
mnemba.season: October to March: the warmest water, often calm seas in the morning and very good visibility on the reef.

around.d: A fishing village facing the atoll, with a long beach and seaweed farms at low tide.
Forest on ancient coral, with caves, birds and monkeys, to explore with a guide.
Remains of a medieval Swahili city, with a mosque and coral-stone houses.

bluebay.vibe: Right next to Mahébourg, a former French town where the Battle of Grand Port lives on in memory, fishermen in pirogues share the lagoon with glass-bottom boats.
bluebay.respect: In the marine park, no fishing, no feeding the fish and no collecting anything: swim at the surface, without touching the coral, within the marked area.
bluebay.season: October to December: calmer trade winds, water already warm and clear, before the cyclone season.

around.d: An islet reserve where the original dry forest, giant tortoises and pink pigeons are thriving again.
A small Creole town on the bay, with a seafront and a lively market.
A colonial mansion tracing the island’s history and the naval Battle of Grand Port.
Ruins of the Dutch fort at Vieux Grand Port, the island’s first settlement.
Protected forest in the Bambous Mountains, with trails and rare endemic species.

tamarinmu.vibe: Between salt pans still in use and Rempart Mountain, Tamarin is a Creole fishing village whose left-hander was revealed to the world’s surfers by a cult film from the 1970s.
tamarinmu.respect: In the line-up, stay humble and give priority to the locals; on a paddleboard, don’t approach the bay’s dolphins, which are already under heavy pressure from boats.
tamarinmu.season: May to September: the southern winter sends in southerly swells, and the trade wind often blows offshore across the bay.

around.d: A UNESCO-listed mountain, once a refuge for runaway slaves, with a hike overlooking the lagoon.
Forests and deep gorges, with trails, viewpoints and endemic birds.
Dunes of volcanic earth in shifting hues, near a beautiful waterfall.
An upland village among sugar cane and forests, with viewpoints over the west coast.
A 19th-century British defensive tower turned into a small museum.
