beauvallon.vibe: One evening a week, the Bazar Labrin fills the beach with Creole stalls and music, while fishermen bring their boats in under the shade of the takamaka trees facing Silhouette Island.
food: Palm heart salad
Raw heart of palm, thinly sliced, nicknamed millionaire’s salad, served as a starter.
beauvallon.respect: Swim between the buoys of the bathing area, as boats and jet skis run offshore, and follow the lifeguards’ flags when the sea picks up.
beauvallon.season: May to October: under the south-east trade wind, the north-west-facing bay stays sheltered and calm.

around.d: Eight islets and their reefs, for snorkelling among turtles and lagoon fish.
Remains of an old mission school in the forest, with a viewpoint over the west coast.
Coco de mer, endemic palms, orchids and giant tortoises.
The capital’s colourful market hall, with the catch of the day, tropical fruit and spices.

saintleu.vibe: A former sugar town of Creole houses, Saint-Leu saw the world’s best surfers battle it out on its left-hander before the shark crisis emptied the line-ups; every day, paragliders glide down from the uplands.
saintleu.respect: Very shallow reef and a risk of sharks: only surf in the zones and time slots authorised by official decree, never alone and never in murky water.
saintleu.season: April to October: the southern winter sends in south-westerly swells that get the left peeling.

around.d: A sea turtle observatory: pools, a care centre and the history of turtle fishing.
A former sugar factory telling the story of sugar cane, vanilla and the island.
An upland Creole estate with collections of plants endemic to the Mascarenes.
A wild basalt cape, with traditional salt pans and a path above the ocean.
The island’s highest point, climbed by night to watch the sunrise from the summit.

ermitage.vibe: On Sundays, Réunionese families settle under the filao trees with pots of carri and mats for long picnics, while the children splash about in the lagoon.
ermitage.respect: The lagoon is part of the marine nature reserve: don’t walk on the coral, don’t feed the fish and stay inside the reef.
ermitage.season: May to November: the dry season, with clear water and a calm lagoon, away from the rains and cyclones of the southern summer.

around.d: A viewpoint at over 2,000 m above the Cirque de Mafate, best seen early before the clouds.
A former sugar plantation, with its master’s house and the memory of slavery.
A white-sand beach lined with coconut palms and terraces, very popular at sunset.
A private botanical garden devoted to sacred, medicinal and tropical plants.
A cave where the island’s first inhabitants are said to have lived, near Saint-Paul.

elgouna.vibe: A new town built on lagoons and canals north of Hurghada, El Gouna combines marinas, domed Nubian-inspired houses and a large community of kiters based on the windward beaches.
elgouna.respect: The shallow lagoons hide coral and sea urchins: wear boots, stay in the centres’ marked zones and give learners plenty of space.
elgouna.season: May to September: the strongest, most consistent northerly wind, and warm water that doesn’t call for a thick wetsuit.

abudabbab.vibe: On the still-wild coast of Marsa Alam, between bare mountains and fringing reefs, the bay lives to the rhythm of turtles grazing on the seagrass, far from the bustle of Hurghada.
abudabbab.respect: Never chase turtles or the dugong: keep your distance, swim at the surface above the seagrass and don’t put your fins down on the bottom.
abudabbab.season: June to October: the warmest water and often calm seas in the morning, ideal for swimming above the seagrass.

djerba.vibe: A flat island of whitewashed houchs and small fortified mosques, Djerba still catches octopus with gargoulettes, clay jars shaped by the potters of Guellala.
food: Djerbian rice
Steamed rice with meat, chard, herbs and spices, the island’s own recipe.
djerba.respect: At El Ghriba, modest clothing is required. In the villages, always ask before photographing people, especially women.
djerba.season: May to October: steady breezes and warm water in the shallow lagoons, with more people in July–August.

around.d: An ancient synagogue with blue tiles, a place of Jewish pilgrimage in spring.
Souks, fondouks and the Borj el-Kebir fort facing the fishing harbour.
A whitewashed Ottoman-era mosque in the heart of Houmt Souk.
The island’s second town, with its market and lively lanes.

sunsetbeach.vibe: On the North Shore, everything follows the winter swells: surfers’ houses, food trucks and rural towns, with the Triple Crown drawing the pros to this coast every season.
food: Kahuku garlic shrimp
Shrimp sautéed in garlic and butter, served with rice from roadside trucks.
sunsetbeach.respect: Here, locals and pros own the peak: watch for a long time from the beach, only paddle out if you can handle big surf, and leave the honu turtles in peace on the sand.
sunsetbeach.season: November to February: the most powerful north-westerly swells; in summer, the ocean goes almost flat.

around.d: A legendary reef barrel, to watch from Ehukai beach on swell days.
The bay for really big days in winter, with calm water and rock jumping in summer.
A sacred Hawaiian valley, with a botanical garden and a path to a waterfall.
Oahu’s largest ancient temple, perched above Waimea Bay.

jaws.vibe: Maui’s north coast of former pineapple and sugar cane fields: Paia, once a sugar town, lives for windsurfing and surfing, and on the days of really big swell everyone heads off to watch Jaws from the cliff.
food: Poke
Cubes of raw fish marinated in soy sauce and sesame oil, often served on rice.
jaws.respect: Jaws is only surfed with a safety team: watch from the cliff, stay on the paths and respect the private farmland on the plateau.
jaws.season: November to March: only big north-westerly swells wake it up, a few days each winter.

around.d: A world-famous windsurfing spot, with turtles hauling out on the beach in the evening.
A forest trail at the entrance to Haleakalā National Park, rich in birdlife.
A tropical garden and taro patches beside the Road to Hana.
A missionary house turned museum of Hawaiian history and crafts.
The history of Maui’s sugar cane plantations and immigrant workers.

kona.vibe: On the Big Island’s leeward coast, lava flows, upland coffee farms and Hawaiian royal sites line calm bays where manta rays come at night to filter plankton.
food: Kona coffee
Grown on the volcanic slopes above the coast, best tasted straight from the farm.
kona.respect: Let the mantas come to you: never touch them, keep your hands on the light board or on the bottom and don’t fin towards them.
kona.season: All year round: the mantas come almost every night, and the sea is often calmer from April to October.

around.d: A former royal place of refuge, with a stone wall, a temple and wooden statues.
A protected marine bay, with reef snorkelling and a monument to Captain Cook.
A sheltered bay ideal for a first snorkel among turtles and fish.
A former summer residence of Hawaiian royalty, now a museum.
A restored coffee farm that tells the story of the planters’ families.

hanalei.vibe: At the end of the north coast road, Hanalei lines up flooded taro fields, one-lane bridges and an old pier, facing a bay where locals grew up on big winter days.
food: Poi
Taro purée, often fermented; the taro grows in the valley just behind the bay.
hanalei.respect: At the one-lane bridges, cars cross in groups, taking turns. On the beach, let the monk seals rest at a good distance.
hanalei.season: October to March: northerly swells get the bay working, for seasoned surfers; in summer, it’s paddleboarding on calm water.

around.d: Dizzying cliffs and hanging valleys, reached on foot or by sea.
A demanding coastal trail along the Nā Pali cliffs.
A lighthouse and seabird colonies on a cliff facing the open sea.
A terraced garden of Hawaiian plants at the foot of the mountains.
A mission house and green wooden church in the heart of Hanalei.

kailua.vibe: On Oahu’s windward coast, Kailua keeps traces of the Hawaiian past, such as the Kawainui fishpond and Ulupō Heiau, behind a beach where the trade winds carry kites and outrigger canoes.
food: Malasadas
Portuguese-style doughnuts rolled in sugar, a speciality of Oahu’s bakeries.
kailua.respect: The Mokulua islets are a seabird sanctuary: only land on the beach of Moku Nui and keep away from the nesting areas.
kailua.season: April to September: the most consistent easterly trade winds, warm water and a lagoon often glassy in the morning.

around.d: Fine sand and turquoise water facing the Mokulua islets.
A cliff in the Koʻolau Mountains with a vast view over the windward coast.
An old crater open to the sea, a marine reserve for snorkelling.
A volcanic cone to climb to the summit, with views over Waikīkī.
A replica of a Japanese temple at the foot of the cliffs, with a koi pond.

rinconca.vibe: On the border of Santa Barbara and Ventura counties, this cobblestone point is a place of pilgrimage for Californian surfing, between the avocado orchards of Carpinteria and a coast once home to the Chumash.
food: Santa Barbara sea urchin
Hand-harvested by divers in the channel and eaten raw at the fishmongers on the harbour.
rinconca.respect: The line-up is crowded and very local: wait your turn at the peak, never paddle inside others and park only in authorised spaces.
rinconca.season: November to March: north-westerly winter swells wrap around the point in long rights.

around.d: A town of white facades and tiled roofs, with a Spanish mission and a pier.
A sheltered family beach, with seals resting on the nearby rocks.
A small artists’ town in a valley of orange groves at the foot of the mountains.
A reservoir surrounded by hills, for peaceful kayaking and fishing.

pointlobos.vibe: Between Carmel and Big Sur, Point Lobos keeps traces of its whalers and abalone fishermen, on a coast of twisted cypresses where Monterey long lived to the rhythm of its sardine canneries.
food: Clam chowder
Creamy clam soup served in a sourdough bread bowl, down on the wharf.
pointlobos.respect: Dives in the reserve must be booked in advance and the number of dive teams is limited. Take nothing and keep your distance from otters and seals.
pointlobos.season: September to November: the upwelling eases, the water clears and the sea often stays calm before the winter storms.

around.d: A huge kelp forest tank, sea otters and local Pacific wildlife.
The old street of sardine canneries, celebrated by Steinbeck.
A village of fairy-tale cottages, galleries and a white-sand beach beneath the cypresses.
A stone house and tower built by hand by the poet Robinson Jeffers.

catalina.vibe: Avalon moves at the pace of golf carts, beneath the Art Deco casino that overlooks the bay; the island owes a great deal to the Wrigley family and keeps bison in its hills.
catalina.respect: Casino Point park is a marine reserve: take nothing, don’t feed the garibaldis and stay within the marked area, away from boats.
catalina.season: July to October: the warmest water of the year and often better visibility in the kelp.

around.d: A garden of plants endemic to the island around a memorial overlooking the valley.
A small town rising like an amphitheatre above the bay, with its promenade and harbour.
A narrow strip of land between two bays, the starting point for wild hikes.
The Wrigleys’ former summer residence, perched above Avalon Bay.

keylargo.vibe: The first of the Keys on the Overseas Highway, Key Largo lives off diving and fishing, among mangroves, wooden marinas and the archipelago’s own “conch” culture.
food: Key lime pie
A Key lime tart on a biscuit base, the emblem of the archipelago.
keylargo.respect: On the reef, tie the boat to the mooring buoys provided, never drop anchor on the coral and don’t put your hands or fins on the coral.
keylargo.season: April to June: often calm seas, warm water and good visibility, before the height of hurricane season.

around.d: A reef very popular with divers, rich in fish and coral spurs.
A large naval ship deliberately sunk to form an artificial reef.
Trails through a tropical dry forest typical of the Keys, rich in birdlife.
The boat from the 1951 film, moored in a Key Largo marina.

cocoabeach.vibe: On the Space Coast, you sometimes surf while watching a rocket lift off from nearby Cape Canaveral; the town lives between its fishing pier, giant surf shops and a laid-back beach culture.
cocoabeach.respect: Around the pier, stay well away from anglers’ lines. In summer, don’t touch the marked sea turtle nests on the beach.
cocoabeach.season: September to November: more frequent hurricane and nor’easter swells, with the water still warm.

around.d: Rockets, the Space Shuttle Atlantis and the history of NASA’s lunar missions.
Mangrove islets in the lagoon to explore by kayak, with manatees and dolphins.
Old launch pads and rockets from the early days of space exploration.

hatteras.vibe: At the elbow of the Outer Banks, the fishing villages of Buxton and Hatteras face the “Graveyard of the Atlantic”, where currents and shoals have swallowed countless ships.
food: Hatteras clam chowder
A clear broth with clams, potatoes and bacon, with no cream or tomato.
hatteras.respect: Only drive on the beach via authorised access points, with a permit, and respect areas closed for turtle and bird nesting.
hatteras.season: September to November: tropical storm and nor’easter swells, water still warm and quieter beaches.

around.d: A black-and-white striped lighthouse, moved back from the shore to escape erosion.
Long wild beaches, dunes and unspoilt marshes along the barrier islands.
Wrecks, shipwrecks and the maritime history of the Outer Banks.

lawrencetown.vibe: On the Eastern Shore, very close to Halifax, a small community of surfers takes on the North Atlantic all year round, not far from the Acadian villages of Chezzetcook and their salt marshes.
food: Nova Scotia lobster
Boiled and served whole or in a roll, in the shacks and restaurants along the coast.
lawrencetown.respect: The beach is a provincial park: park in the car parks, keep off the fragile dunes and give priority to the locals at the peak.
lawrencetown.season: September to November: swells from Atlantic storms and hurricanes, water still bearable in a thick wetsuit.

around.d: Halifax’s naval history, from the Titanic to the 1917 explosion.
The former terminal where immigrants arriving in Canada by sea came ashore.
An old house that brings to life the Acadian families of Chezzetcook.
A fortified islet with a lighthouse in the middle of Halifax Harbour.

puntamita.vibe: At the tip of Banderas Bay, the small fishing village of El Anclote watches the pangas set off for the Marietas Islands, away from the luxury residences that occupy the point.
food: Pescado zarandeado
A fish split in half, marinated in chillies and grilled over embers, a speciality of Nayarit.
puntamita.respect: The Marietas Islands are a national park with limited access: go with an authorised operator and never put your feet on the coral.
puntamita.season: May to October: southerly swells get the points working; in winter, smaller waves ideal for beginners.

scorpionbay.vibe: At the end of long dirt tracks, the fishing village of San Juanico shares its bay with nomadic surfers in vans, under an exceptionally clear desert sky.
scorpionbay.respect: The village is short of water and rubbish collection: save fresh water, take your rubbish away with you and drive at walking pace through San Juanico.
scorpionbay.season: May to October: southerly swells peel along the points, with warmer water at the end of summer.

laventana.vibe: A small fishing village facing Cerralvo Island, La Ventana lives to the rhythm of North American kiters in winter, while the pangas still head out to fish in the Sea of Cortez.
laventana.respect: The fishermen’s pangas have priority on the beach: don’t rig up in their launch area and drive at walking pace through the village.
laventana.season: December to February: the north wind is at its most consistent; the water is cooler, so bring a wetsuit.

ikkil.vibe: Deep in Maya country, near Chichén Itzá, the cenote is a reminder that these natural wells were a vital water source for the Maya and a sacred gateway to the underworld.
food: Cochinita pibil
Pork marinated in achiote and bitter orange, slow-cooked in banana leaves.
ikkil.respect: Take the required shower before entering the water, without sunscreen or insect repellent, to protect this freshwater well.
ikkil.season: November to March: the dry season and bearable heat; come early to avoid the groups coming from Chichén Itzá.

around.d: A great Maya city with the Pyramid of Kukulcán, the ball court and the observatory.
The Maya offering well, at the end of a causeway at Chichén Itzá.
Maya objects found at the site, including offerings from the Sacred Cenote.

soupbowl.vibe: On the Atlantic-battered east coast, Bathsheba lines up mushroom-shaped rocks, fishermen’s houses and rum shops, far from the chic beaches of the west coast.
soupbowl.respect: Shallow reef and a local line-up: watch first, don’t hog the waves and only swim in the sheltered pools, as the currents are fierce.
soupbowl.season: August to March: hurricane and then winter swells from the North Atlantic, which keep the right-hander working.

around.d: A limestone cave with stalactites and underground rivers, toured by little train.
A terraced tropical garden overlooking the Bathsheba coast.
A lush garden tucked in the bottom of a gully, planted with palms and flowers.
A hill beneath mahogany trees with a sweeping view over the wild north-east coast.
A former plantation turned botanical garden in the heart of the hills.

hadicurari.vibe: Nicknamed Fisherman’s Huts after the fishermen’s shacks that once lined the beach, Hadicurari combines colourful sails and diving pelicans, beneath divi-divi trees bent by the trade wind.
hadicurari.respect: Windsurfers and kiters share the water: respect the launch lanes and give way to fishermen heading back to shore.
hadicurari.season: May to August: the trade winds at their strongest and very consistent; the wind drops noticeably from September to November.

around.d: Cactus-covered hills, caves with Amerindian paintings and wild coves.
A stone lighthouse on a limestone plateau, with a fine view over the northern tip.
A large cargo ship scuttled during the war, a wreck popular with divers.
A calm white-sand beach for swimming and snorkelling.
A wetland for watching herons, cormorants and other waterbirds.

playalagun.vibe: In rural Bandabou, the cove still shelters the boats of Lagún’s fishermen, not far from the old plantations where the slave revolt led by Tula began.
playalagun.respect: Leave room for the moored fishing boats, enter the water from the beach without walking on the reef and watch the turtles without following them.
playalagun.season: September to November: weaker trade winds, a very calm sea and often excellent visibility.

around.d: A national park of cacti and hills, with the climb up Mount Christoffel.
A large white-sand beach with turquoise water, surrounded by cliffs.
A cove renowned for diving, with mushroom-shaped corals.
A wild point on the north coast, where the swell spouts up through holes in the rock.

stingraycity.vibe: It all supposedly began with fishermen cleaning their catch in the shelter of the North Sound reef: the rays got into the habit of coming, and the sandbar became a Caymanian meeting place.
stingraycity.respect: Never take a ray out of the water and only feed one with your guide. Shuffle your feet in the sand so you don’t step on one.
stingraycity.season: April to June: calmer trade winds and crystal-clear water over the sandbar, before hurricane season.

around.d: A long coral-sand beach with calm water on the west coast.
Forest trails, flower gardens and endemic blue iguanas.
The island’s oldest stone house, the cradle of its political life.
A trail through primary dry forest and unspoilt wetlands.
A rescue ship sunk as an artificial reef, accessible by snorkel.

roatan.vibe: A sandy street lined with bars on stilts and dive centres, West End mixes the islanders’ Creole English, mainland Spanish and travellers from all over the world, with the reef just a few strokes away.
food: Coco bread
A soft little coconut milk bread roll, a legacy of island and Garifuna cooking.
roatan.respect: Choose a dive centre that ties up to the marine park’s buoys and work on your buoyancy: the reefs close to shore are very busy.
roatan.season: March to September: less rain, calm seas and better visibility before the wet autumn season.

bocasdeltoro.vibe: Wooden houses on stilts, calypso and English Creole on the jetties: the archipelago blends Afro-Caribbean heritage, Ngäbe villages and memories of the banana era, and everything is done by water taxi.
food: Rondón
A Caribbean stew of fish and root vegetables simmered in coconut milk.
bocasdeltoro.respect: On Bastimentos, look at the little red frogs without touching them, and never take the starfish out of the water at Boca del Drago.
bocasdeltoro.season: December to March: Caribbean winter swells on the reefs, with a small second season in June and July.

around.d: Reefs, mangroves and the islets of Cayos Zapatilla, to explore by boat and with a mask.
The Afro-Caribbean village of Old Bank, rainforest and wild beaches such as Red Frog Beach.
The archipelago’s little capital, with colourful wooden houses and restaurants on stilts.
A wooded island facing Bocas Town, with a few reef waves and bars right on the water.
A protected lagoon and marshes on the mainland, a refuge for manatees and sea turtles.

popoyo.vibe: Dirt tracks, cattle ranches and fishermen hauling their boats onto the sand: Popoyo is still a hamlet on the Rivas coast, living to the rhythm of the tides and the wind that comes down from the lake.
popoyo.respect: The reef is exposed at low tide: check the tide times, wear booties and leave the big Outer Reef sessions to seasoned surfers.
popoyo.season: April to October: more powerful South Pacific swells, offshore wind in the morning and fewer people than in the dry season.

elzonte.vibe: A fishing village of volcanic sand turned “Bitcoin Beach”, where you sometimes pay for your pupusas in cryptocurrency and local kids learn to surf on the cobblestone right.
food: Mariscada
A creamy seafood soup, a speciality of the comedores on the La Libertad coast.
elzonte.respect: On the point, the bottom is made of big slippery cobbles: paddle in and out through the channel, and let the village surfers take their waves.
elzonte.season: March to October: consistent southern swells on the right, warm water and showers mostly in the afternoon.

around.d: A lively fishing port with its big pier, its fish market and the Punta Roca wave.
A village in the coastal hills known for its waterfalls, reached on a guided hike.
A quiet little cove with cobbled streets and a gentle wave for beginners.

cousteau.vibe: On the leeward coast, fishermen bring their boats in onto the black sand of Malendure, and Bouillante owes its name to the hot springs that bubble up right into the sea.
food: Fish blaff
Fresh fish poached in a broth with lime, chilli and herbs.
cousteau.respect: In the reserve, fishing is banned and mooring is on buoys only: touch neither corals nor turtles, and fin well away from the bottom.
cousteau.season: December to May: dry season, calm sea on the leeward side and often excellent visibility around the islets.

around.d: A waterfall in the rainforest, with a pool for swimming at the foot of the falls.
A fishing village around a bay, with a botanical garden and Grande Anse beach close by.
A colonial fort overlooking Basse-Terre, a landmark of the resistance to the reinstatement of slavery.
Parc des Mamelles, deep in the rainforest, with a rope bridge above the canopy.

ansedufour.vibe: Fishing yawls pulled up on the sand, nets drying and a little restaurant at the back of the cove: Anse Dufour lives from fishing, a stone’s throw from the dark sand of Anse Noire.
food: Grilled fish with sauce chien
The catch of the day, grilled and topped with a sauce of herbs, lime and chilli.
ansedufour.respect: Keep your distance from the turtles, don’t chase them and swim outside the fishing boats’ channel. The car park is tiny: come early.
ansedufour.season: December to May: dry season, calm sea and clear water for watching the turtles on the seagrass.

around.d: A picture-postcard village with its church facing the sea and its jetty over turquoise water.
White stone statues facing the sea, in memory of the wreck of a slave ship.
A reconstructed village telling the story of slavery and rural life in Martinique.
A Vauban-style fort on the bay of Fort-de-France, still a navy base.
A peaceful small town, birthplace of Empress Joséphine, surrounded by beaches and mangroves.

thunderball.vibe: A string of turquoise cays you get around by small boat: on Staniel Cay, a few colourful houses, an airstrip and a yacht club keep the island going between fishing and sailing.
thunderball.respect: Enter the grotto at slack low tide, as the current is strong the rest of the time, and don’t touch the corals on the ceiling.
thunderball.season: April to June: often calm sea, already warm water and the hurricane season not yet started.

around.d: A beach on Big Major Cay famous for its pigs that swim out towards the boats.
A small inhabited island in the Exumas, a base for boat trips to the neighbouring cays.
An island with a sheltered natural harbour, where you swim with nurse sharks used to the dock.

itamambuca.vibe: Atlantic forest tumbling into the ocean and caiçara culture, that of the fishermen of the São Paulo coast: Ubatuba calls itself the state’s surf capital, and Itamambuca is its heart.
food: Azul-marinho
A caiçara dish of fish stewed with green bananas that turn blue as they cook.
itamambuca.respect: At the peak near the river mouth, the local line-up is close-knit: wait your turn and give priority to those who have surfed here since childhood.
itamambuca.season: April to September: cold fronts and consistent south swells, cooler water and a quiet beach outside the holidays.

around.d: A wooded island with the ruins of an old penal colony, trails and coves for swimming with the fish.
A vast massif of Atlantic forest, with waterfalls and trails above the coast.
An islet with clear water and white sand beaches, perfect for a snorkelling trip.
A coastal town with dozens of beaches and a sea turtle protection centre.

portodegalinhas.vibe: Sailing jangadas, fish sculptures in the streets and a name inherited, so they say, from enslaved people landed in secret under the code word “chickens”: Porto de Galinhas lives to the rhythm of the low tides.
food: Bolo de rolo
A roll cake in very thin layers filled with guava, the pride of Pernambuco.
portodegalinhas.respect: In the natural pools, don’t walk on the reef and don’t feed the fish: stick to the marked areas shown by the jangadeiros.
portodegalinhas.season: September to March: dry season, crystal-clear water, and visit at the big low tides for well-formed pools.

around.d: An unspoilt island with two pale sand beaches, reached by boat for a calm swim.
A cape with coves such as Calhetas and Gaibu, and colonial remains on the heights.

bonito.vibe: In the heart of the fazendas of Mato Grosso do Sul, Bonito has built its tourism on protecting its rivers: every outing is guided, booked and limited in visitor numbers.
food: Ventrecha de pacu
The belly of the pacu, a fish from the Pantanal rivers, served fried or grilled.
bonito.respect: No sunscreen or repellent before getting in the water, and never put your feet on the bottom: you would cloud the water and damage the riverbed.
bonito.season: May to September: dry season, rivers at their clearest and little rain to cloud the water.

praiamole.vibe: Florianópolis keeps the mark of its Azorean settlers: bobbin lace, fishing villages and oyster farms, while Praia Mole, young and bohemian, welcomes surfers and paragliders.
food: Florianópolis oysters
Farmed in the island’s bays, served raw, gratinated or steamed.
praiamole.respect: The rip currents are strong: swim in front of the guarda-vidas posts and leave the peaks near the rocks to the regulars.
praiamole.season: April to August: cold fronts and well-lined-up south swells, but cool water that calls for a wetsuit.

around.d: A large lagoon lined with dunes, bars and restaurants, for paddling or strolling at sunset.
A fishing village at the mouth of the lagoon, with its colourful boats and little coves.
A protected island with turquoise water, known for its rock carvings and guided trails.
The island’s longest beach, wild and backed by the forest of Rio Vermelho park.
A historic suspension bridge linking the island to the mainland, the emblem of Florianópolis.

maragogi.vibe: On the Costa dos Corais, a large marine protected area, the jangadas head out to the reef when the sea pulls back, between coconut groves and the sugar cane fields of the hinterland.
food: Caldinho de sururu
A thick broth of small lagoon mussels, an emblem of Alagoas cooking.
maragogi.respect: Visits to the galés are limited: go with a licensed operator, don’t stand on the coral and don’t feed the fish.
maragogi.season: September to March: dry season, crystal-clear water and big low tides that uncover the pools.

around.d: A village on the Ecological Route of the Miracles, known for its manatee protection project.
A peaceful small town with long palm-lined beaches and natural pools at low tide.
A small colonial inland town, marked by the history of the wars against the Dutch.

pipa.vibe: A former fishing village turned bohemian haunt: cobbled streets full of bars in the evening, ochre cliffs above the sand and dolphins swimming into the bay in the morning.
food: Carne de sol
Salted, dried beef, served grilled with cassava and clarified butter.
pipa.respect: Don’t chase the dolphins of Baía dos Golfinhos, get there at low tide, and don’t sit at the foot of the crumbly cliffs.
pipa.season: September to March: dry season, warm water and small, consistent waves for progressing, with crowds in January.

around.d: A village on the edge of the Guaraíras lagoon, known for its sunsets over the water.
A quiet fishing town at the back of a large bay, with good point waves.
One of the largest remnants of Atlantic forest in the Nordeste, between dunes and lagoons.

prea.vibe: A fishing hamlet with sandy streets where kite schools rub shoulders with jangadas, forró rings out in the evening and buggies race along the beach towards Jericoacoara.
food: Baião de dois
Rice and beans cooked together with queijo coalho, a Ceará classic.
prea.respect: Ride well offshore of the jangadas and the fishermen’s nets, and stay clear of swimmers when you cruise along the beach at Jeri.
prea.season: July to January: strong, steady trade winds, dry skies and lagoons still full at the start of the season.

around.d: Dunes, lagoons and the rock arch of Pedra Furada, to discover on foot or by buggy.
A village with sandy streets, where you climb the big dune to watch the sunset.
A neighbouring town by Lagoa do Paraíso, a freshwater lagoon with hammocks strung above the water.

atins.vibe: A fishing village with no paved road, reached by 4x4 or by boat along the Rio Preguiças, where life unfolds between the river mouth, the white dunes and the fishing huts.
atins.respect: In the national park, vehicles have no business in the dunes: explore on foot or with a local guide, and take all your rubbish away with you.
atins.season: July to December: strong, steady wind, and until September lagoons still full in the dunes.

around.d: A lighthouse you can climb to take in the river mouth, the mangroves and the dunes.
A river lined with mangroves and palms, travelled by boat towards the villages and the sea.

puntahermosa.vibe: A seaside resort for Lima’s residents, with summer houses on the cliff, Punta Hermosa is a cradle of Peruvian surfing: world champion Sofía Mulanovich grew up here.
puntahermosa.respect: At Pico Alto and Punta Rocas, the big sessions belong to the local experts: watch first and strictly respect priority.
puntahermosa.season: April to October: big south swells that wake up the reefs, but cold water and the grey skies of the garúa.

around.d: A vast pre-Inca and Inca archaeological site, with adobe pyramids and a Temple of the Sun.
A colourful fishing port where you board a boat to see sea lions and seabirds.
Rocky islets offshore, home to seabirds and sea lions, visible by boat.
A neighbouring seaside village, perched on the cliff above several point waves.

paracas.vibe: Ochre desert plunging into a cold sea teeming with fish: the Paracas culture, famous for its textiles, lived here, and the fishing boats of El Chaco port come home laden with seafood.
food: Tejas from Ica
Little sweets filled with manjar blanco and fruit, coated in sugar.
paracas.respect: In the reserve, drive only on the marked tracks and keep your distance from the flamingos, sea lions and seabirds.
paracas.season: April to November: stronger afternoon wind over a flat bay; bring a wetsuit, the water stays cool.

around.d: Red cliffs, deserted beaches and seabird colonies on the desert peninsula.
A mysterious giant geoglyph carved into a hillside, visible from the sea.
A wild island home to sea lions, known to surfers for its right reached by boat.
The port town that gave its name to the grape brandy, with its Plaza de Armas.

anakena.vibe: According to tradition, this is where Hotu Matu’a, the first king of Rapa Nui, came ashore: the moai crowned with their pukao watch over the beach, where families come for Sunday picnics.
hello: “hello” in Rapa Nui, which will be returned to you with a smile
food: Umu
Meat, fish and sweet potatoes cooked underground on hot stones, for celebrations.
anakena.respect: Never touch a moai and don’t climb onto the ahu, the sacred platforms: it is forbidden and heavily penalised.
anakena.season: December to March: southern summer, milder water and an often calm sea in the sheltered bay.

around.d: The moai quarry, where dozens of unfinished statues emerge from the slopes of the volcano.
The island’s largest platform, with fifteen moai lined up facing inland.
Seven moai inland, the only ones facing the ocean.
The island’s highest point, to climb on foot for a view of the whole ocean around.

salinasec.vibe: The summer beach of Guayaquil’s residents, lined with tower blocks and a lively malecón, Salinas also lives from big-game fishing and sees humpback whales pass offshore in season.
food: Encebollado
A soup of tuna, cassava and pickled onions, the morning cure on the Ecuadorian coast.
salinasec.respect: At La Chocolatera, a military zone and marine reserve, stay on the marked paths and don’t disturb the sea lions on the rocks.
salinasec.season: December to April: consistent north swells and warm water, before the cold current returns.

around.d: The westernmost point of mainland Ecuador, where waves crash against the rocks.
A reconstructed skeleton of a giant sloth and fossils of prehistoric local fauna.
The provincial capital and its Lovers of Sumpa museum, the prehistoric grave of an embracing couple.

kickerrock.vibe: In Puerto Baquerizo Moreno, the archipelago’s administrative capital, sea lions sleep on the benches of the malecón and fishermen share the harbour with the dive boats.
kickerrock.respect: On the malecón, walk around the sea lions without waking or touching them, and dive at León Dormido only with a park-licensed operator.
kickerrock.season: December to May: warmer water, calm sea and good visibility; from June to November, more hammerhead sharks.

tayrona.vibe: The ancestral land of the Kogi, Arhuaco and Wiwa peoples, the park closes for a few weeks each year to let the Sierra rest, and the ruins of Pueblito recall the Tayrona civilisation.
tayrona.respect: Never swim at Arrecifes, with its deadly currents, and come in without alcohol or single-use plastic, both banned in the park.
tayrona.season: December to March: dry season, clearer sea for snorkelling, but crowds at the end of the year.

nuqui.vibe: With no road to reach it, the Afro-Colombian coast of Chocó lives from canoe fishing and the marimba of currulao, between jungle, hot springs and Emberá villages.
food: Tapao de pescado
Fish braised in a covered pot with green plantain and Pacific herbs.
nuqui.respect: During whale season, insist on boats that keep their distance, and choose community-run accommodation.
nuqui.season: April to October: more consistent South Pacific swells, with humpback whales as a bonus from July.

cabodelavela.vibe: For the Wayuu, the cape is Jepirra, the place where the souls of the dead depart: the rancherías string up their hammocks facing the sea and the women weave colourful mochilas.
food: Friche
Young goat fried in its own fat, a festive dish of Wayuu families.
cabodelavela.respect: You are on Wayuu land: ask before taking photos, buy mochilas from the weavers and save fresh water, which is very scarce here.
cabodelavela.season: December to August: strong, almost daily trade winds, dry skies and flat water in the bay.

losroques.vibe: On Gran Roque, the archipelago’s only village, there are no cars: sandy lanes, colourful posadas and lobster fishermen who head out to the cays every morning.
food: Grilled lobster
Caught in the archipelago during the open season, simply grilled in the posadas.
losroques.respect: It’s a national park: don’t collect shells or coral, and never order lobster outside the fishing season.
losroques.season: April to June: gentler trade winds, calm lagoons and clear water, away from the end-of-year and August holidays.

around.d: Two islets joined by a strip of white sand between two turquoise lagoons.
A village island with colourful houses, and an old lighthouse on the hill for the view.
A long white sand beach and fishermen’s huts, for swimming and eating fresh fish.
Islets home to a research station that raises and releases sea turtles.

lapaloma.vibe: A small summer town nestled in the pines, where fishermen’s huts sit beside holiday homes and Uruguayan surfers stay loyal even in the cold winter wind.
food: Buñuelos de algas
Seaweed fritters from the coast, a speciality of the Rocha beaches.
lapaloma.respect: Cross the dunes on the boardwalks and leave the sea lions resting on the rocks of the point in peace.
lapaloma.season: March to May: consistent autumn swells, water still mild and beaches emptied after the summer.

around.d: A protected lagoon separated from the sea by a sandbar, rich in swans and flamingos.
A village perched on a cliff above the ocean, popular with surfers and artists.
A lighthouse you can visit, with a view over the beaches and the rocks of the point.

puertomadryn.vibe: Born from the arrival of Welsh settlers in the 19th century, Puerto Madryn keeps Welsh teas and chapels in the nearby valley, while its long bay lives to the rhythm of sea lions, divers and the winter return of the southern right whales.
food: Welsh tea and torta negra
A hearty afternoon tea handed down from the Welsh pioneers, with a black fruit cake.
puertomadryn.respect: In the water with sea lions, let them come to you and never approach the pups at the colony. Whale watching is done only with the authorised operators of the Valdés Peninsula.
puertomadryn.season: December to March: the least cold water of the year and playful sea lions; from June to December, the southern right whales fill the gulf.

gilit.vibe: On this motor-free islet, horse carts replace cars, the call to prayer from the Sasak village mingles with the beach bars and turtles graze the seagrass a few strokes from the sand.
food: Ayam taliwang and plecing kangkung
Chilli grilled chicken and water spinach with sambal, the two Lombok classics.
gilit.respect: The island is Muslim: cover up when you leave the beach, especially during Ramadan. Underwater, don’t touch the turtles and don’t rest on the reef, even for a photo.
gilit.season: May to September: dry season, calm sea and good visibility; rain from December to March sometimes clouds the water.

desertpoint.vibe: At the tip of the Sekotong peninsula, a fishing hamlet and a few bamboo huts where surfers watch for the swell for days, hammock strung facing the strait, for a few sessions in the tube.
desertpoint.respect: The reef sits just below the surface at low tide: booties and a helmet are no luxury. When it’s on, the line-up is packed and tense: wait your turn without dropping in on anyone, and bring enough cash.
desertpoint.season: June to September: big south-west swells and offshore south-east trade winds; you need a powerful swell and the right tide.

lakeypeak.vibe: Near the village of Hu’u, in the Muslim, rural east of Sumbawa, a row of losmen faces the reef; between sessions, life follows the fishermen, the maize fields and the call to prayer.
lakeypeak.respect: Sumbawa is conservative: cover your shoulders and knees as soon as you leave the beach. The peak is often busy: respect priority and beware of the sharp reef at low tide.
lakeypeak.season: May to September: dry season, consistent southern swells and offshore wind in the morning, before the trade wind picks up.

wakatobi.vibe: A remote archipelago where the Bajau, a sea people, still live in stilt villages above the lagoon, while fishing canoes glide between untouched coral walls.
food: Kasuami
A steamed cone of grated cassava, the staple of local meals, served with fish.
wakatobi.respect: In Bajau villages, ask before taking photos and buy neither shells nor turtle. The national marine park charges a fee: pay it and don’t touch the reef.
wakatobi.season: April to June and September to December: calm sea and superb visibility; in July and August, the south-east trade wind ruffles the surface.

lembeh.vibe: Facing the tuna port of Bitung, in Christian Minahasa country, fishing boats cross paths with divers searching the black volcanic sand, under the gaze of the volcanoes at the northern tip of Sulawesi.
food: Cakalang fufu
Skipjack tuna smoked on sticks, a Minahasa speciality, flaked and spiced with chilli.
lembeh.respect: Never move a creature for a photo and stay stable above the sand so you don’t kick up a cloud. Limit flash on pygmy seahorses.
lembeh.season: May to October: dry season, calmer sea and plenty of critters, with slightly cooler water in midsummer.

around.d: Rainforest where you can see tarsiers and crested black macaques at dusk.
Sulawesi’s highest volcano, a night climb for a sunrise above the clouds.

krui.vibe: A former export trading post of the Lampung country, Krui lives between its damar resin gardens, its fishing boats and a handful of surf camps scattered along the wild coast.
food: Seruit
Grilled fish mashed with sambal, tempoyak and vegetables, a Lampung sharing dish.
krui.respect: The region is Muslim and rural: cover up in town and in the villages. The local surf scene is growing, so make room for the young local surfers in the line-up.
krui.season: May to September: dry season, consistent Indian Ocean swells and south-east winds that are often offshore.

tubbataha.vibe: In the middle of the Sulu Sea there is no village: only rangers taking turns at their station, among islets where seabirds nest, and dive boats come here only a few months a year.
food: Tamilok
A mangrove worm served raw kinilaw-style, the daring speciality of Puerto Princesa.
tubbataha.respect: The park charges an entry fee and requires a ranger briefing: no gloves, no contact with the coral, and stay with your guide in the open-water currents.
tubbataha.season: Mid-March to mid-June: the only window when the Sulu Sea is calm enough for the overnight crossing, with remarkable visibility.

boracay.vibe: The ancestral land of the Ati, Boracay sets its white-sand west coast, where paraw sailboats head out at sunset, against Bulabog on the windward side, where kite schools line up on the beach.
boracay.respect: On the island, smoking and drinking on the beach have been banned since its rehabilitation. On Bulabog, leave the launch zone to the schools and ride well away from swimmers and boats.
boracay.season: December to March: the north-east amihan blows steadily over flat, warm water protected by the reef.

around.d: White Beach and Puka Beach, white sand and paraw trips at sunset.
The last large lowland forest of the Western Visayas, rich in endemic species.

railay.vibe: A world-class climbing hotspot, Railay lives to the rhythm of the long-tails landing on the sand; in a cave at the foot of the cliffs, fishermen honour a sea princess with offerings.
food: Khua kling
Minced meat dry-fried in a fiery curry paste, typical of southern Thailand.
railay.respect: In Phra Nang Cave, don’t touch the offerings and keep a low profile. In a kayak, keep your distance from the long-tails and don’t feed the monkeys.
railay.season: November to April: north-east monsoon, calm and clear Andaman Sea, ideal for paddling between the limestone pinnacles.

around.d: A white sand islet topped by a limestone pinnacle, a good snorkelling spot.
A small island linked to its neighbours by a sandbar at low tide.
A flat islet with white sand and turquoise water, on the way to the Phi Phi Islands.
A white temple perched above the centre of Krabi, decorated with murals.
A provincial town on its mangrove estuary, with a lively night market.

muine.vibe: A former fishing village on the Cham coast, Mũi Né keeps its round basket boats in the bay and its fish sauce factories, while kites dance in front of the red sand dunes.
food: Gỏi cá mai
Small raw fish marinated in lime, rolled in rice paper with herbs.
muine.respect: Launch and land in the designated zones, away from swimmers and the fishermen’s basket boats. At busy times, give priority to the kiter riding upwind.
muine.season: December to March: the north-east monsoon blows hard almost every afternoon, over a sea that is sometimes choppy further out.

perhentian.vibe: Once a stopover for merchants sailing along the coast, the two islands keep a Malay fishing village on Kecil, jungle trails between the coves and water taxis linking the beaches.
food: Keropok lekor
Fried sticks of fish and sago, dipped in a chilli sauce, an emblem of Terengganu.
perhentian.respect: Terengganu is conservative: cover up in the village and be discreet with alcohol. In the marine park, don’t feed the fish and give the turtles and sharks space.
perhentian.season: May to August: glassy sea and excellent visibility; the archipelago almost entirely closes during the monsoon, from November to February.

tioman.vibe: Tioman strings together fishing kampungs linked by concrete paths and jungle, beneath the granite peaks of the south that legend links to a dragon princess turned into an island.
food: Gulai tempoyak ikan patin
Catfish simmered in a fermented durian curry, the pride of Pahang cooking.
tioman.respect: The marine park charges a fee on arrival and forbids collecting coral or shells. In the kampungs, cover up and share the narrow paths carefully with the scooters.
tioman.season: April to September: calm sea and top visibility; from November to February, the north-east monsoon batters the east coast.

hikkaduwa.vibe: A historic stop for travellers on the hippie trail, Hikkaduwa mixes beach bars, fishermen’s outrigger canoes and small Buddhist temples, on a coast that still remembers the 2004 tsunami.
food: Ambul thiyal
A tangy, almost dry tuna curry with goraka, a speciality of the south coast.
hikkaduwa.respect: Don’t feed or touch the turtles in the lagoon, even if others do. At low tide, don’t walk on the reef’s coral.
hikkaduwa.season: December to March: north-east monsoon blowing offshore, consistent west swells and a calm sea outside the waves.

around.d: A Buddhist temple on an island in the Madu River, reached by boat through the mangroves.
A forest monastery founded by a German monk, on a wooded islet in the lagoon.
The village where the 2004 tsunami struck a packed train, now a memorial site.
A brackish lagoon dotted with islets, calm and rich in birds, to explore by rowing boat.
A village known for its temple dedicated to a local deity, much visited by pilgrims.

kalpitiya.vibe: On this long sandy peninsula, Tamil, Muslim and Catholic fishermen dry fish on the beaches, kite camps set up on the edge of the lagoon and pods of dolphins cruise offshore.
food: Karawala
Salted fish dried in the sun on the beaches, fried or cooked in a curry with rice.
kalpitiya.respect: On the lagoon, steer around the fishermen’s nets and canoes. On a dolphin trip, ask the boat to keep its distance and not to cut across the pods’ path.
kalpitiya.season: May to September: the south-west monsoon blows hard and steadily; from December to March, a gentler wind takes over.

around.d: The country’s largest coral reef, a marine sanctuary for snorkelling and dolphins.
A fishing town at the end of the peninsula, with an old Dutch fort and an old church.

varkala.vibe: At the foot of the cliffs, Papanasam beach is a sacred place where Hindu families come at dawn to pay homage to their ancestors, while cafés and ayurveda centres line the clifftop path.
hello: “hello” in Malayalam, said with palms joined
food: Karimeen pollichathu
Pearl spot fish marinated in spices and cooked in a banana leaf, the pride of Kerala.
varkala.respect: On the part of the beach set aside for rites, dress modestly and don’t photograph the ceremonies. Keep away from the edge of the cliffs, which crumble.
varkala.season: October to March: after the monsoon, clean swells and warm water, with a smoother sea in the morning; from June to September, it is too rough.

around.d: A very old temple dedicated to Vishnu, on the hill above the sacred beach.
A place of pilgrimage where the reformer Sree Narayana Guru rests, visited by devotees in yellow.
A beach where the backwaters meet the sea, between coconut palms and a peaceful lagoon.

havelock.vibe: Settled by Bengali families who arrived after Partition, the island keeps villages and beaches simply numbered, rice paddies between the coconut palms and fishing boats beached in the mangroves.
hello: “hello” in Bengali, said with palms joined
food: Macher jhol
A light Bengali-style fish curry, a legacy of the families who settled on the island.
havelock.respect: Swim at lifeguarded beaches: saltwater crocodiles sometimes frequent the mangroves. Don’t collect coral or shells: taking them off the islands is forbidden.
havelock.season: December to April: calm sea, excellent visibility and dry skies; the monsoon from May to September makes crossings rough.

around.d: A long white sand beach fringed by forest, famous for its sunsets.
A small rural island next door, with a natural rock arch and reefs just below the surface.

cokes.vibe: The wave owes its name to the soft drink bottling plant on Thulusdhoo, a local island where surfers’ guesthouses sit beside fishermen’s homes, the football pitch and the dhonis moored in the harbour.
cokes.respect: In the village, cover shoulders and knees, and wear a bikini only on the bikini beach. The line-up is small and resort boats drop people off there: wait your turn and respect the locals.
cokes.season: March to October: consistent southern swells; the biggest arrive from May to August, ideal for Cokes, with more wind.

hanifaru.vibe: In Baa Atoll, a biosphere reserve, the villages still live from pole-and-line tuna fishing and lacquerware crafts, and fishermen have long known about the mantas’ seasonal gathering.
hanifaru.respect: In the bay, only snorkelling is allowed, in limited groups supervised by rangers: keep your distance from the mantas, don’t touch them and don’t dive beneath the group.
hanifaru.season: June to November, especially July to October: monsoon currents concentrate the plankton and draw mantas and sometimes whale sharks.

around.d: An atoll listed by UNESCO for its reefs, its seagrass beds and its manta gatherings.
The local island closest to the bay, with guesthouses, a village and a sandy beach.

miyazaki.vibe: On the Hyūga coast, land of Japan’s founding myths, Shinto shrines and palm trees line the beaches where generations of Kyūshū surfers meet at dawn before work.
food: Chicken nanban
Fried chicken dipped in sweet vinegar then topped with tartare sauce, born in the prefecture.
miyazaki.respect: Line-up etiquette is taken seriously: one person per wave and priority at the peak. Park in the beach car parks and take all your rubbish away with you.
miyazaki.season: September to November: swells from typhoons and autumn lows, water still warm and beaches quiet after the summer.

around.d: A subtropical islet with its shrine, ringed by the rock slabs of the “Devil’s Washboard”.
A vermilion shrine tucked into a sea cave, where you throw lucky clay balls.
One of Japan’s largest laurel forests, crossed by a great suspension bridge.
A shrine dedicated to Emperor Jinmu, in a wooded park in town.
A hilltop park with its Peace Tower and its garden of haniwa figurines.

ishigaki.vibe: At the heart of the Yaeyama archipelago, Ishigaki lives to the sound of the sanshin and island songs, among red-tiled roofs guarded by shisa, Kabira fishermen and black pearl farming in the bay.
food: Yaeyama soba
Thin, round noodles in a pork broth, seasoned with local long pepper.
ishigaki.respect: At the cleaning station, hang back, settled on the sand or at the surface, and never chase or cut across the mantas’ path. Don’t touch the coral as you fin.
ishigaki.season: June to October: mantas very present off Kabira and the water at its warmest, with possible typhoons in midsummer.

around.d: A turquoise bay dotted with wooded islets, to explore by glass-bottom boat; swimming is forbidden.
A preserved Ryukyu village with sandy lanes, coral stone walls and water buffalo carts.
The highest peak in Okinawa Prefecture, with a trail through subtropical forest.
The former residence of a Ryukyu dignitary, with its rock garden made of coral.
History, canoes, costumes and ritual objects of the archipelago’s culture.

jialeshui.vibe: At the tip of the Hengchun Peninsula, home of folk songs accompanied on the yueqin lute, the coast lines up coral rocks sculpted by the sea, small surf schools and winds dropping down from the mountains in winter.
food: Gangkou tea
A robust tea grown nearby, in Taiwan’s southernmost tea garden.
jialeshui.respect: In the national park, don’t collect coral or shells and stay within the area open to surfing. In winter, the offshore wind can push you out to sea: watch the current.
jialeshui.season: October to March: the north-east monsoon sends a consistent swell; in summer and autumn, typhoons bring powerful sessions.

around.d: A white lighthouse on Taiwan’s southern tip, in a park of uplifted coral.
Gates and walls of the old fortified town, among the best preserved on the island.
A large aquarium devoted to Taiwan’s waters, reefs and the world’s oceans.
Grassland on limestone cliffs facing the Pacific, popular at sunrise and for stargazing.
Tropical forest on uplifted coral, with caves, trails and viewpoints.

riyuebay.vibe: Near Wanning, where Chinese returning from Southeast Asia planted Xinglong coffee, the bay has given birth to a real Chinese surf scene, among fishing villages, coconut palms and surf schools.
food: Hele crab
A meaty crab from the Wanning area, one of Hainan’s four great dishes, steamed.
riyuebay.respect: The bay is full of beginners in lessons: keep your distance from school groups and don’t surf in their zone. The rocks at either end quickly break a board.
riyuebay.season: November to March: the north-east monsoon sends a consistent swell; in summer, only typhoons really make the bay work.

masirah.vibe: An island of fishermen and desert, Masirah lives to the rhythm of dhows and boats pulled up on the sand, flamingos in the lagoons and loggerhead turtles that come in great numbers to nest on its beaches.
masirah.respect: On nesting beaches, no lights at night and no vehicles on the sand, and stay well away from the turtles. When wild camping, take all your rubbish away and cover up in town.
masirah.season: June to September: the south-west monsoon blows hard and relentlessly, with a swell that also wakes up the east coast waves.

aqaba.vibe: Jordan’s only port, Aqaba keeps the memory of the Great Arab Revolt and lives to the rhythm of cargo ships, fishing boats and shisha evenings on the corniche, facing the lights of Eilat.
aqaba.respect: In the marine park, enter the water through the marked access points so you don’t trample the coral, and don’t feed the fish. On the town’s public beaches, locals swim clothed: keep a T-shirt on.
aqaba.season: March to May and October to November: warm water, excellent visibility and desert heat still bearable out of the water.

around.d: A Mamluk then Ottoman caravanserai by the sea, near the great flagpole of the Arab Revolt.
Objects from the ancient Islamic city of Ayla and the history of the Red Sea port.
A lively souk, shisha cafés and fish restaurants where you can try sayadieh after a dive.
An islet on the Egyptian side crowned by a restored medieval fortress, surrounded by reefs.

lennox.vibe: A quiet Northern Rivers village in Bundjalung country, Lennox lives between Lake Ainsworth, its water browned by the tea trees, and the point, where every big swell brings together the cream of the coast’s surfers.
lennox.respect: At the point, getting in and out over the boulders is tricky: watch the regulars before you go. The line-up is very hierarchical: stay in your place and don’t drop in on anyone.
lennox.season: March to July: more consistent south-east swells, south-west winds that groom the point and the summer crowds gone.

around.d: The easternmost point of the mainland, with its white lighthouse and a trail overlooking the whales.
Rocky islets off Byron, famous for diving with rays, turtles and leopard sharks.
Coastal rainforest and small wild coves at the foot of the headland.
A surf and music town with a bohemian spirit, with its long beaches and its markets.
Local maritime history, including a balsa raft that arrived after crossing the Pacific.

kirra.vibe: In Coolangatta, twin town of Tweed Heads sitting on the Queensland border, surfing is a family affair: Michael Peterson and Rabbit Bartholomew shaped a tube-riding culture here that is still alive at the peak.
kirra.respect: When Kirra is on, the line-up is packed with pros and locals: don’t force it on the sets if you don’t have the level, and give priority to whoever is deepest.
kirra.season: February to May: cyclone swells from the Coral Sea and offshore south-east winds that hollow out the sandbanks.

around.d: Gondwana rainforest, waterfalls and lookouts over the Gold Coast hinterland.
A headland on the border between the two states, with views of Snapper Rocks and the whales.
A protected rocky islet where you snorkel among green turtles.
A historic wildlife park to meet koalas, kangaroos and rainbow lorikeets.
A lookout at the top of a Surfers Paradise tower, over the whole Gold Coast.

jervisbay.vibe: Between the HMAS Creswell naval base and Booderee park, jointly managed with the Aboriginal community of Wreck Bay, the bay lives to the rhythm of its resident dolphins and the whales that stop here during their migration.
jervisbay.respect: At Hyams Beach, the car park is full in summer: come early or on foot. In the marine park, sanctuary zones ban all fishing and collecting; keep your distance from the dolphins.
jervisbay.season: December to April: the warmest water of the year, a sea often glassy in the morning and top visibility for snorkelling.

around.d: Forests, white sand coves and a botanic garden, on jointly managed Aboriginal land.
A sheltered cove with turquoise water, ideal for snorkelling facing Bowen Island.
A small village famous for its dazzling white sand that squeaks underfoot.
A lighthouse on the edge of high cliffs at the entrance to the bay, a whale-watching spot.
The remains of a badly sited 19th-century lighthouse, amid the heathland of Booderee park.

lordhowe.vibe: On this volcanic crescent where people get around mostly by bike, island families descend from the first settlers who supplied the whalers and still live from the seeds of the kentia palm, shipped all over the world.
lordhowe.respect: Stay on the trails: the Lord Howe woodhen, saved from extinction by a whisker, nests on the ground. In the lagoon, mineral sunscreen only and no feet on the coral.
lordhowe.season: December to April: the warmest water of the year in the lagoon, good visibility and a kinder sea than in the southern winter.

around.d: The island’s highest point, a guided climb through the cloud forest to the summit.
A string of rocks north of the island, with seabird colonies and renowned dives.
A small uninhabited islet in the middle of the lagoon, reached by kayak on a calm sea.
A basalt peak twinned with Mount Gower, whose sheer walls tower over the south of the island.

coralbay.vibe: An isolated hamlet amid the cattle stations of the Gascoyne, Coral Bay lives entirely to the rhythm of the reef: tour boats, passing anglers and the caravans of nomadic retirees escaping the southern winter.
coralbay.respect: Bills Bay is a sanctuary zone: fishing is banned, and never stand on the coral. With manta rays and whale sharks, keep your distance and don’t touch them.
coralbay.season: April to July: whale sharks and manta rays offshore, milder heat and calmer winds than at the height of summer.

luckybay.vibe: A bay named by Matthew Flinders, who found shelter here while exploring the south coast, at the heart of a park of granite and flowering heathland; the nearby town of Esperance owes its name to a French frigate.
luckybay.respect: Don’t feed the kangaroos, even when they come begging on the sand: bread and scraps make them ill. The park campground fills up fast, so book your spot.
luckybay.season: December to March: the least cold water, long days and an often calm sea in the bay, ideal for kayaking.

around.d: Granite domes, turquoise coves such as Hellfire Bay and the climb up Frenchman Peak.
A wooded island in the Recherche Archipelago, with sea lions, seabirds and clear water.
A large wild bay where the explorer Eyre was rescued by a French whaler.

yallingup.vibe: Yallingup, whose Noongar name is often translated as “place of love”, is one of the cradles of West Australian surfing; between vineyards and eucalyptus bush, you surf the reef in the morning and visit the wineries in the afternoon.
food: Margaret River wines
Renowned chardonnays and cabernets, to taste right at the wineries between sessions.
yallingup.respect: At Main Break, locals have surfed this reef for generations: wait your turn and beware of the shallow reef at low tide. Avoid surfing alone at dawn or dusk.
yallingup.season: March to May: big south-west swells from the Indian Ocean and offshore east winds in the morning, before the winter storms.

around.d: A limestone cave with white and orange formations, open to visitors just above the village.
Granite rocks split by the sea, linked by a walkway above the waves.
An early 20th-century lighthouse at the start of the Cape to Cape Track, overlooking Geographe Bay.
Sheltered coves with calm water and a coastal trail on Geographe Bay.

kaikoura.vibe: Kaikōura means “meal of crayfish” in Māori: a former whaling station, the town now lives from sperm whale watching, started by Ngāti Kurī, and from its roadside crayfish shacks.
food: Kaikōura crayfish
Crayfish grilled or with garlic, sold at the roadside shacks north of town.
kaikoura.respect: Stay at least 20 m from the fur seals on the peninsula rocks and never put yourself between them and the sea. In the Hikurangi Marine Reserve, all taking of marine life is banned.
kaikoura.season: December to March: calmer sea in the morning, the least cold water and long days for paddling among fur seals and dolphins.

around.d: A coastal trail above the limestone cliffs, with fur seal and seabird colonies.
The town’s oldest house, set on whale bones, a witness to the whaling era.
A long climb in the coastal range for a sweeping view over the peninsula and the ocean.
A night sky protected from light pollution, ideal for watching the Milky Way.

poorknights.vibe: Declared tapu by Ngātiwai after a deadly raid in the 19th century, the islands have remained uninhabited; boats leave from Tutukaka marina, and a warm current brings subtropical fish here.
poorknights.respect: Landing on the islands is forbidden without a permit: everything happens in the water or from the boat. In the marine reserve, nothing may be taken, not even a shell.
poorknights.season: January to May: the warmest water of the year, visibility at its best and a sea often calmer than in winter.

gisborne.vibe: On the Tairāwhiti coast, where the ancestral waka and later James Cook came ashore, Gisborne remains one of the most Māori towns in the country; at Wainui, surfing families and early risers meet in the water with the first sun.
gisborne.respect: At Wainui, the peaks are shared among local regulars: say hello and wait your turn. The dunes are being restored, so use only the marked access paths.
gisborne.season: March to June: cyclone swells followed by more consistent easterly swells, offshore winds in the morning and water still mild.

around.d: A former Māori pā overlooking the town and the bay, with a lookout over Tūranganui-a-Kiwa.
A historic reserve telling of the arrival of the Māori waka and of Cook, the first encounter.
A small coastal town surrounded by vineyards, with its port and riverbanks.

beqa.vibe: Beqa is the island of the firewalkers, a ritual handed down by the Sawau clan; on the lagoon side, villages have given up fishing on Shark Reef in exchange for a fee paid by every diver, a model of community protection.
beqa.respect: During the shark feed, stay behind the coral wall, arms by your sides, and follow the guide’s instructions to the letter. The reserve fee keeps the villages going: don’t dodge it.
beqa.season: May to October: dry, cooler season, clearer sea and bull sharks present in numbers on Shark Reef.

around.d: A mountainous island with traditional villages, home of the Sawau clan’s firewalkers.
Tropical gorges and waterfalls to travel down by canoe or raft to the inland villages.
A small town where the dive boats leave from, the hub of the coast’s adventure activities.

rainbowreef.vibe: Taveuni, Fiji’s “Garden Island” crossed by the 180th meridian, lives to the rhythm of its villages and taro plantations; Somosomo is home to the Tui Cakau, the region’s paramount customary chief.
rainbowreef.respect: The sites depend on the tides in the Somosomo Strait: dive with a local guide and keep your fins well away from the very fragile soft corals. In villages, cover your shoulders and knees.
rainbowreef.season: May to October: the dry season, top visibility and soft corals opened out by the tidal currents.

around.d: A forest-covered volcanic island, with the Bouma waterfalls and the Lavena coastal walk.
Taveuni’s chiefly village, seat of the Tui Cakau, on the shore of the strait of the same name.

moorea.vibe: Facing Tahiti, Moorea grows its pineapples deep in the Ōpūnohu valley, where the marae recall ancient Polynesian society; on the lagoon, va’a paddlers glide out at sunrise.
food: Moorea pineapple
A small, very sweet pineapple from the island’s valleys, to enjoy fresh or as local juice.
moorea.respect: Don’t touch the rays and never feed rays or sharks: the lagoon is covered by a management plan. Don’t walk on the coral heads and choose a mineral sunscreen.
moorea.season: May to October: the dry season, cooling trade winds, crystal-clear water and humpback whales late in the season.

around.d: A deep bay framed by green peaks, with the lookout and the valley’s marae further up.
A spectacular bay at the foot of Mount Mouaroa, lined with villages and yachts at anchor.
A dizzying ridge between the two bays, a demanding hike for a view over the whole lagoon.
The island’s highest point, a jagged summit towering over the lagoon from the centre of Moorea.

rangiroa.vibe: Rangiroa, “immense sky” in Paumotu, lives on fishing, pearls and copra; in Tiputa, people watch from the point for dolphins playing in the waves of the pass on the rising tide.
food: Rangiroa wine
A vineyard planted on coral among the coconut palms, whose white and rosé you can taste on site.
rangiroa.respect: In the pass, follow your guide: dives are timed with the very powerful incoming current. Don’t chase the dolphins and never touch the sharks.
rangiroa.season: December to March for great hammerhead sharks in the pass, but dolphins and grey sharks are there all year round.

around.d: A vast lagoon to explore by boat, out to the Blue Lagoon and the Pink Sands.
The atoll’s largest village, with its church and its point on the pass, reached by water taxi.
The atoll’s second, more accessible pass, for drift snorkelling or swimming with mask and snorkel depending on the tide.
The atoll’s main village, with its guesthouses, its church and its pearl farms.

fakarava.vibe: Fakarava lives to the quiet rhythm of Rotoava, its pearl farms and its bicycles; in the south, the hamlet of Tetamanu keeps a coral church, a reminder of the days when it was the capital of the Tuamotus.
fakarava.respect: In the biosphere reserve, don’t collect shells or coral and don’t grab the reef in the pass. Buy your pearls directly from the farms.
fakarava.season: June and July, during the gathering of camouflage groupers in the south pass, which draws even more sharks.

poe.vibe: In Bourail, a land of bush folk and cattle farmers whose agricultural fair brings all of New Caledonia together every year, Poé is the weekend beach: family picnics, kitesurfing in the afternoon and turtles in the lagoon.
food: Bush venison
Stew, skewers or venison sausage, a speciality of the west coast’s farmers.
poe.respect: Stay in the kitesurfing zone, well away from swimmers and snorkellers. At La Roche Percée, loggerhead turtles nest in the southern summer: keep your distance and switch off your torch.
poe.season: September to December: steady afternoon trade winds, a flat lagoon and water warming up before summer.

around.d: A monolith sculpted by the waves at La Roche Percée, facing a long wild beach.
A cove shaded by tall columnar pines, reachable on foot from La Roche Percée.
A vast natural area between hills and lagoon, with trails on foot, by mountain bike or on horseback.
The history of the penal colony and colonisation, in a former prison building.

coolidge.vibe: Luganville was born of the gigantic American Second World War base: at Million Dollar Point, the army dumped its surplus into the sea, and in the evening people meet at the nakamal for a shell of kava.
coolidge.respect: The wreck is protected: don’t bring up any object, or you face heavy penalties. Dive with an approved guide, as the inside of the liner is a real labyrinth.
coolidge.season: April to October: the dry season, calmer sea and better visibility, outside the cyclone period.

around.d: Objects and stories from the American base on Santo and the sinking of the Coolidge.
The country’s second town, with its covered market, its nakamals and its wartime barracks.
A wooded island facing Luganville, with calm coves and snorkelling a few minutes away by boat.
A large rural island of traditional villages and cocoa gardens, south of Santo.

bluecorner.vibe: Palau created the world’s first shark sanctuary: here, a living shark is worth more than a fin, and the guides of Koror know every drop-off of the Chelbacheb islands like their own village.
bluecorner.respect: Hook your reef hook onto dead rock only, never onto living coral, and stay still at the edge of the drop-off. The Rock Islands permit is compulsory.
bluecorner.season: December to April: the dry season, calmer sea and visibility at its best for diving in the current.

around.d: A marine lake in the Rock Islands where you swim among almost harmless golden jellyfish.
A channel cut through the reef, a cleaning station where manta rays come to be groomed.
An island scarred by a terrible battle in 1944, with military remains in the jungle.
A string of limestone islets in a strict nature reserve, to admire from the boat.

jellyfishlake.vibe: In the heart of the Chelbacheb islands, this saltwater lake, cut off from the ocean for millennia, is home to golden jellyfish that follow the sun’s path from one shore to the other; Palauans call it the “fifth lake”.
jellyfishlake.respect: Scuba diving is forbidden: swim gently at the surface, fins in slow motion, so as not to harm the jellyfish. Rinse off every trace of sunscreen before getting in; the lake permit is compulsory.
jellyfishlake.season: December to April: the dry season and a calm sea for the crossing; check beforehand, as jellyfish numbers vary from year to year.

around.d: A legendary reef point where you hook onto the drop-off to watch sharks and schools of fish go by.
A channel cut through the reef, a cleaning station where manta rays come to be groomed.
A string of limestone islets in a strict nature reserve, to admire from the boat.
Koror’s aquarium devoted to the reefs and marine lakes of Palau.

salani.vibe: On Upolu’s south coast, life follows fa’a Samoa: open fale, a council of matai that governs the village and church singing on Sundays; the wave is surfed at the river mouth, facing the fishermen’s canoes.
salani.respect: The reef belongs to the village: go through the surf camp or ask before going in the water. When crossing the village, slow down, say hello and cover your shoulders.
salani.season: May to October: regular southern swells from storms in the Southern Ocean, hitting this south coast head-on.

around.d: Rainforest, the Togitogiga waterfalls and lava cliffs on the south coast.
A long white-sand beach lined with fale, facing the Aleipata islets.
A volcanic islet off Lalomanu, with beach fale and a reef to explore with mask and snorkel.
A deep bay surrounded by forests and traditional villages, a conservation area.

vavau.vibe: Around Neiafu’s Port of Refuge, a natural shelter where Pacific yachts anchor during the southern winter, Vava’u blends Tongan villages, churches with powerful choirs and wooded islets linked by calm channels.
vavau.respect: Only swim with the whales with a licensed operator: small groups, a slow approach and never any contact. On Sundays everything stops, boat trips included.
vavau.season: July to October: the season of humpback whales coming to give birth, clear water and moderate trade winds in the channels.

around.d: The archipelago’s small capital, with a market, churches and sailors’ bars facing the Port of Refuge.
An island next to Neiafu linked by a causeway, with calm coves for paddling.
The country’s first botanical garden, with useful and medicinal plants of the islands.

aitutaki.vibe: The first of the Cook Islands reached by missionaries, Aitutaki keeps an old coral church and its Sunday singing in Arutanga; the Coral Route flying boats once landed on the lagoon, near Akaiami.
aitutaki.respect: The lagoon’s giant clams are protected: don’t touch them and never lift them. On Sundays the island lives to the rhythm of the church, so dress respectfully if you attend the service.
aitutaki.season: April to November: the dry season, steady trade winds for kitesurfing and a crystal-clear lagoon, outside the cyclone period.

around.d: A white-sand motu fringed by turquoise sandbanks, where you can get your passport stamped.
The motu where the Coral Route flying boats used to land, with a beach and shallow water.
An islet in the south-west of the lagoon, with a seabird colony and snorkelling over the coral heads.
The island’s small main town, with its wharf and the oldest church in the Cook Islands.

kavieng.vibe: A former German colonial town at the end of the Boluminski Highway, Kavieng is still a peaceful port of markets and coconut plantations, surrounded by islets where the villages themselves manage surfing on their reefs.
kavieng.respect: The Pacific War wrecks are graves: don’t bring up any object. At the market or in a village, always ask before photographing someone.
kavieng.season: November to April: north-west monsoon swells and light winds, while the rest of the South Pacific is calmer.

envau.vibe: White limestone cliffs, Aleppo pines clinging to the rock and turquoise water: here you arrive on foot or by kayak, like the people of Marseille and Cassis who have always roamed the calanques.
food: Bouillabaisse
Marseille’s rockfish soup, served with rouille and garlicky croutons.
envau.respect: Access to the massif is regulated in summer according to the fire risk: check it is open before setting off, light no fires and take all your rubbish home.
envau.season: May to June and September: the water is already mild, the light is bright and the trails are less crowded than in high summer.

around.d: Coves, cliffs and coastal paths between Marseille and Cassis, on land and at sea.
Among the highest sea cliffs in France, with a huge view from the Route des Crêtes.
A colourful fishing port, with terraces on the quays and the terraced vineyards of Cassis wine.
A long calanque sheltering a marina and old stone quarries.
An island fortress in the harbour of Marseille, made famous by The Count of Monte Cristo.

peyrefite.vibe: On the Côte Vermeille, the terraced vineyards of Banyuls tumble down towards schist coves, and Catalan culture shows everywhere, from the place names to the colourful boats.
food: Collioure anchovies
Salted and matured by hand using age-old know-how, with a glass of Banyuls.
peyrefite.respect: You are in a marine nature reserve: no fishing or collecting, don’t touch the Posidonia seagrass or the wildlife, and follow the marked trail.
peyrefite.season: June to September: the warmest water, an often calm sea and a guided underwater trail in summer.

around.d: France’s first exclusively marine nature reserve, rich in groupers and gorgonians.
A painters’ village with its bell tower rising from the water, flower-filled lanes and pebble beaches.
A massive fortress overlooking the port, once a residence of the kings of Majorca.
A Catalan port surrounded by terraced vineyards, famous for its naturally sweet wine.
A Romanesque abbey perched above Cap de Creus, with a superb view of the sea.

lerins.vibe: Pine forest, shady paths and the fort where the Man in the Iron Mask was held: facing the Croisette, Sainte-Marguerite offers a car-free Côte d’Azur, next door to the monks of Saint-Honorat.
food: Socca and pan bagnat
A chickpea pancake and a Niçois sandwich, perfect for a picnic on the island.
lerins.respect: No fires or camping on the island, and don’t drop anchor on or trample the Posidonia seagrass meadows. Keep an eye on the time of the last boat to Cannes.
lerins.season: June to September: warm water and a calm sea, with visibility often better in early summer.

around.d: A citadel where you can visit the cell of the Man in the Iron Mask, with a view over the bay of Cannes.
The island of the Cistercian monks, among vines, chapels and a still-inhabited abbey.
A medieval tower-monastery standing over the sea at the tip of Saint-Honorat.
The old quarter of Cannes perched on its hill, with lanes and a view over the bay.
Red volcanic rocks plunging into the sea, with trails and wild coves.

pampelonne.vibe: Legendary beach clubs, vines right down to the sand and a pine-covered peninsula: Pampelonne mixes the Saint-Tropez jet set with nature still unspoilt on its capes.
food: Tarte tropézienne
