A brioche filled with a light cream, born in Saint-Tropez and now known everywhere.
pampelonne.respect: Beach car parks are expensive and fill up fast in summer: come early or by bike, and keep out of the marked swimming zones when you paddleboard.
pampelonne.season: June and September: a warm sea, wind often light in the morning and a beach far less crowded than in August.

around.d: A former fishing village of pastel façades, a lively port and the lanes of La Ponche.
A 17th-century fortress housing a maritime history museum, with a view over the gulf.
Pointillist and Fauvist painters who came to Saint-Tropez, in a former chapel by the port.
A hilltop village of winding lanes, surrounded by vines and wooded hills.
A garden of the world’s Mediterranean climates facing the sea, with an underwater trail in summer.

gruissan.vibe: Chalets on stilts facing the sea, an old village coiled around its tower and pink salt pans: Gruissan lives to the rhythm of the tramontane, among lagoons, fishermen and colourful sails.
food: Étang de Leucate oysters
Raised in the nearby lagoon, to enjoy with a glass of La Clape white.
gruissan.respect: When the tramontane blows, the wind comes off the land and pushes you out to sea: never sail alone, stay close to shore and respect the swimming zones.
gruissan.season: April to June and September to October: frequent, strong tramontane, uncrowded beaches and water that’s still pleasant.

around.d: Lanes in a circle around the Barberousse tower, with salt pans and a lagoon at the village gates.
A wildlife park on the edge of the lagoons, with African species seen by car or on foot.
A fishing village perched above the lagoon, with quiet lanes and lovely views over the water.
A limestone plateau dropping into the sea, with cliffs to walk and major board-sports spots.

salagou.vibe: Red earth, volcanic hills and olive trees: Lake Salagou flooded part of the valley, leaving the abandoned village of Celles on its shores, in an almost Martian landscape.
food: Petits pâtés de Pézenas
Small sweet-and-savoury mutton pies, a speciality of the neighbouring town.
salagou.respect: Wild camping and driving off the tracks are forbidden around the lake: the red ruffe soils erode very quickly. Watch out for the wind, which can pick up strongly in the afternoon.
salagou.season: June to September: pleasant water for paddleboarding, windless mornings and a calmer lake than in the middle of August.

around.d: A medieval village nestled at the end of a small valley, around a former Benedictine abbey.
A jumble of dolomite rocks to explore on trails, above a small village.
A near-abandoned village on the lake shore, emptied when the dam was filled.
A former royal cloth manufactory turned into a walled village, out of time.
A deep-cut river beneath the Pont du Diable, with swimming spots and hikes through the garrigue.

monteynard.vibe: Between the Vercors and the Trièves, this green-watered reservoir has become the meeting place for the Alps’ kitesurfers and windsurfers, drawn by an afternoon breeze that is rare in the mountains.
food: Gratin dauphinois
Melting potatoes baked in cream, the great classic of the Dauphiné.
monteynard.respect: Only get in the water from the zones reserved for board sports and stay well away from the pleasure boat. The water stays cool: a wetsuit is a must.
monteynard.season: June to September, especially July and August: a steady thermal breeze in the afternoon and less cold water.

around.d: Limestone cliffs, forests and mountain-pasture plateaus criss-crossed by hiking trails.
A vast, roadless wild plateau, for long hikes through the alpine pastures.
A small area of hedged farmland and villages at the foot of Mont Aiguille, with very open landscapes.
A former anthracite mine to visit to discover the work of the plateau’s miners.
The Champollion family home, devoted to the decipherment of hieroglyphs.

pontdarc.vibe: Colourful canoes under the limestone arch, cliffs riddled with caves and sun-scorched garrigue: around the Pont d’Arc, people left the oldest paintings in the region.
food: Picodon
A small goat’s cheese from the Ardèche and the Drôme, mild when young and sharp when aged.
pontdarc.respect: In the gorges reserve, bivouacking is only allowed at designated sites and must be booked. Leave nothing behind on the pebble beaches.
pontdarc.season: May to June and September: still enough flow, pleasant water and a river far less crowded than in summer.

around.d: A faithful replica of the Chauvet cave and its paintings of lions, horses and rhinos.
A canyon of limestone cliffs to paddle down by canoe or admire from the viewpoint road.
A huge underground chamber with giant formations, plus a museum of prehistory.
A cave of draperies and formations opening onto a balcony above the gorges.
Long galleries with stepped rimstone pools and varied formations, to visit underground.

roquegageac.vibe: Golden stone houses clinging to the cliff, traditional gabarre boats on the river and castles on every promontory: the Dordogne valley keeps the memory of medieval wars.
food: Périgord foie gras and walnuts
Foie gras on toast and walnut cake, two prides of the tables of the Périgord Noir.
roquegageac.respect: Give way to the gabarres taking visitors on trips and only land on the pebble beaches, not on private riverbanks.
roquegageac.season: May to June and September: a decent water level, mild weather and a river much calmer than in high summer.

around.d: A medieval town of golden-stone mansions and a big, lively market.
A fortress perched on top of a cliff, with a spectacular view over the Dordogne.
A medieval fortress housing a museum of warfare in the Middle Ages and its siege engines.
A bastide town perched on a cliff, whose clifftop offers a vast panorama over the valley.
A Renaissance château where Josephine Baker lived, surrounded by formal French gardens.

gorgestarn.vibe: Stone villages huddled at the foot of the causses, boatmen’s punts gliding between the cliffs: in La Malène, life in the canyon has long revolved around the river.
food: Aligot
Stretchy mashed potato with fresh tomme cheese, served piping hot with a sausage.
gorgestarn.respect: Always give way to the La Malène boatmen’s punts, especially in the narrow passage of Les Détroits, and throw nothing into the river.
gorgestarn.season: May to June and September: enough flow, pleasant water and a river far less busy than in summer.

around.d: A labyrinth of strangely shaped dolomite rocks, to explore on trails.
Causses, valleys and wild ridges, criss-crossed by trails and stone villages.
A cave with pink-tinted formations, hollowed out beneath the Causse Noir.
A characterful small town where three rivers meet, gateway to the causses and Mont Aigoual.
A medieval small town crossed by little canals, nicknamed the little Venice of Lozère.

excenevex.vibe: Fine sand and reeds on the shore of Lake Geneva, professional fishermen’s boats and the outline of the Swiss Alps opposite: Excenevex feels like the seaside at the foot of the Chablais.
food: Lake Geneva perch fillets
Pan-fried in butter and served with chips, the great classic of the lakeshore.
excenevex.respect: The bise can whip up short waves very quickly on Lake Geneva: on a paddleboard, stay close to shore and avoid crossing towards Switzerland without experience.
excenevex.season: July to August: Lake Geneva’s water at its warmest, long evenings and a lake that is often calm in the morning.

around.d: A fortified medieval village of flower-decked houses, jutting into the lake between harbour and ramparts.
A garden laid out as a plant labyrinth where you discover plants through sight, smell and touch.
A spa town on a balcony above the lake, with a funicular and the fishing port of Rives.
A Belle Époque spa resort with flower-lined promenades and elegant architecture facing the lake.
Madame de Staël’s home on the Swiss shore, with its salons and its park.

guerledan.vibe: In the heart of the Argoat, far from the sea, the lake flooded part of the Nantes–Brest canal: sunken locks, a towpath and deep forests give the place the charm of inland Brittany.
hello: “hello” in Breton, to greet people the way they do in Central Brittany
food: Crêpes and buckwheat galettes
A galette complète or a salted-butter crêpe, with a bowl of cider.
guerledan.respect: On the towpath, share the space with cyclists and walkers, and on the water keep well away from the dam and its off-limits surroundings.
guerledan.season: June to September: the mildest water of the year and long days to explore the wooded coves.

around.d: A large forest of beeches and heathland overlooking the lake, criss-crossed by trails.
A 15th-century fortified castle with massive towers and moats, in the heart of Pontivy.
A medieval old town and a Napoleonic quarter on a grid plan, on the banks of the Blavet.
A large Gothic pilgrimage chapel in the middle of a granite hamlet.

vassiviere.vibe: On the Millevaches plateau, among heathland, peat bogs and conifer forests, the lake blends swimming, sailing and contemporary art, in a rural and peaceful Limousin.
food: Pâté de pommes de terre
A Limousin pie filled with potatoes and cream, served hot.
vassiviere.respect: On the island, the works in the sculpture wood are part of an art trail: don’t climb on them. Swim at the lifeguarded beaches in summer.
vassiviere.season: July to August: water that is finally mild on this high plateau, lifeguarded beaches and a light wind.

around.d: A wooded island dotted with open-air sculptures, to explore on foot around the lake.
A building with a brick lighthouse housing contemporary art exhibitions.
Heathland, peat bogs and springs on a granite plateau, ideal for hiking.
A rare pacifist memorial where a child shakes his fist beneath the inscription “Cursed be war”.

maubuisson.vibe: Between the pine forest and the dunes of the Médoc, the lake’s fresh, shallow water offers the quiet flip side of the nearby ocean coast, with cycle paths and small marinas.
food: Entrecôte à la bordelaise
Grilled over vine cuttings and coated in a Médoc red wine sauce.
maubuisson.respect: The lake’s shores and reed beds shelter many birds: keep away from the protected areas and bring your gear ashore at the designated beaches.
maubuisson.season: May to September: a steady afternoon sea breeze and water that warms up fast thanks to the shallow depth.

around.d: Trails through marshes, heathland and forest, with shy wildlife to watch.
Wooded dunes, damp dune slacks and unspoilt marshes between the lake and the ocean.
Another large pine-fringed lake, for sailing, paddleboarding or a wave-free swim.
Two brick towers hidden in the pine forest, near the ocean coast.

belharra.vibe: Off the Basque corniche, on days of huge swell, the whole coast crowds onto the cliffs to watch jet skis tow surfers onto immense walls of water.
hello: “hi” in Basque, said with a smile
food: Ttoro
A fish soup of the Saint-Jean-de-Luz fishermen, rich and spiced with Espelette pepper.
belharra.respect: Only venture out for supervised tow-in, with jet-ski safety cover. To watch, park in the corniche car parks without blocking the road.
belharra.season: November to February, only during very big, well-aligned winter swells, a few days a year.

around.d: The neo-Gothic castle of a travelling scholar, on an estate of cliffs and heathland facing the ocean.
A Basque fishing port with half-timbered houses, a sheltered bay and a lively pedestrian street.
A fishermen’s quarter facing Saint-Jean-de-Luz, with Basque houses and the Fort de Socoa.
A fortified manor reworked over the centuries, surrounded by a park.
A small Basque village perched above its harbour and its reef waves.

conchebaleines.vibe: At the tip of the island, white houses with green shutters, salt marshes and bikes everywhere: the Conche keeps a wild side, among dunes, pine forest and a lighthouse watching over the currents.
food: Île de Ré potatoes
Thin-skinned new potatoes harvested in spring, simply cooked with salted butter.
conchebaleines.respect: Only cross the dune by the marked paths, and leave the car behind: the island is easy to explore by bike on its cycle paths.
conchebaleines.season: September to November: regular autumn swells, water still lukewarm and an island much quieter than in summer.

around.d: A tall lighthouse to climb for a view over the whole island, with the old Vauban tower next to it.
A port fortified by Vauban, a UNESCO World Heritage site, with lively quays and lanes.
A village of narrow lanes, recognisable by its black-and-white bell tower that serves as a seamark.
Marshes and mudflats where thousands of birds winter, to watch from the cycle paths.
A small port of white houses, a covered medieval market and quiet quays.

cotesauvage.vibe: Dunes, endless pine forest and an ocean roaring at the foot of the lighthouse: the Arvert peninsula lives between forest, the oyster ponds of the Seudre and wild waves to approach with respect.
food: Marennes-Oléron oysters
Finished in claires in the Seudre basin, to taste straight from the oyster farmer.
cotesauvage.respect: The baïnes and currents here are formidable: only go in the water near lifeguard stations, never alone, and stay on the marked paths across the dune.
cotesauvage.season: September to November: powerful autumn swells, water still lukewarm and an almost deserted beach.

around.d: A Renaissance lighthouse standing at sea, a UNESCO World Heritage site, reached by boat at low tide.
A tall red-and-white tower to climb for a view taking in the ocean, the forest and the estuary.
A huge pine forest on dunes, criss-crossed by cycle paths and trails.
A village of fishermen and oyster farmers with flower-filled lanes, on the edge of the marshes.
A large zoo set beneath the pines, a few minutes from the beaches.

lavezzi.vibe: Wind-sculpted granite boulders, crystal-clear water and a lonely lighthouse: in the middle of the Strait of Bonifacio, the Lavezzi recall the shipwrecks of old, while Bonifacio keeps watch from its cliffs.
food: Aubergines à la bonifacienne
Stuffed, gratinéed aubergines, a family speciality of Bonifacio.
lavezzi.respect: You are in a nature reserve: no fishing, no fires, no camping, and don’t drop anchor on the Posidonia seagrass meadows.
lavezzi.season: June to September: warm water and excellent visibility, but keep an eye on the often strong wind in the strait.

around.d: A fortified old town perched on limestone cliffs overhanging the sea.
The southern tip of Corsica, with a clifftop path and a view of Sardinia.
An almost enclosed cove of white sand and turquoise water, between two headlands.
A small white-sand cove nestled between cliffs, reached on foot.

saleccia.vibe: Sun-scorched maquis, old pastures and dirt tracks: the Agriates, once the farming granary of Cap Corse, have become a protected desert reached by boat or 4×4.
food: Brocciu
A fresh ewe’s or goat’s milk cheese, eaten plain, in an omelette or in fiadone.
saleccia.respect: Wild camping and fires are forbidden in the Agriates: sleep at the beach campsite or head back on the shuttle boat, and bring enough water.
saleccia.season: June to September: a warm, clear sea, with calmer mornings before the boats arrive.

around.d: Wild maquis crossed by the coastal path, from cove to cove.
A neighbouring white-sand beach, served by boat from Saint-Florent.
A lively port at the head of its gulf, with colourful lanes and a Genoese citadel.
A wine village renowned for its wines, among hillsides overlooking the gulf.
Prehistoric megaliths and dolmens scattered through the maquis.

santagiulia.vibe: White sand, a lagoon behind and fragrant maquis: around Porto-Vecchio, southern Corsica mixes postcard coves, an old Genoese citadel and Torrean sites in the hinterland.
food: Fiadone
A lemon-scented brocciu cake, light and melt-in-the-mouth, found on every Corsican table.
santagiulia.respect: The bay is very busy in summer: on a paddleboard or in a kayak, keep out of the marked swimming zones and don’t trample the seagrass or the neighbouring lagoon.
santagiulia.season: June and September: a warm, calm sea, clear water and a beach far less crowded than in August.

around.d: An almost enclosed cove of white sand and turquoise water, between two headlands.
A Genoese old town perched above the salt pans, with lanes and terraces buzzing in the evening.
A Bronze Age stone fortress, perched with a view over the whole gulf.
A small protected archipelago off the coast, a seabird refuge to cruise past by boat.
A high-altitude forest of laricio pines, with a lake, trails and the Piscia di Gallu waterfall.

lemoule.vibe: Cane fields, a rum distillery and a coast pounded by the Atlantic: Le Moule looks out to sea, with local surfers who know every reef in the bay.
lemoule.respect: The line-up is very local and the reefs are shallow: watch before paddling out, give priority to the regulars and say hello at the peak.
lemoule.season: November to March: North Atlantic winter swells, cleaner in the morning before the trade wind picks up.

around.d: Jagged cliffs facing the ocean, a cross at the top and a view of La Désirade.
Collections of Amerindian archaeology tracing the history of the island’s first inhabitants.
A fine-sand beach protected by the reef, with a calm lagoon for swimming.
A small sheltered cove with calm water, popular for swimming and snorkelling.

petiteterre.vibe: Two uninhabited islets, an old stone lighthouse and a turquoise lagoon: Petite-Terre is explored on a day trip from Saint-François, among iguanas and seabirds.
petiteterre.respect: The reserve can only be reached on authorised boats: stay on the trails, don’t touch or feed the iguanas, and keep your distance from the lagoon’s wildlife.
petiteterre.season: December to May: the dry season, steady trade winds and an often crystal-clear lagoon, even if the crossing can be rough.

around.d: Guadeloupe’s oldest lighthouse, rising amid the dry vegetation.
A calm, wild island with deserted beaches and fishing villages far from the bustle.
La Désirade’s highest point, for a climb with a view over the whole archipelago.

grandeanse_deshaies.vibe: Coconut palms, golden sand and green hills tumbling into the sea: Deshaies still feels like a fishing village, with its colourful boats and small fish restaurants.
grandeanse_deshaies.respect: Watch the flags: the swell creates strong currents here. Turtles nest on the beach, so don’t touch the marked nests and avoid lights at night.
grandeanse_deshaies.season: April to June: the end of the dry season and a sea more often calm than in winter, when northern swells hit the coast.

around.d: Protected waters around the Pigeon islets, famous for diving and snorkelling.
A colourful fishing village at the head of its bay, the filming location of a TV series.
A wild islet off the coast, popular with divers for its fish-rich waters.
A wildlife park deep in the rainforest, with a canopy walk.

bonneville.vibe: At the end of the Caravelle peninsula, Tartane is still a fishing village of colourful yoles, now the heart of Martinique surfing with its schools set up facing the bay.
bonneville.respect: Several schools share the bay: avoid the lesson areas, leave the peaks to the regulars and watch out for rocks and sea urchins on the sides.
bonneville.season: November to April: regular Atlantic swells, cleaner in the morning before the trade wind picks up.

around.d: Trails through dry forest, mangroves and cliffs battered by the Atlantic.
The ruins of a former colonial sugar estate, in a wild setting.
A lighthouse perched above the peninsula, with a wide panorama over the Atlantic coast.
The history of agricultural rum and old stills on the site of a distillery.
A lush botanical garden with suspended walkways in the trees.

pointefaula.vibe: In Le Vauclin, small-scale fishing still sets the pace of the town and the yoles rondes, Martinique’s traditional sailing boats, train offshore. The Pointe Faula lagoon serves as a classroom for the south’s kitesurfers.
pointefaula.respect: Stay out of the swimming zone and don’t sail right over the seagrass at low tide: the lagoon is very shallow.
pointefaula.season: December to May, during the carême dry season: strong, steady trade winds, dry weather and warm water.

around.d: Protected islets where terns and seabirds nest, to observe from the sea.
An archipelago of islets and white shallows where you can bathe standing up in the open sea.
Martinique’s largest islet, a refuge of the Lesser Antillean iguana.
Amerindian petroglyphs carved on boulders deep in the forest.
A long beach of golden sand lined with coconut palms at the island’s southern tip.

salines_mq.vibe: At weekends, Martinican families settle under the trees with cool boxes and cooking pots. All around, the lagoon and the dry savannahs of the Sainte-Anne peninsula contrast with the mountainous north.
salines_mq.respect: Spot the manchineel trees marked with a red band: never shelter beneath them, as their sap and fruit are toxic.
salines_mq.season: December to April: the dry season, a calm sea and clear water for swimming and watching the fish.

around.d: An iconic volcanic islet, also a renowned dive site.
White stone statues facing the sea, in memory of the victims of the slave trade.
Protected islets where terns and seabirds nest, to observe from the sea.
The island’s history, from the Amerindians to the sugar estates.
A wild beach on the Atlantic coast, reached by a dirt track.

orientbay.vibe: On the French side of the island, Orient Bay mixes beach bars, fishermen and a Caribbean vibe. People switch from one language to another, and in the evening they head to Grand-Case for seafront barbecues.
food: Grand-Case lolo barbecues
Ribs, chicken and fish grilled in the little seafront canteens.
orientbay.respect: The southern end of the beach is naturist: respect that area. When kitesurfing, stay well away from swimmers and the channel buoys.
orientbay.season: December to April: strong, steady trade winds, the dry season and outside the hurricane period.

around.d: A small white-sand islet reached by shuttle boat, good for snorkelling.
A flat, uninhabited island in the reserve, with deserted beaches and fish-rich waters.
The island’s highest point, with forest trails and a view of the neighbouring islands.
A seaside village renowned for its restaurants and its lolos.
An 18th-century fort overlooking Marigot and its bay.

ngouja.vibe: In the south of Mayotte, outrigger canoes pulled up on the sand and faces masked with msindzano reflect a very much alive Mahoran culture, between the lagoon and Mount Choungui.
ngouja.respect: Keep your distance from the turtles, don’t touch them and don’t follow them. Don’t feed the lemurs that come down from the trees.
ngouja.season: May to October, in the dry season: less rain, clearer water and an often very calm lagoon.

around.d: A sugarloaf volcanic peak, a steep climb and a view over the lagoon.
A white sandbank in the middle of the lagoon, reached by boat.
A marine protected area where turtles come to nest on the beaches.
An old mosque with a carved mihrab, one of the oldest in France.
Traditional salt harvesting on the mudflat, a skill kept alive by women.

borestranda.vibe: Jæren is a windswept farming plain, criss-crossed by dry-stone walls and round pebbles. Norwegian surfers found their first waves here, in thick wetsuits facing the North Sea.
borestranda.respect: The Jæren dunes are protected: stay on the marked paths and park in the designated car parks.
borestranda.season: September to April: North Sea low-pressure systems and sandbanks in good shape, in a thick wetsuit.

around.d: A coastal village with its old church, its bird lake and its long beach.
A farming hamlet with a lighthouse and a small fishing harbour facing the North Sea.
A collection of vintage aircraft and seaplanes near Stavanger airport.

saltstraumen.vibe: With the rhythm of the tides, the channel turns into a swirling river that anglers watch from the rocks for coalfish. In summer, the midnight sun lights up the strait.
saltstraumen.respect: Only dive at slack water, with a local club that knows the current times, and give way to boats.
saltstraumen.season: May to September: very long days to time dives at slack water and milder weather, in a drysuit.

around.d: A plateau above Bodø, with a view of the islands and the midnight sun.
A large museum of civil and military aviation, with Cold War aircraft.
The history of Bodø, coastal fishing and Sámi culture.
A port town of the Far North, the departure point for ferries to the Lofoten Islands.

apelviken.vibe: Varberg sees itself as Sweden’s capital of surfing and boardsports. In summer, families fill the bay; as soon as the westerly gales blow in, riders in wetsuits take over.
apelviken.respect: In summer, respect the areas reserved for swimmers and only launch your kite in the permitted sectors.
apelviken.season: September to November: strong westerly winds and autumn storms, with the beach deserted by holidaymakers.

around.d: A medieval fortress by the sea, with ramparts and a view over the Kattegat.
Inside the fortress, it displays the Bocksten Man, a medieval body found in a peat bog.
Wet meadows and lagoons rich in birds, with observation hides.
A fishing village with its harbour and its huts by the water.

toro.vibe: At the southern tip of the Stockholm archipelago, pine forests and smooth rocks frame a pebble beach. Surfers come here in full wetsuits, sometimes between sheets of ice.
toro.respect: The site is a nature reserve: no fires and no cars outside the car park, and don’t move the pebbles.
toro.season: October to March: Baltic storms raising short waves, in icy water.

around.d: A village on the island of Öja, at the far end of the archipelago, with its lighthouse and its trails.
A small port town, with fish smokehouses and ferries to Gotland.

kosterhavet.vibe: Off Strömstad, Bohuslän lines up pink granite islands, prawn-fishing villages and lobster boats. Below the surface, the Koster trench shelters cold-water coral reefs.
food: Bohuslän prawns
Northern prawns cooked on board, eaten on bread with mayonnaise and dill.
kosterhavet.respect: In the park, some areas are off-limits during bird nesting and seal pupping: check the signs.
kosterhavet.season: June to August: long days, water at its mildest and a sea often calm between the islands.

around.d: Almost car-free islands, to explore by bike between coves and heathland.
A small seaside town and fishing port, the departure point for the boats.
The neighbouring Norwegian marine park, with rocky islets and rich waters.

hvidesande.vibe: Hvide Sande lives around its lock and its harbour: fish auction, trawlers and fish smokehouses. Between the North Sea and the fjord, you sail in the morning and eat smoked herring on the quay in the evening.
food: Smoked fish from the harbour
Wood-smoked herring, mackerel or salmon, sold directly by the smokehouses.
hvidesande.respect: On the fjord, stay in the marked kite zones and keep well away from fishing nets and protected bird areas.
hvidesande.season: May to September: steady westerly winds and a milder fjord; autumn brings strong wind and waves on the sea side.

around.d: An old merchant town of cobbled lanes and colourful houses, on the shore of the fjord.
A protected peninsula of salt meadows, a major stopover for migratory birds.
A preserved fjord-side farm that tells the story of rural life in the past.
Local coastal history and paintings of the dunes and the North Sea.

romo.vibe: Rømø keeps the farms of the commanders, whaling captains of old, and a beach so wide that cars drive on it. In spring and autumn, clouds of starlings darken the sky over the marshes.
romo.respect: The beach is open to cars: drive at walking pace, park outside the traffic lane and only fly your kite in the kite zone.
romo.season: May to September: steady westerly winds and milder water; autumn brings stronger gales.

around.d: Mudflats, sandbanks and seals, to discover on guided outings.
The sailors’ church, surrounded by the carved gravestones of the commanders.
A small Wadden island, reached at low tide by a road that floods.
A double-helix observation tower, with a view over the marshes and the Wadden Sea.
A village in the north of Sylt, in Germany, reached by the ferry from Havneby.

linnansaari.vibe: The park protects the rare Saimaa seal and still keeps up the slash-and-burn farming of the past. You paddle in silence between pine-covered islands and end the day in the sauna, facing the lake.
linnansaari.respect: Only light fires in the designated fireplaces and keep away from the rocks where the Saimaa seal rests.
linnansaari.season: June to August: pleasant water for swimming, light nights and a calm lake for paddling from island to island.

tiree.vibe: A Gaelic island of crofters, Tiree lives among machair meadows, white houses with black roofs and endless beaches. The wind is such that windsurfers from all over the world have made it an autumn gathering.
hello: “hi” in Scottish Gaelic, still spoken on the island
tiree.respect: Don’t drive on the fragile machair, close field gates behind you and let sheep and cows pass on the tracks.
tiree.season: September to November: Atlantic low-pressure systems, strong wind and well-lined-up swell on the west coast.

around.d: An Iron Age stone tower on the north coast, facing the sea.
The island’s main village, with its small harbour and a few shops.

freshwaterwest.vibe: In south Pembrokeshire, dunes, cliffs and fishing harbours make up a rugged landscape. At Freshwater West, a hut recalls the gathering of seaweed for laverbread, a Welsh speciality.
food: Laverbread
A purée of dark seaweed served at breakfast with cockles and bacon.
freshwaterwest.respect: Respect the red flags of the nearby military firing range and beware of the currents, among the strongest in Wales.
freshwaterwest.season: September to November: regular autumn swells, water still lukewarm and a less crowded car park.

around.d: A nature reserve where puffins and shearwaters nest, reached by boat.
An imposing medieval fortress, birthplace of Henry VII.
Castle ruins on the edge of an estuary, with a tidal mill.
A village at the entrance to Milford Haven, with small beaches and a coastal path.

sennen.vibe: At the far end of Cornwall, Sennen Cove keeps its fishing harbour, its lifeboat station and its granite houses. Surfers share the water with seals here when the swell comes in.
food: Cornish pasty
A pastry filled with beef, potato and swede, born among the tin miners.
sennen.respect: Surf between the lifeguards’ black-and-white flags and swim between the red-and-yellow flags.
sennen.season: September to October: regular autumn swells, water at its mildest and a beach emptied after summer.

around.d: An island and castle reached on foot at low tide along a causeway.
Old tin mines clinging to the cliffs, a World Heritage site.
A fishing village of narrow lanes around a granite harbour.
A museum of undersea telegraph cables, in a turquoise bay.
An Iron Age village with its underground passage, the fogou.

kynance.vibe: On the Lizard peninsula, dark serpentine stone, worked by local craftspeople, colours the cliffs and islets. Coastal paths link fishing villages, lighthouses and turquoise coves.
food: Cornish cream tea
Warm scones, strawberry jam and thick clotted cream.
kynance.respect: The beach disappears at high tide: check the tide times so you don’t get stuck on the islets.
kynance.season: June to September, at low tide: the mildest water of the year and plenty of exposed sand.

around.d: The southernmost point of Great Britain, with cliffs and seals.
A fishing hamlet of thatched roofs, with boats pulled up on the shingle.
A historic lighthouse with a visitor centre on navigation.
A quiet fishing village on a sheltered bay.
A centre that cares for stranded seal pups before releasing them.

easkey.vibe: Easkey, whose Irish name evokes an abundance of fish, is home to the Irish Surfing Association. At the water’s edge, a medieval tower keeps watch over the reef slabs and the surfers.
easkey.respect: The reefs are shallow at low tide: give priority to the locals and don’t go out if you don’t have the level.
easkey.season: September to March: big, well-lined-up Atlantic swells on the reefs, in a thick wetsuit.

around.d: A neoclassical mansion linked to the poet Yeats, on the shore of Sligo Bay.
Mountains of moorland and lakes, with wild and little-walked hikes.
A bayside village with its medieval round tower.
A peninsula village, with beaches and a view over Sligo Bay.

inch.vibe: On the Dingle peninsula, Irish can still be heard in the western villages. At Inch, you park on the sand, surf facing the Kerry mountains and finish at the pub with traditional music.
inch.respect: The Inch dunes are protected: only park your car on the permitted part of the beach and stay on the paths.
inch.season: May to September: gentler swells for learning, less cold water and lifeguards on duty in summer.

around.d: A colourful harbour town with traditional music pubs, gateway to the peninsula.
A medieval monastic site with a Romanesque church and an ogham stone.
Sandstone ridges above Tralee and Dingle bays, with fine hikes.
The home village of the explorer Tom Crean, whose pub still keeps his memory alive.
A small archipelago off the Maharees, with the remains of a hermitage.

brouwersdam.vibe: Born of the Delta Works after the great flood, the dam has become a playground: kitesurfers on the sea side, divers on the Grevelingen side, and Zeeland mussels on the table in the evening.
food: Zeeland mussels
Mussels farmed in the waters of the Oosterschelde, cooked with celery and onion.
brouwersdam.respect: Only fly your kite in the marked kite zones and, on the lake side, make way for divers along the dyke.
brouwersdam.season: In spring and from September to October: steady westerly winds, beaches less crowded than in summer.

around.d: A lively seaside resort with wide beaches and wooded dunes.
A moated castle on the edge of Renesse.
A village with a windmill and low houses, between dunes and polders.
A village on the edge of the Grevelingen, a meeting place for Dutch divers.

stpeterording.vibe: A spa resort on the Eiderstedt peninsula, Sankt Peter-Ording lives among salt meadows, lighthouses and restaurants on stilts. The beach is so vast that you drive across it to reach the water.
food: North Sea brown shrimp
Small peeled brown shrimp, served on bread or in a roll.
stpeterording.respect: Never head out alone on the tidal flats when the tide is rising: the sea comes back fast. Kitesurfing is done in the dedicated zones.
stpeterording.season: May to September: steady westerly winds over the tidal flats; in spring and autumn, it blows harder.

around.d: A red-and-white lighthouse surrounded by salt meadows, the emblem of the coast.
Vast mudflats, seals and migratory birds, on a guided walk.
A small port town with gabled houses and a Wadden Sea centre.
Polders, dykes and large farms with tall thatched roofs to explore by bike.

chalupy.vibe: On the Hel Peninsula, a Kashubian land of fishermen, the villages stretch between the Baltic and the Bay of Puck. In summer, kite schools, campsites and fish smokehouses line up along the thin strip of sand.
food: Baltic smoked fish
Smoked flounder, mackerel or herring, sold hot at the smokehouses.
chalupy.respect: Only cross the dunes and pine forest by the marked paths and stay in the kite corridors set by the schools.
chalupy.season: May to September: a flat, shallow bay, milder water and steady winds; crowds in July and August.

around.d: A small old town on the bay, with its square and its Gothic church.
Protected dunes, cliffs and forests along the Pomeranian coast.
A lighthouse on the Hel Peninsula, between pine forest and Baltic beach.
A neo-Gothic manor in a park on the shore of the Bay of Puck.

walchensee.vibe: At the foot of the Bavarian Pre-Alps, the lake’s turquoise reflections inspired the painter Lovis Corinth from his house in Urfeld. Today, windsurfers and hikers meet here over a Brotzeit.
food: Bavarian Brotzeit
Pretzels, obatzda and cold meats, to share under the trees of a Biergarten.
walchensee.respect: Kitesurfing is only tolerated in specific sectors: ask locally and park in the car parks, never at the roadside.
walchensee.season: May to August: the thermal wind picks up almost every sunny afternoon, and the water is finally bearable.

around.d: A summit reached by cable car, with a plunging view over the Walchensee and the Kochelsee.
A glacial lake at the foot of the mountains, fringed with reed beds.
Works by the Expressionist painter and his friends of the Blue Rider.
A large Baroque monastery at the gateway to the Alps.
A Benedictine abbey with a Baroque dome, near Oberammergau.

eisbach.vibe: Where it leaves the tunnel, the river channel swells into a wave that Munich surfers ride in turn. Just behind, the English Garden and its Biergärten embody the Bavarian art of living.
hello: “hi” in Bavaria, for arriving as well as leaving
food: Weißwurst and pretzel
White veal sausage, sweet mustard and a pretzel, served in the morning.
eisbach.respect: Only one surfer at a time: wait your turn in the queue on the bank. The wave is for experienced surfers only, as the bottom is hard and shallow.
eisbach.season: All year round when the flow allows; the wave depends on the upkeep of the riverbed, so check it is working before you come.

around.d: The former palace of the Wittelsbachs, with state rooms and the royal treasury.
Decorative arts, sculptures and nativity scenes, from the Middle Ages to the 19th century.
A contemporary art museum, right next to the wave.
A Renaissance garden with its small temple, at the foot of the Residenz.
A monumental loggia on Odeonsplatz, inspired by Florence.

silvaplana.vibe: In the Upper Engadine, Romansh can be read on houses decorated with sgraffito and the lake slips between larches and peaks. Every summer afternoon, the Maloja wind covers the water with colourful sails.
hello: “hello” in Romansh, the language of the Engadine
food: Engadine nut tart
Shortcrust pastry filled with caramelised walnuts, the pride of Graubünden’s pastry chefs.
silvaplana.respect: At 1,800 metres, the water stays icy even in summer: bring a thick wetsuit and respect the separation between kite and windsurf.
silvaplana.season: June to September: the Maloja wind almost every afternoon and a lake free of ice.

around.d: A large glacier of the Bernina, with a marked trail up to its snout.
A neighbouring lake with wild shores, lined with Engadine villages.
A cable car up to a viewpoint over the lakes and the Bernina massif.
A car-free valley, on foot or by horse-drawn carriage up to the glaciers.
A chic Alpine resort on the shore of its lake, between grand hotels and trails.

podersdorf.vibe: Reed beds, vineyards and the white villages of the Seewinkel: here the Pannonian plain opens onto a flat lake where the wind blows freely, and you end your session with a glass of Burgenland wine.
food: Lake Neusiedl pike-perch
Fish from the lake, pan-fried or grilled in the inns of the lakeside villages.
podersdorf.respect: Kiting is only allowed in designated zones: check with the schools and keep away from the reed beds, a refuge for protected birds.
podersdorf.season: April to June and September: more frequent wind, water that warms up quickly and a less crowded beach than in summer.

around.d: Salt pans, steppe and reed beds where you can watch waterfowl and waders.
Baroque palace of the Esterházy princes in Eisenstadt, where Haydn was Kapellmeister.
Large ruined Roman arch, a remnant of the ancient city of Carnuntum on the Danube.
Small farmhouse in Rohrau turned into a museum devoted to the composer.
The Hungarian side of the lake: marshes, wet meadows and observation trails.

bled.vibe: No engines on this lake: it’s the pletnas, wooden rowing boats handed down from father to son among the boatmen, that take you to the island. Bled is also a stronghold of Slovenian rowing.
bled.respect: Motorboats are banned on the lake: on a paddleboard or in a kayak, give way to the pletnas shuttling to the island.
bled.season: Late June to early September: the water becomes pleasant; come early in the morning to enjoy the lake before the crowds.

around.d: Wooden walkways above a deep turquoise river, all the way to a waterfall.
Karst plateau covered in forest and alpine pastures, a starting point for hikes towards Triglav.
Slovenia’s highest peak and national symbol, climbed by hikers over two days.
Birthplace of the poet France Prešeren, with his house museum and church.

soca.vibe: The valley keeps the memory of the Isonzo Front of the Great War, among trenches and chapels. Today Bovec lives to the rhythm of rafting guides, kayakers and hikers.
food: Bovec cheese
Sheep’s cheese from the valley’s alpine pastures, with a bold, slightly sharp taste.
soca.respect: Paddling on the Soča requires a permit and is only allowed on certain stretches: go through a local club and respect the anglers.
soca.season: April to June: snowmelt swells the river and livens up the rapids; summer is calmer and very busy.

around.d: Slovenia’s only national park: limestone peaks, glacial lakes and mountain streams.
Small town known for its First World War museum and historical trail.
Village at the foot of Mangart, the starting point of the scenic road towards the summit.
Large, wild glacial lake, more peaceful than Bled, surrounded by mountains.

balaton.vibe: Siófok is the Hungarian summer: managed beaches, lángos stands, glasses of fröccs, wine mixed with sparkling water, and lively evenings. Across the water, the north shore is lined with vineyards and volcanic hills.
balaton.respect: Most of Siófok’s beaches are managed “strand”: use the showers and bins, and stay within the marked swimming areas.
balaton.season: June to August: the shallow water warms quickly and becomes some of the mildest of any lake in Central Europe.

around.d: Hilltop village on a volcanic peninsula, lavender fields and views over the lake.
Baroque Benedictine abbey overlooking the lake, with a medieval crypt.
Leafy resort on the south shore, with its marina and promenade.

ohrid.vibe: Ohrid, cradle of Slavic writing with Saint Clement, is lined with Byzantine churches and overhanging houses. In Kaneo, the old fishermen’s quarter, wooden boats still wait at the foot of the rocks.
ohrid.respect: St John at Kaneo is a working church: cover your shoulders and knees to go in, and don’t order wild Ohrid trout, a protected species.
ohrid.season: June to September: the lake water becomes pleasant; June and September avoid the July–August crowds.

around.d: Cobbled lanes, Samuel’s Fortress, an ancient theatre and churches with Byzantine frescoes.
Waterside fishing village, with a small cave church in the cliff.
Albanian village on a peninsula, known for the mosaics of an early Christian basilica.
Village on the east shore, pebble beaches and access to Galičica National Park.

como.vibe: At the north end of the lake, the Alto Lario lives between mountain and water: stone villages, old Spanish forts and fishermen who still dry shad in the sun, following a centuries-old tradition.
food: Missoltini
Lake shad, dried then grilled, served with polenta.
como.respect: Kitesurfing and windsurfing are only allowed in the authorised zones of Colico and Dervio: follow the clubs’ instructions and give way to the ferries.
como.season: May to September: in fine weather the thermal winds are at their most reliable and the lake water warms up.

around.d: Elegant village at the tip where the lake’s two arms meet, stepped lanes and villa gardens.
Waterside abbey on a peninsula, with a lovely Romanesque cloister.
Medieval tower above Varenna, with a sweeping view down over the lake.
Wetland at the mouths of the Adda and Mera, rich in migratory birds.
Ruins of a Spanish fortress on a hill, facing the plain and the lake.

portopollo.vibe: Wind-carved granite, maquis and stazzi, the isolated farmsteads of Gallura: here windsurfers and kiters from all over the world meet between gusts blowing in from the Strait of Bonifacio.
food: Zuppa gallurese
Bread, cheese and broth baked until golden, a peasant dish from Gallura.
portopollo.respect: Windsurfers and kiters share the bay by zones: respect the launch corridors and don’t trample the dunes on the isthmus.
portopollo.season: May to October: the wind funnelled through the Strait often blows hard, especially outside high summer.

around.d: Pink granite islands and crystal-clear water, to explore by boat from Palau.
Wild island linked to La Maddalena by a causeway, pine woods and coves where Garibaldi lived.
Protected island famous for its pink beach, admired from the sea.
Nuragic collective tomb with a large granite stele, near Arzachena.
Bronze Age stone tower surrounded by the remains of its village.

pelosa.vibe: Stintino, a fishing village founded by families driven off Asinara, long lived from its tuna trap. Facing the beach, the Aragonese tower still watches over the passage to the island.
pelosa.respect: Access is limited and requires a paid booking: put your towel on a mat, as the rules require, and take away no sand or pebbles.
pelosa.season: June and September: turquoise water that’s already warm and places easier to book than in July–August.

around.d: Wild island and former penal colony, home to white donkeys; boat trips from Stintino.
Former silver-mining village facing the sea, with restored industrial buildings.

calaluna.vibe: At the foot of the Supramonte, a land of shepherds and nuraghi, the cliffs hide caves where the monk seal once lived. The fishermen of Cala Gonone have become boatmen, but the coast still has no road.
food: Culurgiones
Ravioli sealed in a wheat-ear pleat, filled with potato, pecorino and mint.
calaluna.respect: Camping and fires are banned on the beach: in a kayak, follow the coast away from boat traffic and take all your rubbish home.
calaluna.season: May–June and September: often calm sea, mild water and a cove less overrun by boats than in August.

around.d: Ruins of a village hidden deep in a collapsed sinkhole, at the end of a fine walk.
White-pebble cove overlooked by a limestone pinnacle, reachable on foot.
Huge underground chamber around a giant stalagmite column.
Barbagia village whose façades are covered in politically charged murals.
Karst spring of blue water rising from a fissure at the foot of the Supramonte.

tavolara.vibe: Tavolara nurtures the legend of a tiny island kingdom passed down in one island family. Around it, Olbia’s fishermen and dive centres share a protected sea where the grouper has returned.
food: Olbia mussels
Farmed in the Gulf of Olbia, served sautéed with garlic and parsley.
tavolara.respect: Dive with a centre approved by the marine area: fully protected zones are off-limits, no anchoring on the posidonia and no touching the gorgonians.
tavolara.season: June to October: warm water, good visibility and a sea often calm in the island’s lee.

around.d: Romanesque granite church, the oldest in Olbia, in the heart of the town.
Wild granite island in the marine area, with coves you reach by boat.
Seaside resort with long white-sand beaches, backed by a lagoon with flamingos.
Nuragic collective tomb with a large stone façade, near Olbia.

zingaro.vibe: The reserve was born when locals campaigned against a coastal road. Between dwarf palms and the old tuna traps of Scopello, this coast still lives from fishing, prickly pears and mule tracks.
food: Fish couscous
Hand-rolled semolina and fish broth, the pride of San Vito Lo Capo.
zingaro.respect: There’s an entry fee and water is scarce: bring plenty to drink, stay on the paths, no fires, and take all your rubbish home.
zingaro.season: May–June and September: clear water that’s already warm, and trails more bearable than in high summer.

around.d: Solitary Doric temple and ancient theatre perched facing the hills.
Medieval hilltop town, stone lanes and almond pastry shops.
Hamlet around an old courtyard, with its tuna trap and faraglioni sea stacks.
White village beside a long pale-sand beach, at the foot of Monte Monaco.
Caves sheltering an old hamlet, including the Mangiapane cave and its living nativity.

calarossa.vibe: Favignana lived from its tuff quarries and the Florio family’s tuna trap, where the mattanza of tuna took place. You get around by bike between old quarries turned into gardens and coves carved into the stone.
food: Favignana tuna
Tuna and bottarga, fresh or preserved, a legacy of the island’s tuna traps.
calarossa.respect: In the Egadi Islands marine protected area, don’t take sea urchins or shellfish and don’t drop anchor on the posidonia.
calarossa.season: June to September: warm, clear water; June and September avoid the packed boats of mid-August.

around.d: The Florio family’s former tuna cannery, turned into a fishing museum.
Small, peaceful island, white village and a cave decorated with prehistoric paintings.
Islet in the lagoon with the remains of a Phoenician city and a museum.
Salt pans, windmills and shallow water, magnificent at sunset.
Baroque town renowned for its sweet wine and cellars open to visitors.

conigli.vibe: Lampedusa, closer to Africa than to Sicily, lives from fishing and the sea. A landing point for many migrants, the island also carries a powerful human memory, beyond its coves.
conigli.respect: The beach closes at night during the loggerhead turtles’ nesting season: respect the nest enclosures, the opening hours and the limited number of visitors.
conigli.season: June and September: warm, clear water, and fewer people than in August on a beach with limited access.

around.d: Sculpture facing the sea, dedicated to the migrants lost in the Mediterranean.
Uninhabited offshore rock, renowned for its diving and marine life.

stagnone.vibe: Salt pans, windmills and white heaps of salt line the lagoon, with the Phoenician city of Motya opposite. Between sessions, you taste Marsala wine in the cellars that made the town’s fortune.
food: Busiate with pesto trapanese
Twisted pasta with a pesto of tomato, almonds, garlic and basil.
stagnone.respect: The Stagnone is a nature reserve: kite only in the authorised zones, away from swimmers and from the boat route to Motya.
stagnone.season: April to October: steady wind over the lagoon and flat water, which gets really warm in summer.

around.d: Islet in the lagoon with the remains of a Phoenician city and a museum.
Baroque town renowned for its sweet wine and cellars open to visitors.
Old town on a narrow peninsula, Baroque churches and a port for the Egadi Islands.

around.n: Sanctuary of the Madonna of Trapani
around.d: Revered basilica housing a marble statue of the Virgin, much loved by fishermen.

portofino.vibe: Between the fishermen of Camogli and the Doria abbey, the headland lives facing the sea. The submerged statue has become a symbol for divers, honoured every summer with a ceremony at sea.
food: Focaccia di Recco
Very thin dough filled with soft melting cheese, a speciality of the neighbouring village.
portofino.respect: In the Portofino marine area, dive with an approved centre, don’t drop anchor and don’t touch the red coral on the drop-offs.
portofino.season: June to October: warm water and calm sea; visibility is often best in early autumn.

around.d: Medieval abbey at the head of the cove, with its tower and cloister facing the sea.
Fortress above Portofino harbour, gardens and a view over the bay.
A walk under the pines to the point, looking out to the open sea.
Hilltop sanctuary above Rapallo, reached by cable car, with a wide view.
Riviera resort, seafront promenade and a small castle on the water.

polignano.vibe: Birthplace of Domenico Modugno, the singer of “Volare”, Polignano lives perched on cliffs riddled with sea caves. Its rocks also host international high-diving competitions.
food: Orecchiette with cime di rapa
Small ear-shaped pasta with turnip tops, garlic and anchovies.
polignano.respect: Cliff diving is reserved for supervised athletes: don’t copy it, and come early because the tiny cove fills up fast.
polignano.season: June and September: warm water and a less crowded cove than in July–August.

around.d: Vast karst network of chambers and formations, all the way to the famous White Cave.
Fishing port with blue boats, a white old town and ramparts on the sea.
Norman castle overlooking a small historic town inland.
Fortified abbey on the water’s edge, facing a small fishing harbour.

illetes.vibe: Formentera is best taken slowly, by bike among salt pans, dry-stone walls and propped-up fig trees. Here fishermen still dry fish in the sun, and the posidonia keeps the water so clear.
hello: “good morning” in Catalan, the language of the Balearics
food: Ensalada payesa with peix sec
Sun-dried fish, potatoes and peppers, a Formentera recipe.
illetes.respect: In the natural park, stay on the boardwalks that protect the dunes and never drop anchor on the posidonia, which is protected by law.
illetes.season: June and September: turquoise water that’s already warm and a sandspit less crowded than in July–August.

around.d: Private islet with white-sand beaches, reached by boat from Formentera.
Arid plateau in the south of the island, a lonely lighthouse and cliffs at sunset.
UNESCO-listed fortified old town, white lanes and ramparts.
Remains of a Phoenician village by the sea, on Ibiza’s south coast.

calacomte.vibe: On Ibiza’s west coast, far from the clubs, the pagès countryside keeps its white cube-shaped houses and carob trees. In the evening, locals and travellers gather on the rocks to watch the sun sink into the sea.
hello: “good morning” in Catalan, the language of the Balearics
food: Bullit de peix
Fish and potato stew, followed by rice cooked in the broth.
calacomte.respect: The car park fills up quickly: come early or by bus from Sant Antoni, and don’t drop anchor on the posidonia meadows.
calacomte.season: June and September: warm, clear water, sunsets without the August crowds.

around.d: Dizzying rocky islet rising from the sea, shrouded in legends.
UNESCO-listed fortified old town, white lanes and ramparts.
Sandy cove facing Es Vedrà, with a few fish restaurants.
The island’s highest point, covered in pines, with a view over the whole coast.
Clear-water cove lined with pines and fishermen’s boat shelters.

estrenc.vibe: Behind the dunes, the Es Trenc salt pans still produce fleur de sel, and the countryside of southern Mallorca is lined with stone walls, almond trees and windmills. A beach still free of buildings, defended by the locals.
hello: “good morning” in Catalan, the language of the Balearics
food: Sobrassada
Raw, spreadable paprika sausage, to spread on Mallorcan country bread.
estrenc.respect: The natural park’s dunes are fragile: use the marked access paths, don’t pick any plants and don’t enter the salt pans, which are private.
estrenc.season: June and September: clear, warm water, car parks less packed than in high summer.

around.d: Wild protected islands, a hilltop castle and a blue cave, by boat from the coast.
Small, peaceful fishing port at the head of an inlet, white houses and boats.
Rural village in the south of the island, gateway to the salt pans and Cap de Ses Salines.
Farming town of stone houses, with its weekly market.

capdecreus.vibe: Rocks twisted by the tramontane, the white houses of Cadaqués and fishing boats: this landscape fed Dalí’s imagination. Life here faces the sea, to the rhythm of the north winds.
hello: “good morning” in Catalan, which people will gladly say back to you
food: Suquet de peix
Rockfish and potato stew, a classic of Catalan fishermen.
capdecreus.respect: The tramontane can rise suddenly: check the forecast before setting off in a kayak, and respect the fully protected reserves where diving is banned.
capdecreus.season: June to September: milder water and good visibility, between bursts of tramontane.

around.d: The painter’s labyrinthine home and studio, facing Portlligat bay.

around.n: Monastery of Sant Pere de Rodes
around.d: Romanesque abbey perched on the mountain, with a vast view over the Gulf of Lion.
Fortified enclosure housing the remains of a Greek city and a monastery.
Large Gothic church in the heart of a medieval Empordà town.
Wild protected headland, a path to cliffs plunging into the sea.

monsul.vibe: The driest land in Europe, Cabo de Gata blends extinct volcanoes, old tuna traps and white farmhouses. Its Wild West landscapes have been the backdrop for many film shoots.
food: Migas de Almería
Pan-fried flour semolina, served with fried sardines and peppers.
monsul.respect: In summer, car access is restricted: take the shuttle from San José, don’t climb on the dunes and take your rubbish home.
monsul.season: May–June and September: clear water, bearable heat and easier access than in high summer.

around.d: Wild volcanic coast, coves, cliffs and salt pans home to flamingos.
White village on a bay, a handy base for the park’s beaches.
White inland hamlet, a setting for spaghetti westerns.

larestinga.vibe: A fishing village at the far end of the Canary world, La Restinga lived through the nearby undersea eruption before being reborn around diving. Black lava flows and small-scale fishing shape everyday life.
food: El Hierro cheese
Goat’s and sheep’s milk cheese, often lightly smoked.
larestinga.respect: In the marine reserve, dive only with an approved centre: dive numbers are limited, the fully protected zone is off-limits and fishing is banned.
larestinga.season: All year round, but from June to November the water is warmer and the sea often very calm.

around.d: Isolated lighthouse on lava flows, near the old prime meridian.
The island’s highest point, a hike among volcanic cones and pine forests.
Municipality in the El Golfo valley, terraced vineyards beneath high cliffs.

lascanteras.vibe: The locals’ beach in Las Palmas, where people swim before work and stroll along the paseo in the evening. Card players, La Cícer surfers and swimmers all share the same water.
food: Papas arrugadas with mojo
Small potatoes boiled in salted water, served with a chilli sauce.
lascanteras.respect: Don’t walk on La Barra, the reef that shelters rich marine life; at the La Cícer peak, respect the local surfers’ priority.
lascanteras.season: All year round: pleasant water even in winter; summer brings flat calm behind La Barra.

around.d: Cathedral in the historic Vegueta district, with a view over the city from its tower.
Cave decorated with geometric patterns by the ancient Canarians, with a museum.
Large garden devoted to the Canaries’ endemic flora, in a ravine.
Archaeology museum devoted to the island’s first inhabitants.
Ancient communal granary carved into the cliff by the Canarians.

portomoniz.vibe: On Madeira’s north coast, vines cling to the cliffs, sheltered from the wind by heather hedges. The villages live from fishing and the levadas, the channels that have irrigated the island for centuries.
food: Espada with banana
Fillet of deep-sea black scabbardfish, pan-fried and served with banana.
portomoniz.respect: In heavy swell, follow the lifeguards’ instructions and never swim in the nearby wild pools, which are swept by the waves.
portomoniz.season: June to October: milder water and a calmer sea on this north coast, often battered in winter.

around.d: Path along an irrigation channel to a cirque of waterfalls.
North-coast village, black-sand beach and natural pools.
Lava tubes open to visitors, formed by an ancient eruption.
Lighthouse atop high cliffs, ideal at sunset.
Fishing village at the foot of the cliffs, known to surfers.

berlengas.vibe: Off the big fishing port of Peniche, a block of granite battered by the Atlantic, where hardly anyone lives but the reserve wardens, a few fishermen in summer and colonies of seabirds.
food: Caldeirada de Peniche
Stew of the day’s fish, potatoes and tomatoes, simmered as it is on the boats.
berlengas.respect: Visitor numbers on the island are limited: book your crossing, stay on the paths and keep your distance from nesting birds.
berlengas.season: June to September: calmer sea for the crossing, regular boats and better visibility around the island.

around.d: 17th-century fortress set on an islet, linked to the island by a narrow stone bridge.
Seafront citadel, a former political prison now a museum of the resistance.
Peninsula linked by a sandbar, surrounded by beaches and surf spots.
Vast calm lagoon cut off from the ocean by a sand barrier, ideal for paddling.

myrtos.vibe: Here, almost every village was rebuilt after the 1953 earthquake; only a few northern harbours such as Fiskardo keep their Venetian houses, facing Ithaca.
food: Kefalonian kreatopita
Meat pie with rice and herbs, a speciality of the island’s tables.
myrtos.respect: The road down to the beach is narrow and the car park fills up fast: arrive early. Watch out for the shore break on the pebbles when there’s a swell.
myrtos.season: June to September: warm water and a sea often calm; aim for June or September to avoid the August crowds.

around.d: Small fishing village at the foot of a peninsula crowned by a Venetian fortress.
Harbour of colourful houses spared by the earthquake, quayside tavernas facing Ithaca.
Venetian ramparts on a hill, with a wide view over the south of the island.
The island’s capital: seafront, archaeological museum and loggerhead turtles in the harbour.
White-pebble cove beneath the cliffs of the Paliki peninsula.

portokatsiki.vibe: At the end of the wild peninsula in south-west Lefkada, you head down to the sea among olive trees, goats and white cliffs; caiques from the nearby harbours drop swimmers off here.
food: Lefkada salami
Dry, fragrant pork sausage, the pride of the island’s mountain villages.
portokatsiki.respect: Don’t settle at the foot of the cliffs, which are prone to rockfalls. Arrive early: the small car park at the top of the steps fills up fast in summer.
portokatsiki.season: June to September: warm turquoise water; in the morning, before the boats arrive, the beach stays quiet.

around.d: Long white-pebble beach beneath the cliffs, reached by a staircase or by boat.
Southern harbour village, a windsurfers’ haunt, where the water taxis leave from.
West-coast fishing village, flower-filled lanes and a small sheltered beach.
Small green island with secluded coves, reached by ferry from Nydri.

vassiliki.vibe: A fishing port turned windsurfers’ haunt: the thermal wind the regulars nickname “Eric” picks up in the afternoon and sets the pace of the days, between board centres and quayside tavernas.
food: Lefkada salami
Dry, fragrant pork sausage, the pride of the island’s mountain villages.
vassiliki.respect: Respect the launch corridors in front of the centres and the marked swimming areas; if you’re a beginner, sail in the morning and leave the afternoon to experienced riders.
vassiliki.season: June to September: the thermal blows almost every afternoon, stronger in July and August.

around.d: Turquoise beach at the foot of high white cliffs, reached by boat from the harbour.
Long white-pebble beach beneath the cliffs of the west coast.
Wooded islet once owned by the Onassis family, which you pass by boat.
Small green island with secluded coves and quiet villages.

prasonisi.vibe: At the very south of Rhodes, far from the east-coast resorts, a windswept spit of sand where life follows the rhythm of the board-sports centres, with a few farming villages for neighbours.
food: Pitaroudia
Chickpea fritters served as meze in Rhodian tavernas.
prasonisi.respect: The centres keep kite and windsurf zones separate: ask before rigging up. Don’t drive on the sandbar.
prasonisi.season: June to September: the meltemi blows strong and steady, especially in July and August.

elafonisi.vibe: At the south-western tip of Crete, far from the big towns, a region of olive-growing villages and small mountain roads; Cretan families come here for picnics too.
food: Dakos
Barley rusk topped with grated tomato, mizithra cheese and olive oil.
elafonisi.respect: Natura 2000 site: take no pink sand or shells and don’t walk in the islet’s dunes and junipers.
elafonisi.season: June and September: a warm lagoon, less crowded than in high summer, when the buses arrive from the morning.

around.d: White monastery perched on a rock above the sea.
Large sandy beach facing the sunset, near the remains of an ancient harbour.
Peaceful town on a peninsula, between a sandy beach and a pebble beach.
Seaside hamlet at the mouth of a gorge, a starting point for coastal hikes.

kleftiko.vibe: A volcanic island mined since antiquity for its obsidian and later its minerals, Milos keeps its “syrmata”, fishermen’s houses with colourful doors sheltering boats right at the water’s edge.
kleftiko.respect: At midday, excursion boats crowd into the arches: come early by kayak, don’t climb on the crumbly rock and leave nothing in the caves.
kleftiko.season: June and September: warm water and a sea often calmer than in July–August, when the meltemi stirs up the coast.

goldenbeach_paros.vibe: Paros, island of the white marble sculpted in antiquity, lives between whitewashed inland villages and small harbours where fishing caiques still unload octopus, hung to dry in front of the tavernas.
goldenbeach_paros.respect: Head out through the schools’ marked corridors and keep your distance from swimmers, who crowd the water’s edge in summer.
goldenbeach_paros.season: June to September: the meltemi often blows hard, especially in July and August.

around.d: Fishing port with white lanes, guarded by the ruins of a small Venetian fort.
Small, quiet neighbouring island, renowned for its stalactite cave.
White hilltop village, with windmills and a monastery at the top.
Large neighbouring island: Venetian old town, the gateway of the Temple of Apollo and mountain villages.

kamenjak.vibe: At the tip of Istria, a heath of pines, junipers and wild orchids where dinosaur footprints mark the rock; Pula’s locals come here in summer to dive off the rocks.
food: Fuži with Istrian truffles
Hand-rolled Istrian pasta, topped with grated truffle from the peninsula’s interior.
kamenjak.respect: Protected landscape: car access is paid in summer, drive slowly on the tracks, no fires and no wild camping.
kamenjak.season: June and September: clear, warm water and coves less busy than in high summer.

around.d: One of the best-preserved Roman amphitheatres in the world, still used for concerts.
Intact Roman temple on Pula’s ancient forum.
Double-arched Roman gate, the entrance to Pula’s old town.
Archaeological site of a Histrian, then Roman, town above a bay.
Village at the entrance to the cape, with campsites and water-sports schools.

viganj.vibe: The Pelješac peninsula, land of ocean-going captains, plavac mali vines and stone villages, faces Korčula; in Viganj, windsurfers’ campsites line the water.
food: Ston oysters
Farmed in Mali Ston Bay, at the other end of the Pelješac peninsula.
viganj.respect: Ferries between Orebić and Korčula cross the channel: keep your distance from boats and never sail alone in strong wind.
viganj.season: June to September: the maestral picks up almost every afternoon, most reliably in July and August.

around.d: Fortified town on a peninsula, herringbone lanes and ramparts.
Gothic and Renaissance cathedral in carved stone, in the heart of the old town.
Monastery perched above Orebić, with an open view over the channel and Korčula.
Wooded islet home to a former Franciscan monastery, reached by boat.
Wine village on Korčula, sandy beaches and grk white wine.

ulcinj.vibe: Ulcinj, a mainly Albanian town, blends minarets, a fortified old town and a past as a corsairs’ lair; on the Bojana, fishing huts on stilts spread their big square lift nets.
hello: “hello” in Albanian, the majority language in Ulcinj
ulcinj.respect: Kite only in the schools’ zones, away from swimmers. In town, cover up near mosques and away from the beach.
ulcinj.season: June to September: steady thermal wind in the afternoon, most established in July and August.

around.d: Citadel perched above the sea, cobbled lanes and views along the coast.
Triangular island at the mouth of the Bojana, fish restaurants on stilts.
Delta, lagoons and coastal forests on the Albanian side, a refuge for waterbirds.

cirkewwa.vibe: At Malta’s northern tip, where the ferries leave for Gozo, dive clubs’ vans park in a row; the whole island lives from the sea, from luzzu boats to wrecks turned into reefs.
cirkewwa.respect: The ferries pass very close: stay within the dive area, come up along the edge and deploy a surface marker buoy.
cirkewwa.season: June to October: water between 20 and 26 °C and excellent visibility; the sea stays diveable in winter, just cooler.

around.d: Small, almost uninhabited island, famous for the turquoise water of the Blue Lagoon.
Megalithic temples on Gozo, among the oldest stone buildings in the world.
Nature park of garrigue and cliffs, coastal paths in north-west Malta.
Marian shrine partly carved into the rock, an ancient place of pilgrimage.
Wooden village built for a film, set beside a cove.

zenobia.vibe: Larnaca lives facing the sea: palm-lined promenade, the Church of Saint Lazarus, a fishing harbour and a salt lake where flamingos winter; almost all its dive clubs revolve around the same wreck.
zenobia.respect: Descend along the mooring lines and only enter the wreck with the right training. Bring nothing up: the wreck is protected.
zenobia.season: May to November: warm water, a generally calm sea and very good visibility; you can dive all year in a thick wetsuit.

around.d: Ottoman mosque and mausoleum on the shore of the salt lake, a holy site of Cypriot Islam.
Brackish lagoon where flamingos gather in winter.
Orthodox monastery perched on a rocky peak, with a view over the whole plain.
Collections from ancient Kition: pottery, sculptures and everyday objects.

capegreco.vibe: In the island’s south-east, between red-earth villages where potatoes are grown and the old fishing port of Ayia Napa, the cape remains a plateau of garrigue, cliffs and sea caves.
capegreco.respect: Stay on the park’s paths and don’t drive off the tracks. Avoid jumping off the cliffs: rocky bottoms and swell make jumps dangerous.
capegreco.season: June to October: warm, clear water; in May or October, fewer people on the ladders and in the coves.

around.d: Former fishing village around a 16th-century Venetian monastery.
Bay of pale sand and shallow water facing an islet, ideal for swimming.

oludeniz.vibe: At the foot of Babadağ, paragliders drift down towards the beach while gulets set off for the coves; it’s also the starting point of the Lycian Way, a long-distance coastal trail.
oludeniz.respect: The lagoon is a protected park with an entry fee. On the beach, keep the paragliders’ landing zone clear.
oludeniz.season: May–June and September–October: warm water, a calm lagoon and fewer crowds than in July–August.

around.d: Greek village abandoned in 1923, hundreds of stone houses on the hillside.
Cove at the bottom of a canyon, reached by boat, with a waterfall and butterflies in summer.
Islet covered in ruined Byzantine churches, to explore by boat or kayak.
Summit where the paragliders take off, with a plunging view over the lagoon.
Lycian tomb carved into the cliff above Fethiye, with a temple façade.

alacati.vibe: A former Greek village of stone houses and colourful shutters, overlooked by its windmills, Alaçatı has become a chic hideaway for Izmir; down below, the bay is still the windsurfers’ playground.
food: Çeşme kumru
Hot sandwich of sucuk, cheese and tomato in a soft sesame bun.
alacati.respect: The bay is shared by many schools: respect right of way, stay out of the marina channel and keep your distance from beginners.
alacati.season: June to September: steady, strong northerly wind, especially in July and August, on flat water.

around.d: Lanes of stone houses, windmills on the hill, cafés and shops.
Ruins of an Ionian city above the sea, a theatre and an acropolis.
Quiet fishing village built among the remains of Erythrae.
Long fine-sand beach where hot springs bubble up in the sea.

kas.vibe: Once ancient Antiphellos, Kaş keeps Lycian tombs in the middle of its streets and a theatre facing the sea; from its little harbour you can see the Greek island of Kastellorizo, a ferry ride away.
kas.respect: At Kekova, swimming and diving are banned above the sunken ruins: look at them from your kayak without landing.
kas.season: June to October: warm water and often excellent visibility; September and October are calmer and still warm.

around.d: Roadless hamlet at the foot of a castle, facing the sunken ruins of Kekova.
Small Greek island of colourful houses around a harbour, reached by ferry.
Hellenistic theatre facing the sea and Lycian tombs in the heart of Kaş.
Partly submerged Lycian city, to discover by kayak or snorkelling.
Former fishing village of white houses stacked above a bay.

bureh.vibe: Between forested hills and fishing pirogues pulled up on the sand, the village founded its own surf club, run by local young people who teach and welcome visitors.
bureh.respect: Rent your gear and book your lessons with the community club, and make way for the fishermen when the pirogues come in to the beach.
bureh.season: November to April: dry season, moderate swells for learning; the rainy season brings more waves and heavy downpours.

around.d: Wooded islands reached by pirogue, coves, colonial remains and diving.
Rainforest in the hills above Freetown, a refuge for chimpanzees and birds.
Sandy beach and fishing village beside a river, north of Bureh.

boavista.vibe: Sal Rei owes its name to the salt pans of old: a small town of colourful houses around a square, where fishermen land their catch on the beach and morna fills the evenings.
boavista.respect: Sail within the schools’ zone, away from fishing boats and swimmers, and don’t go out alone when the trade wind picks up offshore.
boavista.season: November to April: steady, strong north-east trade winds, strongest from January to March.

around.d: Rusting hull of a stranded cargo ship, lying on a long wild beach in the north.
Sea of white sand dunes in the heart of the island, among palms and hills.
Huge, deserted pale-sand beach on the south-west coast.
Long beach backed by dunes, with the ruins of an old brickworks.
Islet facing the town, ruins of a fort and small coves, reached by boat.

walvisbay.vibe: A fishing port that remained South African until 1994, Walvis Bay lives among morning fog, oyster beds, flamingos and Namib dunes that run right down to the coast.
walvisbay.respect: The lagoon is a protected wetland: don’t ride through groups of flamingos and other birds, and stay within the usual riding zones.
walvisbay.season: October to March: strong south-westerly wind almost every afternoon; the water stays cold, so bring a thick wetsuit.

around.d: Tall dune to climb at sunrise, with a view over the desert and the town.
Lighthouse at the end of a sandspit, surrounded by seal colonies.
Coastal desert between dunes and ocean, to explore by 4x4 on the permitted tracks.

victoriabay.vibe: A row of beach houses, a railway line along the cliff and a right-hander peeling along the rocks: the cove is a haunt for surfers from George and the Garden Route.
victoriabay.respect: A narrow line-up busy with regulars: wait your turn, don’t paddle to the peak uninvited and exit over the rocks with care.
victoriabay.season: May to September: more consistent south-westerly Southern Ocean swells; the cool water calls for a wetsuit.

around.d: Village among a lagoon, lakes and forests, a starting point for riverside trails.
Historic gravel pass road through the Outeniqua Mountains.
Steam locomotives and vintage cars, the memory of the Garden Route’s railway.
Small sandy bay sheltered by cliffs, calm for swimming.

coffeebay.vibe: On the Wild Coast, the round huts of Xhosa villages dot the hills, cattle wander down to the sand and life follows the rhythm of the fields, the rivers and shore fishing.
hello: “hello” in Xhosa, the language of the Wild Coast villages
coffeebay.respect: Ask before photographing people, go hiking with a guide from the village and avoid driving at night, because of cattle and potholes.
coffeebay.season: April to September: more consistent Southern Ocean swells and offshore winds in the morning; the water stays pleasant all year.

nahoon.vibe: In East London, a port city in the Eastern Cape, surf culture is long-standing and demanding: Nahoon has shaped generations of surfers and bodyboarders used to cool, powerful water.
nahoon.respect: A wave for experienced surfers only: respect the locals’ priority. Don’t surf alone, at dawn, at dusk or in murky water, because of sharks.
nahoon.season: May to August: south-westerly Southern Ocean swells and offshore westerly winds that make the right hollow.

around.d: Natural history museum displaying the first coelacanth identified in the 20th century.
Small seaside resort at a river mouth, beach and wooden boardwalk.
Coastal forest sheltering the rare, endemic umtiza tree, with marked trails.

boulders.vibe: Simon’s Town, a naval port since British times, keeps its Victorian façades and the statue of Just Nuisance, a Great Dane enlisted in the Royal Navy; the penguins nest at the end of the street.
food: Bobotie
Spiced curried minced meat topped with egg, inherited from Cape Malay cooking.
boulders.respect: Stay on the boardwalks, and don’t touch or feed the penguins, which nip hard. Check under your car before you leave.
boulders.season: December to March: southern summer, slightly less cold water and a south-easterly wind often softened in the coves.

around.d: Headland with dizzying cliffs and a lighthouse, at the end of the Cape Peninsula.
Legendary rocky cape of seafaring, coastal paths, ostriches and baboons.
Port town with Victorian façades, a marina and a naval base.
Naval museum housed in the dockyard’s old warehouses.

proteabanks.vibe: On KwaZulu-Natal’s South Coast, divers set off at dawn from Shelly Beach by RIB, punching through the breakers to reach a remote offshore bank, the domain of big sharks.
food: Bunny chow
A curry served in a hollowed-out half loaf of bread, an Indian legacy from Durban.
proteabanks.respect: Dive only with a local club: the surf launch, current and depth call for a surface marker buoy. Never touch the sharks.
proteabanks.season: June to November for ragged-tooth sharks; the southern summer brings tiger and bull sharks instead.

around.d: Wooded canyon carved by the river, with viewpoints, trails and waterfalls.
Small seaside resort at the mouth of the Vungu, with its waterfall and lagoon.
Cast-iron lighthouse standing near the mouth of the Mzimkhulu River.

longbeach_kom.vibe: Kommetjie lives to the rhythm of the cold Atlantic: kelp forests, Slangkop Lighthouse and a community of surfers in thick wetsuits, used to big winter swells on the nearby reefs.
food: Bobotie
Mildly curried spiced mince, baked under an egg custard, a legacy of Cape Malay cooking.
longbeach_kom.respect: The peak is very busy with the village surfers: greet the line-up, wait your turn and never drop in on a local already riding.
longbeach_kom.season: April to September: consistent southern winter swells. The water stays cold all year, so bring a 4/3 mm.

around.d: Cliffside road between Noordhoek and Hout Bay, with dizzying ocean views.
Coves among big granite boulders, home to a colony of African penguins.
Cape Town’s iconic plateau, reached on foot or by cable car, with a view over the whole peninsula.
