Trails through the fynbos, a reservoir and viewpoints over both coasts.
Lively fishing harbour among the mountains, where boats leave for Seal Island.

vilankulo.vibe: In Vilankulo, lateen-sailed dhows set off every morning for the Bazaruto Archipelago, fishermen and small markets liven up the seafront, and low tide reveals vast sandbanks.
vilankulo.respect: When kiting, keep clear of the dhows and of nets set on the sandbanks. In Bazaruto park, keep your distance from dugongs and turtles.
vilankulo.season: August to December: stronger, steadier southerly wind, warm water and sandbanks you can ride at low tide.

around.d: Small island in the Bazaruto Archipelago, fringed with reefs for snorkelling.
Sandy islet in the archipelago, among lagoons and banks exposed at low tide.
Archaeological site of an ancient Indian Ocean trading post.

mafia.vibe: On Mafia, Swahili life follows the tides: dhows and outrigger canoes, octopus fishermen on the reef flats and ruined merchant towns overgrown by baobabs around Chole Bay.
mafia.respect: The marine park charges a fee: keep your receipt. Don’t put a foot or a fin on the coral, and keep your distance from whale sharks without touching them.
mafia.season: October to March: calmer sea beyond the bay, good visibility and whale sharks near Kilindoni.

around.d: Swahili village among the ruins, baobabs and mangroves of the bay.
Remains of a medieval Swahili town on Juani Island, mosques and coral-stone houses.
Large wooded island facing the bay, with lagoons and mangrove channels.
Ruins of an old Swahili port on the island’s west coast.

kendwa.vibe: Kendwa is still a Swahili fishing village facing the sunset: dhows at anchor, nets drying on the sand and traditional boatyards in Nungwi, just to the north.
kendwa.respect: Away from the beach, cover your shoulders and knees in the village. During Ramadan, avoid eating or drinking in public during the day.
kendwa.season: June to October and December to February: dry season and crystal-clear sea; the long rains fall from March to May.

around.d: Private islet surrounded by a protected reef, a top spot for snorkelling with dolphins and turtles.
Large fishing village at the northern tip, where dhows are still built.
East-coast village, between seaweed farms and a long beach facing Mnemba.

kisite.vibe: In the south of the Swahili coast, dhows leave Shimoni for the Kisite reefs; on Wasini there are no cars, just lanes, fishermen and fossil coral gardens.
kisite.respect: The park is run by the Kenya Wildlife Service: pay the entry fee, don’t walk on the coral and let the dolphins come to you without chasing them.
kisite.season: October to March: gentler north-east monsoon, calm sea and better visibility on the reefs.

around.d: Car-free island with Swahili villages, coral gardens and a mangrove boardwalk.
Fishing port known for its caves, linked to the history of the slave trade.
Fishing village at the eastern end of Wasini, facing the mainland.
Mangrove-covered islands, to explore by canoe along the channels.

brothers.vibe: Two rocks lost in the middle of the Red Sea, with an old British-era lighthouse as the only human presence: here you live aboard, to the rhythm of dawn dives and nights at anchor.
brothers.respect: Always dive with the guide: strong currents and open water. Stay grouped against the wall and never chase the sharks.
brothers.season: May to November: warm water, thresher and hammerhead sharks in summer, then oceanic whitetips in autumn.

elphinstone.vibe: On the desert coast of Marsa Alam, between barren mountains and dive villages, Elphinstone Reef is the divers’ legendary trip, reached by boat across an often choppy sea.
elphinstone.respect: With oceanic whitetips around, stay in a group near the reef, don’t linger at the surface and get back on board quickly. No gloves and no touching the coral.
elphinstone.season: October to December: oceanic whitetips are more frequent and the water still warm, despite a sometimes strong north wind.

somabay.vibe: A desert peninsula between red mountains and reefs, Soma Bay lives to the rhythm of the north wind: kites and sails colour the lagoon from late morning, while the dive boats head out to sea.
somabay.respect: Stay within the zone marked out by the centre, away from swimmers. At low tide, watch out for the reef and sea urchins near the shore: keep your booties on.
somabay.season: April to October: stronger, steadier north wind and warm water; winter stays windy but cooler.

around.d: Ferry that sank off Safaga, a moving dive on a site of remembrance.
Port town turned towards the sea, with its souk and dive boats.

dahablagoon.vibe: A former Bedouin camp turned haunt of divers, freedivers and windsurfers, Dahab keeps a slow pace: tea under the tents, cushions by the water and the Sinai mountains as a backdrop.
dahablagoon.respect: In the lagoon, respect the separation between kite and windsurf zones. Always ask before photographing a Bedouin, especially women.
dahablagoon.season: April to October: stronger, steadier north wind; in winter the water stays mild but the wind drops more often.

around.d: Small Sinai seaside town, with its promenade of cafés and shore dive sites.
Sinai desert rocks painted blue by an artist, a surprising art landscape.

giftun.vibe: Hurghada was just a fishing village before becoming the Red Sea’s big port for boat trips; every morning, dozens of boats leave the marina for the Giftun reefs.
giftun.respect: The Giftun protected area charges a fee: don’t feed the fish, don’t collect shells or coral and choose boats that use mooring buoys.
giftun.season: April to June and September to November: warm water, a sea often calm and fewer people than in high summer.

sakalava.vibe: In the north of Madagascar, Diego-Suarez blends the legacy of the former French naval base with Malagasy, Comorian and Indian cultures; on the bay, fishermen in pirogues and kitesurfers share the same lagoon.
sakalava.respect: Give way to the fishermen’s pirogues and don’t inflate your kite in the middle of their nets. Take all your rubbish away: the beach has no collection.
sakalava.season: June to September, the heart of the varatraza season: strong wind almost every day on a lagoon sheltered by the reef.

around.d: Reserve of dry forest and baobabs, trails to caves and a view over the bay.
Huge natural bay guarded by the Sugarloaf, a sacred islet at its centre.
Fishing village and white-sand beach, where pirogues leave for the Emerald Sea.
Port town with colonial façades, lively markets and mixed cuisine.

saintemarie.vibe: Once a pirate hideout, Sainte-Marie keeps its pirate cemetery and fishing villages; on car-free Île aux Nattes, you arrive by pirogue and get around on foot between coconut palms and lagoon.
saintemarie.respect: To see the whales, choose an operator that follows the whale-watching charter: a slow approach, a respected distance, and never getting into the water near a mother and her calf.
saintemarie.season: September to December: a drier season and a clear lagoon; the humpback whales are still around in September.

troubiches.vibe: Under the casuarinas of Trou aux Biches, fishermen’s pirogues and family Sunday picnics set the rhythm of the beach, a stone’s throw from the great Hindu temple of Triolet and the villages of the north.
troubiches.respect: At weekends, Mauritian families picnic under the casuarinas: share the space and leave nothing behind. In the lagoon, stay out of the boat channels.
troubiches.season: September to December: dry season, crystal-clear lagoon and warming water, before the summer rains.

around.d: A historic botanical garden, famous for its giant water lilies and its palms.
The former immigration depot for indentured labourers, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A large Hindu temple dedicated to Shiva, the religious heart of the village of Triolet.
A little red-roofed church facing Coin de Mire, at the northern tip of the island.
A lively capital: central market, Chinatown and the Caudan waterfront.

baieternay.vibe: At the end of Mahé’s north-west coast, granite hills plunge into a bay that has stayed wild; Creole culture lives on in the neighbouring villages, between line fishing, curry and sega.
baieternay.respect: In the marine park, fishing and collecting are forbidden: don’t feed the fish, and keep your fins well above the shallow corals.
baieternay.season: April to May and October to November: between the two monsoons, glassy sea and maximum visibility.

around.d: The remains of a mission school in the hills, with a viewpoint over the west coast.
Islets and reefs facing Victoria, to explore by glass-bottom boat or with a mask.
Coco de mer palms, orchids and giant tortoises in the heart of the capital.
A small granite island off Port Glaud, with a long white-sand beach.

anseintendance.vibe: With no reef to shelter it, Anse Intendance takes the ocean head-on: granite boulders, leaning coconut palms, local surfers at dawn and turtles coming ashore to lay their eggs in the sand.
anseintendance.respect: Hawksbill turtles nest here: keep away from the nests and don’t shine lights on the beach at night. No lifeguards and a powerful shorebreak: don’t swim if it’s pounding.
anseintendance.season: May to October: south-east trade winds and southern swell; the wind often turns onshore, so surf early in the morning.

around.d: A craft village around a traditional Creole house and its workshops.
A restored former colonial plantation, with a rum distillery and garden.
The remains of a mission school in the hills, with a viewpoint over the west coast.

tabarka.vibe: Tabarka lives off red coral, long harvested here and worked by its jewellers, and off the cork oak forests of Kroumirie that run down to the sea, beneath the gaze of the Genoese fort.
tabarka.respect: Red coral is strictly protected: never bring any up and don’t touch the gorgonians. Away from the beach, opt for covering clothing.
tabarka.season: June to October: warmer water and an often calm sea, with better visibility in late summer.

around.d: Tall needles of rock sculpted by erosion, at the water’s edge.
A small mountain town with tiled roofs, in the heart of the Kroumirie forests.

moulaybouzerktoun.vibe: A few fishermen’s houses, argan trees and a wind-battered bay: this hamlet on the Essaouira coast has long drawn windsurfers from all over the world, without losing its calm.
food: Amlou
A spread of roasted almonds, argan oil and honey, eaten at breakfast.
moulaybouzerktoun.respect: An experts-only spot: whoever is riding the wave has priority over whoever is heading out. Watch out for the rocks along the edge, and give way to the locals.
moulaybouzerktoun.season: May to September: the north-east trade wind blows hard almost every day, over smaller waves than in winter.

around.d: A UNESCO-listed walled town of ramparts, souks and white lanes with blue shutters.
A cannon-lined bastion facing the fishing harbour and its blue boats.
A house of memory of Moroccan Judaism, in the heart of the mellah.
A ruined former watchtower, half buried in the beach dunes.

capemaclear.vibe: In Chembe, the day begins with the return of dugout canoes; small fish dry on racks by the water, and in the evening the lake is dotted with the lights of the fishermen.
capemaclear.respect: Avoid swimming near the reeds and the village washing areas, where bilharzia can be present. To reach the islands, pay the park entrance fee.
capemaclear.season: August to November: dry season, warmer and crystal-clear water, ideal for watching cichlids with a mask.

eilat.vibe: At the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, the red desert mountains plunge into one of the northernmost coral reefs in the world, with Egypt and Jordan visible from the beach.
eilat.respect: Enter and exit only via the reserve’s walkways, never stand on the reef and don’t feed the fish.
eilat.season: April to November: warm water and often excellent visibility; in high summer, get in the water early to escape the heat.

around.d: Canyons of colourful granite and sandstone, with trails looking out over four countries.
An aquarium and a submerged tower for seeing the gulf’s reef without getting wet.
An Egyptian islet crowned by a medieval fortress, surrounded by coral.

einbokek.vibe: At the lowest point on the planet, the shores of the Dead Sea are crusted with white salt formations; people come here to float and smear themselves with black mud, facing the mountains of Jordan.
einbokek.respect: Never put your head under the water and don’t splash: the salt burns your eyes. Don’t shave the day before, rinse off in the showers and drink plenty.
einbokek.season: November to April: bearable heat and lukewarm water; in summer, the heat becomes crushing from the morning on.

around.d: Herod’s fortress perched on a plateau, reachable on foot or by cable car.
A mountain of salt carved with caves and pillars, with trails above the Dead Sea.

daymaniyat.vibe: Boats leave the Muscat coast at sunrise, running past beaches where Omani fishermen still haul up their boats, to reach islets of bare rock ringed with coral.
daymaniyat.respect: A nature reserve: no fishing, and some islands are closed to landing while birds and turtles are nesting. Don’t touch any turtle.
daymaniyat.season: October to May: calmer sea and bearable heat; in summer the water is very warm and visibility more variable.

musandam.vibe: At the tip of Arabia, the cliffs of Musandam enclose fishing villages reachable only by sea; in Khasab, excursion dhows rub shoulders with speedboats racing towards neighbouring Iran.
musandam.respect: In the fjord villages, ask before landing or photographing the inhabitants. Let the dolphins come to the boat without chasing them.
musandam.season: October to April: bearable heat and calm water in the khors; summer is crushing.

around.d: The longest fjord in Musandam, between cliffs and isolated villages, visited by dolphins.
An islet in the khor with the ruins of a British telegraph station, ideal for snorkelling.
The highest peak in Musandam, a mountain road with dizzying views over the fjords.
A small coastal town with its traditional fort by the sea.

dubaikite.vibe: Before the towers, Umm Suqeim was a village of fishermen and pearl divers; today, Emirati families stroll here at sunset, between kites and the silhouette of the Burj Al Arab.
dubaikite.respect: Only ride in the marked kite zone and during the permitted hours. When you leave the sand, cover your shoulders and knees for the promenade.
dubaikite.season: November to March: steadier afternoon breeze and bearable heat; summer is stifling and the wind light.

around.d: The tallest tower in the world, with observation decks over the whole city and the desert.
A wetland at the end of Dubai Creek, where you can watch flamingos.
The remains of an old caravan stop from the Abbasid era.

nemberala.vibe: On Rote, life follows the rhythm of the lontar palm, which gives sugar and palm wine, and of the seaweed farms uncovered at low tide in front of Nemberala. The island is also the birthplace of the sasando, a palm-leaf harp.
nemberala.respect: The seaweed farms are the village’s livelihood: don’t walk on them on your way to the peak, and be discreet with your board in the lanes.
nemberala.season: May to September: dry season and consistent southern swells that make the T-Land left peel.

batukaras.vibe: A Sundanese fishing village where outrigger canoes share the bay with surf schools. The local scene is driven by village surfers who have become instructors.
hello: a respectful Sundanese greeting, answered with “Rampes”
food: Nasi timbel
Rice cooked in a banana leaf, served with fried fish, sambal and raw vegetables, Sundanese style.
batukaras.respect: The village is Muslim: cover your shoulders and knees away from the beach. At the peak, give priority on the right to students and locals.
batukaras.season: April to October: dry season, southern swells nicely filtered by the point and often windless mornings.

around.d: A green-water canyon to travel up by canoe or by swimming between mossy walls.
A West Java seaside resort with a fish market and a wooded peninsula full of monkeys.

gerupuk.vibe: A Sasak village focused on fishing and farming lobsters in floating cages. The fishermen have become boatmen: every morning their boats take surfers out to the peaks in the bay.
food: Ayam taliwang
Grilled chicken coated in a very fiery sambal, Lombok’s great speciality.
gerupuk.respect: Agree on the boat price before setting off and pay your boatman. Avoid the lobster cages and stay covered up in the Muslim village.
gerupuk.season: April to October: dry season and consistent southern swells, with lighter winds early in the morning.

around.d: A lively small coastal town, the starting point for the bays and hills of southern Lombok.
A wild cape in eastern Lombok, with sheer cliffs and views over the Alas Strait.
A large, calm bay in south-east Lombok, lined with fishing villages and seaweed farms.

banda.vibe: The Dutch and the English fought over these tiny islands for nutmeg; forts, warehouses and colonial houses still bear witness to it in Banda Neira, facing the cone of Gunung Api.
food: Manisan pala
The flesh of the nutmeg fruit candied in sugar, nibbled all over the Banda Islands.
banda.respect: The corals on the lava flow grow just below the surface: stay at the surface without finning over the coral heads, and ask before entering the nutmeg groves.
banda.season: October to December and March to May: calm sea between the two monsoons and good visibility.

around.d: A pentagonal 17th-century Dutch fort, with views over the bay and the Gunung Api volcano.
The main island: colonial houses, old nutmeg warehouses and a lively little port.
A tiny nutmeg island that the English ceded to the Dutch, who gave up Manhattan.
The ruins of the first Dutch fort on Banda Neira, overtaken by vegetation.

kakaban.vibe: The Derawan archipelago is Bajau country, a people of sailors and fishermen. Kakaban’s lake, cut off from the ocean for millennia, is home to jellyfish that have evolved safe from predators.
kakaban.respect: In the lake: no sunscreen, no finning near the bottom, and don’t take the jellyfish out of the water: they are fragile and unique.
kakaban.season: April to October: a generally calmer sea for the boat crossings and good visibility around the island.

alor.vibe: Alor has dozens of Papuan languages and keeps its moko bronze drums, handed down as dowry. In the hilltop villages, the lego-lego dance and traditional houses carry on a culture that has stayed apart.
alor.respect: The currents in the straits are powerful: dive with a local guide. Always ask before taking photos in the traditional villages.
alor.season: March to November: an often calmer sea; the currents stay strong and the water sometimes cool all year round.

around.d: Alor’s main town at the end of a long bay, with a lively market and a museum of moko drums.
A volcanic island in the Pantar Strait, surrounded by renowned coral walls.

anilao.vibe: On the Mabini coast, the dive centres’ outrigger bancas leave from small coves where fishermen also moor their boats. At weekends, Anilao is the playground of Manila’s macro photographers.
food: Lomi and kapeng barako
A thick noodle soup and strong liberica coffee, two points of pride in Batangas province.
anilao.respect: For macro, never move a nudibranch or a seahorse for a photo, and fin well away from the bottom so as not to stir up the sand.
anilao.season: November to May: dry season and a calmer sea; the water cools down in January and February.

around.d: A colonial town of ancestral wood-and-stone houses, embroidered fabrics and balisong knives.
A huge Spanish-era stone basilica towering over the old town of Taal.
A colonial mansion known as the “wedding gift house”, open to visitors.

puertogalera.vibe: Sabang is a former fishing hamlet turned divers’ village, where bancas and dive centres crowd the shore. In the hills live the Iraya, one of the Mangyan peoples of Mindoro.
puertogalera.respect: Bancas pass right over the reefs: swim with a surface marker buoy and stay within the marked snorkelling areas.
puertogalera.season: November to May: dry season, calm sea and good visibility; typhoons are a threat from June to October.

around.d: A port nestled at the end of a sheltered bay, with long White Beach to the west of town.
A volcanic island in the middle of the passage, renowned for its coral walls for snorkelling.

launion.vibe: An Ilocano town that has become the meeting point for Manila’s surfers, between surf schools, cafés and street stalls. The monsoon swell has given rise to a real community of local surfers here.
hello: “good day” in Ilocano, the language of northern Luzon
food: Pinakbet
A northern Luzon vegetable stew seasoned with bagoong, a fermented fish paste.
launion.respect: The Urbiztondo line-up is packed with beginners: keep your distance, don’t let go of your board and give priority to whoever is closest to the peak.
launion.season: October to March: north-east monsoon swells and late typhoon-season swells, warm water.

around.d: The capital of La Union, with its hilltop Taoist Ma-Cho Temple and its market.
A coastal town known for its pebble beach and its old Spanish watchtower.
A colonial church in Luna, a Marian shrine revered throughout northern Luzon.
A peninsula south of San Fernando, with a lighthouse and views over the Lingayen Gulf.

baler.vibe: Philippine surfing is said to have been born here after the filming of Apocalypse Now, when the crew left their boards to the local kids. Baler also keeps the memory of the siege of its church by a Spanish garrison.
baler.respect: The beach break forms powerful rip currents: swim near the surf schools and ask the locals for advice before paddling out.
baler.season: October to February: north-east monsoon swells and Pacific typhoon swells, warm water.

around.d: A small town and its stone church, scene of the 1898–1899 siege.
A museum devoted to Baler’s history, from the Spanish siege to the beginnings of local surfing.

balicasag.vibe: Balicasag is a small fishing island whose reef has long been protected. Every morning, outrigger bancas shuttle across from Panglao in the low light over the Bohol Sea.
hello: “good morning” in Cebuano, the language of Bohol
food: Calamay
A Bohol sweet of sticky rice, coconut and sugar, sold in a coconut shell.
balicasag.respect: The sanctuary limits visitor numbers: go through an accredited operator, never stand on the reef flat and keep your distance from the turtles.
balicasag.season: March to June: glassy sea, very warm water and visibility at its best around the drop-off.

around.d: A coral island linked to Bohol, with white-sand beaches, freshwater caves and an old church.
Panglao’s lively white-sand beach, the departure point for dive boats.

redang.vibe: Off Terengganu, a Malay state attached to its painted fishing boats and its traditions, Redang lives to the rhythm of the green turtles that come to nest on its beaches and of the island’s fishing villages.
food: Keropok lekor
A fried fish-and-sago sausage, nibbled with a chilli sauce, the pride of Terengganu.
redang.respect: Pay the marine park fee, don’t feed the fish and stay well away from the turtle nesting beaches at night, without a torch.
redang.season: April to September: calm sea and crystal-clear water; the island slows right down during the north-east monsoon.

around.d: A small neighbouring island with quiet beaches and fringing reefs good for snorkelling.
An island that once held a camp for Vietnamese refugees, of which remains and a memorial are left.

tarpark.vibe: Facing Kota Kinabalu, these islands live to the rhythm of the harbour’s water taxis and of the Bajau, a seafaring people of Sabah’s west coast. In town, the waterfront markets overflow with grilled fish.
hello: a greeting in Kadazan-Dusun, the language of Sabah’s first people
food: Hinava
Raw fish marinated in lime, ginger and chilli, a Kadazan-Dusun recipe from Sabah.
tarpark.respect: Don’t feed the fish, stay within the marked swimming areas and keep your park entry ticket on you.
tarpark.season: March to September: calmer sea and better visibility, before the heavy year-end rains.

around.d: Sabah’s capital, with waterfront markets, mosques and views of Mount Kinabalu.
The state museum on Sabah’s peoples, crafts and nature, with traditional houses.
The park’s large wooded island, with forest trails and stilt villages.
A mangrove in the middle of the city, crossed by boardwalks for watching birds and crabs.
A living museum showcasing the houses, skills and dances of Borneo’s peoples.

kata.vibe: Kata is the birthplace of Phuket’s small surf scene: in summer, shapers and board-hire stands take back the beach when the tourists desert it. The island keeps a Sino-Portuguese heritage and active temples.
food: Moo hong
Pork braised with black pepper and garlic, handed down by Phuket’s Hokkien families.
kata.respect: During the monsoon, rip currents are deadly: respect the lifeguards’ red flags and never swim alone outside the patrolled area.
kata.season: May to October: the south-west monsoon pushes consistent waves into the bay, cleaner early in the morning.

around.d: A white marble Buddha on a hilltop, with views over the bays of southern Phuket.
Phuket’s most revered temple, with its great chedi decorated with murals.
A small neighbouring beach at the foot of the hills, quieter than the main bay.
Two islands off Phuket, with clear water and reefs for snorkelling.

sailrock.vibe: Between Ko Pha-ngan and Ko Tao, diving keeps a host of small centres going, and fishing boats cross paths with dive boats at dawn. Hin Bai, the “sail rock”, is a landmark for the gulf’s fishermen.
sailrock.respect: In the chimney, wait your turn and don’t touch the rock. If a whale shark passes by, keep your distance and don’t chase it.
sailrock.season: March to September: calm sea and better visibility, before the north-east monsoon stirs up the gulf at the end of the year.

around.d: A wooded island with many coves, waterfalls and temples, well beyond its party reputation alone.
An isolated beach in northern Ko Pha-ngan, reachable by boat or along a trail.
Ko Pha-ngan’s main port, with its night market rich in street food.

honmun.vibe: In Nha Trang Bay, fishermen still steer round bamboo basket boats, and the islands’ cliffs shelter swiftlet nests, harvested in the region for a long time.
food: Bún chả cá
A rice vermicelli soup with fish cakes, a speciality of Nha Trang’s canteens.
honmun.respect: Don’t stand on the coral when getting off the boat, and turn down any coral or shells offered for sale.
honmun.season: February to September: calm sea and good visibility; from October to December, rain and rough sea.

around.d: A lively seaside city with markets, Cham towers and a seafront lined with cafés.
A neo-Gothic stone cathedral built on a mound during the French colonial era.

lanha.vibe: Among the limestone karsts, fishing families still live in floating houses and on fish farms, as in the village of Cái Bèo, one of the oldest settlements on Cát Bà.
food: Bánh đa cua
A soup of reddish rice noodles in crab broth, a Hai Phong speciality.
lanha.respect: By kayak, go around the floating farms without landing on them, and leave nothing behind in the enclosed lagoons.
lanha.season: April to June and September–October: warm water and clearer skies, between the winter mists and the summer storms.

around.d: A large island with a forested national park, hiking trails, caves and small beaches.
Thousands of limestone islets in an emerald sea, with caves and floating villages.
An islet in the bay with a small beach and a summit viewpoint over the karsts.

mykhe.vibe: From dawn, Da Nang’s residents swim and exercise on the beach, while fishermen haul their round basket boats up the sand. American soldiers nicknamed it China Beach.
food: Mì Quảng
Yellow rice noodles in just a little broth, with prawns, pork and a toasted rice cracker.
mykhe.respect: Swim between the lifeguards’ flags: the currents strengthen quickly in winter. And leave room for the basket boats.
mykhe.season: May to August: calm, warm sea, perfect for swimming; the surfing waves arrive from October to March.

around.d: Five marble hills riddled with caves, pagodas and stairways leading to viewpoints.
The finest collection of sandstone sculptures from the kingdom of Champa, in a colonial building.
A wooded peninsula home to douc langurs, with a large pagoda facing the sea.
A covered bridge topped by a small temple, the emblem of Hội An’s old town.
A dragon-shaped bridge over the Hàn River that breathes fire and water on certain evenings.

condao.vibe: A former penal colony of the colonial era and then of the war, Côn Đảo remains a place of remembrance and pilgrimage for the Vietnamese. All around, the sea is protected and green turtles come back to nest.
condao.respect: Trips to Bảy Cạnh are run by park-approved operators. To watch the turtles, follow the rangers, with no torch or flash.
condao.season: March to June: calm sea and better visibility; the turtles nest mainly in summer and early autumn.

around.d: The main island: former prisons, Hàng Dương Cemetery and a peaceful little town.
Tropical forest criss-crossed by trails leading to coves and protected reefs.

kohrong.vibe: Sok San is a Khmer fishing village at the end of a long beach, where colourful boats sit alongside a few bungalows. At night, bioluminescent plankton makes the water sparkle around swimmers.
kohrong.respect: The island struggles with its waste: take your plastics back to the mainland, and cover up when walking through the fishing village.
kohrong.season: November to April: dry season, glassy sea and crystal-clear water on the west coast.

around.d: A quieter neighbouring island, with white-sand bays and turquoise water good for snorkelling.
A marine protected area around the islands, with seagrass beds and reefs to explore with mask and snorkel.

palolem.vibe: In the south of Goa, Palolem blends Catholic and Hindu village life, fishermen’s canoes pulled up on the sand and huts taken down every monsoon. Konkani is spoken here, and the white churches recall the Portuguese past.
food: Xacuti
A Goan curry with roasted coconut and toasted spices, often made with chicken.
palolem.respect: Nudity and topless sunbathing are banned in Goa. When kayaking to the islet, give way to fishing boats coming home to the north of the bay.
palolem.season: November to March: end of the monsoon, calm sea and bearable heat for paddling.

around.d: A wild beach lined with casuarinas where olive ridley turtles come to nest.
A Western Ghats forest with trails and watchtowers for spotting wildlife.

netrani.vibe: Long used as a target range by the navy, Netrani is gradually opening up to divers. On the coast, Murudeshwar’s fishermen set out beneath the giant statue of Shiva that towers over the headland.
hello: “hello” in Kannada, said with palms joined
food: Neer dosa
Thin rice crêpes from the Karnataka coast, served with a fish curry.
netrani.respect: The island lies far offshore: dive with an accredited centre in Murudeshwar and take home no coral or shells.
netrani.season: December to May: calm sea and good visibility; the monsoon halts trips from June to September.

around.d: A temple with a tall gopuram and a giant statue of Shiva on a headland facing the sea.
The monastery-temple of the Chitrapur Saraswat community, in the heart of the village of Shirali.

rishikesh.vibe: A holy city where the Ganges leaves the Himalayas, Rishikesh lives among ashrams, temple bells and evening ceremonies on the ghats. The Beatles meditated here, and both yoga and white water draw the whole world.
food: Vegetarian thali
Rice, dal, vegetables and chapatis: the holy city is vegetarian and alcohol-free.
rishikesh.respect: Meat and alcohol are banned in town. Cover up on the ghats and don’t swim outside the supervised areas: the current is treacherous.
rishikesh.season: March to May and October–November: good water levels; rafting trips stop during the monsoon.

around.d: A large ashram on the banks of the Ganges, famous for its Ganga aarti ceremony at dusk.
An abandoned ashram in the forest, its walls covered in murals, where the Beatles meditated.
A suspension footbridge over the Ganges, surrounded by temples and shops.
A Shiva temple in the forest, the goal of a hike or pilgrimage from Rishikesh.
Forests in the Himalayan foothills, home to elephants, deer and tigers.

covelong.vibe: A Tamil fishing village where kattumarams, log rafts that gave us the word catamaran, now sit alongside surfboards. The village children have become the first local surfers.
hello: “hello” in Tamil, said with palms joined
food: Meen kuzhambu
A tangy tamarind fish curry, cooked every day in Tamil villages.
covelong.respect: The beach is the fishermen’s workplace: don’t put your board down on the nets or boats, and cover up in the village.
covelong.season: March to September: southern swells running up the Bay of Bengal, modest and consistent waves.

around.d: An 8th-century granite temple standing on the Bay of Bengal at Mahabalipuram.
A huge bas-relief carved into the rock, populated by gods, elephants and ascetics.
Five monolithic temples, each carved from a single block of granite.
An artists’ community founded in the 1960s, with a gallery and studios.

mirissa.vibe: A fishing village on the south coast, where colourful boats return to the little harbour at dawn while tuk-tuks speed along the coast road lined with coconut palms and surfers’ cafés.
food: Ambul thiyal
A dry, sour tuna curry made with goraka, a preserving recipe typical of the south coast.
mirissa.respect: For the whales, choose an operator that keeps its distance and doesn’t cut across the animals’ path. On the reef right, give priority to the locals.
mirissa.season: November to April: the monsoon has passed, the sea is smooth on the south side and the swell arrives clean on the reef.

around.d: A tall white lighthouse on the southernmost point of Sri Lanka.
A small star-shaped Dutch fort, with a moat and an ornate gate.
A rocky islet crowned by a villa, set in Weligama Bay.
A lagoon dotted with islets to explore by boat, between mangroves and temples.
The writer’s birthplace and a museum of Sinhalese rural traditions.

pigeonisland.vibe: The Tamil and Muslim north-east coast, where Nilaveli’s fishermen still haul nets from the beach. Offshore, the rocky islet shelters a reef, and rock pigeons nest there, which gave it its name.
hello: “hello” in Tamil, said with palms joined
pigeonisland.respect: In the national park, never stand on the coral and don’t feed the sharks. At Koneswaram Temple, cover your shoulders and legs and take off your shoes.
pigeonisland.season: May to September: the east coast is sheltered from the monsoon, the sea is calm and the water crystal clear.

around.d: A Hindu temple perched on Swami Rock, above the sea.
A Portuguese and later Dutch fort where deer wander among the ramparts.
Seven hot-water wells at different temperatures, a place of pilgrimage.
The ruins of an ancient Buddhist monastery, in the countryside north of Trincomalee.

pastapoint.vibe: It was in this corner of North Malé Atoll that Maldivian surfing took off, around the first surf camps. Around it, the local islands live off pole-and-line tuna fishing and the comings and goings of dhonis.
pastapoint.respect: Pasta Point is reserved for the resort’s guests: don’t try to surf it from another island. On the local islands, cover up outside the bikini beaches.
pastapoint.season: March to October, often with the cleanest conditions in April–May and in September, when the wind drops.

around.d: A lively local island, with surfers’ guesthouses and a neighbouring reef wave.
A mosque of carved coral stone, a jewel of Maldivian heritage.
Royal artefacts, pre-Islamic sculptures and the history of the archipelago.
A small, quiet inhabited island, fringed with mangroves and lagoons.

maeda.vibe: On Okinawa’s west coast, land of the old gusuku castles of the Ryūkyū Kingdom, the sea draws divers and growers of umibudo, the sea grapes that the village of Onna has made its speciality.
food: Gōyā chanpurū
A stir-fry of bitter melon, tofu, egg and pork, Okinawa’s family dish.
maeda.respect: Don’t touch the coral, and don’t go down the steps when the red flag is up: the swell makes getting out of the water dangerous.
maeda.season: May to October: warm water and good visibility, but keep an eye out for typhoons in late summer.

around.d: The curved ramparts of a UNESCO-listed gusuku, with views over the coast.
A museum village of old houses, Okinawan crafts and dances.
A village renowned for its yachimun pottery workshops and old kilns.

niijima.vibe: A volcanic island administered by Tokyo, famous for its pale kōgaseki stone, used for moyai statues and glass. The village lives to the rhythm of fishermen, open-air onsen and surfers from the capital.
food: Kusaya
Dried fish marinated in a fermented brine, the pungent pride of the Izu Islands.
niijima.respect: The beach is long and unpatrolled outside summer: never surf alone when the swell comes in. At the onsen, wash before getting into the bath.
niijima.season: September to October: consistent typhoon swells, still-warm water and a beach deserted after the summer.

around.d: A small island of rocky coves and hot springs by the sea.
Stone moyai statues, a glass studio and a free onsen facing the open sea.
A cone-shaped island covered in camellias, which yield a renowned oil.

yonaguni.vibe: At the far end of Japan, the island keeps its own language, its small horses and a marlin fishing port. On clear days, the mountains of Taiwan appear on the horizon.
food: Yaeyama soba
Thin wheat noodles in a clear broth, topped with pork and kamaboko.
yonaguni.respect: The currents are powerful: dive only with a local club and stay with your guide. Yonaguni’s horses roam free; don’t feed them.
yonaguni.season: December to March for the schools of hammerhead sharks, at the cost of an often rough and cool sea.

around.d: The westernmost point of Japan, facing Taiwan, ideal at sunset.
Cliffs, pastures of free-roaming horses and fishing villages.

yoshino.vibe: On Miyako Island, fringed with reefs and sugar cane fields, the villages of the east coast keep a quiet life turned towards the sea and their own island language.
food: Miyako soba
Wheat noodles in a light broth, with the pork traditionally hidden beneath the noodles.
yoshino.respect: Don’t walk on the coral at low tide, and beware of the currents at the lagoon’s exit. Wear mineral sunscreen.
yoshino.season: May to June and October: warm water, a calm lagoon and less risk of typhoons than in high summer.

around.d: A long, wild peninsula ending in a lighthouse, with cliffs and views over the reef.
A long white-sand beach facing Kurima Island and its bridge.
The history, wildlife and traditions of the Miyako Islands, in Hirara.
A shady botanical garden planted with tropical species.

jukdo.vibe: On the Gangwon coast, between pine forests and fishing ports, Yangyang has become the cradle of Korean surfing, where young people from Seoul come at weekends to learn to ride waves.
food: Songi mushrooms
Matsutake picked in Yangyang’s pine forests in autumn, grilled or in soup.
jukdo.respect: In summer, respect the marked zones separating swimmers and surfers. At weekends, the line-up is full of beginners: keep your distance.
jukdo.season: October to March: winter low-pressure systems raise more consistent swells; bring a thick wetsuit.

around.d: A wooded mountain in the Taebaek range, with trails and ancient Buddhist temples.
A bustling fishing port and its large fish and squid market.

munseom.vibe: In the south of Jeju, Seogwipo lives among tangerine orchards, basalt cliffs and small harbours. The haenyeo, the island’s free-diving women, still harvest abalone and sea urchins here.
food: Jeju black pork
Thick slices of black pork grilled over charcoal, dipped in an anchovy sauce.
munseom.respect: The currents around the islet are strong: dive with a local club. Don’t pick up any shellfish; these waters are worked by the haenyeo.
munseom.season: September to November: the water is at its warmest of the year and visibility improves after the typhoons.

around.d: A waterfall that drops straight into the sea, at the foot of the cliffs.
A waterfall at the end of a wooded gorge, beautiful at nightfall.
Trails to the summit of the volcano, the highest point in South Korea.
A bustling covered market: fish, tangerines and Jeju street snacks.
An estuary of green water between lava walls, to explore by boat.

greenisland.vibe: Once a prison island for political dissidents, Lüdao has become an island of fishermen and divers that you tour by scooter, among reefs, hot springs and strangely shaped rocks.
greenisland.respect: Don’t touch the large massive corals and avoid finning over the bottom. On the coast road, ride your scooter carefully: it is narrow and windy.
greenisland.season: May to September: calm sea and regular boats from Taitung; in winter, the monsoon often cancels the crossings.

around.d: A rare saltwater hot spring, with open-air pools facing the sunrise.
A former political prison turned place of remembrance of the martial-law era.
A volcanic rock shaped like a reclining woman, seen from the coast.
A park devoted to sika deer, once raised in large numbers on the island.

penghu.vibe: An archipelago of basalt and coral where villages shelter their vegetable plots behind low stone walls against the wind, and where fishermen built stone fish traps on the foreshore.
food: Brown sugar cake
A soft steamed cake made with brown sugar, Penghu’s emblematic sweet.
penghu.respect: The winter wind is violent and the sea cold: never ride alone and tell someone before you head out. Keep clear of the swimming area.
penghu.season: October to March: the north-east monsoon blows strong and steady, for experienced, well-equipped riders.

around.d: A temple to the sea goddess Mazu, considered the oldest in Taiwan.
Traditional basalt-and-coral houses in a preserved village on Xiyu.
A small island ringed by basalt columns, reached by boat from Magong.
A 19th-century artillery fort with vaulted galleries, facing the strait.

hoihawan.vibe: At the tip of the Sai Kung peninsula, old Hakka villages, lime kilns and coastal trails recall rural Hong Kong, far from the towers, with a protected bay as its showcase.
food: Sai Kung seafood
Choose fish or crabs from the harbour’s tanks, cooked on the spot.
hoihawan.respect: In the marine park, fishing and collecting are forbidden. Come by minibus from Sai Kung: the access road is closed to unauthorised cars.
hoihawan.season: May to October: warm water and calm sea; the drier end of the season is best, and keep an eye out for typhoons.

around.d: Four wild white-sand beaches linked by a coastal trail.
A fishing island with a Tin Hau temple and windswept meadows above the sea.
A 19th-century fortified Hakka village and its old lime kiln.
An islet in Kiu Tsui Country Park, with a pebble tombolo to cross at low tide.

turquoisebay.vibe: Between the ochre Cape Range and Ningaloo Reef, life revolves around the sea: whale sharks, manta rays and turtles draw van travellers and campers here from Exmouth.
turquoisebay.respect: Enter the water at the south end of the bay and get out before the sand spit: beyond it, the current races out to sea. Don’t touch the coral; the area is a sanctuary.
turquoisebay.season: April to June: still-warm water, lighter winds and whale sharks passing along the reef.

around.d: Limestone gorges such as Yardie Creek and Mandu Mandu, and rock wallabies.
The tip of the peninsula, with Vlamingh Head Lighthouse and whales in winter.

yongala.vibe: Lost with all hands in a cyclone in the early 20th century, the steamship was only found decades later. Divers now set out from Alva Beach, amid the sugar cane fields of the Ayr region.
yongala.respect: The wreck is a grave and a protected historic site: entering it or touching the hull is forbidden. Descend along the mooring line.
yongala.season: August to December: the trade winds ease, the sea calms down and visibility is often better.

ladyelliot.vibe: Once stripped bare by guano miners, this coral island has been replanted and now lives to the rhythm of seabirds, nesting turtles and an old lighthouse.
ladyelliot.respect: Stay on the paths while birds and turtles are nesting, with no torch on the beach at night. Keep your distance from the manta rays.
ladyelliot.season: May to October: crystal-clear water and plenty of manta rays, even if the sea is cooler than in summer.

tangalooma.vibe: A former whaling station turned holiday spot, Tangalooma lies on a sand island explored by 4WD, Quandamooka country, where dolphins and dugongs frequent Moreton Bay.
tangalooma.respect: Don’t climb on the rusty wrecks, and keep clear of the channel where boats anchor. On the island, you can only get around by 4WD and with a permit.
tangalooma.season: October to April: warmer water and an often calm sea on the bay side; avoid very windy days.

around.d: Giant dunes for sandboarding, freshwater lakes and wild beaches.
A small, isolated coral reef, a dive site rich in turtles and rays.
Second World War gun batteries and bunkers in the dunes.

pointlookout.vibe: On Minjerribah, Quandamooka country, the village of Point Lookout overlooks the Pacific from its headland, where you watch for whales, dolphins and turtles. Here, life is lived barefoot between beach and bush.
pointlookout.respect: Main Beach has strong rip currents: swim between the flags. In the water, give priority to the headland’s locals.
pointlookout.season: February to May: more consistent cyclone and trade-wind swells, still-warm water and the summer holidays over.

around.d: The North Gorge walk, with turtles, rays and whales in season.
A perched lake with tea-coloured water, stained by tea trees.
A crystal-clear freshwater lake hidden in the bush, at the end of a trail.
Aboriginal history, shipwrecks and island life, in Dunwich.

agneswater.vibe: A small coastal town surrounded by national parks, near the spot where James Cook landed in 1770, hence the name of the neighbouring village. You learn to surf here before heading off to the islands of the southern Great Barrier Reef.
agneswater.respect: In the nearby parks, turtles nest in summer: no torches on the beach at night. Swim between the flags, patrolled by the local club.
agneswater.season: December to April: cyclone swells and trade winds bring the most consistent waves, often gentle.

around.d: Dunes, deserted beaches and coves, turtle nesting sites.
A village on a peninsula, with sunsets over the water and trips out to the islands.
A monument on the beach where Cook came ashore on his 1770 voyage.
Mangroves, coastal forests and wild beaches reachable by 4WD.

crescenthead.vibe: A small village in Dunghutti country where longboarding is almost a religion: long boards glide along the point, and kangaroos graze on the headland grass at sunset.
crescenthead.respect: The line-up is crowded and full of longboards: one person per wave, and never drop in on someone else’s wave. Don’t feed the headland’s kangaroos.
crescenthead.season: March to June: south-east and cyclone swells wrapping around the headland, often with offshore winds in the morning.

around.d: Dunes, swamps and rocky headlands, with a trail to Smoky Cape Lighthouse.
A quiet village beside a clear river, ideal for swimming or paddling.
Wild beaches, flowering heathland and sand tracks between lagoons and ocean.

angourie.vibe: A National Surfing Reserve, Angourie drew shortboard pioneers from the 1960s, who came to live near the point. The village keeps a low-key spirit, away from the bustle of Yamba.
food: Yamba prawns
Clarence River prawns landed at the harbour, to enjoy by the water.
angourie.respect: The point is for experienced surfers only, and the local line-up is demanding: watch for a long time before paddling out, and let the regulars go.
angourie.season: March to July: southerly swells and offshore south-westerly winds make the point peel along the rocks.

around.d: A small fishing town at the mouth of the Clarence, with cafés and varied beaches.
World Heritage-listed littoral rainforest, with a trail to the sea.
Long beaches, dark rivers and Aboriginal sites north of the Clarence.
A lighthouse on Yamba’s headland, a lookout over the ocean and the whales in winter.

narrabeen.vibe: Sung about by the Beach Boys, Narrabeen has produced generations of champions in one of Sydney’s most demanding line-ups. The neighbourhood lives between lagoon, surf life saving club and suburban surf culture.
narrabeen.respect: The local line-up is very sharp: no room for beginners at the peak. After heavy rain, avoid surfing near the mouth: the lagoon water is polluted.
narrabeen.season: March to June: more frequent autumn swells, offshore wind in the morning and still-mild water.

around.d: A steep climb up to the lighthouse, with views over Palm Beach and Pittwater.
A protected rock platform, teeming with rock-pool life at low tide.
A lake in the bush, with swimming, a loop walk and mountain-bike trails.
A 1950s modernist house turned museum, in the northern bush.

flypoint.vibe: On Port Stephens, Worimi country, Nelson Bay lives off fishing, dolphin-watching trips and oysters. Underwater, the marine sanctuary teems with small, colourful creatures.
food: Port Stephens oysters
Rock oysters farmed in the estuary, served natural or with just a squeeze of lemon.
flypoint.respect: Fly Point is a sanctuary: take nothing. Dive at high-tide slack water, because the current quickly becomes very strong in the channel.
flypoint.season: May to September: the water cools, but visibility is often the best of the year.

around.d: A climb to the top of Tomaree Head, with views over the islands and whales in winter.
Second World War guns and bunkers on the headland.
A village of river and dunes, with koalas in the trees and calm beaches.
A reserve for the rare Gould’s petrel, to be observed only from the boat.

woolamai.vibe: On Phillip Island, Bunurong country, shearwaters nest in their thousands on Cape Woolamai and little penguins come home every evening. You surf here in cold water from Bass Strait.
woolamai.respect: The rip currents are fearsome: don’t surf alone, and swim only between the flags. On the cape, stay on the path to spare the shearwater burrows.
woolamai.season: March to May: consistent south-westerly swells, calmer winds and the water at its mildest of the year.

around.d: The Penguin Parade at dusk, koalas and a seal-watching centre.
A historic farm, old gardens and sheep-shearing demonstrations, linked by a bridge.
Offshore rocks home to a large colony of fur seals.
A fishing village where you can watch the pelicans being fed on the jetty.

squeaky.vibe: At the tip of the mainland, the Prom is a land of granite, bush and empty beaches, where wombats and emus wander among the tents at Tidal River. Melbourne families have camped here for generations.
squeaky.respect: Never feed wombats, emus or ravens, and store your food away. The beach is unpatrolled: don’t stray far from the shore.
squeaky.season: January to March: the water reaches its peak, still cool, and the days are long and bright.

around.d: Trails up Mount Oberon, deserted beaches and bush wildlife.
The southernmost point of the Australian mainland, at the end of a long walk.
Granite seabeds, kelp forests and fur seals, for experienced divers.

wineglass.vibe: On Tasmania’s east coast, pink granite and orange lichen, the fishing shacks of Coles Bay and oyster farms: here, life follows the rhythm of the tides, the kayaks and the unshy wallabies.
food: Freycinet oysters
Farmed in the cool waters around Coles Bay, best tasted freshly shucked.
wineglass.respect: A Tasmanian parks pass is required at Freycinet. Stay on the marked trails and never feed the wallabies.
wineglass.season: December to March: long southern-summer days, less cold water and an often calmer sea for paddling.

around.d: A granite range towering over the bay, crossed by the park’s trails.
A clifftop boardwalk with views over the coast and the granite islets.
A small sheltered cove between granite boulders, ideal for a calm swim.
Long, wild white-sand beaches pounded by the Tasman Sea.
A wild island south of the peninsula, reached by boat or sea kayak.

busselton.vibe: A quiet seaside town on Geographe Bay, built around its historic jetty. Families come here for picnics on the grass, fishing trips and the whales that cruise along the bay in the southern spring.
food: Margaret River wines
The neighbouring wine region pairs beautifully with the bay’s fish.
busselton.respect: Along the jetty, don’t touch or pull anything off the pylons: the soft corals and sponges are fragile. Stay within the marked swimming area.
busselton.season: December to April: warmer water and a calm bay in the morning, before the afternoon sea breeze.

around.d: A rare forest of tuarts, tall coastal eucalypts, to explore on foot.
A 19th-century settlers’ farm, restored and open to visitors.
A wetland where you can watch black swans and waterbirds in great numbers.
A small coastal town, the gateway to Cape Naturaliste and its coves.

lancelin.vibe: A crayfishing village turned haunt of windsurfers and kiters, facing its islets. Between fishing boats, white dunes and riders’ vans, the mood stays simple and all about the wind.
food: Western rock lobster
Caught in pots by the Lancelin boats, best tasted grilled during the season.
lancelin.respect: Respect the launch zones and give way to windsurfers already out on the water. Off the permitted tracks, don’t drive on the dunes.
lancelin.season: November to March: a strong, steady sea breeze every afternoon of the southern summer.

around.d: A protected islet facing the village, sheltering the lagoon from the ocean waves.
A small neighbouring coastal village, another spot loved by windsurfers and kiters.

goatisland.vibe: The country’s first marine reserve, created on the initiative of researchers at the Leigh marine laboratory. The small fishing harbour nearby now also welcomes families who come to see the fish that have returned to the shore.
goatisland.respect: A no-take marine reserve: take nothing, neither fish nor shellfish, and don’t feed the fish, it’s forbidden.
goatisland.season: January to April: the warmest water of the year and often good visibility close to shore.

around.d: A peninsula fenced off to protect native birds, with beaches and trails.
A long white-sand beach lined with dunes, ideal for walking.
A wooded island in the Hauraki Gulf, with Governor Grey’s historic mansion.
A small neighbouring cove lined with rocks, for a quiet picnic.
A fishing village on Omaha Cove, with its little harbour and cafés.

taupo.vibe: In the heart of Ngāti Tūwharetoa country, the lake lives between trout fishing, steaming vents and pumice beaches. The Mine Bay carvings are a reminder that this lake is first and foremost Māori land.
taupo.respect: The lakebed belongs to Ngāti Tūwharetoa: be discreet in front of the Mine Bay carvings and don’t land on Motutaiko Island.
taupo.season: December to March: milder water, settled weather and a lake often glassy in the morning before the wind.

around.d: Boardwalks among steaming craters and active geothermal ground.
A volcanic dome whose summit looks out over the whole lake.
A geothermal area north of Taupō, all steam and hot pools.
A peaceful little village on the lake’s northernmost bay.

milford.vibe: Piopiotahi to the Māori, this fjord’s only village is a small harbour and a few wharves. Rain, waterfalls and cliffs set the pace of life here, where fur seals and dolphins cross paths with kayaks.
milford.respect: Keep your distance from fur seals and dolphins, and stay close to the walls, out of the boats’ path. Bring repellent against the sandflies.
milford.season: December to March: long days and less cold water; after rain, the waterfalls multiply.

around.d: An iconic peak soaring out of the fjord, to admire from the water or the shore.
The fjord’s dark waters, where black corals and deep-sea life thrive.
A famous alpine hike through lakes, ridges and glacial valleys.
A wild rainforest valley with trails and waterfalls.

stclair.vibe: The beach of a city founded by Scottish settlers, with its esplanade, cafés and surf club. Dunedin’s students brave water here that comes straight from the Deep South.
stclair.respect: Keep at least 20 m between you and the sea lions resting on the sand. In the line-up, wait your turn: there are plenty of regulars.
stclair.season: March to June: consistent southern swells and more frequent offshore winds, with a thick wetsuit.

around.d: A castle-style mansion on the Otago Peninsula, with gardens and views.
Otago’s Māori and colonial history told in a lively museum.
Dunedin’s central square, lined by the cathedral and the town hall.
A fenced forest where you can spot rare native birds and tuatara.
A classical Chinese garden, a tribute to Otago’s first Chinese immigrants.

natadola.vibe: On the south coast of Viti Levu, Fijian villages still live from fishing and their gardens. Children on horseback on the sand, fishers in the lagoon and kava shared in the evening set the tone.
natadola.respect: Stay inside the lagoon: near the reef passes, the current gets strong. Horse rides offered by villagers are negotiated politely.
natadola.season: May to October: dry season, moderate trade winds and an often crystal-clear lagoon.

around.d: A small sandy islet offered as a day trip from the coast.
A lively Coral Coast town with its fruit and vegetable market.

drawaqa.vibe: In the Yasawas, small fishing villages and bungalow resorts share roadless volcanic islands. Evening singing, kava and boat trips back and forth set the rhythm of life.
drawaqa.respect: Don’t touch the mantas or dive down onto them: stay at the surface, off to the side. To visit a village, bring kava as sevusevu.
drawaqa.season: May to October: manta ray season in the channel, drawn by plankton carried on the currents.

around.d: A large neighbouring volcanic island, with traditional villages and hills to climb.
An island with spectacular ridges, criss-crossed by trails to its summits.
A small rocky island in the southern Yasawas, popular for snorkelling.

tikehau.vibe: Around the village of Tuherahera, people live from copra and fishing: the lagoon’s stone fish parks feed the atoll. Deserted motu, pink sand and ukulele parties do the rest.
tikehau.respect: Dive the pass with the local club, on the incoming current. Don’t touch the fishers’ fish parks and don’t feed the sharks.
tikehau.season: April to November: drier season, moderate trade winds and excellent visibility in the pass.

iledespins.vibe: Land of the Kunié people, where outrigger canoes still glide across Upi Bay. Columnar pines, traditional huts and the remains of the penal colony where the Communards were deported tell a singular story.
food: Isle of Pines snails
The island’s big snails, served grilled with parsley butter in the small restaurants.
iledespins.respect: The path to the natural pool crosses customary land: stay on the trail, don’t walk on the coral and don’t pick anything up.
iledespins.season: September to December: fairly dry weather, warming water and clear light, before the cyclones.

jinek.vibe: On Lifou, life follows the custom of the chiefdoms: round huts, yam fields and vanilla grown by the tribe. At Easo, fishers and children share the bay with the turtles.
jinek.respect: The bay belongs to the Easo tribe: pay the access fee asked on site and never set foot on the coral.
jinek.season: September to December: drier weather, clear water and an often calm sea, before the cyclone season.

around.d: High limestone cliffs in the north of the island, with a plunging view over the lagoon.
A coastal village overlooked by a chapel perched on a panoramic headland.

amedee.vibe: The metal lighthouse, made in France and reassembled here piece by piece, watches over the Boulari Pass. At weekends, Nouméa locals arrive by boat to picnic and swim.
amedee.respect: The banded sea kraits, sea snakes very common on the islet, are venomous: watch them without touching. Fishing is forbidden in the reserve.
amedee.season: September to December: fairly dry weather, warming water and an often calm lagoon.

around.d: Fluorescent corals, nautiluses and New Caledonian lagoon fish shown in tanks.
Kanak and Oceanian collections: carvings, currencies and everyday objects.
Nouméa’s shady heart, with its bandstand and fountain.
A wooded hill by the lagoon, with views over the islets and the bay.
A small islet facing Anse Vata, with an underwater snorkelling trail.

champagnebeach.vibe: Coconut plantations, ni-Vanuatu villages and roadside stalls: Santo’s east coast keeps a slow pace, between copra, fishing from dugout canoes and family swims on Sundays.
champagnebeach.respect: The beach belongs to customary landowners: pay the entry fee requested and, if possible, avoid cruise-ship days.
champagnebeach.season: May to October: dry season, gentler heat and crystal-clear water.

around.d: A French-speaking village on a long beach, with islets you can reach on foot.
A neighbouring village on Santo’s east coast, between plantations and beaches.

bonegi.vibe: On Guadalcanal’s north coast, the remains of the Pacific War are part of the everyday landscape. Families swim on the black sand between two wrecks that have become reefs.
bonegi.respect: The wrecks are places of remembrance: take nothing away. An access fee is charged by the beach’s customary landowners.
bonegi.season: May to November: drier season, an often calm sea on the north coast and good visibility on the wrecks.

around.d: The capital’s big market for fish, fruit, vegetables and betel nut.
Traditional objects, shell money and the history of the archipelago.
The hill of a 1942 battle, with a memorial and views over the plain.

kimbe.vibe: Between forested volcanoes and oil palm plantations, the bay’s villages live from fishing by canoe. Divers come here for some of the richest reefs in the Coral Triangle.
kimbe.respect: On the pinnacles, keep your distance from gorgonians and sea fans, with no gloves and no contact. The dive fees paid to villages help protect the reefs.
kimbe.season: April to June and September to November: an often calm sea and excellent visibility on the pinnacles.

around.d: A volcanic peninsula with hot springs and a caldera lake at its tip.
A lively provincial capital with its market of local produce.

lalomanu.vibe: Village families run beach fale here, rebuilt after the 2009 tsunami. Shared meals, songs and fiafia nights keep fa’a Samoa, the Samoan way of life, alive.
lalomanu.respect: At dusk, respect sa, the evening prayer: lower your voice and don’t walk through the village. Ask before settling in front of a fale.
lalomanu.season: May to October: dry season, refreshing trade winds and an often crystal-clear lagoon.

around.d: A small island off the coast, with beach fale and a trail to the summit.
A remote village renowned for its woodcarvers and its protected forest.
Uninhabited volcanic islets off the eastern tip, rich in seabirds.

muri.vibe: On the Ngatangiia side, tradition holds that voyaging canoes set off from Avana for Aotearoa. Today, outrigger canoes, kites and Sunday barbecues share the lagoon.
muri.respect: Launch well away from swimmers and paddlers. Watch out for the current in the Avana passage, which can pull you towards the reef.
muri.season: May to October: steady south-easterly trade winds over the lagoon and drier weather.

around.d: A rocky spire in the heart of the island, a stop on the cross-island hike of Rarotonga.
A small capital by the harbour, with its Punanga Nui market on Saturdays.
A small museum on the culture, crafts and navigation of the Cook Islands.
Canoes, carvings and traditional objects from the archipelago’s different islands.

chuuk.vibe: Among the lagoon’s volcanic islands, Chuukese people live from fishing and their gardens. Kimiuo Aisek, a witness to the 1944 bombing, guided the first divers to the sunken fleet.
chuuk.respect: The wrecks are protected war graves: take nothing, and don’t touch human remains or munitions.
chuuk.season: December to April: drier season, a calm lagoon and good visibility on the wrecks.

around.d: The lagoon’s former Japanese headquarters, dotted with wartime remains.
Objects and stories from the Pacific War and the fleet sunk in the lagoon.
Tunnels dug into the hill on Weno, where Japanese guns remain.

yap.vibe: Yap keeps its customs: giant stone money lined up along the paths, men’s houses on stilts and traditional loincloths. Here, tradition comes before tourism.
yap.respect: Ask permission before entering a village or taking photos. Never touch the stone money and cover your thighs.
yap.season: December to April: dry season and the mantas’ mating display in the reef channels.

around.d: A traditional village with a men’s house, stone money and a beach.
Traditional houses, stone money and craft demonstrations.
A large traditional faluw with a thatched roof, built at the water’s edge.
A harbour islet linked to the 19th-century stone money trade.

germanchannel.vibe: Palauans have long practised bul, a system of fishing bans that inspired the protection of their waters. Painted bai, clans and wartime remains mark the archipelago.
germanchannel.respect: Reef-toxic sunscreens are banned in Palau: bring a mineral one. At the cleaning station, keep your distance from the mantas.
germanchannel.season: November to April: drier season, an often calm sea and excellent visibility.

around.d: Hundreds of forest-covered, mushroom-shaped limestone islets above a turquoise lagoon.
A marine lake filled with golden jellyfish, to explore with mask and snorkel.
A famous current-swept drop-off, frequented by sharks and schools of fish.
An island marked by a 1944 battle, with military remains and memorials.

lencois.vibe: In Barreirinhas, boats head down the Rio Preguiças to fishing villages, and rugged 4x4s take visitors into the dunes. In the evening, the squares come alive to the sound of forró.
food: Arroz de cuxá
Maranhão rice with vinagreira and dried shrimp, served with fish.
lencois.respect: Only enter the park with a licensed guide and leave no litter: the rainwater lagoons are fragile.
lencois.season: June to September: lagoons filled by the rains, with warm turquoise water.

abrolhos.vibe: Caravelas, a small fishing town on the edge of a mangrove, lives to the rhythm of the whales and the boats to the archipelago, which Darwin visited aboard the Beagle.
abrolhos.respect: Only Siriba Island can be visited on land, with the park rangers. Don’t touch the chapeirões and keep your distance from the whales.
abrolhos.season: December to March: an often calmer sea and good visibility; from July to November, it’s whale time.

ilhadomel.vibe: No cars, sandy trails and caiçara communities who still live from small-scale fishing. In the evening, forró echoes through the villages of Encantadas and Nova Brasília.
food: Barreado
Beef slow-cooked for hours in a sealed clay pot, a speciality of the Paraná coast.
ilhadomel.respect: The trails cross protected restinga: don’t stray from the paths and take your rubbish back to the mainland.
ilhadomel.season: April to September: more consistent southern swells and empty beaches, with cool water.

around.d: Paraná’s oldest town, with a colonial centre and the port the boats leave from.
Rocky islets offshore, seabird colonies and protected waters.

silveira.vibe: A coast of Azorean heritage where small-scale mullet (tainha) fishing still sets the rhythm of winter, and where southern right whales come to calve offshore while surfers watch for the southern swells.
food: Sequência de camarão
Shrimp served in several dishes one after another, a ritual of the Santa Catarina coast’s tables.
silveira.respect: During the tainha fishing season, some beaches close to surfing: respect the flags and leave room for the fishers’ nets.
silveira.season: April to September: more consistent southern swells, cool water (wetsuit) and less crowded line-ups than in summer.

around.d: A fishing village of Azorean origin on its bay, where whale-watching trips set off.
A port and wild beaches to the south, on the coast protected for southern right whales.
An isolated beach at the southern tip of Santa Catarina Island, reached by a forest trail.

guardaembau.vibe: A car-free surf village where you cross the river with your board under your arm: a bohemian vibe, fishers on the sandbar and the park’s Atlantic Forest tumbling down to the sand.
food: Florianópolis oysters
Farmed in the bays south of the island, eaten raw or gratinated.
guardaembau.respect: Cross the Rio da Madre where the current is weak, and at the river-mouth wave, wait your turn: the locals surf it every day.
guardaembau.season: April to August: well-lined-up southern swells on the river-mouth sandbanks and a quieter village than in summer.

around.d: A large park of Atlantic Forest, restinga and mountains, with trails and protected beaches.
A steep climb to a summit overlooking the bay and Florianópolis Island.
A wild beach in the south of Santa Catarina Island, reached by a forest trail.
A fishing village of Azorean origin, the starting point for watching southern right whales.

arpoador.vibe: Where Cariocas discovered surfing, the Arpoador rock gathers a crowd every evening that applauds the sunset behind the Dois Irmãos.
food: Biscoito Globo and mate gelado
Puffed cassava biscuits and iced mate tea, hawked on the sand.
arpoador.respect: The peak is crowded and has a pecking order: wait your turn, don’t take wave after wave and stay well away from the swimming zone.
arpoador.season: May to September: southern swells wrapping along the rock, milder air and fewer storms.

around.d: A cable car to the summit for views over Guanabara Bay and Rio’s beaches.
The summit of Christ the Redeemer, reached by a little train through the Tijuca Forest.
An avenue of imperial palms, greenhouses and rainforest at the foot of Corcovado.
A lagoon lined with a cycle path and kiosks, ringed by mountains.
A fort at the tip of Copacabana, with an army museum and cafés facing the sea.

taiba.vibe: A village where jangadas, the sail rafts of Ceará’s fishers, still come back onto the sand below ochre cliffs, while kites zip across the lagoon.
food: Baião de dois
Rice and beans mixed with coalho cheese, an iconic dish of Ceará cuisine.
taiba.respect: Give way to the jangadas heading out or coming back, and never rig your kite among the boats pulled up on the beach.
taiba.season: July to December: strong, steady trade winds, dry skies and constant heat, peaking from August to November.

barragrande.vibe: A sandy village on Piauí’s short coastline where kiters cross paths with crab fishers, and where you head out by boat into the mangroves in search of seahorses.
food: Caranguejo
Mangrove crab cooked in a spicy broth, cracked with a mallet at the barracas’ tables.
barragrande.respect: On seahorse trips, leave them in the water and don’t touch the mangrove; at low tide, ride well away from the nets.
barragrande.season: July to December: steady trade winds every afternoon and flat lagoons at low tide, perfect for learning.

around.d: A small neighbouring coastal town, between beaches, mangroves and the delta’s protected areas.
A mangrove-lined estuary to explore by boat, rich in birds and crabs.

guajiru.vibe: A Ceará fishing coast dotted with currais, wooden fish traps planted in the water, where a small kite community has settled facing the sand island.
food: Baião de dois
Rice and beans mixed with coalho cheese, an iconic dish of Ceará cuisine.
guajiru.respect: Spot the fishing currais and nets before you ride, and keep your lines well away from them: they are the village’s livelihood.
guajiru.season: July to December: strong, steady trade winds, flat water in the lagoon and skies that are almost always dry.

lagoaparaiso.vibe: A rainwater lagoon surrounded by dunes where life happens in the water: hammocks and tables just above the surface, barracas on the shore and kite sails in the afternoon.
food: Tapioca
A cassava-starch pancake filled with coalho cheese or coconut, sold all over Jijoca.
lagoaparaiso.respect: The hammocks in the water belong to the barracas: order something to use them, and leave nothing in the lagoon.
lagoaparaiso.season: July to November: the lagoon still full after the rains, dry skies and steady wind for kiting in the afternoon.

around.d: Dunes, lagoons and sculpted rocks like the Pedra Furada, to explore by buggy or on foot.
A village of sandy streets where you climb the big dune for sunset.

morrosp.vibe: A car-free village where luggage travels by wheelbarrow from the pier, between the ruins of a small fort, a lighthouse on the hill and numbered beaches where Bahian music plays late into the night.
food: Acarajé
A black-eyed-bean fritter fried in dendê oil, filled with shrimp and vatapá.
morrosp.respect: At low tide, don’t walk on the coral to get into the natural pools, and wear mineral sunscreen.
morrosp.season: September to March: dry season, calm sea and clear water in the natural pools at low tide.

around.d: Lanes, ruins of the colonial fort and a hilltop lighthouse with views over the beaches and the island.
An island of mangroves and coconut palms to discover by boat, with villages and deserted beaches.

praiadoforte.vibe: A former fishing village overlooked by the ruins of Garcia d’Ávila’s castle, now a stronghold of sea turtle protection, where the TAMAR base monitors nesting on the beaches.
food: Acarajé
A black-eyed-bean fritter fried in dendê oil, filled with shrimp and vatapá.
praiadoforte.respect: From September to March, the turtles nest: no torches or fires on the beach at night, and don’t go near the marked nests.
praiadoforte.season: September to March: dry season, calm sea and crystal-clear natural pools at low tide.

paraty.vibe: A port on the old gold route, with cobbled streets that the spring tides sometimes lap, surrounded by caiçara communities who still live from fishing and dugout canoes.
food: Azul-marinho
A caiçara stew of fish and green banana that turns bluish as it cooks.
paraty.respect: In the protected bays, drop anchor well away from the seagrass beds and take your rubbish back: the caiçara communities live from this sea.
paraty.season: April to October: drier season, calm water and light wind, away from the summer thunderstorms.

around.d: Cobbled streets, baroque churches and white colonial houses with colourful doors.
A narrow inlet lined with mangroves and mountains, to explore by kayak.
A wild peninsula of caiçara beaches linked by trails through the Atlantic Forest.

maresias.vibe: São Paulo’s weekend beach, between parties and Atlantic Forest, and a breeding ground for Brazilian surfing: Gabriel Medina grew up here, and the local kids train on the same sandbanks.
food: Azul-marinho
A caiçara stew of fish and green banana that turns bluish as it cooks.
maresias.respect: The rip currents are strong and the line-up very local: surf near the lifeguard towers and leave the waves to the regulars.
maresias.season: April to September: more powerful southern swells and a far less crowded beach than in summer.

around.d: A mountainous, forest-covered island with beaches, waterfalls and wrecks to explore.
Preserved Atlantic Forest, with trails to waterfalls and secluded beaches.
A small colonial historic centre facing the channel and the ferry to Ilhabela.
A long beach with calmer water, popular with families for swimming.

piramides.vibe: A village of sandy streets facing the gulf, living to the rhythm of southern right whales and sea lions: you head out to sea with fishers turned guides.
food: Patagonian lamb
Cordero slow-roasted on a cross by the embers, a speciality of Chubut’s estancias.
piramides.respect: A protected reserve: by kayak or when diving, keep your distance from whales and sea lions, and leave the approach to authorised boats.
piramides.season: December to March: the least cold water and playful sea lions; the whales are here from June to December.

nahuelhuapi.vibe: An Andean shore of wood and stone houses inherited from Swiss and German settlers, where you paddle facing snowy peaks before heading back to taste Bariloche chocolate.
food: Bariloche chocolate
Chocolate branches from the town’s chocolate shops, also to enjoy as hot chocolate.
nahuelhuapi.respect: The wind picks up fast and the water stays icy: set off in the morning, stick to the shore and wear a buoyancy aid even in calm weather.
nahuelhuapi.season: December to March: southern summer, often light wind in the morning and slightly less cold water for paddling.

around.d: Argentina’s oldest national park: lakes, coihue forests and mountain trails.
A cable car to a summit with a panoramic view over the lake and the Andes.
A stone-and-wood civic centre, chocolate shops and a lively lakefront.
A village of Swiss settlers, known for its craft fair and its curanto.
A smaller, sheltered lake at the foot of Cerro Catedral, with beaches and trails.

marmol.vibe: A land of ranchers and pioneers along the Carretera Austral, where the glacial lake has carved the marble into blue-veined vaults that you visit from a tiny village.
food: Cordero al palo
Patagonian lamb roasted on a spit in front of the fire, the festive dish of Aysén.
marmol.respect: Don’t touch or climb the fragile marble walls, and only go out by kayak with a guide: the lake’s wind shifts fast.
marmol.season: December to March: southern summer, a turquoise lake that is calmer early in the morning, before the wind picks up.

puntachoros.vibe: A caleta of loco and seaweed fishers at the gateway to the desert, now the base for boats heading out to see the reserve’s Humboldt penguins, marine otters and bottlenose dolphins.
puntachoros.respect: On Isla Damas, stay on the marked trails; Isla Choros can only be seen from the boat, landing there is forbidden.
puntachoros.season: December to March: a more manageable sea, slightly less cold water and regular crossings to the island.

around.d: A fishing village where whale- and dolphin-watching trips set off.
A rocky island in the reserve, with penguin and seabird colonies seen from the boat.

totoralillo.vibe: A fishing cove among rocks and cacti, where surfers from La Serena and Coquimbo come looking for the reef peaks when the swell arrives, facing surprisingly clear water.
food: Tongoy ostiones
Pacific scallops gratinated with parmesan, a speciality of the nearby caletas.
totoralillo.respect: The beach is small and popular in summer: take your rubbish with you, and on the reef peaks, let the locals have their waves.
totoralillo.season: April to September: more consistent south-westerly swells; in summer, an often calm, clear sea for swimming.

around.d: A huge concrete cross on a hill in Coquimbo, with a lookout over the bay.
A large sheltered bay, a sandy beach and a caleta where you eat fresh fish.
An iconic lighthouse at the end of Avenida del Mar, symbol of La Serena.
An Andalusian-Moroccan-style mosque with a minaret, a surprise on Coquimbo’s hill.

futaleufu.vibe: A town of wooden houses right by the Argentine border, where farmers, rafting guides and kayakers from all over the world meet around a turquoise river of rare power.
food: Cordero al palo
Patagonian lamb roasted on a spit in front of the fire, the festive dish of southern Chile.
