futaleufu.respect: Only run the rapids with a local guide and a safety kayaker: the class V sections leave no margin for error.
futaleufu.season: December to March: southern summer, favourable water levels, less icy water and long days on the river.

mompiche.vibe: A fishing village on the Afro-Ecuadorian coast of Esmeraldas, lulled by the marimba, where canoes come back onto the sand while surfers watch for the left at the end of the bay.
food: Encocado de pescado
Fish simmered in coconut milk, the emblem of Esmeraldas’ Afro-Ecuadorian cuisine.
mompiche.respect: The point-break left draws a crowd: respect priority, paddle out through the channel and watch out for the rocks at low tide.
mompiche.season: December to April: north-westerly swells that make the point peel, warm water and a lively beach.

around.d: Hills of tropical rainforest, rich in birds and howler monkeys.
A town on a mangrove island, with a long beach and fishing boats.

caboblanco.vibe: A fishing hamlet at the foot of desert cliffs, once famous for marlin fishing and its club where Hemingway stayed, now known for its legendary left-hand barrel.
food: Seco de chabelo
Green plantain and dried meat sautéed together, a typical dish of Piura.
caboblanco.respect: A shallow reef wave with a narrow peak: don’t paddle to the peak without the level for it, and give priority to the locals.
caboblanco.season: December to March: north-westerly swells and offshore wind in the morning, for the best barrels of the year.

pacasmayo.vibe: An old port in northern Peru with its long pier and republican-era houses, battered by the desert wind, where surfers come for a left that seems never to end.
food: Arroz con pato
Green rice with coriander and beer cooked with duck, a classic of northern Peru.
pacasmayo.respect: On such a long left, one surfer per wave: don’t steal priority by paddling back up around the point.
pacasmayo.season: April to October: southern swells that light up the point and often offshore wind in the morning.

around.d: A vast pre-Hispanic archaeological site of adobe pyramids, facing the ocean.
The malecón, the old iron pier and the colonial houses of the former port.

isladelaplata.vibe: A dry, wild island where blue-footed boobies and frigatebirds nest, reached from Puerto López, a fishing village that also lives to the rhythm of the humpback whales of the southern winter.
food: Viche de pescado
A Manabí soup of fish, peanut, green plantain and corn, very filling.
isladelaplata.respect: Stay on the trails with the Machalilla park guide, don’t go near the nests and never put your fins on the coral.
isladelaplata.season: December to April: warmer, clearer water; from June to September, humpback whales during the crossing.

tortugabay.vibe: At the end of a trail lined with opuntia cacti, a beach where marine iguanas, reef sharks and pelicans share the water with Puerto Ayora locals who come for a swim after work.
food: Pescado brujo
A local Galápagos fish served fried or as encocado at the kiosks of Puerto Ayora.
tortugabay.respect: Only swim at Playa Mansa, as the main beach has strong currents; let the iguanas pass and respect the park’s opening hours.
tortugabay.season: December to May: warm season, milder water and a calm sea, ideal for swimming and paddling in the cove.

around.d: Highlands where giant tortoises roam free, lava tunnels and twin craters.
A small port town, with its fish market frequented by sea lions and pelicans.
Santa Cruz’s natural harbour, home to the Charles Darwin Research Station.

puntacarola.vibe: The beach of the Galápagos capital’s residents, where sea lions sleep on the sand, frigatebirds circle above the hill and a small crew of surfers watches the reef.
food: Pescado brujo
A local Galápagos fish served fried or as encocado in the port’s restaurants.
puntacarola.respect: Sea lions share the beach and the water: keep two metres away and never pass between a mother and her pup.
puntacarola.season: December to April: northern swells that wake up the reef, warmer water and good visibility.

around.d: A freshwater crater lake in the highlands, where frigatebirds come to bathe.
A lively malecón where sea lions take over the benches and the docks.
The easternmost island: Kicker Rock, sea lion beaches and a giant tortoise reserve.

rosario.vibe: A string of coral islets home to Afro-Caribbean fishing communities, between mangroves, boats from Cartagena and little houses on the water.
food: Cocadas
Coconut sweets sold by Cartagena’s palenqueras and on the beaches.
rosario.respect: Never stand on the coral, use mineral sunscreen and buy fish and crafts from the islanders.
rosario.season: December to April: dry season and clear water, even if the trade winds sometimes make the crossing choppy.

providencia.vibe: A Raizal island that has stayed away from mass tourism: colourful wooden houses, English creole, reggae and small-scale fishing around a lagoon of a thousand shades of blue.
food: Rondón
A stew of fish, conch and root vegetables simmered in coconut milk, a Raizal dish.
providencia.respect: Stay in the navigation lanes on the lagoon and never walk on the reef: it lies at the heart of the Seaflower reserve.
providencia.season: February to May: dry season, gentler trade winds and the best visibility on the reef.

around.n: Old Providence McBean Lagoon National Park
around.d: Mangroves, lagoon and Crab Cay, where you snorkel among reef fish.
An islet linked by a floating bridge, with remains of small forts and the Morgan’s Head rock.

malpelo.vibe: A bare volcanic rock pounded by the Pacific, uninhabited apart from a small military post: here, life is underwater, in schools of sharks as far as the eye can see.
malpelo.respect: Landing is forbidden without a permit. Underwater, stay with your group, with no gloves and no contact, and let the sharks come to you without chasing them.
malpelo.season: January to April for a calmer sea; June to November for silky sharks and sometimes the whale shark.

capurgana.vibe: A car-free Afro-Colombian village where you get around on foot or on horseback between jungle and coves, and where life follows the arrival of the lanchas from Necoclí and Turbo.
capurgana.respect: The village has no reliable cash machine: bring cash. To walk to La Miel, on the Panamanian side, keep your passport on you.
capurgana.season: December to April: dry season, fewer downpours over the jungle, but a sometimes rough lancha crossing.

cabopolonio.vibe: A hamlet of fishers’ and artists’ shacks with no grid electricity, where the lighthouse beam sweeps the dunes at night and where sea lions were once hunted.
food: Buñuelos de algas
Fried seaweed fritters, the speciality of the shacks on the Rocha coast.
cabopolonio.respect: Keep your distance from the sea lions at the foot of the lighthouse and stay on the trails: the park’s dunes are protected.
cabopolonio.season: March to June: more consistent southern swells, water still mild at first and a village returned to calm.

around.d: A lighthouse on the rocky point, with views over the islands and the sea lion colony.
A small, rustic seaside village of shacks on a long beach of the Rocha coast.

marialagorda.vibe: A Cuban land’s end beyond the tobacco fields of Pinar del Río, named after a pirate legend, with only a handful of buildings for a village, facing the drop-offs.
marialagorda.respect: You are in Guanahacabibes National Park: take away no coral or shells, and leave the turtles that nest in summer in peace.
marialagorda.season: November to April: dry season, a glassy sea in the bay and good visibility, away from the cyclones.

jardinesreina.vibe: A maze of cays and mangroves named in honour of the Queen of Spain, kept almost untouched thanks to strict protection and the complete absence of any village.
jardinesreina.respect: Don’t feed the mangrove crocodiles or the sharks, and take nothing away: corals and shells stay in the park.
jardinesreina.season: November to April: dry season, a calmer sea for outings and a cyclone-free period.

puntaperdiz.vibe: A stretch of the Zapata Swamp coast marked by the 1961 landing, with memorial stones along the road, between marshes, crystal-clear sinkholes and fishing villages.
puntaperdiz.respect: In spring, thousands of crabs cross the coast road: drive slowly. Enter the water via the designated access points.
puntaperdiz.season: November to April: dry season, a calm sea on the bay and fewer mosquitoes from the marshes.

negril.vibe: A former fishing village turned hippie hideaway and then beach resort, where reggae drifts out of the beach bars and everyone gathers on the cliffs for sunset.
negril.respect: With beach vendors, a smiling “no thanks” is enough. Before jumping off the cliffs, watch the locals and check the depth.
negril.season: December to April: dry season, calm, clear sea, away from the hurricane season.

around.d: A white late-19th-century lighthouse on the cliffs of the island’s western point.
A cove in the West End cliffs, riddled with caves and passages over clear water.

bostonbay.vibe: A green, rainy corner of Portland parish, where smoke from the jerk pits rises by the roadside and the village kids learn to ride waves in the little bay.
food: Boston jerk pork
Pork marinated in chilli and smoked over pimento wood, in the roadside shacks.
bostonbay.respect: The line-up is tiny and very local: say hello, wait your turn and rent your board from the guys on the beach.
bostonbay.season: December to March: more consistent north-easterly swells and a drier season on the coast.

around.n: Blue and John Crow Mountains National Park
around.d: UNESCO-listed mountain forests, trails and Blue Mountain coffee plantations.
A peaceful trip down the river on a bamboo raft steered by a raftsman.
A banana port with twin bays, a market, old houses and a laid-back feel.
A public beach dear to Jamaicans, with grilled-fish shacks and calm water.
A wide, wild crescent of white sand on the east coast, lined with coconut palms.

catalina_do.vibe: Off a town born from sugar cane, the uninhabited island welcomes the boats of Bayahíbe’s fishers, now turned ferrymen to the reef, every day.
catalina_do.respect: Never stand on the Aquarium reef, choose a mineral sunscreen and avoid the times when the big catamarans arrive.
catalina_do.season: December to April: dry season, calm sea and good visibility, away from the hurricanes.

around.d: A fishing village where boats leave for the islands and East National Park.
A river carved deep into the jungle, admired from the village of Altos de Chavón.

playarincon.vibe: A coconut-palm peninsula partly settled by descendants of freed African Americans, where cooking is done with coconut milk and whales come to calve in winter.
food: Pescado con coco
Fish simmered in a coconut-milk sauce, the signature dish of the Samaná peninsula.
playarincon.respect: For grilled fish on the beach, agree the price before it’s cooked. Take your rubbish back: there are hardly any bins.
playarincon.season: February to April: drier season, calm sea and humpback whales still present in Samaná Bay.

around.d: A fishing village at the end of the peninsula, the starting point for the wild beaches.
A small port town where humpback whale-watching trips set off.
A white-sand islet in the middle of Samaná Bay, for a quiet swim.

jobos.vibe: A north-west coast nicknamed the island’s surfers’ corner, where Puerto Rican families come at weekends and the chiringuitos serve alcapurrias and cold beers facing the right-hander.
jobos.respect: The right breaks over a shallow reef and a current pulls out to sea: give priority to the locals and swim in the sheltered part.
jobos.season: November to March: consistent northern Atlantic swells and trade winds that are often calm in the morning.

around.d: A blowhole in the coastal rock, linked to the legend of a farmer and his cow.
An old railway tunnel on the edge of the cliffs, with a lookout over the Atlantic.
Ruins of the old Spanish lighthouse and the current lighthouse at the island’s north-west tip.
A planters’ mansion turned house museum, amid former cane fields.

flamenco.vibe: An island municipality that got the US Navy to leave after years of protest, still peaceful with its rental jeeps, its little town of Dewey and its turtle bays.
flamenco.respect: Turtles nest on the island’s beaches: don’t walk on marked nests and avoid any light on the sand at night.
flamenco.season: April to August: winter swells are over, and the water is calm and clear at the head of the bay; avoid long weekends.

around.d: Wild islet with natural pools, beaches and a lighthouse from the Spanish era.
Protected islet reached by kayak or water taxi, for snorkelling among turtles.
Refuge for seabirds and nesting beaches, spread across the island and its cays.
The island’s little town, with its ferry port, colourful houses and restaurants.

mosquitobay.vibe: An island long occupied by the US Navy and handed back to its residents in the early 2000s, where free-roaming horses wander between the villages and still-wild beaches.
mosquitobay.respect: Swimming is forbidden in the bay: no sunscreen or insect repellent on your skin before the trip, and no flash.
mosquitobay.season: All year round, but pick a night close to the new moon: without moonlight, the blue glow stands out far better.

around.d: Former military land turned into a refuge, with wild beaches and lagoons.
Long beach on the south coast, with turquoise water and an islet you can swim to.
The last Spanish fort built in the Americas, now a museum of the island’s history.
Small coastal village with a lively malecón, the starting point for kayak trips.

thebaths.vibe: On the island Columbus is said to have named “the fat virgin” for its outline, charter yachts anchor off the boulders and locals live to the rhythm of the sea.
thebaths.respect: Arrive early, before the cruise-ship excursions, and give up on swimming if the red flag warns of swell.
thebaths.season: April to July: winter swells have eased, the sea is calm between the rocks and there are fewer people.

around.d: Stone ruins of a 19th-century copper mine, perched above the waves.
Protected islet with granite boulders like those at the Baths, explored by boat.
The island’s town, with its marina, small eateries and market.
Rainforest trails up to the highest peak in the islands, on Tortola.

rhone.vibe: In the heart of the charter-yacht archipelago, the wreck made famous by the film The Deep tells of the hurricanes that have always shaped life on these islands.
rhone.respect: Take nothing from the wreck, not even a scrap of copper: moor to the park buoys and don’t touch the corals covering it.
rhone.season: March to July: the sea is often calm, visibility good and the water warm, before the peak of hurricane season.

around.d: Islet with natural salt ponds, where salt was once harvested, and the Rhone’s graveyard.
Small, quiet island with a beach, snorkelling and a popular stop for yachts.
Wild islet linked to the pirate song “Fifteen men on a dead man’s chest”.
Rainforest trails up to the highest peak in the islands, on Tortola.

trunkbay.vibe: An island two-thirds protected since Laurance Rockefeller’s gift of land, where the ruins of Danish sugar mills sleep under the forest above the bays.
trunkbay.respect: On the underwater trail, stay at the surface without resting on the coral, and pay your park entry fee when you arrive.
trunkbay.season: April to July: calm sea on the north coast, clear water and the winter crowds gone home.

around.d: Coastal trails, sheltered bays and dry forest over most of the island.
Ruins of a sugar mill at the end of a trail that passes Taíno petroglyphs.
Remains of a beachside Danish plantation, with a short waymarked trail.
Bohemian hamlet in the east of the island, with its sailors’ bars and sheltered bay.

carlislebay.vibe: Below the UNESCO-listed capital, racehorses from the Garrison sometimes come down for a morning swim and yachts anchor above the wrecks.
carlislebay.respect: Swim with the turtles without touching or feeding them, and stay within the marked areas: boats and jet skis cross the bay.
carlislebay.season: December to May: dry season, a glassy sea in the bay and great visibility over the wrecks.

around.d: Former British garrison listed by UNESCO, with its racecourse.
Colonial capital with its neo-Gothic Parliament, markets and rum shops.
One of the oldest synagogues in the Americas, with a museum and ritual bath.
House where the young George Washington stayed, now a small museum.

tobagocays.vibe: A yacht anchorage where the boat boys paddle out to sell fruit and bread, and where lobster is grilled in the evening on the beach at Petit Bateau.
tobagocays.respect: Bargain politely with the boat boys before buying anything, and never stand on Horseshoe Reef, which shelters the islets.
tobagocays.season: December to June: dry season, steady trade winds and clear water on the reef, before the hurricanes.

around.d: Tiny inhabited island, with its hilltop village, its church and Salt Whistle Bay.
Mountainous island with the port of Clifton, a base for boats to the cays and a kitesurfing spot.

moliniere.vibe: On the Spice Island, among the fishing villages of the west coast and the scent of nutmeg, the underwater statues tell Caribbean history as they slowly become covered in coral.
moliniere.respect: Don’t stand on the statues or touch them: the coral colonising them is fragile and part of the artwork.
moliniere.season: January to May: dry season, calm sea on the leeward coast and the best visibility.

around.d: 18th-century fort perched above the harbour, with views over the Carenage.
Small museum in an old colonial building, on the island’s history and spices.
Stone cathedral overlooking St George’s, restored after Hurricane Ivan.

champagnereef.vibe: A volcanic island that has stayed green and lightly built, where people speak Kwéyòl, where the Kalinago live and where the earth’s heat escapes even under the sea.
champagnereef.respect: Enter from the pebble beach without trampling the sponges, and stay above the bubbles without touching the bottom.
champagnereef.season: February to May: dry season, calm sea on the leeward coast and maximum visibility.

around.d: Fishing village at the end of an isthmus between the Atlantic and the Caribbean Sea.
Village with sulphurous hot springs, where you can bathe in natural pools.
Village in the Roseau Valley, the gateway to the twin Trafalgar Falls.
Colonial garden at the foot of the hills, with tropical trees and endemic parrots.
Former market square in the heart of the capital, with craft stalls.

ansechastanet.vibe: At the foot of the Pitons, around the island’s former French capital, people speak Kwéyòl, live from fishing and farming, and the earth still steams at the sulphur springs.
ansechastanet.respect: Swim in the marked zone off the beach: dive boats manoeuvre right next to the reef.
ansechastanet.season: February to May: dry season, calm sea in the lee of the Pitons and good visibility on the drop-off.

around.d: Two UNESCO-listed volcanic peaks; the guided climb of Gros Piton is superb.
Steaming geothermal field and hot mud pools where you can bathe.
Tropical garden around the Diamond waterfall and its old mineral baths.
Colourful little town on the bay, with its church and fishermen’s market.
Small neighbouring beach of dark sand, lined by a former plantation.

thousandsteps.vibe: An island where shore diving is a way of life: yellow stones mark the sites along the coast road, among pink salt pans, flamingos and cacti.
food: Stoba di kabritu
Goat stew slow-cooked with spices, a classic of Bonaire’s kitchens.
thousandsteps.respect: Don’t leave anything valuable in your car at the car park, and take the steps down carefully with your tank on your back.
thousandsteps.season: All year round: warm water, remarkable visibility and an island generally spared by hurricanes.

around.d: The island’s wild north, with dirt tracks, flamingo lagoons and snorkelling coves.
The island’s oldest village, with colourful houses nestled in a valley.
Pink salt flats, salt pyramids and flamingos in the south of the island.
Small capital with a colourful seafront, cafés, a fort and shops.

deansbluehole.vibe: A rural, peaceful island where people live from fishing and small-scale farming, and where the white churches built by Father Jerome watch over Clarence Town.
deansbluehole.respect: Never freedive alone, and give space to the freedivers training on the lines above the hole.
deansbluehole.season: April to June: very calm sea in the bay, water already warm, before hurricane season.

smithsreef.vibe: Around Turtle Cove, Provo’s small historic marina, local life still revolves around conch, caught, cooked into fritters and salads, and the boats that speed off to the cays.
smithsreef.respect: Keep clear of the Turtle Cove entrance channel, used by boats, and never stand on the coral heads.
smithsreef.season: April to June: the sea is often calm, the water warm and visibility good, before hurricane season begins.

bloodybay.vibe: On Little Cayman, the smallest and quietest of the three islands, the day revolves around the dive boats; on the roads, iguanas have right of way.
bloodybay.respect: Moor only to the marine park buoys, control your buoyancy along the wall and touch neither sponges nor corals.
bloodybay.season: April to October: the north coast is generally calm and visibility excellent; in winter, northerly gales can close the site.

around.d: Protected lagoon home to a large colony of red-footed boobies and frigatebirds.
Hull of Donald Crowhurst’s trimaran, beached on Cayman Brac after a solo race.

losislotes.vibe: From the La Paz malecón, pangas set off every morning for the desert islands of the gulf; here, the Sea of Cortez is lived between small-scale fishing and encounters with sea lions.
losislotes.respect: Let the sea lions come to you without touching or chasing them, and stay well away from the rocks where the males defend their territory.
losislotes.season: September to November: the water is still warm, the young sea lions playful and the sea calm before the winter northerlies.

around.d: Protected desert island with turquoise coves and red cliffs, ideal by kayak.
Espíritu Santo’s neighbour, separated by a shallow channel, with beaches and sheltered anchorages.

grancenote.vibe: For the Maya, cenotes were both the only water sources in a Yucatán without rivers and gateways to the underworld; today Tulum lives between ruins, jungle and cave diving.
food: Cochinita pibil
Pork marinated in annatto and bitter orange, slow-cooked and served in tacos.
grancenote.respect: Shower before getting in the water, with no sunscreen or repellent, and touch neither the stalactites nor the turtles that live in the pool.
grancenote.season: All year round, the water stays cool and crystal clear; come early in the morning, outside the winter holidays, to avoid the crowds.

around.d: Fortified Maya city perched on a cliff facing the Caribbean Sea.
Wild strip between lagoons and sea, in the Sian Ka’an Biosphere Reserve.

barradelacruz.vibe: A village of fishers and farmers on the Oaxaca coast, Barra de la Cruz chose to manage its own beach: no concrete, a few palapas and a right-hander that made its name.
food: Tlayuda
Large crispy tortilla topped with beans, quesillo and meat, an emblem of Oaxaca.
barradelacruz.respect: The beach is run by the community: pay the access fee at the entrance and give priority to the village surfers at the peak.
barradelacruz.season: May to September: south swells get the right-hander peeling, especially in the morning before the breeze.

around.d: River run by raft, which meets the sea near Huatulco.
The lively heart of Huatulco, with its zócalo, church and small restaurants.

loreto.vibe: The first capital of the Californias, Loreto keeps its stone mission and quiet streets; across from the malecón, the islands of the marine park draw fishers, kayakers and, in winter, whales.
food: Almejas chocolatas
Brown-shelled clams from the bay, often roasted under embers, known as tatemadas.
loreto.respect: The marine park requires an access wristband: get it before you set off, don’t fish without a permit and keep your distance from the sea lions.
loreto.season: October to May: mild temperatures; watch for days without the north wind, common in winter, to cross to the islands.

around.n: Mission of Our Lady of Loreto
around.d: The first Jesuit mission in the Californias, founded in 1697, with a small museum next door.
Remains of the short-lived first Jesuit settlement on the coast, north of Loreto.

bacalar.vibe: A former Spanish stronghold against pirates, Bacalar lives to the slow rhythm of its lagoon, among wooden jetties, balnearios and stromatolites, some of the oldest forms of life.
food: Cochinita pibil
Pork marinated in annatto and bitter orange, slow-cooked and served in tacos.
bacalar.respect: Don’t walk on or touch the stromatolites: these living formations are fragile. Swim without sunscreen.
bacalar.season: November to April: the dry season and clear skies bring out the lagoon’s shades of blue.

around.d: Village on the lagoon shore, overlooked by the San Felipe fort and its museum.
Capital of Quintana Roo, with its bayfront and its museum of Maya culture.

santamaria.vibe: Between two resorts, this cove recalls the Baja California of old: cactus desert plunging into a turquoise sea and pelicans skimming the rocks.
santamaria.respect: The bay is a protected area: no fishing or collecting, and stay in the marked swimming area, away from the boats.
santamaria.season: June to November: warm water and good visibility, but keep an eye on hurricane alerts in late summer.

around.d: Lively town at the tip of the peninsula, the departure point for boats to El Arco.

around.n: Cabo San Lucas Natural History Museum
around.d: Small museum on the wildlife, plants and fossils of the Cape region.

atitlan.vibe: Around the lake, each Maya village keeps its own language and dress; in San Marcos, fishermen in wooden cayucos cross paths with yoga lovers who have come in search of calm.
food: Patín
Small lake fish cooked in a spicy tomato sauce, wrapped in leaves.
atitlan.respect: In San Marcos, keep a low profile in the Maya village, cover up out of the water and use the jetties or the reserve to swim.
atitlan.season: November to April: dry season; paddle in the morning, before the Xocomil, the afternoon wind, whips up waves.

around.d: Large Tz’utujil town, with its market, colonial church and the cult of Maximón.
Village of weaving cooperatives using natural dyes, with painted streets.
Guided climb through coffee fields to a bird’s-eye view of the lake.
Gateway to the lake, with its craft market and boats to the villages.

elparedon.vibe: A black-sand village at the end of a road lined with plantations, El Paredón lives between fishing from small boats, the nearby mangroves and a small surf scene that has stayed simple.
elparedon.respect: Make room for the fishermen hauling in their boats and respect the sea turtle nests; the black sand burns at midday, so keep your sandals on.
elparedon.season: March to October: regular south swells; surf early in the morning, before the wind picks up.

around.d: Mangroves and channels to explore by boat or kayak, rich in birdlife.
Neighbouring seaside town, another base for surfers on the Pacific coast.

eltunco.vibe: A former fishing hamlet turned El Salvador’s surfer hangout, El Tunco comes alive at night around its beach bars, while cobblestone peaks line up along the coast.
eltunco.respect: On the cobblestone peaks, watch out for sea urchins and let everyone take their turn, especially at Sunzal, where the line-up fills up fast.
eltunco.season: March to October: regular South Pacific swells and offshore winds in the morning, in water that’s warm all year round.

around.d: Neighbouring surf village, with its right-hander over rock and its laid-back feel.
Port town with a fishing pier where you can buy fish and seafood.
Hill village known for its waterfalls, reached on a guided hike.

lasflores.vibe: In eastern El Salvador, far from the bustle of La Libertad, the fishermen of El Cuco and a few surfers share a coast that is still rural and lined with coconut palms.
lasflores.respect: On this point break, don’t paddle into the surfers’ path: go round via the channel and respect priority at the peak.
lasflores.season: March to October: south swells get the right-hander peeling along its full length, in warm water.

utila.vibe: An island of English-speaking islanders with Caribbean roots, Utila has become a haven for trainee divers; on the Utila Cays, fishermen’s houses crowd onto tiny islets.
food: Coconut bread
Soft bread made with coconut milk, an Anglo-Caribbean legacy of the Bay Islands.
utila.respect: With whale sharks, don’t touch them, no flash, and slip into the water calmly, at a distance, following the boat’s instructions.
utila.season: March to September: calmer sea and good visibility, with peak whale shark sightings in spring.

maderas.vibe: Once a stop on the gold-seekers’ route between the two oceans, the bay of San Juan del Sur mixes fishing boats, surfing and lively nights; Maderas is its wild beach.
maderas.respect: At the peak, give priority to the locals and avoid paddling through the many surf school students in the inside.
maderas.season: April to October: regular South Pacific swells and morning offshore winds blowing across from Lake Nicaragua.

around.d: Fishing town at the head of a curved bay, with its market and wooden houses.
Giant statue on the hill, with a wide view over the bay of San Juan del Sur.

apoyo.vibe: Around the crater, the “pueblos blancos” live from pottery, plant nurseries and crafts; down below, the warm lake is shared by swimmers, howler monkeys and birds.
food: Vigorón
Yuca, chicharrón and cabbage salad served on a banana leaf, a Granada speciality.
apoyo.respect: In the reserve, no soap or greasy cream in the lake, and carry your rubbish back up: the wooded shore is home to monkeys and birds.
apoyo.season: December to April: dry season, clear and warm water; late in the day, the breeze can ripple the surface.

around.d: Colonial city with colourful façades, churches and horse-drawn carriages on the shore of Lake Nicaragua.
Active volcano whose crater sometimes reveals a glowing lava lake.
Village of plant nurseries with a mirador looking straight down on the lagoon.
Archipelago of volcanic islets in Lake Nicaragua, to explore by boat.
Potters’ village where you can visit workshops making decorated ceramics.

isladelcoco.vibe: Only park rangers live on this island covered in forest and waterfalls, which has fuelled legends of pirate treasure; here, everything happens from the boat.
isladelcoco.respect: Stay with your dive group, don’t touch or chase the sharks, and only land on the island with the park rangers’ permission.
isladelcoco.season: June to November: rainy season, nutrient-rich water and larger schools of hammerheads; calmer sea from December to May.

bahiasalinas.vibe: In this corner of Guanacaste near Nicaragua, the sabanero culture of the cattle ranches sits alongside a handful of kite schools, and the papagayo wind sets the rhythm of the dry season.
food: Rosquillas
Small crunchy rings of corn and cheese, a traditional Guanacaste snack.
bahiasalinas.respect: Leave the beach free for swimmers when rigging and launching, and sail well away from the fishing boats at anchor.
bahiasalinas.season: December to April: a strong, steady papagayo wind through the dry season, over water that’s often flat in the bay.

around.d: Tropical dry forest, trails and the historic La Casona hacienda.
Small protected bay with calm water, for swimming and snorkelling.
Forest corridor climbing from dry forest to the slopes of the volcanoes.

salsabrava.vibe: Puerto Viejo carries the Afro-Caribbean heritage of the Limón coast: English creole, calypso, coconut-milk cooking and local surfers proud of their reef.
food: Rice and beans
Rice and red beans cooked in coconut milk, a pillar of local Caribbean cooking.
salsabrava.respect: Salsa Brava is a locals’ wave over a very shallow reef: if you don’t have the level, watch from the beach and never drop in.
salsabrava.season: December to March: Caribbean winter swells get the reef working, with a possible second window in June and July.

around.d: Rainforest, wild beaches and reefs all the way to the Panamanian border.
Caribbean village and its coastal national park, with a forest trail and coral reef.
Rehabilitation centre for wild animals, open for guided visits.
Indigenous community offering guided walks in the rainforest.

santacatalina.vibe: Long isolated at the end of a dirt track, this fishing village in Veraguas made its name with its wave, then with the boats that head out to explore the islands of Coiba.
santacatalina.respect: The point breaks over volcanic rock: work out the way in and out before you go, and respect the locals at the peak.
santacatalina.season: April to October: the most regular South Pacific swells, which wake up the point.

coiba.vibe: Long home to a penal colony, Coiba stayed out of reach of people and industrial fishing; today only park rangers live there, and boats come over from Santa Catalina.
coiba.respect: In the park, no fishing or collecting, no chemical sunscreen, and register at the ranger station before landing.
coiba.season: December to April: dry season and an often calmer sea for the long boat crossing from the coast.

sanblas.vibe: An autonomous territory of the Guna people, the archipelago lives from fishing, coconut palms and the craft of molas, the layered embroidery that women wear every day.
food: Tule masi
Guna stew of fish, plantain and coconut milk, cooked over a wood fire.
sanblas.respect: Each island belongs to a community: pay the access fees, don’t pick coconuts and ask before taking any photo.
sanblas.season: March to June: the trade winds ease, the sea is calmer for crossings and the water crystal clear over the reefs.

around.d: Densely populated Guna island, with lanes of bamboo houses and a small cultural museum.
Islets of sand and coconut palms in turquoise water, sheltered by a reef.

holchan.vibe: A former lobster-fishing village, San Pedro is explored by golf cart; people switch constantly between Spanish, Kriol and English, between trips out to the barrier reef.
holchan.respect: Don’t touch the nurse sharks or rays at Shark Ray Alley, even when they come close, and follow your guide, who is compulsory in the reserve.
holchan.season: April to June: the sea is often calm, trade winds moderate and visibility good before the rainy season.

around.d: Small car-free island with a slow pace, and its swimming channel, The Split.
Colourful town on Ambergris Caye, with sandy streets, seafood restaurants and piers.
Shallow coral heads in the north of the island, ideal for snorkelling.

sandharbor.vibe: Ancestral land of the Washoe, the lake later supplied timber for the Comstock silver mines; its Nevada shore is still wooded, scattered with granite boulders and lightly built.
sandharbor.respect: Clean, drain and dry your paddleboard or kayak before launching so you don’t introduce invasive species, and arrive early: the car park fills up fast.
sandharbor.season: July to September: the least cold water and windless mornings; paddle early, before the afternoon breeze.

around.d: 1930s stone mansion on the lakeshore, open for guided tours.
Summit in the Carson Range, a day hike with views over the lake and the desert.
Small mountain lake, the start of the famous Flume Trail above Lake Tahoe.
Housed in the old mint, it tells the story of Nevada’s mining, nature and history.

crystalriver.vibe: A small town that has stayed very “Old Florida”, Crystal River lives from fishing and the summer scallop harvest; in winter, manatees swim upriver in search of the springs’ warmth.
crystalriver.respect: Watch the manatees without touching or chasing them, float at the surface without kicking hard and never enter the marked sanctuary areas.
crystalriver.season: November to March: manatees gather in the warm springs of Kings Bay as soon as the Gulf cools down.

around.d: Mounds and shell middens left by pre-Columbian Native American peoples.
Spring where you can see manatees and Florida wildlife, with an underwater observatory.
Salt marshes and riverside trails, rich in coastal birds.
Remains of a 19th-century plantation sugar mill, in stone and cast iron.

ginnie.vibe: In the heart of north Florida, a land of cypress trees and springs, the banks of the Santa Fe draw families on inner tubes as well as cave divers from all over the world who come to explore the flooded passages.
ginnie.respect: Never enter the caves without a cave-diving certification: these caverns have already killed divers. In the pools, avoid stirring up the sand to keep the water clear.
ginnie.season: April to May and September to October: the water stays at 22 °C all year round, the air is mild and the summer crowds are gone.

around.d: Crystal-clear spring-fed river to float down on an inner tube or by kayak under the cypresses.
Turquoise spring in a wooded park on the Santa Fe, ideal for a swim.
Forest trails where the Santa Fe disappears underground before resurfacing further on.
Small railway town with old shopfronts, antique shops and dive stores.

scorpionanchorage.vibe: Santa Cruz is the Limuw of the Chumash, whose plank canoes sometimes come back to land here; at Scorpion, the old ranch buildings recall sheep farming, on an island with no shops at all.
scorpionanchorage.respect: Store your food in the campground’s fox-proof boxes: the island fox is protected. You are in a national park with no services, so take all your rubbish back on the boat.
scorpionanchorage.season: August to October: the warmest water of the year, a sea that’s often calm in the morning and good visibility in the kelp.

around.d: Trails to Cavern Point and Potato Harbor, with the island’s endemic scrub-jay along the way.
Volcanic islet with gull-covered cliffs, famous for its Arch Rock.
Protected kelp forests where garibaldi, sea lions and sometimes dolphins cruise by.
White lighthouse perched on the island, watching over the entrance to the Santa Barbara Channel.

shortsands.vibe: The park is named after the governor who made Oregon’s beaches public; you walk down a trail under the spruces, board under your arm, to surf cold water in a thick wetsuit.
food: Clam chowder and Tillamook cheddar
Creamy clam soup and cheese from the nearby Tillamook creamery.
shortsands.respect: Parking along the 101 fills up fast: never park outside the marked spaces. The line-up is packed, so wait your turn and beware of currents near the rocks.
shortsands.season: September to November: clean autumn swells, wind more often calm in the morning and fewer people than in summer.

around.d: Wooded cliffs and coastal viewpoints, with trails down to wild coves.
Switchback hike to a summit overlooking the ocean and Nehalem Bay.
Village of galleries facing Haystack Rock, a huge rock teeming with seabirds.
Beach with a waterfall and caves, and an old road cut into the rock at low tide.
Sand spit between ocean and bay, great for walks and seal watching.

sanjuanpark.vibe: A border island known for the “Pig War” between the British and the Americans, San Juan lives to the rhythm of the ferries and the resident orcas, which locals recognise one by one.
sanjuanpark.respect: Keep your distance from the orcas, the law is strict: never cut across their path. Haro Strait has strong currents and icy water, so check the tides before setting off.
sanjuanpark.season: June to September: calmer sea in the morning, long days and the best chance of meeting orcas along the west coast.

around.d: Small lighthouse on the rocks, one of the best spots for watching orcas from shore.
Museum dedicated to the orcas of the Salish Sea and their families.
Ferry port with wooden houses, a marina and small seafood restaurants.
The British and American camps of the Pig War, with meadows and farms along the roads.

molokini.vibe: A crescent-shaped islet that Hawaiian legends link to the goddess Pele, Molokini long served as a navy target before becoming a sanctuary; every morning, a flotilla sets off from Māʻalaea and Kihei.
food: Poke
Cubes of raw tuna marinated in soy sauce and sesame oil, sold by weight.
molokini.respect: Boats moor to buoys, never on the reef. Don’t touch the coral, don’t feed the fish and use mineral sunscreen, as required by Hawaiian law.
molokini.season: May to September: weaker trade winds in the morning, a calm sea inside the crater and visibility that’s often exceptional.

around.d: Black lava flow and protected reef coves, to explore with a mask.
Big Beach, a long golden beach at the foot of the Puʻu Ōlaʻi volcanic cone.
Bay of raw lava at the end of the road, the start of a trail along the old King’s Highway.
Aquarium devoted to Hawaiian reefs, with a tunnel under a large tank.
Coastal wetland for watching Hawaiian stilts and migratory birds.

honolua.vibe: A lush valley and a bay sacred to Hawaiian surfers, Honolua long rallied residents against property developments; in winter, the point gathers Maui’s best surfers.
food: Shave ice
Shaved ice drenched in tropical syrups, a sweet ritual after the session.
honolua.respect: The bay is a marine reserve: no fishing or collecting of any kind, and mineral sunscreen is compulsory. At the peak, locals have priority, so stay humble and keep your distance.
honolua.season: November to March: northwest swells get the right-hander peeling below the point, for experienced surfers only.

around.d: Rugged lava coast and a spectacular blowhole, to be watched from a distance in big seas.
Taro village tucked at the head of a valley, on a narrow, dizzying coastal road.
Small neighbouring sandy cove, also protected, good for snorkelling in summer.
Lifeguarded, tree-lined beach, handy for a family swim.

twostep.vibe: In Kona coffee country, Hōnaunau keeps the memory of kapu: anyone who broke the sacred law could find absolution by swimming to the nearby place of refuge.
food: Kona coffee
Grown on the slopes above the bay, to taste straight from the farms.
twostep.respect: Don’t settle on the park’s sacred grounds for a picnic. Stay well away from turtles resting on the lava and from spinner dolphins, protected by law in the bay.
twostep.season: April to October: the Kona coast is sheltered, the sea often glassy in the morning and the water crystal clear at around 26 °C.

around.d: Ancient sacred place of refuge with its great stone wall, rebuilt temple and wooden statues.
Historic bay where James Cook died, with very rich reefs reached by kayak.
Small wooden church whose walls are entirely painted with naive biblical scenes.
Japanese pioneers’ farm where you can discover coffee growing as it used to be.
Plants used by the ancient Hawaiians, grown as they were before European contact.

tunnels.vibe: At the foot of the Nā Pali cliffs, Hāʻena lives among taro valleys, ancestral hula sites and beaches where monk seals come to rest, far from the bustle of southern Kauaʻi.
food: Taro poi
Fermented taro purée, from the taro fields of the Hanalei Valley.
tunnels.respect: Keep your distance from monk seals lying on the sand. The car park is tiny: don’t park on private driveways, and the nearby state park must be booked in advance.
tunnels.season: May to September: the sea is often glassy and the water crystal clear; in winter, north swells make the reef dangerous.

around.d: Legendary trail on the Nā Pali coast, between dizzying cliffs and wild valleys.
Garden of ancient taro terraces and endemic plants, facing the mountains.
Large half-moon bay with its pier, mountain backdrop and surf village.
19th-century mission house and green church in the heart of Hanalei.
Clifftop lighthouse and colonies of boobies, frigatebirds and albatrosses.

sandybeach.vibe: At the foot of Koko Crater, Sandy’s is the playground of Oahu’s bodyboarders and bodysurfers, who come to take on the shore break after work under the lifeguards’ watchful eye.
food: Plate lunch
Rice, macaroni salad and grilled meat, the Hawaiians’ everyday favourite meal.
sandybeach.respect: Listen to the lifeguards and respect the flags: the shore break causes serious injuries every year. If you’re a beginner, watch from the sand and leave room for the locals.
sandybeach.season: May to September: south swells and trade winds hollow out the shore break; in winter, the coast is often calmer.

around.d: Collapsed crater flooded by the sea, a marine reserve renowned for snorkelling.
Easy trail to a lighthouse and a viewpoint over the windward coast and its islets.
Spout of water bursting from a lava tube in rough seas, beside the coast road.
Dryland plants, plumerias and cacti in the hollow of an old crater.
Fine sand and turquoise water facing the two Mokulua islets.

apostle.vibe: Land of the Ojibwe and of fishermen from Scandinavia, the Bayfield Peninsula lives from the lake: whitefish fishing, apple orchards and, in winter, walks out to the frozen caves when the ice holds.
food: Lake Superior whitefish
White fish caught locally, smoked or grilled in Bayfield’s restaurants.
apostle.respect: The lake is icy and gets rough quickly: only set out in calm weather, well equipped, as the cliffs offer no shelter for kilometres. Don’t climb into the fragile caves.
apostle.season: July to August: slightly less cold water and a lake that’s more often calm; set off early, as the wind strengthens in the afternoon.

around.d: Small harbour town with Victorian houses, orchards all around and a ferry to Madeline Island.
Restored lighthouse with a keeper’s house, reached by boat from Bayfield.
Brown sandstone lighthouse at the north tip of the island, facing the sculpted cliffs.

northbar.vibe: According to an Anishinaabe legend, a mother bear waits here for her cubs, who became the Manitou Islands; around it, life goes on among dunes, cherry orchards and old life-saving stations.
food: Cherry pie
The region’s tart cherries fill the farms’ pies and jams.
northbar.respect: Stay on the marked trails, as the dune vegetation is fragile. The channel linking the small lake to Lake Michigan sometimes creates a current: keep an eye on children.
northbar.season: Mid-July to late August: the small lake warms up quickly and becomes pleasant, while Lake Michigan stays cool.

around.d: Tall dunes to climb and a scenic drive with overlooks on Lake Michigan.
Wild island reached by ferry, with a lighthouse, old farms and giant cedars.
Former life-saving station turned maritime museum, with demonstrations.
Lake with turquoise water surrounded by wooded hills, good for swimming and paddleboarding.

looekey.vibe: The reef is named after a British frigate that ran aground here in the 18th century; the Lower Keys live to the slow rhythm of fishermen, tiny deer and an underwater music festival.
food: Key lime pie
Key lime tart on a biscuit base, born in the archipelago.
looekey.respect: Boats moor to buoys, never anchoring on the coral. The heart of the reef is a protected zone: touch nothing, don’t fish and don’t feed the fish.
looekey.season: May to September: the sea is often flat and the water warm; keep an eye on the weather during hurricane season, especially from August.

around.d: Pine forests and mangroves where you may spot the tiny Key deer, endemic to the archipelago.
Flooded former quarry for watching alligators, turtles and waterbirds.
Freighter sunk deliberately to form an artificial reef, a dive for experienced divers.

drytortugas.vibe: Named for their turtles and their lack of fresh water, the Tortugas are home to a never-finished fort that served as a prison, notably for the doctor convicted after Lincoln’s assassination.
food: Conch fritters
Fried conch fritters, a Key West speciality, served with a spicy sauce.
drytortugas.respect: The neighbouring islet of Bush Key closes for part of the year for nesting terns: respect the buoys. There are no services or fresh water here, so bring everything and take your rubbish back.
drytortugas.season: April to June: the sea is often calm for the crossing, the water already warm and hurricane season not yet under way.

around.d: Wild island where loggerhead turtles nest, fringed by reefs to explore with a mask.
Tall black-and-white lighthouse towering over Loggerhead Key and the archipelago.

southpadre.vibe: A barrier island at the very south of Texas, South Padre lives between Port Isabel’s shrimp fleet, the Kemp’s ridley turtles that return to nest on its beaches and the influx of students in spring.
food: Gulf shrimp
Shrimp from the Port Isabel fleet, grilled, fried or in tacos.
southpadre.respect: Pump up and launch your kite in the designated zones, away from swimmers. Shuffle your feet as you walk and wear booties: the lagoon is home to stingrays and sharp shells.
southpadre.season: March to May: the most regular southeasterly winds and warming water, before the crushing heat of summer.

around.d: Rehabilitation centre for injured sea turtles, open to the public and very educational.
Historic lighthouse to climb for views over the lagoon, the bridge and the island.
Fishing port with colourful shrimp boats and seafood restaurants on the quay.

sebastian.vibe: On the “Treasure Coast”, where a Spanish fleet laden with gold sank in 1715, Sebastian is the benchmark wave for Florida surfers, while anglers occupy the jetty day and night.
sebastian.respect: The peak is tight and very local: wait your turn and don’t drop in on anyone. Keep clear of the anglers’ lines on the jetty and beware of the current in the inlet.
sebastian.season: October to December: swells from the northeast and from distant hurricanes, more frequent offshore winds and water that’s still warm.

around.d: The first national wildlife refuge in the United States, with brown pelicans on the lagoon.
Small museum on the wreck of the 1715 fleet, on the site of a survivors’ camp.
Some of the most important beaches in the world for loggerhead turtle nesting.
Gold coins, jewellery and objects recovered from wrecked Spanish galleons.

blueheron.vibe: Here, everything revolves around high tide: at slack water, divers and photographers gather under the bridge in search of tiny creatures, in an urban lagoon facing the yachts of Palm Beach.
blueheron.respect: Deploy your dive buoy and stay out of the channel, as boats pass very close. Don’t handle seahorses or frogfish, not even for a photo.
blueheron.season: All year round at high tide; from May to September, the water is very warm and the lagoon often clearer.

around.d: Island of billionaires’ grand villas, with Worth Avenue and its lakeside promenade.
Long turtle-nesting beach, with a rehabilitation centre and a fishing pier.
Barrier island with wild beaches, and John D. MacArthur State Park to the north.
Mass grave of the hurricane’s Black victims, a moving place of remembrance.

resurrectionbay.vibe: The terminus of the Alaska Railroad, Seward lives from fishing and the boats that head out to the glaciers; every 4th of July, the whole town turns out to watch runners race up and down Mount Marathon.
food: Alaskan salmon and halibut
Caught in the bay, served grilled or as fish and chips on the harbour.
resurrectionbay.respect: Keep your distance from otters and seals: if they change their behaviour, you’re too close. The water is icy, so paddle suitably equipped and close to shore.
resurrectionbay.season: June to August: long days, calmer sea and active wildlife; the wind often picks up in the afternoon in the fjord.

around.d: Aquarium and rehabilitation centre for marine mammals: sea lions, seals and seabirds.
Steep trail above the town, with a bird’s-eye view over the whole bay.
Second World War bunkers perched on Caines Head, reached on foot or by kayak.
Small harbour town with murals, a marina and cruise departures to the fjords.

tadoussac.vibe: A fur-trading post from the earliest days of New France, Tadoussac lives to the rhythm of the whales, among dunes, an old wooden chapel and whale-watching boats leaving from the wharf.
hello: “hello” in French, the language of Quebec, said without fuss
food: Tourtière du Lac-Saint-Jean
Deep pie of meats and potatoes, a speciality of the neighbouring region.
tadoussac.respect: In the marine park, approach distances for whales are regulated, even more so for the beluga, an endangered species: never chase them. Currents and fog change quickly.
tadoussac.season: July to September: slightly less cold water, plenty of whales at the river mouth and a sea that’s often calm in the morning.

around.d: Fjord with tall wooded cliffs, to explore by boat or along the trails on its banks.
Village on the bay with its Indian chapel, its grand white hotel and its dunes.
Village on the opposite shore, with a lookout for spotting belugas at the river mouth.

grotto.vibe: On the territory of the Anishinaabeg of the Saugeen Ojibway Nation, the tip of the peninsula is a mecca for freshwater diving: its cold, clear waters preserve sunken schooners.
food: Whitefish fish and chips
Fried Great Lakes whitefish, served on the harbour in Tobermory.
grotto.respect: In summer, parking at Cyprus Lake must be booked in advance through Parks Canada. Cliff jumping causes injuries every year: get into the water from the rocks.
grotto.season: Mid-July to late August: Georgian Bay finally reaches a bearable temperature; come early to avoid the crowds.

around.d: Harbour village at the tip of the peninsula, the departure point for glass-bottom boats.
19th-century schooner sunk in a shallow cove, visible from the surface.
Stone lighthouse on an island in Fathom Five National Marine Park, surrounded by wrecks.

algonquin.vibe: The historic heart of canoeing in Ontario, Canoe Lake is also the lake where the painter Tom Thomson disappeared, whose canvases fixed the image of this land of pines, loons and portages.
algonquin.respect: In the backcountry, a permit is compulsory and cans and glass bottles are banned. Hang your food out of bears’ reach and take all your rubbish out with you.
algonquin.season: Late August to September: fewer blackflies, water still pleasant and maples blazing by the end of the month.

squamish.vibe: On the lands of the Squamish Nation, the town has become a haven for climbers and mountain bikers; in summer, a riders’ association runs the spit and the launches at the foot of the Chief.
squamish.respect: The spit is run by an association: buy your day pass and follow its launching rules. The fjord water is icy, so a full wetsuit is compulsory.
squamish.season: May to September: on sunny days, the thermal breeze funnels up the fjord in the afternoon, strong and steady.

around.d: Huge granite dome, a climbing paradise, with a steep trail to its summits.
Spectacular waterfall tumbling down the cliff in several drops, a stone’s throw from the road.
Former copper mine toured by underground train, at the foot of the huge mill.
In winter, hundreds of bald eagles gather for the salmon.
Forest-fringed lake, ideal for swimming and family walks.

hopewell.vibe: Here the sea rises and falls by more than ten metres twice a day; all around, the Acadians once reclaimed the salt marshes from the sea with their aboiteaux, and life goes on between farms and mudflats.
food: Poutine râpée
Ball of grated potato stuffed with pork, an Acadian speciality of the southeast.
hopewell.respect: Respect the posted cut-off time for climbing back up from the ocean floor: the tide comes in fast and cuts off the beaches. Never climb on the “flowerpots”, which are fragile and unstable.
hopewell.season: June to September: less cold water and outings at high tide; always plan your day around the tide times.

around.d: UNESCO-listed cliffs where the tide reveals fossil trees from the Carboniferous.
Star-shaped French fort, taken by the British in 1755, with views over the marshes.
Cradle of the Acadian renaissance, with the Monument-Lefebvre and its farms.
Mudflats where huge flocks of migrating sandpipers land in summer.
